0.title: 1 Chronicles — Seek His Presence
0.overview:
The message. First Chronicles was written for a small, poor and discouraged people, home from exile in Babylon, with no king, a modest temple and a city that had burned, who were asking whether God had finished with them. Its answer is that he had not. By retelling their story from Adam to David, the Chronicler shows them that they still belong to God’s people, that the promise God made to David still stands, and that the worship David set in order is still the way to draw near to him. Its watchword is the call of the psalm David gave the singers: “Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!” (16:11). Kings may fall and temples burn, but the throne of David was always “the throne of the LORD” (29:23), and he will keep his word.

Background: the writer. The book does not name its author, whom readers call the Chronicler. Jewish tradition credited Ezra, and the link is natural: 2 Chronicles ends with the decree of Cyrus letting the exiles go home (2 Chronicles 36:22–23), and Ezra opens with the same words. Many scholars now think Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah come from different hands, because their language and emphases differ; faithful Christians hold both views, and nothing in the book hangs on the name. His love for the Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers suggests a man who served at the temple. He drew on older records, which he names (9:1; 29:29). This commentary takes him to be an unnamed, inspired historian of the restored community.

When and where. Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC. About 538 BC Cyrus of Persia let the exiles return, and under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest they rebuilt the temple, finished about 516 BC. The Chronicler wrote some generations later. David’s line in 3:17–24 runs several generations past Zerubbabel, and the gifts for the temple are counted partly in darics (29:7), a Persian coin, so the book belongs to the Persian period, probably about 400 BC; some place it a little earlier, in Ezra’s day. Judah was then a small Persian province under a Persian governor, with no army and few people, asking who it now was.

The kind of writing. Chronicles is history, but preached history. Its Hebrew title means “the events of the days”; the Greek translators called it “the things left out”, as if it were a supplement to Samuel and Kings. It was one book with 2 Chronicles until the Greek translation divided it. The Chronicler knew Samuel and Kings, expected his readers to know them, and often copies them almost word for word, so where he leaves out, adds or rearranges, the change usually shows what he is teaching. Much is his alone, such as the men who came over to David (chapter 12), the orders of priests, singers and gatekeepers (chapters 23–26), and David’s last charge and prayer (chapters 28–29). The lists are not filler. For people rebuilding their life, a name in the register was a title deed.

How the book makes its case. Nine chapters of genealogies [1–9] set Israel inside the story of all mankind, from Adam through Noah and Abraham to the twelve tribes, with Judah and David’s line first [2–4], Levi at the centre [6], and every tribe counted, even those long lost [5; 7–8]. They end with the reason for the exile, “Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith” (9:1), and with the names of those who came back [9]. Then the story. Saul dies, for “he did not seek guidance from the LORD” (10:14), and the kingdom passes to David [10]. All Israel makes him king, and men come over to him one by one [11–12]. He brings up the ark, failing the first time because, as he confesses, “we did not seek him according to the rule” (15:13), then succeeding with joy [13–16]. At the centre stands God’s promise to build David a house [17], and around it the victories God gives [18–20]. The census and the plague end at a threshing floor, which becomes the temple site [21]. The last chapters are all preparation [22–29]: materials, the orders of priests and Levites, singers, gatekeepers and officers, the plan given “in writing from the hand of the LORD” (28:19), the people’s glad offerings, and Solomon seated on the LORD’s throne. Saul who did not seek the LORD (chapter 10) and David’s charge to seek him (28:9) frame the whole.

Does Chronicles polish the story? Readers notice what is missing: the years of civil war, David’s sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, Absalom’s rebellion, and the whole history of the northern kingdom. Some scholars conclude that the Chronicler idealised David, and doubt the book’s worth as history. But he hides nothing his readers did not know: they had Samuel and Kings, and he points them to the prophets’ fuller records (29:29). He keeps the census, a grave sin that brought death on Israel (chapter 21), because it led to the temple site, and he records that David was barred from building because he had “shed much blood” (22:8). Some of his numbers differ from those in Samuel and Kings; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, and takes these as slips in copying that touch nothing the book teaches, though a few remain hard to explain. This commentary’s view is that the Chronicler is a selective but faithful historian: he chose what his readers needed, and what he wrote is true.

Where it leads: to Christ. First Chronicles leads to Christ first by promise. God said of David’s son, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son … I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever” (17:13–14). Solomon sat on that throne for a time; then the line ran down into captivity and obscurity, until the angel said of Mary’s child, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32–33). Hebrews applies 17:13 to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5), and this commentary holds, with Peter (Acts 2:30–36), that he reigns on that throne now, at the Father’s right hand. It leads to him by its genealogies: Matthew opens with “the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and Luke traces him back to “the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38), where Chronicles begins. And it leads by pattern. The temple was built on the threshing floor where judgment stopped at a sacrifice and the angel put his sword back into its sheath (21:26–27; 2 Chronicles 3:1). Jesus, “something greater than the temple” (Matthew 12:6), spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21), and at the cross the judgment that stopped on Ornan’s floor fell on him, once for all.

For us. Christians can feel like the Chronicler’s first readers: few, overlooked, and wondering whether God’s promises still hold. First Chronicles says that they do, and why: “Yours is the kingdom, O LORD” (29:11), and its King has risen. It tells us we belong, because God keeps the register, and those who are Christ’s are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27). It teaches us to worship God as he has said, gladly and generously, for “all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (29:14). And it repeats David’s charge to every generation: “If you seek him, he will be found by you” (28:9). We may seek him with confidence, because in Jesus Christ he first came to seek us.

1.title: From Adam to Abraham: The Universal Scope of Grace

The chiefs of Edom were: chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,<sup>52</sup>Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,<sup>53</sup>Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,<sup>54</sup>Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom.
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the first chapter of the book and the first of nine chapters of names (see the introduction). Before a single story is told, the Chronicler opens the family register of the whole human race.

The message. Israel’s story is not a small tribal history but the centre of God’s dealings with all mankind. Every nation comes from the one man God made, and God keeps a record of them all; yet out of the many he chose one line, through Shem to Abraham, Isaac and Israel, to carry his promise. Brothers with longer lists and earlier crowns are honoured and set aside: God’s purpose runs by his choice, not by size or strength.

Why it was said. The first readers were a handful of returned exiles in a Persian province, wondering whether they still counted for anything among the empires (see the introduction). The chapter answers by placing them in a line that runs unbroken from Adam, through every catastrophe, to themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. Ten names carry the race from Adam to the flood (vv. 1–4). The nations spread out from Noah’s sons (vv. 5–16). Shem’s line narrows through Eber and Peleg to Abraham (vv. 17–27). Abraham’s other sons, Ishmael’s twelve and Keturah’s six, are honoured first (vv. 28–33); then Isaac’s two sons are named, Esau and Israel (v. 34), and Esau’s descendants are listed with the clans of Seir (vv. 35–42). The chapter ends with the kings and chiefs of Edom, who reigned “before any king reigned over the people of Israel” (vv. 43–54).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise. The line it follows is the line of the woman’s offspring promised in Genesis 3:15, and of Abraham, in whom “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). Matthew opens with “the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and Luke runs this same list back to “the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). The nations of verses 5–23 are not forgotten when the line narrows: the narrowing was for their sake, and in Christ a multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” will stand before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

For us. You did not invent yourself, and you are not lost in the crowd of history: God made the first man and keeps the record of every one of his descendants. In Christ he gives what no ancestry can, the right to become his children (John 1:12). And because his promise runs by grace and not by size, a small church in a large world need not lose heart.
1.theology:
Two doctrines are carried by the shape of the chapter. The first is that election, God's choosing of one line to carry his promise, narrows without leaving the others with nothing: the brothers outside the line are named and given real futures. God's choice of one has never meant abandoning the rest.

The second is providence, God's ruling of events, at work over centuries. Edom reigns while Israel waits, and a genealogy is the least dramatic form providence takes and one of the most convincing: nobody in it knew what he was part of.
1.examples:
Fifty-four verses of names are the last thing a modern reader wants, and they were the first thing the first readers needed, because a name in a register is a fact that does not depend on how a man feels about himself. A believer who cannot see what his life has amounted to is in the position of one of Joktan's thirteen sons in verse 22: no story attached, no deed recorded, and set down in the book of God all the same.

The record is still being kept, and the names in it now are written where nothing can burn them: the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 21:27), which is the register this one was always leading to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Adam to Abraham the Chronicler shows that Israel’s story begins with the whole human race, and that God was narrowing it towards his promise from the start. Ten names carry the race from creation to the flood (vv. 1–4). The nations spread out from Japheth and Ham (vv. 5–16), and only Nimrod, the first mighty man, whose kingdom began at Babel, is given a sentence. Shem’s line is then followed more closely, forking at Eber’s two sons, Peleg and Joktan (vv. 17–23), and walking on through ten more names to the man God renamed: “Abram, that is, Abraham” (v. 27). Every nation is counted, and one line is followed.
verseByVerse.theology: Beginning at Adam rather than at Abraham is a theological decision. Israel is not an alternative to the nations but a branch of the one human family, which is why the list can run forward to a Gospel preached to every nation. Paul carries the line to its end: Adam was a type, a pattern set in advance, of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14), and Christ is the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), head of a new humanity gathered from every nation.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a believer whose world has shrunk can still say whose he is. The exiles' identity was given by God, not granted by Persia, and the same holds in Christ: a Christian's standing rests on the God who called him out of darkness (1 Peter 2:9–10), not on what he owns or controls.

verseByVerse.quote: Adam, Seth, Enosh; Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared; Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech; Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole human race comes from one man whom God made, and Israel’s story, and ours, begins there.

Adam, Seth, Enosh. Nine chapters of names stand before the first story, and they begin with no sentence at all, only a name, and then another. The ten names from Adam to Noah have no deeds attached, and the God who has kept the record since then has not lost one of them.

The first reader. Picture the man who first read it in Jerusalem, generations after the return: a smaller temple, no king, no army, and Persia deciding what happens in his city. His question is whether his people are still anybody, and the answer he is handed is a list that begins not at Abraham, or Sinai, or the lost throne, but at the first man God made. Everything that could be taken from that community had been taken except the register: an empire can burn a palace, but it cannot make a man not be his father’s son.

Identity received, not invented. We are told that identity is something you discover inside and then create. It sounds like freedom, and it is exhausting: a self you invent you must also defend, prove and perform, and it is only as secure as your last success. The first reader was not asked to invent himself; he was handed a name, a father and a line. The gospel goes further. It does not simply return us to our ancestors, who in the next chapter turn out to be a troubled lot; it gives us a Father: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). An identity you achieve can be lost on a bad day. One God gives cannot be taken by an empire, a failure or the passing of years.

The son of Adam, the son of God. That is why Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy, and Luke runs the line back through these names to “the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). The chain that starts here did not stop at the exile.

Do these genealogies have gaps? Some biblical lists skip generations (Matthew 1:8 passes over three kings), and Luke includes a Cainan found in the Greek Old Testament but not in the Hebrew (Luke 3:36), so the names cannot be added up to an exact date for creation; but they trace one real line from Adam to Abraham. Gaps of a few generations do not stretch that line across vast ages, and with the six ordinary days of Genesis 1 it points, in this commentary’s view, to a young creation, though faithful Christians who hold an old earth read the gaps more widely.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles was written after the exile, probably in the 400s BC, to show the returned community that they still belong to God’s story. It begins with Adam to place Israel within all humanity. In most printed Hebrew Bibles it is the last book.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim. The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Cush fathered Nimrod. He was the first on earth to be a mighty man. Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim. Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth, and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the nations are one family descended from Noah’s sons, and Israel is a branch of it before it is a nation.

The sons of Japheth … the sons of Ham. Some forty names, many of them peoples, cover the world as Israel knew it, from the Greeks (Javan) to Egypt and Canaan. The Philistines are named inside a parenthesis (v. 12), as though four centuries of Israel’s grief were a footnote.

One family of nations. A small people surrounded by larger ones is always under pressure to define itself against them. The Chronicler will not allow it. The families in these verses, the sons of Japheth and Ham, are not simply enemies; they are relatives.

He was the first on earth to be a mighty man. One man is given a sentence of his own: Nimrod, whose kingdom in Genesis began at Babel, that is Babylon (Genesis 10:8–10). The readers’ people had walked home from there, and the Chronicler adds nothing. That restraint is itself the argument: Babel is given one verse, and the line that runs to David nine chapters.

Uncertain wording. Genesis 10:4 has Dodanim where verse 7 has Rodanim. In Hebrew d and r look very alike, so one is probably a copying variant of the other; Rodanim may be the people of Rhodes.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. And the sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber. To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg (for in his days the earth was divided), and his brother's name was Joktan. Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chronicler slows down for Shem’s family, because the promise runs through it, and at Eber the line forks.

The sons of Shem. Japheth’s descendants were given a paragraph and dropped; Shem’s are walked one generation at a time.

To Eber were born two sons. Peleg carries the line; Joktan is given thirteen sons, peoples of Arabia such as Sheba and Ophir, and is never heard of again. The Chronicler is establishing a pattern: of two brothers, the one with the longer list drops out of the story, and numbers never decide it. Ishmael will have twelve princes and Esau kings before Jacob has a tent.

Uncertain wording. Peleg means “division”, and “in his days the earth was divided” (v. 19) is usually taken to mean the scattering at Babel, which Genesis tells straight after this list (Genesis 11:8–9). Others think of a dividing of the land among the clans, or of irrigation channels, since the word can also mean a stream. Babel is the likeliest.
verseByVerse.note: “Peleg” means “division” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah; Eber, Peleg, Reu; Serug, Nahor, Terah; Abram, that is, Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten more names bring the line to Abraham, and the list halts on the name God gave him, because everything that follows grows from its promise.

Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah. Ten names from Shem to Abram match the ten from Adam to Noah.

Abram, that is, Abraham. The Chronicler retells none of the call out of Ur, the covenant or the son given when the body was as good as dead. He sets the two names side by side and lets the second do the work: exalted father becomes father of a multitude, a name given to a man of ninety-nine whose wife had never borne a child. God changes what a man is called, and then spends centuries making the name true.

Father of a multitude of nations. That is what God called Abraham (Genesis 17:5), and Paul says the promise rests on grace so that it holds for all his offspring, believing Gentiles included (Romans 4:16–17). The nations of verses 5–23 are the families Abraham’s offspring, Christ, was sent to bless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–42 — The Brothers Named and Set Aside
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God honours the sons who do not carry the promise, yet the promise does not go with them. Abraham’s sons are named, Isaac first, and then Ishmael’s twelve princes are listed in full, as God had promised Abraham (vv. 28–31), with Keturah’s sons and grandsons after them (vv. 32–33). Only then come Isaac’s sons, Esau and Israel (v. 34). The Chronicler finishes with Esau’s descendants and the Horite clans of Seir among whom he settled (vv. 35–42), giving the side branches their full due before the story returns to the line it is following.
verseByVerse.theology: God gave Ishmael princes because he had promised to (Genesis 17:20), and Esau a kingdom. Being passed over for the line of promise did not mean being forgotten.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who feels defined by past failures: the record God keeps of his people is the name his grace gave them, not the tally of their struggles, and in Christ that is true of every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael. These are their genealogies: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael. The sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the descendants of Keturah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s sons who do not carry the promise are honoured first and in full, for God keeps his word to them too.

The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael. Isaac is named first as the heir, but the son who is not the heir receives his full honours first. Ishmael’s twelve princes are set down by name, a promise kept and not a slight (Genesis 17:20). Keturah’s sons and grandsons follow, more than twenty men in all, each the father of a people. Being outside the line of promise did not put them outside God’s notice.

Wife or concubine? Genesis 25:1 calls Keturah Abraham’s wife; here, as in Genesis 25:6, she is counted a concubine, a wife of lower standing whose sons received gifts but not the inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham fathered Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line narrows to Isaac’s two sons, and the younger is called by the name God gave him.

Esau and Israel. He writes Israel, not Jacob, stepping over the bought birthright, the stolen blessing, the years with Laban and the night of wrestling at the ford, as though the new name had always been there. Jacob wrestled until daybreak for it; here it takes one word. A genealogy compresses everything a man suffered into the name he ends up with, and that name is the one God gave him.

Chosen before they were born. Paul reads the choice of the younger twin as pure grace, “not because of works but because of him who calls” (Romans 9:11–12). The line to Christ was never kept going by the merit of the men in it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz, and of Timna, Amalek. The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. The sons of Lotan: Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna. The sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau’s family and the clans of Seir are recorded in full, and one name among them, Amalek, prepares for the book’s first story.

The sons of Esau. Eight verses cover Esau’s descendants and the Horite clans of Seir, the people already in the land Esau settled; the Chronicler is finishing with the side branches.

And of Timna, Amalek. One name carries a history. Timna appears as the mother of Amalek (v. 36; a concubine, Genesis 36:12) and as Lotan’s sister (v. 39). Amalek cut down the stragglers on the way out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 25:17–18), and Saul was ordered to destroy it and spared it. When the genealogies end and the first story begins, it is Saul’s death, and the reason given is a command he did not keep (10:13). Nothing in a list like this is dead weight.

Textual note. As it stands, the Hebrew of verse 36 seems to list Timna among the sons of Eliphaz; the ESV follows the Greek Old Testament and Genesis 36:12 in making her Amalek’s mother.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom had kings long before Israel did, and the Chronicler records them without envy, for the line with a future was the one still waiting on God’s promise. Eight kings are named, each with his city or homeland, all reigning “before any king reigned over the people of Israel” (vv. 43–50), and no son succeeds his father. Then Hadad dies, and the list ends with eleven chiefs of Edom (vv. 51–54). To a people with no king, verse 43 was a quiet lesson in patience: the first crown is not the crown that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: God's delays are not defeats. The verse is written by a man who knows the throne came; it dates Edom's kings before Israel's, and so admits that Israel had to wait.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the oldest ache in the life of faith, and Scripture never pretends it away: the people not waiting on God appear to be doing better, for a long time. Asaph could not resolve it until he went into the sanctuary (Psalm 73:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel: Bela the son of Beor, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan, the son of Achbor, reigned in his place. Baal-hanan died, and Hadad reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pai; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom had kings while Israel had none, and the Chronicler records it without envy, because the promise of kings belonged to Jacob’s line.

Before any king reigned over the people of Israel. Read verse 43 with the eyes of a man who has no king. The family outside the promise was governed and crowned while the family inside it was still shepherds waiting on God. Yet no king here is the son of the one before: Edom had crowns but no dynasty, while Judah’s throne will pass from father to son for fifteen generations (3:10–14).

The line with a future. The man writing that clause knows the throne came, and knows the King it pointed to. Edom’s crowns were real, but the promise that “kings shall come from your own body” was made to Jacob (Genesis 35:11). Being first is not the same as being blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were: chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom’s record closes: God keeps account of every nation while working his purpose through one line.

These are the chiefs of Edom. The kings give way to eleven chiefs, and Edom is finished. In this book it returns only as a conquered enemy (18:12–13).

Where the record narrows. Fifty-four verses have shown that God keeps a record of everyone, though none of these nations, brothers or crowned men is the main line. When the record narrows, it will narrow to Israel, then Judah, then Jesse, then a boy nobody thought to call in from the sheep. The God who wrote down every chief of Edom was working the whole time on that single line, and at the end of it stands “Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1).

Edom’s last word. Amos promised that David’s fallen house would be raised to possess “the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name” (Amos 9:12), and James heard it fulfilled as Gentiles turned to Christ (Acts 15:16–17). The brother set aside here is invited back through the Son of David.

keyVerse.quote: Abram, that is, Abraham.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter funnels towards this line. The nations are listed and Shem’s line followed until it reaches the man God called and renamed “the father of a multitude of nations” (Genesis 17:5), through whose offspring every family on earth would be blessed. That offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16).

1.reflection:
The Chronicler begins his answer to discouraged exiles not with their own history but with Adam. Why might it help a struggling church to remember that its story begins with God’s creation of all mankind?

The nations of verses 5–23, Philistines and Egyptians included, are listed as Israel’s relatives. How should the truth that every person descends from the one man God made shape the way we think about people of other races and nations?

Again and again the brother with the longer list or the earlier crown (Joktan, Ishmael, Esau) is not the one who carries the promise. What does this teach about how God works, and where are you tempted to measure blessing by size or speed?

John 1:12 says that all who receive Christ are given the right to become children of God. How does an identity received from God differ from one you build for yourself, and what difference does that make on a bad day?

2.title: The Sons of Israel: Jacob's Family and Judah's Line

Now Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death.<sup>4</sup>His daughter-in-law Tamar also bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.<sup>5</sup>The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all.<sup>7</sup>The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing;<sup>8</sup>and Ethan's son was Azariah.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Hezron that were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.<sup>10</sup>Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah.<sup>11</sup>Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz,<sup>12</sup>Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse.<sup>13</sup>Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third,<sup>14</sup>Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,<sup>15</sup>Ozem the sixth, David the seventh.<sup>16</sup>And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three.<sup>17</sup>Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.<sup>18</sup>Caleb the son of Hezron fathered children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.<sup>19</sup>When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur.<sup>20</sup>Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel.<sup>21</sup>Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub.<sup>22</sup>And Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.<sup>23</sup>But Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair, Kenath, and its villages, sixty towns. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur.<sup>29</sup>The name of Abishur's wife was Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died childless.<sup>31</sup>The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.<sup>32</sup>The sons of Jada, Shammai's brother: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died childless.<sup>33</sup>The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.<sup>34</sup>Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, but Sheshan had an Egyptian slave whose name was Jarha.<sup>35</sup>So Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his slave, and she bore him Attai.<sup>36</sup>Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad.<sup>37</sup>Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed.<sup>38</sup>Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah.<sup>39</sup>Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah.<sup>40</sup>Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum.<sup>41</sup>Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama.<sup>42</sup>The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mareshah his firstborn, who fathered Ziph. The son of Mareshah: Hebron.<sup>43</sup>The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema.<sup>44</sup>Shema fathered Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem fathered Shammai.<sup>45</sup>The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon fathered Beth-zur.<sup>46</sup>Ephah also, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran fathered Gazez.<sup>47</sup>The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.<sup>48</sup>Maacah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.<sup>49</sup>She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.<sup>50</sup>These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,<sup>51</sup>Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader.<sup>52</sup>Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had other sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth.<sup>53</sup>And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.<sup>54</sup>The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites.<sup>55</sup>The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 traced mankind from Adam to Israel. Now the register names Israel’s twelve sons and turns at once to Judah, the royal tribe, following its line to David and then out through its clans and towns.

The message. The family God chose to bring the king into the world was not chosen for its purity, and it was not kept going by its own goodness. Its story includes a son put to death by the LORD, a scandal with a daughter-in-law, a thief, men who died childless and an Egyptian slave, and God carried the promise through all of it. Grace, not pedigree, makes the royal line, and its door was always wider than its doorkeepers wanted.

Why it was said. The returned exiles knew that their nation had been sent to Babylon for its “breach of faith” (9:1), and they were debating who truly belonged to Israel (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that the royal family itself was made of sinners and outsiders whom God had written in.

How the chapter makes its case. Israel’s twelve sons are named, and Judah is followed (vv. 1–2). Judah’s family begins with a Canaanite wife, a son put to death and Tamar (vv. 3–4), and Zerah’s line includes Achan, “the troubler of Israel” (vv. 5–8). Quiet generations run from Ram to Jesse (vv. 9–12), and Jesse’s sons end with David the seventh, while his sisters’ sons become his commanders (vv. 13–17). The register then works through Hezron’s other houses: Caleb’s line to Bezalel and Jair’s lost towns (vv. 18–24), Jerahmeel’s line with two men who died childless (vv. 25–33), and an Egyptian slave who married into Judah (vv. 34–41). It closes with Caleb’s towns (vv. 42–50), Bethlehem among Hur’s, and the Kenite scribes (vv. 51–55).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. Jacob had said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10), and the New Testament draws the line to its end: “our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). Matthew’s genealogy repeats these names, Tamar included (Matthew 1:3–6), and the “town too small” of verse 51 is Bethlehem, where the ruler was to be born (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6). The pattern is grace: the Son of God was born into a family like this, and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

For us. No one is too compromised, too foreign or too obscure to be written into God’s family by grace. If your history is tangled, so was the line of the Messiah. And the generations who are given no story here remind us that faithfulness in ordinary, unrecorded years is never wasted in God’s hands.
2.theology:
The chapter puts the book's main claim inside a name (see v. 7): the exile is explained not as bad luck or Babylonian strength but as Israel breaking faith with God, and the explanation is set down before the story starts.

Against that runs God's persistence in using unworthy people. Grace is not a late New Testament softening of an earlier severity; it is in the oldest documents Israel had.
2.examples:
The register is not a list of achievements: one man is in it because he stole and was stoned (v. 7). A believer who reads his own life as a ledger of what he has produced is reading the wrong document.

And the chapter is quietly walking towards a village. Bethlehem is filed in verse 51 between two others, with no star over it: God was a thousand years from finishing and had already written down the address.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Line to David, and What Is in It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The royal line to David runs through failure and grace, and God keeps it unbroken. The twelve sons of Israel are named (vv. 1–2), and the Chronicler follows Judah. The line begins badly: a Canaanite wife, a firstborn put to death for his wickedness, an heir by a daughter-in-law (vv. 3–4), and among Zerah’s descendants Achan, “the troubler of Israel” (v. 7). Then come the quiet names from Ram to Jesse (vv. 10–12), and Jesse’s sons, David last of them, with his two sisters, whose sons became the hard men of his reign (vv. 13–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler does not clean this line, and Matthew keeps Tamar in it on purpose, because the Son at the end of it came for sinners (Matthew 9:13).
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a believer who thinks his family history disqualifies him has not read this genealogy properly. It is the royal line of the Son of God, with a dead man in verse 3 and a stoning in verse 7.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chronicler follows Judah first, because God chose the king’s tribe, not the firstborn’s.

These are the sons of Israel. Twelve names are given, and eleven set aside for Judah, fourth in birth order and neither the eldest nor the favourite.

Not by birth order. The Chronicler explains himself in 5:1–2 (Reuben forfeited the birthright, and the ruler came from Judah); here he simply does it. Jacob had said the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and the New Testament draws the line to its end: “it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan and Shelah; these three Bath-shua the Canaanite bore to him. Now Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death. His daughter-in-law Tamar also bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The royal line begins in sin and shame, and God carries it on anyway.

He put him to death. Three verses into the royal genealogy there is already a corpse: Judah’s firstborn, put to death by the LORD, not by battle or illness but by sentence. The mother of those sons is “Bath-shua the Canaanite”, from the people Abraham’s family had refused to marry into (Genesis 24:3; 28:1).

His daughter-in-law Tamar. Then the line goes on through Tamar, Judah’s widowed daughter-in-law. Denied the youngest son Judah had promised her, she veiled herself, sat by the road, and conceived by Judah himself. Genesis does not praise the deception, but it records Judah’s verdict: “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26). Perez, born of that night, carries the royal line.

Written in without apology. The Chronicler could have started at verse 5. He writes all this into the opening lines of the Messiah’s family, and Matthew does the same, putting Tamar in his first paragraph (Matthew 1:3). The line is not clean, and the Son of God, born at the end of it, did not come into a clean family. He came to make it clean.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all. The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing; and Ethan's son was Azariah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Achan is named to introduce the sin the whole book traces: breaking faith with God.

The sons of Zerah. Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara are probably the wise men with whom Solomon was compared (1 Kings 4:31, where the last is Darda).

Achan, the troubler of Israel. Then a name lands like a bomb. Achan stole from the plunder devoted to God at Jericho (Joshua 7), and here the Hebrew spells his name Achar, which sounds like the word for trouble, as Joshua said over him (Joshua 7:25–26). He belongs to the family, and the Chronicler will not remove him.

Breaking faith, the book’s theme. The phrase “broke faith” translates a verb that 1 Chronicles uses at just four points, and together they are its whole account of what went wrong in Israel: Achan here; the tribes across the Jordan who “broke faith with the God of their fathers” (5:25); Judah carried to Babylon “because of their breach of faith” (9:1); and Saul, whose obituary reads, “So Saul died for his breach of faith” (10:13). A thief, then two and a half tribes, then the nation, then the king: the main claim of the book is hidden in a list of names.
verseByVerse.note: Achan is the man whose theft of devoted things at Jericho troubled Israel (Joshua 7). The devoted thing was plunder placed under the ban (Hebrew herem), given wholly to God and not to be taken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hezron that were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah. Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven quiet generations carry the line to Jesse, and God carried his promise through each of them.

Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah. Four verses give names and nothing else. Nahshon led Judah’s camp in the wilderness, Salmon lived through the conquest, and Boaz settled a matter at the gate about a foreign widow: the centuries between the promise and the throne, in about twenty-five words. (Chelubai, v. 9, is the Caleb of v. 18.)

Ruth left out. The register drops one story in particular. Boaz is here; Ruth is not, though without her there is no David. Matthew will put her back (Matthew 1:5).

Generations without lines. God’s work in a family is carried by generations who are given no lines to speak, and the God who required none of them to be remarkable brought his own Son out of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third, Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth, Ozem the sixth, David the seventh. And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three. Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David, the king God chose, is the youngest of Jesse’s sons, and his nephews will be the hard men of his reign.

David the seventh. Jesse’s sons are counted off, and the king is the youngest. God had told Samuel, “the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7), and the boy left with the sheep was his choice.

Seven sons or eight? 1 Samuel says Jesse “had eight sons” (1 Samuel 17:12), and seven pass before Samuel before the youngest is fetched (1 Samuel 16:10–11). Most likely one son died without children: a genealogy records descent, and a man who leaves none may leave no entry. The Chronicler is not contradicting Samuel; he is doing a different job with the same family.

And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. Verse 16 quietly explains a great deal. Zeruiah and Abigail are David’s sisters, so Joab, Abishai, Asahel and Amasa are the king’s nephews. The men he could neither control nor dismiss were family.

The father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite. Abigail is “daughter of Nahash” in 2 Samuel 17:25: most likely Nahash was her mother’s first husband. Jether was an Ishmaelite by descent or by residence.
verseByVerse.note: Zeruiah's sons Joab and Abishai were David's commanders; Amasa, Abigail's son, led Absalom's army (2 Sam. 17:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–41 — Hezron's Other Houses, and an Egyptian Slave
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Away from the royal line, God’s record keeps hold of people of every kind. Hezron’s other sons are traced: Caleb’s line produces Bezalel, the Spirit-filled builder of the tabernacle (v. 20), and Jair’s twenty-three towns are lost to Geshur and Aram (vv. 21–23). Jerahmeel’s line runs on without fame, pausing twice on men who “died childless” (vv. 30, 32). Then Sheshan, who has no son, gives his daughter to his Egyptian slave Jarha, and thirteen generations of their descendants are counted in Judah (vv. 34–41).
verseByVerse.theology: The wall between Israel and the nations was never as high as Israel tried to make it (see vv. 34-41), and Christ in the end broke it down (Ephesians 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone without children, verses 30 and 32 are tender. In a world where a man lived on through his sons, the register still kept Seled and Jether. God's care for a person never depended on descendants: he promises the childless who hold fast to him a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Caleb the son of Hezron fathered children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur. Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel. Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub. And Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. But Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair, Kenath, and its villages, sixty towns. All these were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead. After the death of Hezron, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the wife of Hezron his father, and she bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezron’s other descendants include the Spirit-filled builder of the tabernacle and a man whose towns were won and lost.

Uri fathered Bezalel. Three generations down from Caleb sits a name the reader of Exodus knows. Bezalel is the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and he was filled in order to work gold and cut stone for the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–5). He belongs to the tribe the temple builder will come from. The tent he built, where God lived among his people, pointed to the day when the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair. Around him is ordinary loss: Hezron’s grandson holds twenty-three towns in Gilead, and Geshur and Aram take them (v. 23).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 24 is hard. As it stands it seems to say that Hezron died “in Caleb-ephrathah” and that his wife Abijah bore him Ashhur after his death. The ESV follows the Greek translation, in which Caleb takes his father’s widow Ephrathah (compare v. 19). Either way Ashhur, “the father of Tekoa”, belongs to Hezron’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron: Ram, his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel also had another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam. The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. The name of Abishur's wife was Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid. The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died childless. The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai. The sons of Jada, Shammai's brother: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died childless. The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men are written down because they died childless: God’s record of a person is not a record of usefulness.

The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron. Jerahmeel is traced for nine verses, and the line produces no king, no prophet and no city. Twice the register pauses on the same fact: “Seled died childless” (v. 30), “Jether died childless” (v. 32). In a document whose whole purpose is descent, two men are recorded because their lines ended.

Written down anyway. A genealogy could have passed over them in silence. Instead their names were kept. Those who have no children, by grief or by circumstance, may take this to heart: God promised the childless who hold fast to him “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, but Sheshan had an Egyptian slave whose name was Jarha. So Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his slave, and she bore him Attai. Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad. Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah. Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah. Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum. Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An Egyptian slave marries into Judah and his descendants are counted: the door was wider than many thought.

Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters. Sheshan gives his daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian slave, and their line is traced for thirteen generations, more patiently than most of Judah.

A foreigner given the future. A man with no heir gives a foreigner from the nation that once enslaved Israel his daughter and his future. Israel spent much of its history arguing about who was properly inside. Its own family papers say a slave out of Egypt married into the royal tribe and his children were counted. In Christ that door is thrown open: “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

Uncertain wording. Verse 31 gives Sheshan a son, Ahlai. He may have died young, leaving Sheshan without a son to inherit, or Ahlai may be the name of the daughter Jarha married (a man of David’s guard is called “son of Ahlai”, 11:41). The text does not say.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–55 — Caleb, Bethlehem, and the Scribes at Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register becomes a map of Judah, and it ends with outsiders keeping Israel’s records. Caleb’s descendants are traced as much through towns as through people, the founders of Ziph, Hebron, Maon and the rest, with his daughter Achsah at the end (vv. 42–50). Hur’s line gives Kiriath-jearim and Salma, “the father of Bethlehem” (v. 51), a village that would one day be the birthplace of the King. The chapter closes on the clans of scribes at Jabez, who were Kenites, not Israelites by birth (v. 55).
verseByVerse.theology: Providence lays its groundwork where nobody is watching. The chief priests would one day quote Micah's word about this little town to Herod (Matthew 2:4–6).
verseByVerse.examples: Some of the people who preserved Israel's records were outsiders (v. 55): God's book has always been kept by those he brought in.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mareshah his firstborn, who fathered Ziph. The son of Mareshah: Hebron. The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. Shema fathered Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem fathered Shammai. The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon fathered Beth-zur. Ephah also, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran fathered Gazez. The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. Maacah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah. These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb’s descendants are listed as towns as much as people, because the list was a title deed to the land.

The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel. Ziph, Hebron, Maon, Beth-zur: this is a survey as much as a genealogy, who holds what and by what right. In these lists “the father of” a town usually means its founder or the head of the clan that settled it, which is why people and places can stand in the same line.

The title deed. To families home from exile, finding others farming their land, this was not old history but a title deed: this ridge, these terraces.

The daughter of Caleb was Achsah. At the end comes one daughter, who, given a field in the Negeb, asked her father for the springs as well, and got them (Joshua 15:16–19). She is remembered for asking for water in a dry place, which is not the worst thing to be remembered for.

Which Caleb? Achsah’s father was Caleb the son of Jephunneh (4:15), not Hezron’s son, who lived generations earlier. Most likely the famous Caleb, a Kenizzite who joined Judah (Numbers 32:12), was counted within the older Calebite clan.

verseByVerse.quote: Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader. Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had other sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth. And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites. The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites. The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bethlehem enters as a small entry in a survey, and the chapter ends with outsiders keeping Israel’s records.

Salma, the father of Bethlehem. Hur’s line runs out into the villages of Judah, and one of them stops the eye, though the list moves straight on. Bethlehem is small enough that Micah will call it “too little to be among the clans of Judah” before promising that the ruler comes out of it (Micah 5:2), and Matthew will quote that promise at the birth of Jesus (Matthew 2:6).

The scribes who lived at Jabez. The scribes at Jabez were Kenites, the people of Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, and from them came the house of Rechab, whose faithfulness Jeremiah held up to Judah (Jeremiah 35). Some of the men who kept the records of the covenant nation had come in from outside it.

What the chapter holds. The chapter that began with a Canaanite mother ends with foreign scribes; between them stand an executed son, a thief, an Egyptian slave and a town too small to count. This is the line God chose, kept and came down into. He was never looking for material he could be proud of; he was making something in which he would be glorified.

keyVerse.quote: Ozem the sixth, David the seventh.
keyVerse.note: Every strand of the chapter runs towards this name, the goal of Judah’s line, and he comes last among his brothers. Through sin, scandal and silent generations God kept the line to the king God had chosen, and through David it runs on to the Son of David, born in the little town of verse 51.

2.reflection:
The royal line includes a son put to death by the LORD, Judah and Tamar, and Achan the thief (vv. 3–7). Why do you think God chose to bring his Son into a family like this, and why did the Chronicler refuse to tidy the record?

Seven generations from Ram to Jesse are given no story at all (vv. 9–12). How does it encourage you that God carried his promise through ordinary, unrecorded lives? What would faithfulness in an unremarkable season look like for you?

An Egyptian slave, Kenite scribes and other outsiders are written into Judah’s register (vv. 34–35, 55). How should that shape the welcome your church gives to people who seem not to belong?

Two men are recorded simply because they “died childless” (vv. 30, 32). How might this chapter comfort someone who feels that their life has left nothing behind?

3.title: The House of David: The Covenant Line Continues
3.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite,<sup>2</sup>the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith;<sup>3</sup>the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah;<sup>4</sup>six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel;<sup>6</sup>then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,<sup>7</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>8</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.<sup>9</sup>All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.<sup>10</sup>The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,<sup>11</sup>Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,<sup>12</sup>Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,<sup>13</sup>Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,<sup>14</sup>Amon his son, Josiah his son.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum.<sup>16</sup>The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;<sup>17</sup>and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,<sup>18</sup>Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah;<sup>19</sup>and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister;<sup>20</sup>and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah.<sup>22</sup>The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 brought Judah’s line to David, “the seventh” of Jesse’s sons (2:15). Chapter 3 now sets out David’s own house: his sons, the kings who followed him, and the generations who lived on after the throne was gone.

The message. God kept his promise to David’s house through everything: a family scarred by sin, kings good and bad, and an exile that left no throne at all. The line did not end, because God’s word to David could not fail. A king list that keeps being written after the kingdom has fallen is a confession of faith that the true King is still to come.

Why it was said. The first readers lived under a Persian governor, generations after Zerubbabel, with David’s descendants living as private men (see the introduction). They needed to know whether God’s promise of an everlasting throne (17:12) was still alive. This register, carried down to their own day, says that it was.

How the chapter makes its case. David’s sons are listed: six born at Hebron, each with his mother (vv. 1–4), and thirteen at Jerusalem, Solomon among the four sons of Bath-shua, with Tamar their sister last (vv. 5–9). The throne passes from Solomon to Josiah in one unvarying formula, fifteen kings in five verses (vv. 10–14). Josiah’s sons bring the collapse, down to Jeconiah, who went to Babylon (vv. 15–16). Then “Jeconiah, the captive”, Zerubbabel who led the return, and further generations of a royal house with no crown (vv. 17–24).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by covenant and promise. God had sworn of David’s son, “I will establish his throne forever” (17:12), and the clerks who kept this list in the dark were keeping the family line of the King. Matthew runs these names on to “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16), and the angel told Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). Risen and ascended, he reigns on that throne now (Acts 2:30–36).

For us. When God’s promises seem to have gone underground, they have not lapsed. God’s faithfulness is not measured by the quality of the people it passes through, so we can trust him with families and churches that look broken. Like the men who kept writing the names, we keep praying, worshipping and waiting, because the King has come and will come again.
3.theology:
God’s covenant with David was a promise with no conditions attached, but the way it worked out in history was painful. This chapter shows an unbroken succession through men who in many cases deserved to end it, and then the throne is lost and still the family line does not break. God does not always keep his word by preventing disaster; he keeps it through disaster, which is harder to watch and much harder to doubt afterwards.

The omissions matter too. Uriah is not in verse 5, and Manasseh's reign is not in verse 13. A genealogy answers one question: not what the fathers deserved, but whether the promise survived them.
3.examples:
Anani, the last man named here, ends the Old Testament's record of the house of David, and he did nothing anyone wrote down. Faithfulness in a family very often looks like that: someone in a bad century keeps the records, teaches the children, and never learns what it was for.

Every clerk who copied these names was working on the genealogy of Jesus of Nazareth, and not one of them knew it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David’s house is set out in full, with its blessings and its sorrows left for the reader to remember. Six sons are born at Hebron, each named with his mother (vv. 1–3), and thirteen more at Jerusalem, the reign split across the two cities (v. 4). Four of the Jerusalem sons are by Bath-shua, that is Bathsheba, and Solomon is the last of them (v. 5). The sons of concubines are mentioned without names, and the roll closes with a line that has no business in a list of sons: “and Tamar was their sister” (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: A register can be merciful in a way a narrative cannot: it tells the truth about who existed without retelling what they did.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone wronged within a family, it matters that God's record names Tamar and does not file her under her abuser: the Lord sees what was done (Psalm 10:14), and the abused should seek safety and help at once.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite, the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah; six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s Hebron sons are listed without comment, though among them are the sons whose sins broke his heart.

These are the sons of David. Three of these names are the reason David’s old age was a misery. Amnon the firstborn raped his half-sister; Absalom killed him for it, seized the kingdom and died in a tree; Adonijah crowned himself while his father was still breathing. None of that is said.

Why the mothers are named. In a royal house a prince’s standing depended on his mother; Absalom’s was a princess of Geshur, where he fled after the murder. The six mothers are also a quiet warning: the king was not to “acquire many wives for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:17), and the rivalries among these half-brothers were part of the price.

Names that differ. Some of David’s sons have two names in Scripture: Daniel is Chileab (2 Samuel 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel; then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine. All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon is listed quietly among Bathsheba’s sons, and the roll ends by naming Tamar, whose suffering her family ignored.

Four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel. Bath-shua is Bathsheba, and Ammiel is her father Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3) with the two parts of his name reversed. Of her four sons Solomon is the fourth; another, Nathan, is the son through whom Luke traces Jesus (Luke 3:31).

What the Chronicler omits. Nothing is said of the rooftop, Uriah’s murder, Nathan’s rebuke or the child who died. Matthew will not leave it there: at the same point in the line he writes that David was the father of Solomon “by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6). One writer keeps the family’s record; the other keeps the family’s conscience, and Scripture gives both. The Son of David was born into a line that needed forgiving.

And Tamar was their sister. Named after nineteen brothers, with what was done to her left to another book (2 Samuel 13), she is simply counted, which is more than her family managed at the time. God does not overlook those whom families silence. If you have been abused, it was not your fault: tell someone you trust, a pastor or counsellor, and if you are in danger, seek help today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Fifteen Kings in Five Verses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The throne passes from father to son for generations, and God keeps the chain unbroken whatever the kings are like. From Rehoboam to Josiah the succession is given in one formula, fifteen reigns in five verses with no verdict on any of them (vv. 10–14). Then come Josiah’s four sons, three of whom reigned in the last chaotic years (v. 15), and the line runs down to Jeconiah, the king who surrendered Jerusalem and went to Babylon (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything Kings spends chapters weighing is compressed here into succession alone, to establish the one fact the exiles needed: the line held.
verseByVerse.examples: The worst king Judah ever had is a name in the middle of verse 13, with nothing said about him. Yet Chronicles alone will record that he humbled himself in captivity and God heard him (2 Chronicles 33:12–13): the line held, and so did mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son, Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son, Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son, Amon his son, Josiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chain of kings from Solomon to the exile held, because God’s promise held.

The son of Solomon was Rehoboam. Elsewhere these reigns are weighed at length; here the formula never varies, and Asa the reformer and Ahaz who burned his children get the same three words.

Whether the chain held. To a man reading this in a ruined city, the question was not which ancestors had been admirable but whether the chain had held from Solomon to the burning of Jerusalem, and this list answers without adjectives: it did. God’s faithfulness to a promise is not measured by the quality of the people it passes through; if it were, it would have stopped at verse 11.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum. The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah’s sons bring collapse and exile, yet God keeps his word to David.

The sons of Josiah. With Josiah’s four sons the succession goes wrong at once. Johanan the firstborn never reigns, and Judah burns through four kings in twenty-three years, three of them brothers. Shallum is Jehoahaz, who reigned three months (Jeremiah 22:11).

A good father’s sons. Josiah was the best king since David (2 Kings 23:25), and these are his sons. A good father cannot guarantee the generation after him, and a grieving parent need not read that as his own failure.

Christ and the curse on Jeconiah. Jeremiah said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Jesus is Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father (Matthew 1:11–12, 16), but, born of a virgin, not Joseph’s physical son, and Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31). Luke also names a Shealtiel and a Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27); whether they are the same men is debated. Either way, the throne passed to a Son of David in a way that kept God’s word on every side.

Uncertain wording. The Zedekiah of verse 16 is either an otherwise unknown son of Jeconiah, or Josiah’s son Zedekiah (v. 15), listed here because he followed Jeconiah on the throne. The text does not settle it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Line That Keeps Going After the Throne Is Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The royal line goes on after the throne is gone, because God’s promise to David has not lapsed. Jeconiah is given a title rather than a kingdom, “the captive” (v. 17), and the register carries on through his sons: Shealtiel, Pedaiah, and Zerubbabel, who led the first return and rebuilt the temple (vv. 17–19). After him come further generations of men who never ruled anything, down to Anani and his brothers (vv. 19–24), still recorded because the family of David still mattered to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise to David did not depend on his descendants holding office. Keeping this list for generations after the throne was gone was an act of faith in a covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: When God's promises seem to have gone quiet, remember this line: it does not end in a blaze but trails off into names nobody remembers, and it stays alive there.

verseByVerse.quote: and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah; and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister; and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king becomes “the captive”, yet the royal line goes on in exile and comes home in Zerubbabel.

The sons of Jeconiah, the captive. “The captive” is a title now. He was eighteen when he surrendered Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8; most Hebrew copies of 2 Chronicles 36:9 read eight, probably a copying slip), and spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison.

Yet the line goes on. Zerubbabel led the first return and laid the foundation of the second temple. God later called him his “signet ring” (Haggai 2:23), the very picture he had used in casting off Jeconiah (Jeremiah 22:24): the line had been disciplined, not discarded.

The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. Here Zerubbabel is the son of Pedaiah; Ezra, Haggai and Matthew call him the son of Shealtiel. A likely explanation is the law for exactly this case (Deuteronomy 25:5–6): Shealtiel died without a son, his brother raised up an heir to his name, and Zerubbabel was legally the one man’s son and by birth the other’s.
verseByVerse.note: Jeconiah is Jehoiachin. Zerubbabel was a leader of the first return from exile (Ezra 2:2; 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah. The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six. The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three. The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long after the throne was lost, David’s descendants were still recorded, because God had promised him a throne forever.

Still keeping the record. After Zerubbabel the register keeps writing, down to Anani and his brothers, generations past the last event the Old Testament records.

One reason to keep writing. There was no throne, no army, a Persian governor in the citadel, and one reason not to let the record lapse: God had said of David’s son, “I will establish his throne forever” (17:12), and men who could see no evidence of it went on writing down the names.

Keeping the family line of the King. They were right to. Centuries later a young woman in Nazareth was told that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32), and Matthew opened his Gospel by running this list forward until it reached Joseph, a carpenter, the husband of Mary. The clerks who kept this chapter going in the dark were keeping the family line of the King.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 21 is hard to follow, and the Greek Old Testament reads it as one line of fathers and sons, so counts after Zerubbabel range from about six generations to eleven. Verse 22 also says “six” but names five sons of Shemaiah; perhaps Shemaiah himself is counted, or a name has dropped out in copying.

keyVerse.quote: the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son
keyVerse.note: The king has become “the captive”, and still the register goes on to his sons. This is the hinge of the chapter: the throne has fallen, but God’s promise to David has not, and the line runs on through exile and return to Jesus, the Son of David (Matthew 1:12–16).

3.reflection:
The Chronicler lists Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah without comment, while Matthew writes “by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6). Why might Scripture give us both the family’s record and the family’s conscience? What does each teach us about God’s grace?

Fifteen kings, good and evil, are passed over with the same three words (vv. 10–14). How does it comfort you that God’s faithfulness is not measured by the quality of the people it passes through?

Josiah was a godly king whose sons did evil (v. 15). How should Christian parents think about their responsibility, and about God’s grace, when grown children turn away?

Generations after the throne was lost, people kept recording David’s line because they trusted God’s promise (vv. 17–24). Where are you tempted to give up on a promise of God because you cannot yet see it fulfilled, and how does Christ’s coming strengthen your hope?

4.title: Judah and Simeon: Names Preserved, Prayers Answered
4.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.<sup>2</sup>Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites.<sup>3</sup>These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi,<sup>4</sup>and Penuel fathered Gedor, and Ezer fathered Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem.<sup>5</sup>Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah;<sup>6</sup>Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan.<sup>8</sup>Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel, the son of Harum.<sup>9</sup>Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, "Because I bore him in pain."<sup>10</sup>Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, "Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!" And God granted what he asked.<sup>11</sup>Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton.<sup>12</sup>Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah; and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai.<sup>14</sup>Meonothai fathered Ophrah; and Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam; and the son of Elah: Kenaz.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. These are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married; and she conceived and bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa.<sup>18</sup>And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah.<sup>19</sup>The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea;<sup>22</sup>and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem (now the records are ancient).<sup>23</sup>These were the potters who were inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the king's service.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul;<sup>25</sup>Shallum was his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son.<sup>27</sup>Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.<sup>28</sup>They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual,<sup>29</sup>Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad,<sup>30</sup>Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag,<sup>31</sup>Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until David reigned.<sup>32</sup>And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities,<sup>33</sup>along with all their villages that were around these cities as far as Baal.
