These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record.<sup>34</sup>Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah,<sup>35</sup>Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel,<sup>36</sup>Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah,<sup>37</sup>Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah—<sup>38</sup>these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.<sup>39</sup>They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks,<sup>40</sup>where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham.<sup>41</sup>These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks.<sup>42</sup>And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.<sup>43</sup>And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 2 and 3 traced Judah’s royal line down to the Chronicler’s own day. Chapter 4 goes back over Judah, this time clan by clan, and then gives Simeon, the tribe that lived inside Judah’s territory, its own short record.

The message. God knows and keeps ordinary people, and he hears those who call on him. Craftsmen, potters, a foreign princess and a shrinking tribe are all written down, and in the middle of the lists a man named for pain asks the God of Israel to bless him and be with him, and “God granted what he asked”. God’s purposes do not lapse when great men fail; they are carried on by people no one remembers.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were few, poor and squeezed into a small territory (see the introduction). They needed to know that small and fading families still counted with God, that he still answers prayer, and that what he has said he will finish.

How the chapter makes its case. Judah’s clans are traced sideways, household by household, with Hur again “the father of Bethlehem” (vv. 1–8). Then the list stops for Jabez, who prays and is answered (vv. 9–10). The clans run on through Othniel the judge, a valley of craftsmen, Caleb, and Mered’s marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter (vv. 11–20), to linen workers and royal potters (vv. 21–23). Simeon’s line is short, for it did not multiply like Judah (vv. 24–27); its towns are listed “until David reigned”, and it kept its records (vv. 28–33). Some of its families grew (vv. 34–38), and two expeditions close the chapter, one for pasture and one that destroyed the last of Amalek (vv. 39–43).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by showing God’s character, which is revealed fully in him. The God who granted Jabez’s request is the Father who will “give good things to those who ask him” (Matthew 7:11), and Jesus teaches us to ask in his name. Jabez prayed to be kept from pain; Christ, “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3), did not ask to be spared but drank the cup, so that the presence Jabez asked for could be promised to his people for ever.

For us. Bring God specific needs, as Jabez did, but want the Giver more than the gift. Do not despise ordinary work or a small church: God writes down potters and fading tribes. And trust that what God has said he will do, he will finish, even if it is finished by people no one remembers.
4.theology:
Jabez is the centre of the chapter’s teaching and easily mishandled in two ways: his prayer is neither a formula (see vv. 9-10) nor an oddity to be embarrassed by. God is presented as the rest of Scripture presents him, able to be asked and pleased to answer.

The second theme is providence working through decline. Simeon shrinks and is absorbed, and yet its princes' houses increase and its men complete an unfinished command of God.
4.examples:
A reader who was handed the Jabez prayer as a method and found that his own borders did not move has been badly served. Jabez asked for a specific thing out of a specific pain, and rested it all on that your hand might be with me. A prayer built on that clause can survive not getting what it asked for. A prayer that rests on getting more land cannot.

And the man whose name sounded like pain, who asked to be kept from it, belongs to the tribe of one who was named before birth as the one who would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). He asked his Father in a garden whether the cup could pass, and it did not. He bore the pain, and because he did, everyone who is his can pray with Jabez's confidence that God's hand is with them: the Father who did not spare his own Son will not withhold what is truly good (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Judah's Clans, and the Prayer of Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s record holds ordinary households, and the God who keeps it hears prayer. Judah’s line is worked through a second time, sideways, by clans and households (vv. 1–8), with Hur again “the father of Bethlehem” (v. 4). Then the list stops for two verses. A man whose name sounds like the word for pain calls on the God of Israel, asking for blessing, more land, God’s hand with him and protection from harm, and “God granted what he asked” (vv. 9–10). It is the first prayer in nine chapters of names.
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer breaks into the record. This is the first prayer in nine chapters of names, and one of only two answered prayers in them; the other is in the next chapter (5:20).
verseByVerse.examples: If you carry a name, a past or a wound that someone else gave you, Jabez shows what to do with it: take it to God. He asks not for escape from the name but for blessing inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites. These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi, and Penuel fathered Gedor, and Ezer fathered Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem. Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah; Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah. The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan. Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel, the son of Harum.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is traced again, clan by clan, because God’s record holds ordinary households as well as kings.

Judah from another angle. This time the tribe is traced sideways, clan by clan and town by town. Bethlehem surfaces again (v. 4), still a village belonging to Hur. And a sister is named in verse 3, Hazzelelponi, with nothing recorded about her but that somebody knew her name.

History from the inside. This is what most of a nation’s history looks like from the inside: households, villages, a trade, a well, and far more people than ever reach the narrative books.

verseByVerse.quote: Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, "Because I bore him in pain." Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, "Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!" And God granted what he asked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man named for pain asked the God of Israel for blessing and his presence, and God answered: he is a God who can be asked.

Because I bore him in pain. After nine chapters of names, the list stops and a man speaks, introduced by his mother’s suffering. Whatever happened at that birth, she named the child after it, and he carried a name that sounded like the word for pain every time anyone called him to dinner. Yet he was “more honorable than his brothers”, and the honour is set beside his prayer.

Jabez called upon the God of Israel. What he does with his name is the point. He makes four requests, and the last answers his own name: keep me from pain. The middle two are the substance. “Enlarge my border” sits in a chapter of land allotments; it is a farmer asking for ground. “That your hand might be with me” is what the request rests on, and it makes the other three safe to pray.

And God granted what he asked. The God of nine chapters of silent record-keeping had been listening the whole time.

Not a technique. This prayer has been sold as a technique: a small book on it sold millions of copies around the turn of this century, offering what our age wants most, a dependable method for getting more out of an uncertain future. The chapter refuses that reading. Prosperity teaching treats God as a supplier, and wellness culture does much the same with the universe; in both, the one being asked matters only for what he delivers. But a technique has no one on the other end. It cannot say no, and so it can never love you; it can only be used. Around Jabez are dozens of men given no enlargement, and the register does not suggest they failed to say the words. Nor is it a promise of being spared pain or given property: Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and that too was an answer.

Magic wants the gift; prayer wants the Giver. Jabez is not working a formula on the world. He is asking a person, and the hinge of his prayer is not the larger border but “that your hand might be with me”. And the Giver has gone further than Jabez asked. The one man who could rightly have asked to be kept from harm prayed in Gethsemane for the cup to pass, and then drank it, so that God could say to his people for good, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Uncertain wording. The end of the prayer is compressed in Hebrew. The ESV takes it as a plea to be kept from harm so that it does not bring him pain; others read it as a prayer that he might not cause pain. The general sense, protection from the harm his name seemed to forecast, is clear.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the name Jabez transposes two letters of the word for pain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–23 — Craftsmen, Potters, and Pharaoh's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The clans of Judah include people of every rank and origin, and all of them are counted. The list runs through Othniel, Israel’s first judge (v. 13), a valley named for its craftsmen (v. 14), and the family of Caleb son of Jephunneh (v. 15). Mered marries Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, and their children are recorded in Judah alongside those of his Judahite wife (vv. 17–18). The section closes with Shelah’s descendants: the linen workers of Beth-ashbea and the potters who lived and worked in the king’s service (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's family has always been less tidy than its members would like, and that is good news for outsiders.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, ordinary work done well is part of God's record. Clans of Judah are remembered for linen and clay rather than battles (vv. 21-23).

verseByVerse.quote: Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton. Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah. The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah; and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai. Meonothai fathered Ophrah; and Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen. The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam; and the son of Elah: Kenaz. The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel. The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. These are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married; and she conceived and bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite. The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s clans include Israel’s first judge, a valley of craftsmen and an Egyptian princess, all counted alike.

The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. Othniel is Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9–11), who married Achsah, the woman who asked for springs (2:49). A valley is named for its trade, “because they were craftsmen” (v. 14). Caleb son of Jephunneh appears in his own right (v. 15; see on 2:42–50).

The daughter of Pharaoh. Then comes a marriage with no explanation. Mered’s wife Bithiah is the daughter of Pharaoh (v. 17), given a Hebrew name that appears to mean daughter of the LORD. Like the Egyptian slave of 2:34–35, she is written into the family of the Messiah, and the Chronicler never stops to justify it. He will not let the record be tidier than the family was.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 17–18 is jumbled, and the ESV moves the clause about Bithiah from verse 18 into verse 17. The likeliest sense is that Mered had two wives, an Egyptian and a Judahite, and both sets of children are listed.
verseByVerse.note: “Ge-harashim” means “valley of craftsmen” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea; and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem (now the records are ancient). These were the potters who were inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the king's service.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Linen workers and potters are written in beside princes and judges: to God ordinary work is not filler.

They lived there in the king’s service. The register does not rank these craftsmen below the princes or below Jabez. A way of reading Scripture that treats one as important and the other as filler is not the Chronicler’s, and a way of living that treats ordinary work as second-class is not the gospel’s: whatever we do, we do for “the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:24).

Uncertain wording. Verse 22 is obscure. “Ruled in Moab” may mean “married into Moab”, since the Hebrew verb can mean both, and “returned to Lehem” may be part of a name. “The records are ancient” admits that the source was old and brief.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–43 — Simeon: The Tribe That Shrank
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Simeon was a shrinking tribe, yet God kept its record and used its people to finish what Saul had left undone. Its genealogy is short, for its clans did not multiply like Judah’s (v. 27), and its towns are listed as theirs only “until David reigned” (v. 31). Still, it kept a genealogical record (v. 33), and some of its families grew greatly (vv. 34–38). Two expeditions close the chapter: one to Gedor in Hezekiah’s day for pasture (vv. 39–41), and one to Mount Seir that destroyed the remnant of the Amalekites (vv. 42–43).
verseByVerse.theology: The same judgment can fall on two people and God may do different things with each. Jacob's words scattered Simeon and Levi alike (see vv. 24-27).
verseByVerse.examples: A believer in a dwindling congregation or a family that seems to be fading can take heart from Simeon. The decline is written down honestly, but it is not the last word: a tribe going down is not a tribe God has finished using.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul; Shallum was his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son. The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon’s tribe shrank, as Jacob had said it would, and the record says so honestly.

Nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah. Simeon’s genealogy is short, and verse 27 gives the reason out loud: a hard sentence to have in your family papers. One man has sixteen sons and six daughters, and even he cannot lift the average. The tribe is fading while the record is kept, and the record says so.

As Jacob had said. Jacob had said it would be like this, for their violence at Shechem (Genesis 49:5–7). Levi was scattered into the priesthood and given the LORD himself as an inheritance; Simeon was scattered into Judah and slowly disappeared. The same sentence fell on both, and grace made one of them a blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until David reigned. And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities, along with all their villages that were around these cities as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon lost its towns to Judah but kept its genealogy, and so it is still here.

These were their cities until David reigned. After that these were no longer Simeon’s towns. They lay inside Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1, 9), and in the end the tribe was absorbed by the neighbour it lived among.

They kept a genealogical record. The last thing said about them is that a shrinking tribe went on writing down who its people were, which is why they are in this chapter at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah— these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within a shrinking tribe some families grew greatly, and the Chronicler names them.

Princes in their clans. Thirteen princes are named, and the reason comes at the end: “their fathers’ houses increased greatly”.

Increase in a shrinking tribe. So there was increase in a tribe that did not increase. The Chronicler will not let the general statement hide the families that did grow, the same care he showed the men who died childless in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks, where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham. These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks. And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeonites found pasture and destroyed the last of Amalek: God’s word of judgment, which Saul had left undone, was carried out by forgotten men.

To seek pasture for their flocks. Men from a tribe with too little land go out to find some. One party came back with grazing land in Hezekiah’s reign. The other destroyed “the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped”.

The remnant of the Amalekites. That clause finishes something. Amalek entered this book as a name (1:36); Saul was ordered to destroy it and spared its king and the best of the sheep (1 Samuel 15). Generations later five hundred men of the smallest tribe finish the job, with no song and no prophet present.

Purposes handed on. God’s purposes do not lapse when the man commissioned to carry them out refuses. They are handed on, quietly, to people nobody remembers, and completed.

A judgment long declared. God had placed Amalek under judgment for attacking the faint and weary at the back of Israel’s column (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; 1 Samuel 15:2). Chronicles records what happened; it is no pattern for taking land or for violence today. That judgment belonged to Israel’s unique calling under the old covenant; the church’s warfare is not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12), and its King conquers by the gospel.

keyVerse.quote: Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, “Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!” And God granted what he asked.
keyVerse.note: In nine chapters of names this is the only prayer, and its centre is not the larger border but God’s hand with him. It shows that the God who keeps the record also hears the people in it, and it points to the Father who gives good things to those who ask in Jesus’ name.

4.reflection:
Jabez’s prayer has often been treated as a formula for getting more from God. How does the chapter itself, and Paul’s unanswered request in 2 Corinthians 12:7–9, correct that reading? What is the difference between using God and asking him?

The heart of Jabez’s prayer is “that your hand might be with me”. How would your own prayers change if you wanted God’s presence more than the things you ask him for?

Linen workers, potters and craftsmen are written into the register beside princes (vv. 14, 21–23). How does this shape the way you see your own ordinary work, and the work of others in your church?

Saul failed to carry out God’s command, and generations later unnamed men of a fading tribe finished it (vv. 42–43). How does it encourage you that God’s purposes do not depend on the famous or the strong?

5.title: Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh: Faithfulness and Failure East of the Jordan
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son;<sup>2</sup>though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),<sup>3</sup>the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,<sup>5</sup>Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,<sup>6</sup>Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites.<sup>7</sup>And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,<sup>8</sup>and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.<sup>9</sup>He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead.<sup>10</sup>And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah:<sup>12</sup>Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.<sup>13</sup>And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven.<sup>14</sup>These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz.<sup>15</sup>Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses,<sup>16</sup>and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits.<sup>17</sup>All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.<sup>18</sup>The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war.<sup>19</sup>They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.<sup>20</sup>And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.<sup>21</sup>They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive.<sup>22</sup>For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.<sup>23</sup>The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.<sup>24</sup>These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses.<sup>25</sup>But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them.<sup>26</sup>So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
5.overview:
Where we are. After the long lists of Judah (chapters 2–4) and the small tribe of Simeon (4:24–43), the Chronicler crosses the Jordan to the two and a half tribes who settled on its eastern side: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. They were the first of Israel to go into exile, and that ending shadows their register.

The message. God can give his people land, increase, victory and an answer when they cry to him, and they can still turn from him; and then the God who answered their prayer judges them. Faithfulness is not inherited, and a past answer to prayer does not secure it. Two sentences carry the lesson: “they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him” (v. 20), and “they broke faith with the God of their fathers” (v. 25).

Why it was said. The first readers had come back from an exile brought on by their fathers’ “breach of faith” (9:1; see the introduction). The eastern tribes showed them how such an ending comes, and what keeps a people from it: trusting the LORD now, not living on earlier mercies.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens by settling why Reuben, the firstborn, does not lead (vv. 1–2). Reuben’s clans spread east with their flocks, down to a chief deported by Assyria (vv. 3–10). Gad’s clans stand beside them (vv. 11–17). Then the high point: the eastern tribes cry to God in battle against the Hagrites and he gives the victory, “because the war was of God” (vv. 18–22). Half-Manasseh is numerous and famous (vv. 23–24), then breaks faith, and God stirs up Assyria to carry all three tribes away (vv. 25–26).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. “A chief came from” Judah (v. 2): David first, and at the end of the line “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Revelation 5:5). And the eastern tribes show what Israel needed and could not supply: hearts that would go on trusting after the battle was won. One Israelite cried to God and trusted him to the end, and “he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). He bore the judgment unfaithfulness deserved, so that people who had broken faith could be brought home.

For us. An answered prayer is a gift, not a guarantee. Let the memory of what God has done send you back to him today, and teach your children to trust him for themselves. And if you have broken faith, the God who judged is the God who receives everyone who returns to him through Christ.
5.theology:
Verse 20 shows prayer and skill working together, and the Chronicler feels no tension between them. Human skill is not a rival to God’s action; it is one of the ways God acts.

Verse 26 says the same about judgment. God stirred up a pagan king, the king did what pagan kings do, and the exile was both Assyrian policy and divine act. The book will need this when it explains why Jerusalem fell: not that God lost, but that God was acting in judgment.
5.examples:
Read verse 20 beside verse 25. A man can look back on a time he cried out and was heard and treat the memory as proof that he stands well with God. These tribes had such a memory, and it did not keep their descendants faithful.

What holds is not the memory of an answered prayer but the God who answered it, and he was as present in the deportation as in the victory. That is the comfort for anyone whose own record has broken down: God's faithfulness, not ours, is what keeps his people, and the way back for those who have wandered is the confession he has always heard (Psalm 32:5). The tribes carried into Assyria did not stop being his: their names are in this chapter, written in Jerusalem centuries after their nation had ceased to exist. And the northern tribes were never wholly lost: when the infant Christ was brought to the temple, Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Asher, was there to give thanks and speak of him (Luke 2:36–38).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reuben came first by birth but not by blessing, and his story is one of good grazing that ended in exile. The opening verses explain why the firstborn does not lead: Reuben defiled his father’s bed, so the double portion went to Joseph’s sons and the leadership to Judah, from whom a chief came (vv. 1–2). Then Reuben’s clans are traced (vv. 3–8). One chief, Beerah, was carried off by Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (v. 6). The tribe spread east towards the desert because its flocks multiplied in Gilead (v. 9), and it fought the Hagrites in Saul’s day (v. 10), a first glimpse of the war told in full in verses 18–22.
verseByVerse.theology: The birthright, the double portion and the throne are separated here. Reuben lost all of it by one act; Joseph received the inheritance and Judah the crown, and neither was the eldest. Putting the eldest son first is the world's way of ordering a family, and God overrules it in nearly every generation of this book.
verseByVerse.examples: A single night's sin cost Reuben's descendants a status they never recovered, though the register still names him first.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son; though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben the firstborn lost his birthright through sin, and God divided its honours: the double portion to Joseph, the leadership to Judah. This answers a question the book raised three chapters ago: why does Israel’s genealogy begin with Judah, who was fourth?

Because he defiled his father’s couch. Reuben slept with his father’s concubine (Genesis 35:22; 49:4). The firstborn’s birthright, a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), went to Joseph, whose two sons Jacob adopted as his own (Genesis 48:5).

Yet the birthright belonged to Joseph. The birthright and the crown did not travel together: the double portion went to one brother, the leadership to another, and the eldest got neither. The chief who came from Judah was David (the same word is translated “prince” in 11:2).

Not decided by the order of birth. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah and Joseph over Reuben, David over seven brothers: by now God’s passing over the obvious man is not a surprise but a signature. Grace, not rank, decides; yet Reuben lost what was his by right through what he did.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah. At the end of the line stands “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Revelation 5:5). In him the birthright and the crown meet again, for he is both the firstborn (Colossians 1:15) and the king, and he shares the inheritance with people who, like Reuben, had forfeited every claim (Romans 8:17).
verseByVerse.note: The firstborn’s rights were split: the double portion went to Joseph, the leadership to Judah.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son, Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son, Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites. And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah, and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon. He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead. And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben’s clans spread east of the Jordan for the sake of their flocks, and the list already marks where that would end: in exile under Assyria.

Because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead. Good grazing on the far side of the river, chosen when Reuben and Gad asked not to cross the Jordan (Numbers 32:1–5). It was a reasonable request, and Moses granted it once they promised to fight beside their brothers. But it put them first in the path of anything coming from the north.

Whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile. Verse 6 records the result almost in passing (about 733 BC; 2 Kings 15:29): the empire that ended the northern tribes enters this book inside a list of fathers and sons.

A decision about pasture. A decision taken for sound reasons by men who meant no harm set the geography that centuries later decided who went into captivity first. Choices made for prosperity, a job, a house, a move, are worth weighing by where they will leave us and our children before God, not only by the grass.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The War That Was of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the eastern tribes cried to God in battle, he heard them, because they trusted him. Gad’s clans are first set beside Reuben’s in Bashan and Gilead, from a register made in the days of Jotham and Jeroboam (vv. 11–17). Then the three eastern tribes muster 44,760 trained fighting men and go to war against the Hagrites and their allies (vv. 18–19). The Chronicler tells the victory twice, once as an army’s triumph and once as God’s answer: “they cried out to God in the battle”, and “the war was of God” (vv. 20–22). They held the land “until the exile”, a phrase that prepares for the end of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 puts prayer in the right order: they cried out, and he granted it because they trusted. Trust is the reason, crying out the act; neither numbers nor expertise is offered as the explanation.
verseByVerse.examples: Someone good at their work can pray in the middle of it as earnestly as anyone; expertise does not make prayer unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah: Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan. And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven. These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz. Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses, and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits. All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gad’s clans settled beside Reuben in Bashan and Gilead, and their names survived because someone wrote them down while they still lived there.

All of these were recorded in genealogies. The register was made under Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel (v. 17), in the eighth century BC, just before Assyria came. The document outlived the tribes it surveyed, and a scribe in Jerusalem still had it three hundred years later, after his own city had burned. A people who lost their land did not lose their place in the record.

Uncertain wording. Sharon (v. 16) cannot be the coastal plain of that name, far from Gad. It is probably pasture east of the Jordan (the word means a level plain), not mentioned elsewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war. They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him. They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive. For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes won because they cried to God in the battle and trusted him; their skill was real, but the victory was his. The battle is told twice, once in terms of the army and once in terms of God, and the two accounts do not compete.

They cried out to God in the battle. Not the night before or at a shrine, but in the fighting itself, by men expert with shield, sword and bow. God answered not their skill but their trust: because they trusted in him. So work hard, use every gift, and cry to him while you are doing it, in the exam room or the hospital corridor.

The war was of God. The plunder is counted like an inventory, and the explanation is five words long. They lived in their place until the exile: the victory was real, but the phrase already looks ahead to verse 26.

Heard because of his reverence. The pattern reaches its height in Christ, who prayed “with loud cries and tears” and “was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). Those who trust him cry to the Father sure of being heard for his sake.

Does that make any war a holy war? No. This was the covenant nation defending the land God had given it. No nation today stands in Israel’s place, and Christ’s people fight with the gospel and prayer (Ephesians 6:12–18).

Uncertain wording. As a people the Hagrites appear only in this chapter and in Psalm 83:6, though one of David’s officials is called Jaziz the Hagrite (27:31). Since Jetur and Naphish are sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15), they were probably Arab tribes of the desert edge, and the name suggests descent from Hagar, though that is not certain. If so, Reuben was fighting distant relatives over grazing (v. 10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — And Then They Broke Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people God had blessed broke faith with him, and the God who had given them victory gave them into exile. Half-Manasseh was numerous, spread north to Mount Hermon, and led by famous warriors (vv. 23–24). But they worshipped the gods of the nations God had driven out before them (v. 25), so God stirred up the king of Assyria to carry Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh away to the far north, where they remained “to this day” (v. 26). The first tribes to settle were the first to go.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler's verb returns. Achan broke faith and Israel lost a battle; these tribes lost a territory; Judah will lose the temple (9:1); Saul lost a kingdom (10:13). One word carries the book's account of why things went wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: Assyria is not the subject of verse 26. God is. The king who deported them was stirred up by the God they had left, a more frightening reading of the news than the political one.

verseByVerse.quote: The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon. These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses. But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them. So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes, blessed with numbers, fame and an answered prayer, turned to other gods, so the God who had given them victory sent Assyria to carry them away.

But they broke faith with the God of their fathers. Half-Manasseh is numerous and famous, and the chapter has gone well since verse 18. Then one word, But, turns it over. Broke faith is the Chronicler’s word for the treachery that ended Saul (10:13) and sent Judah into exile (9:1).

Whom God had destroyed before them. The sting is the last clause: they took up the worship of nations that were no longer there, nations God had removed for that very worship.

Verse 25 against verse 20. The men who cried to God and were heard became, generations later, worshippers of the gods round them. An answered prayer is no guarantee of faithfulness: it settles nothing about the next generation, or the next decade of the same one.

The God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul. Assyria is the tool, not the actor: the God who granted their plea in verse 20 moved Assyria in verse 26, no less faithful in the judgment than in the victory. The same words close the Chronicler’s history in hope: “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus” (2 Chronicles 36:22), who sent the exiles home.

Brought near. Christ, the one Israelite who never broke faith, bore the judgment the unfaithful deserved, so that “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

What it does not mean. Not that every disaster is judgment for a particular sin (Luke 13:1–5). The Chronicler can say it of this exile because God’s word says so; we may not read our neighbours’ troubles that way.

Uncertain wording. Halah, Habor and the river Gozan lie in northern Mesopotamia (2 Kings 17:6). Hara appears nowhere else and its location is unknown, perhaps among “the cities of the Medes” that 2 Kings names instead.
verseByVerse.note: Pul is another name for Tiglath-pileser III.

keyVerse.quote: And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.
keyVerse.note: This is the high point of the chapter and the measure of everything around it. The same tribes who were heard because they trusted are the ones who break faith in verse 25, so the verse shows both what God gladly does for those who rely on him and what no past answer to prayer can secure on its own.

5.reflection:
Reuben lost the birthright through one sin, yet Judah and Joseph, neither of them the eldest, received it (vv. 1–2). What does this chapter teach about how God chooses, and how does Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, bring the birthright and the crown together for undeserving people?

The eastern tribes settled where the grazing was good, and that choice later put them first in the path of Assyria (vv. 9, 26). What decisions in your life are you weighing mainly by prosperity, and how might you weigh them before God?

The men of verse 20 cried to God in the middle of the battle and were heard. What would it look like for you to pray in the middle of your work and struggles, not only before and after them?

Verse 25 follows verse 20. Why does a past answer to prayer not guarantee future faithfulness, and what helps a church, a family or a believer keep trusting God after the battle is won?

6.overview:
Where we are. The eastern tribes have gone into exile (chapter 5), and the Chronicler now comes to the centre of his genealogies: Levi, the tribe set apart to serve at God’s house. It is the longest chapter in the book, standing among the tribes as the sanctuary stood in the middle of Israel’s camp.

The message. God gave a sinful people a way to live near him: priests to make atonement, singers to lead praise, and Levites spread through the land to serve and teach. That appointed service ran unbroken from Aaron to the exile, and its record told the returned exiles that the way to God he had appointed was still open to them.

Why it was said. The returned community had a rebuilt temple but no king, and its life centred on the priests, Levites and singers (see the introduction). It needed to know who might serve at the altar (compare Ezra 2:61–63), and that its worship stood in an unbroken line from Aaron and David.

How the chapter makes its case. The high priests run from Levi through Aaron to Jehozadak, who went into exile (vv. 1–15). The three Levite clans are traced, with Korah and Samuel among them (vv. 16–30). Then David’s singers, Heman, Asaph and Ethan, each with a pedigree back to Levi (vv. 31–48). One verse states what the priests were for, “to make atonement for Israel” (v. 49), and the chapter ends with a map of the Levites’ towns among all the tribes, every city of refuge among them (vv. 50–81).

Where it leads. By pattern. Aaron’s sons made atonement morning and evening for centuries, and every priest in the list died with the work unfinished; Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and sat down (Hebrews 10:12). The cities of refuge, where a killer was safe until the high priest died, picture those who “have fled for refuge” to him (Hebrews 6:18). And the sons of Korah, the rebel the earth swallowed, became singers before the altar, a small sign of the grace that turns rebels into worshippers.

For us. Every believer now belongs to “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), with the LORD himself as our portion. Our access to God rests not on our pedigree but on Christ’s finished offering; our praise is a service to be ordered gladly; and hidden work in God’s house is never unseen by him.
6.theology:
Two offices stand on equal footing. Priests offered blood, singers offered song; both were appointed, both had to prove descent, both are recorded with the same care. Israel's worship was never a service with music added.

Underneath the whole tribe lies verse 49: atonement is why Levi exists, and it was work that no offering ever finished.
6.examples:
Korah's descendants are the pastoral centre of this chapter (vv. 22-33). Nobody chooses his ancestor, and the children of a rebel became a prophet's family and the singers of the house he had tried to storm. No family history puts a person beyond God's mercy.

Every name in this chapter served a system that pointed beyond itself. The priests stood daily at the altar because no sacrifice could take away sins; Christ, a priest for ever, offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:23–27). The singers sang before an ark; the church sings to the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The High Priests, Down to the Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priesthood ran unbroken from Aaron to the exile, because God kept the line of atonement going. The chapter begins with Levi’s three sons, Amram’s children, Aaron, Moses and Miriam, and Aaron’s four sons (vv. 1–3). It follows Eleazar, since Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD, through Phinehas and Zadok (vv. 4–8), and on through the priest of Solomon’s temple to Jehozadak, who went into exile “when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar” (vv. 9–15). The list stops in captivity, and its first readers, back in the land, were what happened next.
verseByVerse.theology: The priesthood was handed from father to son, not chosen as a career, and the line is unbroken from Sinai to Babylon. The list stops at the deportation without comment, but a line that goes into exile has not ended (see v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples: A family record that keeps Nadab and Abihu in it is honest: the register does not tidy away the members whose story ended badly.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi’s family is traced to Aaron, because the line this chapter needs is the priesthood, not the prophet. (In Hebrew Bibles verses 1–15 are numbered 5:27–41.)

The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Of Levi’s three sons the chapter follows the middle one, and of Amram’s children it follows Aaron and lets Moses go.

Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. That is startling editing. The man who brought Israel out of Egypt is named once, between his brother and sister, because the line this book needs runs through the priest.

Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire and died before the LORD (Leviticus 10:1–2). The register names them without a word about it, lists them because they were born, and passes on to Eleazar because the priesthood did.

verseByVerse.quote: Eleazar fathered Phinehas, Phinehas fathered Abishua, Abishua fathered Bukki, Bukki fathered Uzzi, Uzzi fathered Zerahiah, Zerahiah fathered Meraioth, Meraioth fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Ahimaaz,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priesthood passed from father to son through Phinehas and Zadok, whose stories the list assumes rather than tells.

Eleazar fathered Phinehas. Phinehas drove a spear through an Israelite and a Midianite woman in the middle of a plague and was given a covenant of perpetual priesthood (Numbers 25:7–13). His zeal for God’s honour ended a plague of judgment. It belonged to Israel under the old covenant and is never a licence for private violence.

Ahitub fathered Zadok. Zadok went out with David when Absalom took the city and carried the ark back at David’s command (2 Samuel 15:24–29), and his house held the high priesthood until the time of the Maccabees, in the second century BC.

Neither story told. The list records only who held the office and handed it on. What a man did in it belongs to the narrative books.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahimaaz fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Johanan, and Johanan fathered Azariah (it was he who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem). Azariah fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Shallum, Shallum fathered Hilkiah, Hilkiah fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Seraiah, Seraiah fathered Jehozadak; and Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priests served on for centuries until God himself sent Judah into exile, and the list stops there, leaving its readers to supply what came next.

When the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile. Twenty-two generations, and then the sentence the list has been travelling towards. The LORD sent Judah into exile; Nebuchadnezzar was only the hand he used. The Chronicler will not let his readers think of Babylon as a defeat God suffered.

Jehozadak went into exile. And then the list simply stops. Yet its readers knew that Jehozadak’s son Jeshua, Joshua the high priest, had come home with the first company and stood at the rebuilt altar (Ezra 3:2). The line is left in captivity, and the readers are expected to supply the rest, because they themselves, back in the land, are what happened next.

Not a complete roll. The list leaves out Eli’s house, descended from Aaron’s youngest son Ithamar, and men such as Jehoiada; it traces Zadok’s line, the line that came home.

Uncertain wording. The remark in verse 10 that Azariah served “in the house that Solomon built” may belong with the Azariah of verse 9, Solomon’s contemporary (1 Kings 4:2), and have shifted a line in copying; or it may mark this later Azariah as serving in the temple rather than the tent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gave his worship a whole tribe of servants, and among them singers whose pedigrees are as careful as any priest’s. The three Levite clans are traced, with Korah and Samuel inside Kohath’s branch (vv. 16–30). Then David appoints the service of song (vv. 31–32), and the three chief singers are named, one from each clan: Heman, Samuel’s grandson and Korah’s descendant, in the centre (vv. 33–38), Asaph on his right (vv. 39–43) and Ethan on his left (vv. 44–47). The rest of the Levites, unnamed, are appointed “for all the service of the tabernacle” (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: Music in Israel's worship is not an atmosphere or a preference. It is an office, with a charter from the king, a place in the building and a genealogy behind it.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who lead a church's singing today hold no hereditary office, but the principle stands: leading praise is a service to God and his people, not a performance, offered in response to the God who has already come near. It is rightly done with preparation and order (1 Corinthians 14:40), and with the word of Christ dwelling richly in those who sing (Colossians 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. And these are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their fathers. Of Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son, Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, Jeatherai his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of Levi is recorded as carefully as the high priests, because every servant of God’s house mattered to him.

These are the clans of the Levites according to their fathers. The three clans again in more detail (Gershom is another spelling of Gershon), because the priests were only one family inside Levi; the rest of the tribe served alongside them.

No office, no story, no second class. Gershom’s and Merari’s descendants have no office attached and no story told. These are the men who carried frames and curtains across a desert and then kept the doors and stores of a temple for four hundred years. The register gives them the same treatment as the high priests: in the tribe that existed to serve near God, there was no second class.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son, Elkanah his son, Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son, Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son. The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth, Elkanah his son, Zophai his son, Nahath his son, Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son. The sons of Samuel: Joel his firstborn, the second Abijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inside Kohath’s line stand Korah the rebel and, generations later, Samuel the prophet: God’s mercy ran on through a family that had deserved destruction.

Korah his son. A name that ought to stop the reader. Korah led the rebellion against Moses and Aaron, and the ground opened under him (Numbers 16:31–33). Ten chapters later Numbers adds, “But the sons of Korah did not die” (Numbers 26:11).

The sons of Samuel. This is what became of them. Samuel, the child who heard his name called in the dark at Shiloh and anointed Israel’s first two kings, descends from the man who tried to seize the priesthood by force. The God who judged Korah kept his children, as the God who sent his Son “to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15) still does.

Was Samuel a Levite or an Ephraimite? 1 Samuel 1:1 calls his father an Ephrathite of the hill country of Ephraim, which describes where the family lived; Levites lived among the other tribes, as the end of this chapter shows. This chapter tells where the family came from.

Uncertain wording. Korah’s father is Amminadab here (v. 22) but Izhar in verse 38 and Exodus 6:21; Amminadab may be another name for Izhar, though no explanation is certain. The repeated Elkanahs of verses 23–27 are also hard to sort into generations.

Textual note. Older English versions call Samuel’s firstborn Vashni in verse 28. The Hebrew word taken as a name means “and the second”, and Joel’s name seems to have dropped out in copying; the ESV restores it from verse 33 and 1 Samuel 8:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son, Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, and Asaiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Merari’s line belongs to the clan God charged with carrying the sanctuary, a charge the book will show was not to be taken lightly.

The sons of Merari. Seven names, no comment, closing the section.

Uzzah his son. One is a name the reader will meet again. An Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark on a new cart and died beside it (13:9–10). That Uzzah is probably not this man, but this list belongs to the tribe God charged with carrying the sanctuary: the Merarites its frames, the Kohathites the ark on poles (Numbers 4:15, 31). Chapter 13 is about what happens when it is carried the wrong way.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men whom David put in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there. They ministered with song before the tabernacle of the tent of meeting until Solomon built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they performed their service according to their order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David gave Israel’s praise its own appointed servants, who sang in response to God’s presence and did it in good order.

The service of song. Song is a service, the word used of the sacrifices, and it has an appointment from the king.

After the ark rested there. It begins once the ark is in place (chapters 15–16): a response to God’s arrival, not a device for summoning him.

According to their order. Israel’s praise was rostered, with a rota, a place to stand and a move from tent to temple to manage, and none of that was thought to be in tension with its being worship.

I will sing your praise. Behind these singers stands the one who leads his people’s praise himself: “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). Christ is the true worship leader, and his church sings with him.
verseByVerse.note: Heman, Asaph and Ethan (or Jeduthun) were the leading musicians; several psalms bear their names.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men who served and their sons. Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief singer, Heman, was Samuel’s grandson and Korah’s descendant: the family of a rebel was given a place of praise before the altar.

Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel. The chief singer’s pedigree runs back twenty generations to Levi, as carefully kept as the high priests’ own, and through Korah.

A place before the altar. The family whose father the earth swallowed for wanting a place at the altar was given, centuries later, a place in front of it with a harp. Eleven psalms carry the heading “of the sons of Korah”, the first of them the prayer of a soul panting for God as a deer pants for flowing streams (Psalm 42).

Mercy without comment. The register draws no attention to it. A reader who knows Numbers finds the mercy for himself, and finds the gospel’s shape in it: those who once grasped at God’s place are brought near and given a song.

verseByVerse.quote: and his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, namely, Asaph the son of Berechiah, son of Shimea, son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malchijah, son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah, son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei, son of Jahath, son of Gershom, son of Levi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asaph, from Gershom’s clan, stood at Heman’s right hand, so that every branch of Levi shared in leading Israel’s praise.

Who stood on his right hand. The three chief singers came one from each clan, so no branch owned the music.

Asaph’s psalms. Asaph’s name stands over twelve psalms, some of the bleakest in the book: one admits he almost stumbled from envying the wicked until he went into the sanctuary (Psalm 73); another asks how long God will be angry with his people’s prayers (Psalm 80:4).

Leading with doubts. The man appointed over Israel’s praise put his worst doubt into the hymn book, and Israel sang it for centuries. A man does not need to have every doubt settled before he leads God’s people in worship.

verseByVerse.quote: On the left hand were their brothers, the sons of Merari: Ethan the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi. And their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ethan of Merari stood on the left, and the rest of the Levites served in God’s house unnamed: hidden service is no lesser honour.

On the left hand. Ethan and the Merarites stood on the left: Kohath in the centre, Gershom right, Merari left.

Appointed for all the service of the tabernacle. Then verse 48, and the vast majority of the tribe: no names, no pedigrees, no instrument. One sentence covers thousands of men whose working lives were spent inside that building. To be covered by that sentence was no lesser gift; the service was the honour, and being recorded was never the point.

The idol of being seen. Our age has made a currency of visibility: followers, views, a name in the credits, and much modern anxiety is the fear of going unnoticed. By that standard verse 48 is a list of failures. But these men served in the house of the God who sees, who needed no register to know them. The approval we chase must be won again every morning and is withdrawn the moment we stop performing. The gospel gives its verdict once: the Father who “sees in secret” (Matthew 6:4) has looked on us in his Son and called us his own. People who know that can do hidden work for a lifetime and count it an honour, because the only audience that finally matters is already in the room.

Uncertain wording. Ethan leads in this role again in 15:17, but in 16:41 and 25:1 the third leader is Jeduthun. Many think they are one man under two names; it is not certain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–81 — Aaron's Altar, and Forty-Eight Towns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole tribe existed for one purpose, atonement, and God spread it through every part of the land. One verse states what the priests did: they offered on the altars “to make atonement for Israel” (v. 49). Aaron’s line is repeated to Ahimaaz (vv. 50–53), and the chapter becomes a map: thirteen priestly towns out of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (vv. 54–60), and the rest of Levi given towns by lot among all the tribes, forty-eight in all (vv. 61–81). The tribe with no land of its own held every city of refuge in Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The one tribe with no territory held all six cities of refuge (vv. 57, 67): the tribe that served the altar of atonement also kept the shelters for the guilty.
verseByVerse.examples: Anathoth (v. 60) is a priestly town like any other. Centuries later Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, bought a field there with the Babylonian army outside the walls, as a sign that fields would be bought in this land again (Jeremiah 32:6–15).

verseByVerse.quote: But Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense for all the work of the Most Holy Place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded. These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son, Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son, Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son, Zadok his son, Ahimaaz his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests existed to make atonement for Israel exactly as God commanded, a work they could never finish and Christ has finished.

To make atonement for Israel. After forty-eight verses of descent, one verse says what it was for. Everything else in the chapter, the towns, the singers, the twenty-two generations, exists around that one function: blood carried to an altar so that a guilty people could go on living beside a holy God. According to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded: the way near was the way God gave, not one Israel devised.

One offering, finished. It took a whole tribe, a portable sanctuary, forty-eight towns and many centuries to keep that work going, and it was never finished. The same offerings were made every morning and evening for a thousand years, and every priest in this list died with the work undone. The Son who ended it made one offering and sat down (Hebrews 10:11–12), and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near through him (Hebrews 7:25). Those who trust him stand before God on that finished work, not on their own.

verseByVerse.quote: These are their dwelling places according to their settlements within their borders: to the sons of Aaron of the clans of Kohathites, for theirs was the first lot, to them they gave Hebron in the land of Judah and its surrounding pasturelands, but the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests received Hebron and its pasture while its fields stayed with Caleb: the division honoured both the priests’ calling and an old soldier’s promise.

They gave Hebron in the land of Judah. The map opens on Hebron, where Abraham buried Sarah and David reigned seven years.

But the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Caleb. Caleb had asked Joshua for that hill country at eighty-five, forty-five years after Moses promised it to him, because he had followed the LORD wholly (Joshua 14:6–14). He got the farmland; the priests got the town and enough grass for their animals.

Fair to both. Nobody was cheated. The tribe that lived on the offerings needed no farmland, and the old soldier who had waited for a promise was not asked to give up his fields.

verseByVerse.quote: To the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge: Hebron, Libnah with its pasturelands, Jattir, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands, Hilen with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands, Ashan with its pasturelands, and Beth-shemesh with its pasturelands; and from the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon, Geba with its pasturelands, Alemeth with its pasturelands, and Anathoth with its pasturelands. All their cities throughout their clans were thirteen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests’ towns included Hebron, a city of refuge, so that the tribe of atonement held the places of safety for the guilty.

What a city of refuge was. A place where a man who had killed somebody without meaning to could run and live. He fled to the gate, stated his case to the elders, and stayed inside the walls until the high priest died, safe from the avenger of blood, the dead man’s relative, who had the legal right to kill him outside (Numbers 35:9–28; Joshua 20). Six such towns were appointed in Israel, and the priests and Levites held all six.

Refuge in Levi’s keeping. So the tribe with no land of its own, whose office was atonement, was given custody of every place in the country where the killer could not be touched.

Freedom by a high priest’s death. Many Christians have seen here a picture of Christ, and the New Testament gives them the language: believers are those who “have fled for refuge” to the hope set before them (Hebrews 6:18). The fugitive’s freedom came by a high priest’s death; the guilty sinner’s comes by the death of the great High Priest, who lives for ever to keep those who have fled to him.

Uncertain wording. The cities of refuge is plural, though Hebron is the only city of refuge in this list (as in Joshua 21:13, “Hebron, the city of refuge for the manslayer”). The plural is probably a shorthand carried over from the fuller lists; it does not mean the other towns here were places of refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest of the Kohathites were given by lot out of the clan of the tribe, out of the half-tribe, the half of Manasseh, ten cities. To the Gershomites according to their clans were allotted thirteen cities out of the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Manasseh in Bashan. To the Merarites according to their clans were allotted twelve cities out of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. So the people of Israel gave the Levites the cities with their pasturelands. They gave by lot out of the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin these cities that are mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites’ towns among the other tribes were assigned by lot, so that the decision was God’s, not any tribe’s.

They gave by lot. No tribe chose its Levites and no Levite his neighbours. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33): the method that put a teaching family in every district took the decision out of everybody’s hands and left it in God’s.

Uncertain wording. Verse 61 is compressed. Joshua 21:5 says these ten towns came from Ephraim, Dan and half-Manasseh, and verses 66–70 list towns from Ephraim and Manasseh, so words naming Ephraim and Dan seem to have dropped out here.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the clans of the sons of Kohath had cities of their territory out of the tribe of Ephraim. They were given the cities of refuge: Shechem with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, Gezer with its pasturelands, Jokmeam with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands, Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands, and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner with its pasturelands, and Bileam with its pasturelands, for the rest of the clans of the Kohathites. To the Gershomites were given out of the clan of the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands and Ashtaroth with its pasturelands;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim and Manasseh gave up towns they had fought for, Shechem and Golan among them, so that the landless tribe could live among them.

Shechem with its pasturelands. The refuge formula returns with Shechem (v. 67), where Joshua gathered Israel to choose whom they would serve and Joseph’s bones were buried (Joshua 24), and Golan in Bashan (v. 71).

Given up by other tribes. Every town here belonged to somebody else: Ephraim and Manasseh gave up settlements they had fought for, so the tribe with no inheritance could live among them.

verseByVerse.quote: and out of the tribe of Issachar: Kedesh with its pasturelands, Daberath with its pasturelands, Ramoth with its pasturelands, and Anem with its pasturelands; out of the tribe of Asher: Mashal with its pasturelands, Abdon with its pasturelands, Hukok with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, Hammon with its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim with its pasturelands. To the rest of the Merarites were allotted out of the tribe of Zebulun: Rimmono with its pasturelands, Tabor with its pasturelands, and beyond the Jordan at Jericho, on the east side of the Jordan, out of the tribe of Reuben: Bezer in the wilderness with its pasturelands, Jahzah with its pasturelands, Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead with its pasturelands, Mahanaim with its pasturelands, Heshbon with its pasturelands, and Jazer with its pasturelands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last towns complete the map: Levi had no territory of his own, but a home in every tribe and the LORD as his portion.

The last cities of refuge. Kedesh (v. 76), Bezer (v. 78) and Ramoth in Gilead (v. 80) complete the six. Forty-eight towns, none in Levi’s own country, because Levi had none.

No acres for Levi. Every other tribe walked away from the division of the land holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the well. Levi was handed no acres, no boundary stones, no deed, but a house in each of his brothers’ territories, enough grass for the animals, and a promise that the LORD himself was his portion. The arrangement was practical too: scatter the teaching tribe across every border and no family in Israel lives far from a man whose whole life is the law of God.

Levi was given God. The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

What it means to have the LORD as your portion. A portion is your share of the estate, the thing you live on. To Aaron God said, “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20). Most of us quietly want God and a secure field as well, and the field is what we would miss first: whatever we feel we could not live without has become our real portion. The psalmist learned to say, “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26). And every believer now stands where Levi stood, part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9).

Nowhere to lay his head. Christ made that possible by becoming the one with no share at all. “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and on the cross he lost even the sense of his Father’s presence, so that God himself could be ours. That is why losing a job, a house or a plan cannot touch your inheritance. This week, when something you counted on is taken, say that psalm out loud before you start doing the sums. See Inheritance.

keyVerse.quote: But Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense for all the work of the Most Holy Place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.
keyVerse.note: After forty-eight verses of names, this verse says what the whole tribe existed for. Every priest, singer, gatekeeper and town in the chapter served this one work of atonement, done as God commanded; and its endless repetition points to the one offering of Christ that finished it.

6.reflection:
Verse 49 says the whole priestly line existed “to make atonement for Israel”, a work repeated daily for centuries. Read Hebrews 10:11–14. What difference does it make to your confidence before God that Christ’s offering is finished?

Korah rebelled and was swallowed by the earth, yet his descendants included Samuel and Heman the chief singer (vv. 22–38). What does this tell you about God’s mercy to families with a dark past, including your own?

David gave Israel’s praise appointed leaders, an order and a place (vv. 31–48), and Asaph’s psalms include some of the Bible’s most honest doubts. How should careful planning and honest feeling both shape the worship of your church?

Levi received no land but had the LORD as his portion (Numbers 18:20). What would you miss first if it were taken from you, and what would it mean in practice to treat God himself as your inheritance?

7.title: The Northern Tribes: Every Name Counted
7.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four.<sup>2</sup>The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses, namely of Tola, mighty warriors of their generations, their number in the days of David being 22,600.<sup>3</sup>The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men.<sup>4</sup>And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons.<sup>5</sup>Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And their enrollment by genealogies was 22,034.<sup>8</sup>The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher.<sup>9</sup>And their enrollment by genealogies, according to their generations, as heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, was 20,200.<sup>10</sup>The son of Jediael: Bilhan. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.<sup>11</sup>All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war.<sup>12</sup>And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah.<sup>14</sup>The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead.<sup>15</sup>And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters.<sup>16</sup>And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem.<sup>17</sup>The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh.<sup>18</sup>And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son,<sup>21</sup>Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock.<sup>22</sup>And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.<sup>23</sup>And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. And he called his name Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house.<sup>24</sup>His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah.<sup>25</sup>Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son,<sup>26</sup>Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,<sup>27</sup>Nun his son, Joshua his son.<sup>28</sup>Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and to the east Naaran, and to the west Gezer and its towns, Shechem and its towns, and Ayyah and its towns;<sup>29</sup>also in possession of the Manassites, Beth-shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, Dor and its towns.
