In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah.<sup>31</sup>The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith.<sup>32</sup>Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua.<sup>33</sup>The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet.<sup>34</sup>The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.<sup>36</sup>The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah.<sup>37</sup>Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.<sup>38</sup>The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.<sup>40</sup>All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
7.overview:
Where we are. After Levi at the centre (chapter 6), the Chronicler turns to the tribes of the north: Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher, six tribes in forty verses. Most of the entries are muster rolls from old army records, and Benjamin will receive a chapter of its own next.

The message. God remembers every tribe of his people, even tribes long since scattered, and inside their brief records he keeps the people the world forgets: a grieving father, daughters with no brother, a woman who built towns, a sister named for no reason anyone records. Israel was meant to be twelve tribes, one people, and the gaps in the list are honest about what had been lost.

Why it was said. Assyria had scattered these northern tribes three centuries before (5:26; see the introduction). The returned community, drawn mostly from Judah and Benjamin, needed to know that all Israel still mattered to God, and some of Ephraim and Manasseh were already living among them in Jerusalem (9:3).

How the chapter makes its case. Issachar’s 87,000 warriors come first (vv. 1–5), then Benjamin briefly (vv. 6–12), Naphtali in one verse (v. 13), and Manasseh, whose line pauses on Zelophehad’s daughters (vv. 14–19). Ephraim’s list breaks into one of the genealogies’ rare stories: two sons killed in a cattle raid, a father who mourned many days and named the next child for the disaster, a daughter who built three towns, and at the end of the line Joshua (vv. 20–29). Asher closes the rolls with a sister named and 26,000 men (vv. 30–40). Dan and Zebulun receive no genealogy at all.

Where it leads. By the character of God, revealed fully in Christ, and by pattern. The God who records a father’s grief and the names of overlooked women is the God who in Christ wept at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35) and tells his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). And Ephraim’s line ends in Joshua, who led Israel into the land; Jesus bore the same name, and gives the rest that Joshua could not (Hebrews 4:8).

For us. Grief that lasts is not unbelief, and God does not hurry the mourner. Your name and your work are known to God even if no one else could say why they matter. And the incomplete rolls of Israel point to the only complete one, the Lamb’s book of life.
7.theology:
The numbers record past greatness, not present strength. The point is continuity: the small community reading this book is the same people as those tribes, and it remained that people because its identity never depended on its numbers.

Against that stands an honest gap, two tribes missing and unexplained (see vv. 36-40). The completeness belongs to God's memory, not Israel's paperwork.
7.examples:
Ephraim is the pastoral centre of the chapter. A father buried two young men, grieved a long time while his brothers sat with him, and carried the loss into the next child's name, and nobody in the text hurries him or suggests a believer should be further along by now.

The loss stays a loss; later blessings do not explain it away. But the household that grief nearly ended went on to produce Sheerah and Joshua (vv. 24, 27), and what God does after a disaster in a family is rarely visible to the generation that suffered it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps the record of tribes great and small, and does not forget the people inside them. Issachar’s entry is an army list, 87,000 mighty warriors counted in David’s day (vv. 1–5). Benjamin is given briefly, with more than 59,000 warriors (vv. 6–12), before its own chapter. Naphtali receives a single verse (v. 13). Manasseh’s line runs through Machir, the father of Gilead, and pauses on a man with no sons whose daughters changed Israel’s law of inheritance: “Zelophehad had daughters” (vv. 14–19).
verseByVerse.theology: These are counts of fighting men, kept by a community with no army, a record of what the tribes once were.
verseByVerse.examples: Five sisters once asked Moses that their father's name not disappear for want of a son, and the law was changed for them (Numbers 27:1–11). Speaking up for the overlooked is not presumption.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four. The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses, namely of Tola, mighty warriors of their generations, their number in the days of David being 22,600. The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men. And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons. Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Issachar is remembered as a tribe of many fighting men, numbers written down by a people who were now few, and kept to the credit of the God who had made them many.

Enrolled by genealogy. Issachar’s entry reads like an army list: houses, chiefs and 87,000 men, counted “in the days of David” (v. 2).

Why the numbers. These numbers are not pride. The men holding this book could not have raised a thousand soldiers; Jerusalem was a small town in a Persian province. These figures are a record of what the tribes had been, written by people who were now something much smaller.

Two ways to remember. One way of remembering a great past poisons the present; another steadies it. The difference is whether the memory is of what we were or of what God did, and the Chronicler keeps the credit with God, who will yet gather “a great multitude that no one could number” (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three. The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And their enrollment by genealogies was 22,034. The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher. And their enrollment by genealogies, according to their generations, as heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, was 20,200. The son of Jediael: Bilhan. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar. All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war. And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin, once cut down to six hundred men, is recorded here with nearly sixty thousand warriors: a tribe God had restored from the edge of extinction. This is a brief entry before Benjamin’s own chapter (chapter 8).

Benjamin’s recovery. After the civil war of Judges 20, Benjamin was reduced to six hundred men hiding at a rock (Judges 20:47), and these numbers are its recovery. That tribe produced Israel’s first king, and later a Pharisee from Tarsus who listed being “of the tribe of Benjamin” among the things he counted as loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:5–8).

Uncertain wording. Verse 12 is obscure: Hushim is the son of Dan in Genesis 46:23, and “Aher” means “another”, so many think the verse keeps a fragment of Dan’s genealogy; some think the whole section first belonged to Zebulun, the other tribe missing from these chapters. Neither suggestion can be proved.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah. The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead. And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters. And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem. The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh. And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah. The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naphtali receives one line and Manasseh a tangled one, yet in it God remembers five daughters whose case changed Israel’s law.

The descendants of Bilhah. Naphtali is named as descended from Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, without apology.

Zelophehad had daughters. A clause inside Manasseh’s line that stops the eye. Those five women, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, asked for their father’s inheritance before Moses and the assembly, and God told Moses, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” (Numbers 27:7). The law of inheritance changed for every family in Israel.

A few words in a genealogy. Here the whole affair is a few words in a list, which is the fate of most things that changed the world. The God who heard the case of five women with no brother still hears those others overlook, and in Christ all who believe, sons and daughters alike, are “heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29).

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 is among the hardest in the genealogies. As it stands, Machir takes a wife “for Huppim and for Shuppim” (Benjaminite names from v. 12), both his sister and his wife are called Maacah, and “the second” has no first. Words have probably been lost in copying. The main line, Machir, Gilead and Zelophehad’s daughters, is clear from Numbers 26:29–33.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Ephraim: A Father Who Mourned, and a Daughter Who Built
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of Ephraim’s list God lets us see a father’s grief and a daughter’s work. Two of Ephraim’s sons are killed by the men of Gath in a cattle raid; he mourns many days, his brothers come to comfort him, and he names the next son Beriah, “because disaster had befallen his house” (vv. 20–23). His daughter Sheerah builds Lower and Upper Beth-horon and Uzzen-sheerah (v. 24). The line runs on to Joshua the son of Nun (vv. 25–27), and the section closes with the towns of Joseph’s sons, from Bethel to Megiddo and Dor (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture gives grief time and company. Ephraim's brothers sat with him, and the Son of God wept at a friend's tomb before he raised him (John 11:35), so no believer need be ashamed of mourning long.
verseByVerse.examples: Sheerah is one of very few people in nine chapters of genealogy credited with building anything (Shemed is another, 8:12), and her towns guarded the pass armies used for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son, Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock. And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him. And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. And he called his name Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim lost two sons and mourned them long, and Scripture keeps his grief and the name he gave his next son without rebuke.

Ezer and Elead. Without warning, the list becomes a story: two sons killed in a cattle raid involving the men of Gath, and then one of the few sentences in these chapters with a heart in it.

And Ephraim their father mourned many days. Nothing is explained, not whether the raid was justified or the boys foolish. We are told how long the grief lasted, many days, and that his brothers came and sat with him.

Because disaster had befallen his house. Then he had another son and named him Beriah, which sounds like the Hebrew for disaster. A father who buried two children gave the next one a name like that, and every time he called the boy in from the field he said the word out loud. Scripture does not tell him to stop, and does not treat it as a failure of faith. The register carries the name down the generations, in a list that had no obligation to mention it.

The hurry to get over it. Our culture is uneasy with grief that lasts. We talk of closure and moving on, and quietly worry when someone is still sad a year later. Christians can add a pressure of their own: if I really trusted God, surely I would not feel like this. C. S. Lewis, after his wife died, opened A Grief Observed with the sentence, “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear,” and many have found its honesty a better comfort than cheerful advice. Scripture is on the side of the honest. Ephraim mourns many days, his brothers come and sit with him, and nobody hurries him. That is not unbelief; it is love going on after its object has gone.

Jesus wept. Christians have a stranger warrant still. Standing at the tomb of a friend he was about to raise, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). Paul tells believers not to grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13): not an instruction to stop grieving, but a promise that grief is not the end. If grief does not lift and begins to crush you, tell your pastor or a biblical counsellor and see your doctor too; seeking help is no failure of faith.

How could Ephraim mourn sons killed at Gath? He lived in Egypt, and Gath is in Canaan. The raid probably happened while Israel was in Egypt, when Ephraim’s sons went up to Canaan, or “Ephraim” here means a later descendant who bore the tribe’s name.

Uncertain wording. “They came down to raid their livestock” (v. 21) can be read either way: Ephraim’s sons went down to take the cattle of Gath, or the men of Gath came down to take Ephraim’s. The Hebrew allows both; most translations take it the first way.
verseByVerse.note: “Beriah” sounds like the Hebrew for “disaster” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah. Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son, Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son, Nun his son, Joshua his son. Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and to the east Naaran, and to the west Gezer and its towns, Shechem and its towns, and Ayyah and its towns; also in possession of the Manassites, Beth-shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, Dor and its towns. In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim’s line includes a daughter who built towns on Israel’s most fought-over pass, and ends with Joshua, who led Israel into the land.

His daughter was Sheerah. Hundreds of men in these chapters fathered somebody. Very few built something, and one who did is a woman who built three towns, one of them bearing her name.

Lower and Upper Beth-horon. Beth-horon is not a village on a hill. It is the pass, the road up from the coastal plain into the highlands, the route invading armies took. Joshua chased the five kings down it the day the sun stood still (Joshua 10:10–14), and armies fought over it for centuries. A woman built towns on that ascent, and her name stayed on the map.

Nun his son, Joshua his son. Three verses later the line reaches Joshua: the family that lost two sons to a cattle raid also produced the man who led Israel into the land.

Another day. Joshua’s name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus. He brought Israel into Canaan, but not into God’s final rest: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The greater Joshua leads his people into the rest that remains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–40 — Asher, and the Two Tribes That Are Missing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asher’s line is recorded with unusual care, and then the tribal rolls end with two tribes missing. Asher’s four sons and their sister Serah head the list (v. 30), which runs through Beriah and Heber, naming another sister, Shua (vv. 31–39), and closes on 26,000 approved warriors (v. 40). With that the Chronicler has finished the tribes outside Judah, Levi and Benjamin, and Dan and Zebulun have received no genealogy at all.
verseByVerse.theology: Dan and Zebulun have no genealogy anywhere in 1 Chronicles. The register that insists God keeps track of everyone is itself silent about two tribes.
verseByVerse.examples: Some find a fragment of Dan in verse 12, since Genesis names Dan's son Hushim (Genesis 46:23), though the Hebrew is uncertain. Either way, the record has holes, and the God whose record it is does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith. Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet. The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram. The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asher’s register names a sister, Serah, whom Scripture records three times without ever saying why: her name is kept because God keeps it.

And their sister Serah. Asher’s register does something rare: it names a sister. Serah is named in Genesis among the seventy who went into Egypt (Genesis 46:17) and in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:46), and nothing is recorded about her. Three documents centuries apart wrote her name, and none explains why.

Written by God. That is one of the quiet arguments these chapters make. A person can be in the book of God for no reason anyone can reconstruct, and stay there, because it is God who wrote the name, not the person. Jesus told his disciples that the thing to rejoice in was not their achievements but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah. Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera. The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara. The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia. All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asher closes the tribal rolls with 26,000 warriors, and with the rolls complete, two tribes are missing.

Dan and Zebulun missing. The genealogies of the tribes are finished, and two of the twelve have not appeared. The Chronicler, who gave eighty-one verses to Levi and three chapters to Judah, does not account for the omission.

Whatever the reason. Whatever the reason (records lost, a scroll damaged, tribes no longer traceable), the effect on a returning exile from either tribe is not softened by the explanation. He opened the book and his family was not in it.

The last roll of Israel. Set that beside the last roll of Israel in Scripture, twelve thousand sealed from every tribe, which this commentary takes as a picture of the whole church (Revelation 7:4–8). Zebulun is named there; Dan is still absent, and Ephraim appears under Joseph. So the two rolls do not match, and neither settles the matter. The names that finally count are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27), and no scroll in Jerusalem was ever the master copy.

keyVerse.quote: And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of muster rolls this is the verse with a heart in it. It shows the God who keeps Israel’s records keeping a father’s grief as well, without hurry and without rebuke, and it points to the Saviour who wept with the bereaved before he raised the dead.

7.reflection:
The Chronicler’s readers were few and weak, yet he records the large musters of the past (vv. 1–12, 40). When you remember better days in your life or church, how can you remember them in a way that steadies you rather than poisons the present?

Ephraim mourned many days, his brothers came to comfort him, and he named his son for the disaster (vv. 22–23). What does this teach about grief and about how to comfort someone who is grieving? Where are you tempted to hurry yourself or others?

Zelophehad’s daughters, Sheerah and Serah are named in lists dominated by men (vv. 15, 24, 30). What does God’s record of them tell you about the value he places on people the world overlooks?

Dan and Zebulun are missing from these chapters. How does the promise that the names that count are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27) comfort someone who feels left out or forgotten?

8.title: Benjamin: The Tribe of Saul and the Background of David's Kingdom
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,<sup>2</sup>Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.<sup>3</sup>And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud,<sup>4</sup>Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,<sup>5</sup>Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.<sup>6</sup>These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath):<sup>7</sup>Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.<sup>8</sup>And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives.<sup>9</sup>He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,<sup>10</sup>Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses.<sup>11</sup>He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns,<sup>13</sup>and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee);<sup>14</sup>and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.<sup>15</sup>Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,<sup>16</sup>Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah.<sup>17</sup>Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,<sup>18</sup>Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal.<sup>19</sup>Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,<sup>20</sup>Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,<sup>21</sup>Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.<sup>22</sup>Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,<sup>23</sup>Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,<sup>24</sup>Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,<sup>25</sup>Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak.<sup>26</sup>Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,<sup>27</sup>Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham.<sup>28</sup>These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>29</sup>Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah.<sup>30</sup>His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,<sup>31</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zecher,<sup>32</sup>and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>33</sup>Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal;<sup>34</sup>and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.<sup>36</sup>Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>37</sup>Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>38</sup>Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third.<sup>40</sup>The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
8.overview:
Where we are. The tribal genealogies end with Benjamin, given a chapter of its own after its brief entry in 7:6–12. Benjamin had stayed with Judah when the kingdom divided, shared Jerusalem with it, and with Judah formed the core of the people who came home (Ezra 1:5).

The message. God keeps faith with the families of his people through all their failures, and he tells the truth about them. Benjamin’s record holds exiles, a broken marriage, builders and fighters, the families who lived in Jerusalem, and at last the house of Saul, the king God rejected; yet their names are kept, not erased. The chapter sets Saul’s line in place so that the story can begin with his fall.

Why it was said. Many of the first readers were Benjaminites, and Jerusalem after the return was half empty and needed families with a claim to live in it (Nehemiah 11:1–4; see the introduction). This chapter gave them their family papers and their place in the city.

How the chapter makes its case. Benjamin’s sons and the houses of Ehud come first, with an exile to Manahath (vv. 1–7). Shaharaim’s families follow, one begun in Moab after he sent away his wives (vv. 8–11), and then the builders of Ono and Lod and the men who put Gath to flight (vv. 12–14). Long lists of chiefs end, “These lived in Jerusalem” (vv. 15–28). Last comes Saul’s family from Gibeon, through Saul and Jonathan to Merib-baal and on for a dozen generations to Ulam’s archers (vv. 29–40). The list is repeated at 9:35–44, and leads straight into Saul’s death in chapter 10.

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Saul of Benjamin was the king the people asked for, and his house ended in failure; the true King would come from Judah. Yet in Saul’s own line the Chronicler keeps Merib-baal, Jonathan’s lame son, whom David brought to eat at his table for Jonathan’s sake (2 Samuel 9), a picture of what the Son of David does for sinners. And another Saul of Benjamin, the apostle Paul, found in Jesus the King his namesake had failed to be.

For us. God does not erase the failures in his people’s families, and he does not erase the families either. Whatever your family history, you may sit at the King’s table for the sake of another, and take your place in the city God has prepared for his people.
8.theology:
The chapter shows how the Chronicler works. He writes Eshbaal and Merib-baal where the books of Samuel write Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, most likely because his sources have them that way. A historian who leaves the name Baal in a king’s family is copying his documents faithfully, not tidying them.

And the theological weight is in the arrangement: Saul's genealogy closes the nine chapters, kept in the archive of the dynasty that replaced him. Rejection from an office is not erasure from the record.
8.examples:
Whole households here are remembered for nothing but an address: they lived in Jerusalem while it mattered. That is closer to most Christian lives than anything heroic.

And the last family in the genealogies is the one that failed publicly, written down carefully with its children and its skill with a bow. God keeps a family in his record even when its story is one of failure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin’s families are recorded honestly, exiles, a broken marriage and victories alike. Benjamin’s five sons head the list, with the sons of Bela and the houses of Ehud at Geba, who were carried into exile to Manahath (vv. 1–7). Shaharaim fathers families in Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara (vv. 8–11). Elpaal’s sons build Ono and Lod, and the heads of houses at Aijalon put the people of Gath to flight (vv. 12–14). Nothing is polished away: the tribe’s record keeps its losses and its failures beside its achievements.
verseByVerse.theology: Benjamin produced the first king and stayed with Judah when the ten northern tribes broke away, so the returned community was essentially Judah, Benjamin and Levi.
verseByVerse.examples: A deportation, a man divorcing two wives and starting again in Moab: the register carries small domestic catastrophes without a syllable of judgment, and carries their children into the tribe of the first king.

verseByVerse.quote: Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third, Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth. And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram. These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath): Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin receives a full chapter because his families were among those reading it, and already in its first verses there is an exile.

A chapter for Benjamin. Only Judah and Levi also receive a chapter to themselves. These are not antiquarian notes about a vanished world; they are the family papers of the men reading the book.

They were carried into exile to Manahath. Already in verse 6 there is an exile, at a time and for reasons nobody records. Deportation did not come from nowhere in 586 BC, when Jerusalem fell; it had been happening in smaller ways for a long time.

Uncertain wording. Verses 6–7 are obscure. “The sons of Ehud” appear without any link to the names before them; this may be the left-handed judge Ehud, a Benjaminite and “the son of Gera” (Judges 3:15), since a Gera is named here, but that is not certain. “Gera, that is, Heglam” may give Gera a second name, or the Hebrew word may mean “he carried them into exile”, so that Gera was the one who led them away.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives. He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses. He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who sent away his wives and started again in Moab is recorded, and his children counted, without the record approving what he did.

After he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives. One verse here has a marriage in it, and the marriage has ended. A man divorced two women, left the country and started a family somewhere else, and his children are in the official genealogy of the tribe of Israel’s first king. The register records that these people exist and how they came to.

Recording is not approving. Scripture’s teaching on marriage stands elsewhere (Malachi 2:16; Matthew 19:3–9). The point here is that the children of a broken home are counted.

Why he is not left out. A writer anxious for appearances would have left him out. Scripture does not guard its reputation that way. The genealogy of Judah, the Messiah’s tribe, already has a Canaanite wife, a deceived father-in-law and an Egyptian slave in it (chapter 2); Benjamin’s line has a divorce. The Saviour came from families like these, and for them.

Uncertain wording. Shaharaim appears with no link to the names before him, and the Hebrew of verse 8 is awkward. “Sent away” is the usual word for divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1), and most read it that way.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns, and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee); and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin’s record notes builders whose towns outlived them and fighters who drove back Gath, and keeps both in the same archive.

Who built Ono and Lod. Shemed built Ono and Lod, and both towns long outlived him. Ono is where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah down from the wall, and Nehemiah replied that he was doing a great work and could not come down (Nehemiah 6:2–3). Lod is Lydda, where Peter told a man bedridden eight years that Jesus Christ healed him (Acts 9:32–35). Both were lived in again after the exile: the men of Lod, Hadid and Ono were among the first to come home (Ezra 2:33), and Benjaminites settled in Lod and Ono once more (Nehemiah 11:35), so the first readers could see Shemed’s towns inhabited by his own tribe.

Who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee. In the previous chapter the men of Gath killed two of Ephraim’s sons (7:21). The text draws no moral, but the city that took two sons from one tribe was put to flight by another, and both facts are kept in the same archive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — The Heads of Houses Who Lived in Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin had families living in Jerusalem, and the record of them mattered to a city that needed people. Five houses of chiefs are listed, the sons of Beriah, Elpaal, Shimei, Shashak and Jeroham, without a word about any of them (vv. 15–27). Then comes the clause the section exists for: “These lived in Jerusalem” (v. 28). For returned exiles trying to fill a half-empty city, those words were a family’s written claim to a place in it.
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem sat on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and Benjaminites lived in it from the beginning. The record of who lived there mattered enormously to a generation trying to repopulate it.
verseByVerse.examples: A half-empty city needed ordinary families willing to move in (Nehemiah 11:1–2). Being where God's people need you can be a real service, even if it is all anyone remembers.

verseByVerse.quote: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder, Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah. Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal. Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three houses and not a word about any of them: a family’s claim to belong, preserved for those who would need it.

The barest of lists. Three houses in seven verses: the genealogies at their barest. Every name is somebody’s grandfather, and somebody after the return from exile needed it written down.

verseByVerse.quote: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak. Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham. These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These Benjaminite families lived in Jerusalem, a written precedent that mattered to returned exiles trying to fill a half-empty city.

These lived in Jerusalem. Benjaminites had houses in the city from the start, and that mattered to the people holding this book, because Jerusalem after the return was half empty. The people cast lots to bring one family in ten into the city, and blessed those who volunteered (Nehemiah 11:1–2).

A record to point to. These verses are the precedent: a written record that Benjamin had always lived there. Somebody arguing about a ruined street after the return could put his finger on verse 28 and say his family had held it before Babylon burned the city.

A city prepared. Christians belong to a city that no one can burn. God is not ashamed to be called the God of his people, “for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16), and their names are recorded there by Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The genealogies end with the house of Saul, the king God rejected, kept in the record and told truthfully. The family of Gibeon, Jeiel and his wife Maacah, leads to Ner, Kish and Saul, whose sons were Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal (vv. 29–33). Jonathan’s son Merib-baal carries the line on (v. 34), and it runs for a dozen generations more to the sons of Ulam, mighty archers with a hundred and fifty sons and grandsons (vv. 35–40). When the list appears again (9:35–44), it leads straight to Saul’s death.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogies close on the family that failed, and the narrative's first report is Saul's death on Gilboa. Nine chapters are arranged so the story opens at a funeral.
verseByVerse.examples: Even the last names (v. 40) are remembered for a skill. A family's record includes its gifts as well as its failures.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah. His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal; and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s line arrives through a family of Gibeon, and its names still carry the story of Jonathan’s lame son, whom David honoured.

Jeiel the father of Gibeon. The line the book has been walking towards arrives quietly, through a man in Gibeon and his wife Maacah. The father of Gibeon probably means the founder or chief of the town, as the father of Bethlehem does in 2:51.

Ner was the father of Kish. Ner and Kish were both sons of Abiel (1 Samuel 9:1; 14:51); here Ner is named as the father of a Kish, most likely a second Kish in the family, or the list names a grandfather as father.

Eshbaal … Merib-baal. Eshbaal is 2 Samuel’s Ish-bosheth, and Merib-baal is Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son. Most scholars think the names were altered in Samuel: baal, which meant lord or master and was once used innocently, was replaced with bosheth, shame. In Saul’s generation a man could name his son Eshbaal and mean nothing by it. By the time Samuel was copied, Baal meant the false god Elijah opposed on Mount Carmel, and the scribes probably would not write it in a man’s name. The Chronicler keeps what are probably the original forms, as his older documents had them.

The son of Jonathan was Merib-baal. He is the lame son of Jonathan whom David sought out for Jonathan’s sake and seated at the king’s table for life (2 Samuel 9). Many Christians have seen there a picture of the gospel: the heir of a fallen house, unable to walk, brought to eat with the king for the sake of another. The greater Son of David does that for sinners.

Textual note. The Hebrew of verse 29 lacks the name Jeiel, which the ESV supplies from the parallel list in 9:35. That list also includes Ner among Jeiel’s sons (9:36), where verse 30 here does not.
verseByVerse.note: Esh-baal and Merib-baal are probably the original names of Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel. The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third. The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s family goes on for generations, ending in archers, and the genealogies close on the house God rejected, kept in the record and not erased.

Mighty warriors, bowmen. Saul’s family goes on generation after generation, ending with Ulam’s sons, mighty warriors, bowmen. The archers of Gilboa wounded Saul (10:3), and his descendants are remembered for the bow. Nothing is made of it.

All these were Benjaminites. Here the list ends, though chapter 9 will repeat Saul’s line. From Adam to a hundred and fifty Benjaminite archers, and the last family named is the house God rejected.

A merciful arrangement. That arrangement is deliberate and merciful. A chronicler serving the house of David wrote Saul’s line into the record of the kingdom that replaced it. God did not erase the family that failed; he kept their names in the book, and then told the truth about what happened.

Another Saul of Benjamin. Centuries later another Benjaminite who bore the king’s name persecuted the Son of David until he met him. Then he could write, “I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin” (Romans 11:1), as living proof that God had not rejected his people.

keyVerse.quote: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal
keyVerse.note: The genealogies of the tribes close on this line, and the story of the kingdom will open with Saul’s fall (chapter 10). The verse shows the Chronicler keeping the house that failed in the record, truthfully and without spite, while the kingdom passes to David and finally to the Son of David.

8.reflection:
This chapter records an exile, a man who sent away his wives, and builders and fighters side by side (vv. 6–13). Why do you think Scripture keeps the failures in Benjamin’s family on record? How might that help someone ashamed of their own family history?

“These lived in Jerusalem” (v. 28) gave returning families a claim to a place in the city. What gives a Christian a secure place in God’s people and God’s city (Hebrews 11:16)?

Merib-baal, Jonathan’s lame son, was brought to eat at David’s table for Jonathan’s sake (v. 34; 2 Samuel 9). In what ways is that a picture of what Christ does for us?

The genealogies end with the house of Saul, the king God rejected, kept in the record rather than erased. What does this show about how God deals honestly and mercifully with failure, and how should it shape the way we speak of those who have failed?

9.title: The Returned Remnant and the Gatekeepers of the Holy
9.text: <sup>1</sup>So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith.<sup>2</sup>Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.<sup>3</sup>And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:<sup>4</sup>Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah.<sup>5</sup>And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690.<sup>7</sup>Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah,<sup>8</sup>Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah;<sup>9</sup>and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.<sup>10</sup>Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin,<sup>11</sup>and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God;<sup>12</sup>and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer;<sup>13</sup>besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God.<sup>14</sup>Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;<sup>15</sup>and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph;<sup>16</sup>and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.<sup>17</sup>The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief);<sup>18</sup>until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites.<sup>19</sup>Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance.<sup>20</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him.<sup>21</sup>Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>22</sup>All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust.<sup>23</sup>So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards.<sup>24</sup>The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south.<sup>25</sup>And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these,<sup>26</sup>for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God.<sup>27</sup>And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.<sup>28</sup>Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out.<sup>29</sup>Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices.<sup>30</sup>Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices,<sup>31</sup>and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes.<sup>32</sup>Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath.<sup>33</sup>Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night.<sup>34</sup>These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>35</sup>In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah,<sup>36</sup>and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab,<sup>37</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth;<sup>38</sup>and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>39</sup>Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.<sup>40</sup>And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah.<sup>41</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz.<sup>42</sup>And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>43</sup>Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>44</sup>Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 closes the nine chapters of genealogies that open the book. Having traced every tribe from Adam onwards, the Chronicler names the reason for the exile and then the people who came back from it, before the story proper begins with Saul’s death in chapter 10.

The message. God’s people lost everything through unfaithfulness, and God brought them back in faithfulness. The restored community is not described by its king or its army, for it had neither, but by the house of God and the men who kept its doors, baked its bread and sang its praise. Its life rested on God’s presence, and that presence was served by ordinary people in faithful, daily work.

Why it was said. The first readers were these people or their grandchildren: a few thousand back in a small, half-ruined Judah, wondering whether they still counted (see the introduction). The chapter tells them that the exile had a reason, that the return was God’s gift, and that their names, their families and their humble duties at the temple mattered to him.

How the chapter makes its case. One verse gives the cause of the exile, “their breach of faith”, and the next begins the return (vv. 1–2). The settlers in Jerusalem are counted, Judah and Benjamin first (vv. 3–9), then the priests and Levites (vv. 10–16). The gatekeepers take most of the chapter: their descent from Korah, their charter from David and Samuel, their “office of trust” and their daily round (vv. 17–27). Others look after the utensils, spices and bread, and the singers serve day and night (vv. 28–34). Saul’s family tree is repeated (vv. 35–44) to lead straight into his death.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. Israel’s history ended in a breach of faith that no list of names could repair; it needed someone who would keep faith where they had not, and bear the judgment of the faithless. That is Christ, who is “faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:6). The gatekeepers who opened God’s house every morning point to the one who said, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

For us. Unfaithfulness to God is serious: it cost Israel the land and the temple. But God is faithful to the unfaithful who return to him, and he keeps the register. No service in his house is too ordinary for him to notice: whoever unlocks the building, counts the offering or bakes for the church is named before him.
9.theology:
Verse 1 gives the reason for the exile, and the reason concerns God, not politics. The Chronicler knew how strong the empires were; he refuses to let them be the explanation.

Against the breach of faith stands the doorkeeping. The chapter’s answer to Israel’s unfaithfulness is not a reform programme but a rota: men enrolled by name, opening a building every morning, counting the vessels, baking the bread every Sabbath. And the rota exists only because God brought them back. Faithfulness in Scripture is far more often a duty performed at dawn, by people God has already taken back, than a decision made at a crisis.
9.examples:
The men in this chapter are remembered for opening a door, counting spoons, mixing spices and making flat cakes. It is the closest the Bible comes to describing a normal working life among the people of God, written with the same care as the covenant with David.

And the family at the centre is Korah's (v. 19). God’s mercy to a disgraced family was not to give it the priesthood Korah had grasped at but to give it something better to want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Exile, and the First to Come Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exile was God’s judgment on unfaithfulness, and the return was his mercy to a people who had not earned it. One verse closes the genealogies and gives the reason for everything before it: “Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith” (v. 1). Then the page turns. The first to settle again in their towns are Israel, the priests, the Levites and the temple servants (v. 2), and men of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh live in Jerusalem (v. 3). The households of Judah’s three clans and of Benjamin are named and counted to the man (vv. 4–9), so that a returning family could find itself in the record and know that it belonged.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler’s word for breaking faith is now used of a whole nation, which loses the city and the temple. The exile is explained by unfaithfulness to God’s covenant, not by Babylon’s power.
verseByVerse.examples: The returned are counted by household, as a community small enough to count is. A returning family could find itself in verse 8 and know it had a place.

verseByVerse.quote: So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith. Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants. And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogies end by naming the reason for the exile, unfaithfulness to God, and turn at once to the return: God brought his people home to their towns.

Because of their breach of faith. The verb has run through the book. Achan “broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing” (2:7) and Israel lost a battle; the eastern tribes broke faith and lost their land (5:25). Now the whole nation breaks faith and loses the city and the house of God.

What is not the reason. Not Babylon’s siege engines, not Nebuchadnezzar’s army, not a failed alliance with Egypt: all true, none mentioned. The catastrophe is explained by unfaithfulness to God.

The first to dwell again in their possessions. Verse 2 turns the page: the people are back in their towns. The temple servants were probably descended from foreigners given to the sanctuary for its heavy work, as the Gibeonites were made woodcutters and water carriers for the altar (Joshua 9:27). The list closely parallels Nehemiah 11, probably drawn from the same records. And verse 3 names Ephraim and Manasseh among those in Jerusalem: men of the northern tribes had come home too, so the small community around the temple could still call itself all Israel (v. 1).

Home because God kept faith. They came back not because they had kept faith but because God kept his. God’s faithfulness to the faithless took flesh in the one Israelite who never broke faith and who bore their judgment on the cross. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah. And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690. Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah, Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah; and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The households of Judah and Benjamin who resettled Jerusalem are named and counted to the man, because every returning family mattered to God.

From the sons of Perez the son of Judah. Judah’s three clans are all here: Perez (v. 4), the Shilonites, probably the clan of Judah’s son Shelah (v. 5), and Zerah (v. 6). Then the Benjaminites, named to the grandfather and beyond (vv. 7–9).

Counted with care. A few thousand people in a half-ruined city are counted as carefully as the great armies of earlier chapters, because the counting was never a measure of strength. A man reading verse 8 could find his own family in it. That is why the number is written down: God knows his people by name (John 10:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–34 — The Men Who Kept the Doors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The restored community is described by the people who kept God’s house, because his presence was the one thing it could not do without. The priests, 1,760 of them, are called “mighty men for the work of the service” (vv. 10–13), and the Levites include the families of the singers (vv. 14–16). Most space goes to the gatekeepers: descendants of Korah, 212 in all, set in their “office of trust” by David and Samuel (vv. 17–22), guarding four sides, serving a week at a time and opening the house every morning (vv. 23–27). Others counted the utensils, mixed the spices and baked the bread (vv. 28–32), and the singers were on duty day and night (vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology: A community with no king and no army is described by its priests, Levites, gatekeepers and singers: a God to worship, and men set apart to keep that worship going. The house came first because God's presence was the one thing they could not do without.
verseByVerse.examples: Mattithiah is named for making the flat cakes (v. 31). Whatever unseen work someone does for God's people, baking, counting or locking up, God does not overlook it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer; besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God. Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph; and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests and Levites came home too, traced to their fathers, so that the worship of God could begin again in its proper order.

Of the priests. The priests’ descent runs through Zadok and Ahitub (v. 11), the high-priestly line of chapter 6, and Azariah is “the chief officer of the house of God”.

Mighty men for the work of the service. That is a soldier’s phrase, used of men whose work was sacrifice and instruction.

In the villages of the Netophathites. One Levite lived in the villages around Netophah, near Bethlehem. The temple staff came in from the villages for their turn of duty, as they always had (v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief); until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites. Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance. And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him. Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief gatekeepers descend from Korah, the rebel against Moses: God gave the rebel’s family the honour of keeping the doors of his house.

Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah. Korah stood up against Moses and Aaron with two hundred and fifty leaders of the congregation, accused them of setting themselves above the LORD’s people, and went down alive into the earth (Numbers 16). Numbers adds, almost in passing, “But the sons of Korah did not die” (Numbers 26:11).

Keepers of the thresholds of the tent. Centuries later the house their ancestor tried to storm, his descendants open in the morning and shut at night, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD (v. 19).

Phinehas the son of Eleazar. Their overseer in the wilderness was Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson (Numbers 25:10–13). The LORD was with him: the guards of the holy place needed God’s presence first.

The psalms of the sons of Korah. Eleven psalms carry their name. One of them says, “I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psalm 84:10). For them it was a job description.

Given the doorway. God did not give Korah’s family the priesthood their father had grasped at. He gave them the doorway, and they made a song of it that Israel sang for a thousand years. That is grace: a rebel’s children set to keep the house of God. In Christ, former enemies become “members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

Uncertain wording. “Until then” (v. 18) may mean “up to now”, that is, in the Chronicler’s own day this family still kept the king’s gate on the east side. The king’s gate is not described elsewhere; it was probably an east entrance kept for the king.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust. So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards. The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south. And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these, for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God. And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gatekeepers held an office of trust, set up by David and Samuel, and their faithfulness in ordinary duties answered the nation’s breach of faith.

David and Samuel the seer established them. A king and a prophet, jointly over a rota of doormen: the office is neither improvised nor menial. Samuel died before David became king, so the phrase probably means that Samuel began organising the gatekeepers while David was young, and David completed it.

In their office of trust. The Hebrew word behind “trust” means faithfulness, and it comes again in verses 26 and 31 (“entrusted”). The chapter that began with Judah’s “breach of faith” (v. 1) describes the restored community by men who were faithful in small things.

They had charge of opening it every morning. Four sides, a week on and then home (v. 25), the treasures, the night watch. Somebody had to get up early and unlock the house of God. Every morning for centuries, in the rain and the cold and on the mornings when he did not feel like it, a man walked to a door and opened it so that Israel could come in and meet God.

Faithful in a very little. Jesus said, “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10), and he is himself the perfectly faithful one: “Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out. Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices. Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices, and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes. Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath. Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night. These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Counting the utensils, mixing the spices and baking the bread were holy work, and the singers kept God’s praise going day and night.

Required to count them when they were brought in and taken out. In the house of God there was no line between sacred and domestic work. Only priests mixed the holy spices (v. 30; Exodus 30:34–38); a Levite, Mattithiah, “was entrusted with making the flat cakes” (v. 31); and Kohathites prepared the showbread for every Sabbath (v. 32; Leviticus 24:5–8).

Free from other service, for they were on duty day and night. The singers were excused from carrying and counting because they were needed around the clock (v. 33). In the temple’s ordered life the praise did not stop, and somebody had to staff the night.

Unseen work. Whoever bakes, counts, locks up or sings for God’s people today does work God notices.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by repeating Saul’s family tree from chapter 8, and the repetition is a hinge. The lists close on the household of the king who lost the kingdom (vv. 35–44), and the next verse is the battle in which he dies (10:1). Before the reader meets David, he must see where a king who did not seek the LORD ended; so must the returned exiles, who had to learn from their history before they could hope in it. Yet through Jonathan’s son Merib-baal the line runs on for many generations (vv. 40–44): God’s judgment on Saul did not blot out his descendants.
verseByVerse.theology: The repetition has a purpose: it hands the reader straight from the lists to the battle on Mount Gilboa.
verseByVerse.examples: The restored community, having just read of the return, is handed Saul's family again and then a funeral. It may not read its own history without first reading how a king was lost.

verseByVerse.quote: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah, and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth; and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah. The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s family is listed again to lead straight into his death: the genealogies hand the reader from the lists to the story, and to the king who did not seek the LORD.

Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul. The list repeats, almost word for word, 8:29–38. This is no accident of copying but a doorway: the moment the list ends, Israel falls on Mount Gilboa, and before the reader is told anything about David he is shown what happens to a king who does not seek the LORD (10:13–14).

Where the genealogies end. The genealogies end as they began, with a register and a God who keeps it: from Adam, through a Canaanite wife, an Egyptian slave, a thief and a rebel’s children, down to a man unlocking a door at dawn. Not one name was lost. And at the end of the line came the Son of David who said, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

keyVerse.quote: So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith.
keyVerse.note: The verse says in one clause what the nine chapters of genealogies were leading to: the exile came because of unfaithfulness to God, not because Babylon was strong. It explains the past to the returned exiles, and the rest of the chapter, with the people home and the doors of God’s house opened by faithful men, shows God’s answer to it.

9.reflection:
Verse 1 explains the exile by one thing, a “breach of faith”, though many political causes were also true. How does seeing God’s hand behind events change the way we read our own history, or our nation’s?

The descendants of Korah, the rebel, became keepers of God’s doors and singers of his praise (v. 19; Psalm 84:10). What does that teach about God’s grace to the families of people who sinned grievously, and to us?

The gatekeepers held an “office of trust” and opened the house every morning (vv. 22, 27). What ordinary, unseen tasks in our church are like this, and how can we honour those who do them?

Jesus is the door (John 10:9) and the Son who is faithful over God’s house (Hebrews 3:6). How does his faithfulness give hope to people whose own record is one of broken faith?

10.title: The Death of Saul: Unfaithfulness and Its Wages
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.<sup>3</sup>The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.<sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.<sup>5</sup>And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.<sup>6</sup>Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together.<sup>7</sup>And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.<sup>8</sup>The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.<sup>9</sup>And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people.<sup>10</sup>And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.<sup>11</sup>But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul,<sup>12</sup>all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.<sup>13</sup>So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance.<sup>14</sup>He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
10.overview:
Where we are. After nine chapters of genealogies the story begins, and it begins with a funeral. Chapter 9 ended by repeating Saul’s family; now Saul dies with his sons on Mount Gilboa. It is the only part of his reign the Chronicler tells.

The message. A king who does not seek the LORD cannot keep the kingdom, however gifted he is, and it is the LORD, not the Philistines, who decides who rules his people. Saul’s death was a battle lost and a verdict given: “He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David” (v. 14). Even in judgment God was carrying forward his purpose for his people.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had lost king, land and temple through the same unfaithfulness (9:1; see the introduction). Saul is their history in one man: he broke faith and lost everything. The chapter warns them, and points them to the way of life the rest of the book commends: to seek the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. Israel is routed and Saul’s sons are killed (vv. 1–3). Wounded, Saul asks to be killed and then falls on his own sword; his dynasty ends, and Israel loses its towns in the valley (vv. 4–7). The Philistines carry his head and armour into their temples as a triumph for their gods (vv. 8–10), and the men of Jabesh-gilead rescue the bodies (vv. 11–12). Then the verdict, the reason the chapter exists (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by promise. Saul shows what Israel’s kings could not be on their own: a king who seeks God in everything. The kingdom turned over to David is the kingdom that arrives at Christ, as Paul preached (Acts 13:22–23). Surrounded by enemies who would shame him, Saul took his life into his own hands; Jesus “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Saul died for his own breach of faith; Jesus died for the breach of faith of others.

For us. Gifts, height and courage do not make a life right with God; seeking him does. When God was silent Saul went everywhere but to him; we are to wait on him in his word and in prayer. And if we have looked everywhere but to God, the way back is still open: “Seek the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The story begins with defeat, because the Chronicler wants his readers to see first where a king who does not seek God ends. Israel flees before the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, and Saul’s sons, Jonathan among them, are struck down (vv. 1–2). Wounded by archers, Saul begs his armour-bearer to kill him before the “uncircumcised” can mistreat him; refused, he falls on his own sword, and the armour-bearer follows him (vv. 3–5). “All his house died together” (v. 6): the dynasty ends in a day. The men of the valley abandon their towns and the Philistines move in (v. 7). Readers who knew the full story from 1 Samuel 31 are told only how the reign ended.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler assumes his reader knows the reign and tells only how it ended. A king introduced by his death is introduced as a warning.
verseByVerse.examples: The battle takes a few verses because the first readers knew it from 1 Samuel 31. What they are to take away is the reason, held back to the last two verses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story opens on a battle already lost: Israel flees, Saul’s sons fall, and the king is left wounded and alone on the hill his army has abandoned.

The Philistines fought against Israel. Saul is not introduced; the reader is put on a hillside in a rout. The order matters: Israel flees, Saul is overtaken, the sons die, then the archers find him. The people had asked for a king to “go out before us and fight our battles” (1 Samuel 8:20); he is the last man on a hill his army has left, and the arrows arrive while he is alone.

The Philistines struck down Jonathan. Jonathan had long known the throne was not coming to him, and said so to David in a wood at Horesh while Saul was hunting David: “You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you” (1 Samuel 23:17). It never happened. He died on the hill his father had lost, and this is his only mention in the book outside the genealogies. A man can love the right person and tell the truth about God’s choice against his own interest, and still go down with the house he was born into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wounded and afraid of being taken alive, Saul asks his armour-bearer to kill him, and when he will not, takes his own life: the last decision of a king who did not seek God.

Lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me. The chapter’s one conversation is a request to be killed. Saul is not asking to escape death but to control it. What he cannot bear is the shame of what the Philistines will do to a captured king.

But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Then Saul falls on his own sword, and the armour-bearer, having refused to kill the king, kills himself. Being afraid to do a wrong thing is not the same as trusting God, and on Gilboa it saved nobody. Saul’s last decision as king is made without reference to God, which is exactly what verse 14 says of his life.

Another anointed King. Centuries later the Son of David was surrounded by uncircumcised soldiers who did mistreat him, stripping and mocking him. He did not take his life into his own hands to escape the shame. He “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), and laid down his life for others when he could have saved his own.

Is suicide a sin, and is it unforgivable? Taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment, a grave sin against the God who gives life (Exodus 20:13). But it is not the unforgivable sin, which is the settled rejection of Christ (Mark 3:28–29). A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Romans 8:38–39). If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today: a pastor or biblical counsellor, a trusted friend, a doctor; treatment for depression is no failure of faith. If you are in danger now, call the emergency services at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together. And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s dynasty ended on Gilboa, and Israel lost the heart of its land in a day.

All his house died together. A reader who knows Samuel will stop here, because not all Saul’s family died that day: Ish-bosheth reigned two years afterwards, Mephibosheth lived at David’s table for decades, and this book has just traced Saul’s descendants for generations (9:39–44). The Chronicler is not contradicting any of that. He means that the dynasty died on Gilboa: Saul’s house never ruled all Israel again.

They abandoned their cities and fled. Verse 7 measures the defeat in geography: the men of the valley walked out of their towns and the Philistines moved in. For readers who had lost far more than a valley, the history begins by showing the loss of land following a king who would not seek God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — The Head in the Temple of Dagon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines treat Saul’s death as a victory for their gods, but the reader knows better. They strip the body, send the “good news” around their land, and fasten Saul’s head in the temple of Dagon (vv. 8–10), the god who once lay broken and headless before the ark of the LORD (1 Samuel 5:1–5). Then comes the chapter’s one act of loyalty. The valiant men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had rescued at the start of his reign, carry the bodies home, bury them under the oak and fast seven days (vv. 11–12). Idolatry and gratitude, shame and honour, stand side by side.
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's head is nailed up in the house of the god who fell, headless, before the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–5). The Chronicler sets the two stories side by side without comment.
verseByVerse.examples: Kindness done long ago is not wasted: the town Saul once rescued was the only one in Israel to come for his body.
