verseByVerse.quote: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people. And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines parade Saul’s head and armour in their temples as a victory of their gods; the Chronicler shows that it was really the LORD’s verdict on Saul.

To carry the good news to their idols. What the Philistines do with the body is a religious act. They send messengers to announce it to their gods as good news, and the Greek translators used the word that becomes the New Testament’s word for preaching the gospel. They believe their gods have beaten Israel’s God.

Fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. Samuel adds that the body was fastened to the wall of Beth-shan and the armour put in the temple of the Ashtaroth (1 Samuel 31:9–10); each account records a different part of what was done. The reader is meant to notice the name Dagon. When the captured ark stood in Dagon’s house at Ashdod, the god was found face down before it, his head and hands broken off on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:1–5). Now the head of Israel’s king hangs in the same god’s temple. A god who could not stand before the ark is given the head of a king who did not seek God at the ark (13:3). The trophy is a verdict on the man, not a victory over his God.

Good news of another King’s death. The apostles’ gospel was also news of a king’s death, but of a King who died for his people, rose again, and by his cross disarmed the powers that thought they had won (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of Jabesh-gilead risk their lives to give Saul an honourable burial, repaying the rescue he gave them at the start of his reign.

All the valiant men arose. One act of decency in fourteen verses, from a town nobody expects. The men of Jabesh-gilead crossed the Jordan to a Philistine-held hill, carried the bodies home, buried the bones under an oak and fasted seven days. Samuel adds that they burned the bodies first and calls the tree a tamarisk (1 Samuel 31:12–13); both words describe a great tree that marked the grave.

Why Jabesh came. Their reason was decades old (Acts 13:21 gives Saul’s reign as forty years; the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 is damaged and gives no reliable figure). Nahash the Ammonite had besieged Jabesh and offered to spare it for the right eye of every man. Saul raised the country, marched through the night and broke the siege at dawn (1 Samuel 11). It was the best day of his life. When everything else about the man had gone wrong, one town remembered the morning he came, and David blessed them for it (2 Samuel 2:5). Kindness done long ago is not wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: These two verses are why the chapter exists: they give the LORD’s verdict on Saul. He “died for his breach of faith”: he did not keep the LORD’s command, and he consulted a medium instead of the LORD (v. 13). So the LORD himself put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David (v. 14). The two key words of the whole book stand here together. Breaking faith is what sent Judah into exile (9:1); seeking the LORD is the measure every king after Saul will be judged by, and the charge David will give his son (28:9).
verseByVerse.theology: Both the book's key verbs are here: he broke faith, and he did not seek the LORD, which will become the measure of every king after him.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's failure was not a lack of gifts: he was tall, brave and anointed. What a church should look for in its leaders, and in itself, is whether they seek the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul died because he broke faith with the LORD and sought a medium instead of God; so the LORD himself ended his reign and gave the kingdom to David. These two verses are the reason the chapter is in the book.

He broke faith with the LORD. Broke faith has run through the genealogies, from Achan at Jericho (2:7), through the eastern tribes (5:25), to Judah carried to Babylon (9:1). Here it is used of its smallest subject, one man. The command he did not keep is not named, but a reader of Samuel would think of Gilgal, where Saul offered the sacrifice rather than wait for Samuel (1 Samuel 13:8–14), and of Amalek, where he spared what God had devoted to destruction (1 Samuel 15:22–23): Achan’s sin again, in a king.

He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Seek is the word the rest of the book is built on. Saul was seeking urgently at the end, at Endor, in the one place forbidden to him (1 Samuel 28:7). The charge is not that he never asked but that he asked everyone except God.

Seeking in the chapters ahead. Watch what the word does from here. David will say the ark must come back, “for we did not seek it in the days of Saul” (13:3). He will inquire of God twice before battle and win twice (14:10, 14). When the ark goes wrong he will admit, “we did not seek him according to the rule” (15:13). He will write into a psalm, “let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice!” (16:10). And at the end of his life he will hand his son the kingdom with one sentence attached: “If you seek him, he will be found by you” (28:9).

Therefore the LORD put him to death. Saul died of an arrow and a sword in a battle the Philistines won, and the Chronicler says the LORD put him to death. Both are true, the second is the reason for the first, and this book never sets the two against each other.

Turned the kingdom over to David. Paul preached this transition at Pisidian Antioch: God removed Saul, raised up David, and “of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised” (Acts 13:23). The kingdom turned over to David is the kingdom that arrives at Christ, the King who never once failed to seek his Father, and whose faithfulness covers those who, like Saul, have looked everywhere but to God. The way back is still open: “Seek the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6).

Asking is not seeking. Saul “did not seek guidance from the LORD”, though 1 Samuel 28:6 says he inquired and got no answer. His asking was not true seeking: when God was silent he went to a medium. Is it wrong today to use psychics, horoscopes or tarot? Yes: God forbids it (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). To seek the LORD is to come to him in his word and in prayer, waiting on him, helped by the Spirit he gives to those who ask (Luke 11:13).

10.theology:
The chapter states the doctrine of providence the book assumes (v. 14). The arrows and the sword were real causes, and God worked through them; he was not one more cause beside them. The same logic explained the exile (ch. 9) and Assyria (ch. 5).

The two governing verbs are set as opposites. To break faith is to treat what belongs to God as ours to take; to seek is to go to God for what only he can give. Saul was desperate enough at the end to visit a medium in the dark. Desperation is not seeking God. What matters is not how urgently a man asks but whom he asks.
10.examples:
Saul's last decision is about how his body will look to his enemies, the instinct of a man who spent a career managing appearances and once begged Samuel to honour him before the elders after he had been rejected. A life organised around not being humiliated ends on a hill with nobody left to see.

Against that stands Jabesh-gilead. They could not fix the reign or win the battle, but they could walk a long way, bury a man properly and go hungry for a week. Where nothing can be mended, that is often the whole of what love can do, and Scripture records it beside the verdict of God.

keyVerse.quote: He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
keyVerse.note: This is the verdict the whole chapter was written to deliver, and it introduces the book’s great theme: seeking the LORD. Saul died in battle, yet the Chronicler says the LORD put him to death, and in the same breath the LORD hands the kingdom to David, so that judgment on one king becomes the opening of the line that leads to Christ.

10.reflection:
Saul was tall, brave and anointed, yet he “did not seek guidance from the LORD” (v. 14). What does it look like for a gifted person, or a gifted church, to rely on gifts rather than seek God?

Saul died by an arrow and his own sword, yet verse 14 says the LORD put him to death. How does the Bible hold together human actions and God’s rule over them, and how does that help us in our own hardships?

When God was silent, Saul went to a medium (v. 13; 1 Samuel 28:6–7). Where are we tempted to turn when God seems silent, and what does it mean to wait on him?

The men of Jabesh-gilead remembered a kindness done decades before (vv. 11–12). How does Christ, who died for people who were his enemies, shape the gratitude and loyalty we show?

11.title: David Crowned and His Mighty Men: The King Who Draws Loyal Hearts

And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And David set him over his bodyguard.<sup>26</sup>The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,<sup>27</sup>Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite,<sup>28</sup>Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth,<sup>29</sup>Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,<sup>30</sup>Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah,<sup>31</sup>Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon,<sup>32</sup>Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,<sup>33</sup>Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,<sup>34</sup>Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite,<sup>35</sup>Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,<sup>36</sup>Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,<sup>37</sup>Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai,<sup>38</sup>Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri,<sup>39</sup>Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,<sup>40</sup>Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,<sup>41</sup>Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai,<sup>42</sup>Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him,<sup>43</sup>Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite,<sup>44</sup>Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,<sup>45</sup>Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,<sup>46</sup>Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,<sup>47</sup>Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
11.overview:
Where we are. Saul is dead, and the LORD has turned the kingdom over to David (10:14). Passing over the years of civil war told in 2 Samuel 2–4, the Chronicler moves straight to the day all Israel made David king at Hebron, and then to the men who helped him.

The message. God keeps his word: the king he promised is crowned, the city he chose is taken, and the men he raised up stand round the throne. David’s rise is explained not by his gifts or his soldiers but by God: “David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him” (v. 9). Human courage is honoured, but the victories are the LORD’s (v. 14).

Why it was said. The returned exiles had no king and a small, battered Jerusalem (see the introduction). This chapter reminded them how the kingship and the city began: by God’s promise, through a covenant, with a people united round the man God chose. If God did that once, his promise to David’s house still stood.

How the chapter makes its case. All Israel comes to Hebron, a covenant is made, and David is anointed “according to the word of the LORD” (vv. 1–3). He takes Jebus, which becomes the city of David, and grows greater because the LORD is with him (vv. 4–9). Then the mighty men: the chiefs, Eleazar in the barley field, the three who brought water from Bethlehem, Abishai and Benaiah (vv. 10–25), and a long roll of names from every quarter, foreigners and Uriah the Hittite among them (vv. 26–47).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. David is made king as the shepherd of God’s people, and God later promised “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23), a promise kept in Jesus, the good shepherd who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). David poured out the water bought with his men’s lives; Jesus poured out his own blood and gives it to his people to drink. And the mixed roll of David’s men foreshadows the King who gathers his people from every nation.

For us. Our King has been crowned according to God’s word, and God is with him. Serve him gladly, in whatever rank you stand: no faithful service is forgotten. And receive what he bought with his blood, for unlike David’s water it was given to be taken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Covenant at Hebron, a Stronghold at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David becomes king of all Israel and takes the city that will bear his name, because God had promised it and was with him. All Israel comes to Hebron, claiming kinship, remembering that David led them even under Saul, and quoting the LORD’s word that he would shepherd them (vv. 1–2). He makes a covenant with them before the LORD and is anointed (v. 3). Then he takes the stronghold of Zion despite the Jebusites’ taunt, and Joab wins the command by striking first (vv. 4–6). David builds up the city (vv. 7–8), and the section ends on the sentence that explains the reign: “the LORD of hosts was with him” (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The kingship rests on three things: the people choose him, the LORD had already appointed him, and a covenant is made between king and nation before God. Israel’s monarchy never rested on conquest alone or on the people’s choice alone.
verseByVerse.examples: The elders could follow David because he had already served them. God's people still do well to look for leaders who have shepherded before they are given a title (1 Timothy 3:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel makes David king at Hebron, because he is their kinsman, because he has already led them, and above all because God has spoken; and he binds himself to them by a covenant before the LORD.

Then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron. Between chapters 10 and 11 lie seven and a half years the Chronicler does not mention: no civil war, no Ish-bosheth, no Abner (2 Samuel 2–4). Saul dies, and all Israel gathers to David.

We are your bone and flesh. They claim kinship and give two reasons: experience, for he had led them even under Saul, and the word of God. They wanted a competent soldier and they knew God had chosen him, and the text does not treat the second as spoiled by the first.

You shall be shepherd of my people Israel. The office God names first is not king but shepherd. It is what David was doing when Samuel sent for him, and the word God uses of himself when the kings have failed and he promises to search for his sheep himself (Ezekiel 34:11), setting over them “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23) long after David was dead. A king who is called a shepherd is bound to care for his people, and only one Son of David did so perfectly: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. The king binds himself, in God’s presence, to the people giving him the throne: obligation runs both ways, and the king stands under God (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). The anointing confirms the one at Bethlehem years before (1 Samuel 16:13); God’s word came first.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles passes over David’s seven years at Hebron and his sin with Bathsheba; it focuses on David as builder of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, "You will not come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. David said, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander." And Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief. And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David takes Jerusalem, a Canaanite fortress no Israelite had held, and it becomes the city of David, the city of God’s promises.

Jerusalem, that is, Jebus. Centuries after Joshua a Canaanite city still sat unconquered on the ridge between Judah and Benjamin (Judges 1:21), confident enough to shout down, “You will not come in here.” The spur has steep valleys on three sides, yet the assault takes a single sentence.

Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first. Joab already led David’s men at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:13); by one act of nerve he wins command of all Israel’s army. David spent his reign with a general he could neither control nor dismiss, who would murder Abner in a gateway, Amasa on a road, and Absalom in a tree against a direct order.

The account in Samuel. Samuel tells the capture differently, with the taunt about the blind and the lame and a water shaft (2 Samuel 5:6–8), and does not name Joab. The two accounts add to each other; they do not conflict.

Therefore it was called the city of David. A Canaanite fortress with no history in Israel becomes, in one sentence, the city of God’s covenant promises. Every prophecy about Zion for a thousand years is about this hill, and until this verse it belonged to somebody else, as every citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem once did (Hebrews 12:22).

verseByVerse.quote: And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David grew greater and greater, and the reason was not his skill but God’s presence: the LORD of hosts was with him.

He built the city all around from the Millo. David’s first act in the city is building. The Millo was probably a terrace or filled platform on the slope, the engineering that made a steep spur usable. The Chronicler, whose whole book is heading towards a building, notices.

For the LORD of hosts was with him. This is the sentence the reign hangs on. The reason given for the greatness is not the man: not his generalship, not the loyalty of the thirty, not the strength of the ridge. The LORD of hosts commands every army in heaven and earth; David’s own was never his real strength.

God with us. What was said of David became the name of his greater Son, Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who promised his people, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
verseByVerse.note: The Millo was probably a terraced structure supporting buildings on the hill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–25 — The Three, and the Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mighty men are honoured for their courage, but the victory and the kingdom belong to the LORD. The roll opens with the chiefs who made David king “according to the word of the LORD” (v. 10). Jashobeam kills three hundred at one time (v. 11), and Eleazar holds a barley field when the army runs, and “the LORD saved them” (vv. 12–14). Three men break through to the well at Bethlehem, and David pours the water out to the LORD rather than drink their lifeblood (vv. 15–19). Abishai and Benaiah win great names beside the three, though they never reach them (vv. 20–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Courage is real, but it is not what won the battle: Eleazar’s stand is honoured, and the victory is credited to the LORD (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: These men are loyal to David before he has given them anything, drawn by the king God had chosen and was with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the chiefs of David's mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. This is an account of David's mighty men: Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s mighty men are honoured because they helped make him king according to the word of the LORD: their courage served God’s purpose.

Who gave him strong support in his kingdom. The roll opens with what the mighty men were for. They made him king, a human act, deliberate and costly; all Israel did it with them; and it happened according to the word of the LORD. Human action and God’s word sit in a single verse, and it is never suggested that the more God did, the less they did.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Here Jashobeam kills 300 at one time; in 2 Samuel 23:8 it is eight hundred. Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error, and takes such differences as copying slips; none touches what the passage teaches.

verseByVerse.quote: And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite. He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines were gathered there for battle. There was a plot of ground full of barley, and the men fled from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and killed the Philistines. And the LORD saved them by a great victory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleazar held a barley field when Israel ran, and the LORD gave the victory: the courage was his, the salvation God’s.

He was with David at Pas-dammim. Probably the Ephes-dammim of 1 Samuel 17:1, where the Philistines camped when David fought Goliath: the same enemy on the same ground.

A plot of ground full of barley. Not a pass, not a citadel, not a bridge, but somebody’s crop. He stood in it because it was Israel’s, and stayed while everyone he knew ran away behind him.

The LORD saved them by a great victory. The clause keeps the chapter honest: not Eleazar saved them, but the LORD. A man had just done something extraordinary, and the credit is handed straight past him. God uses the courage of his servants, but the glory is his.

verseByVerse.quote: Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David at the cave of Adullam, when the army of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem. And David said longingly, "Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!" Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David. But David would not drink it. He poured it out to the LORD and said, "Far be it from me before my God that I should do this. Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? For at the risk of their lives they brought it." Therefore he would not drink it. These things did the three mighty men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men risk their lives to bring David water from Bethlehem, and he will not drink it: he pours it out to the LORD, because a gift bought with men’s lives belongs to God.

Three of the thirty chief men went down. The finest story in the chapter changes nothing in the war. David is in the stronghold; the Philistine garrison is in Bethlehem, sitting on the town he grew up in.

David said longingly. He is homesick, not giving an order: a man in a cave remembering the water of one particular well. Three men hear him, break through the Philistine camp, draw the water and bring it back.

Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? He calls the water their blood, because that is what it cost, and pours it out to the LORD. In Israel the blood, which carries the life, belonged to God alone (Leviticus 17:11), so he gives it to God. He wanted it and had every right to it, but would not enjoy a comfort bought with other men’s risk. Some gifts are too costly to be spent on ourselves, and the fit thing to do with them is to give them back to God.

Bought so that it could be drunk. Christians can hardly read this without thinking of another son of Bethlehem, who poured out his blood at a cost nobody could repay. That gift is not too costly to receive. It was bought precisely so that it could be drunk, and he puts the cup into his people’s hands: “Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:27–28).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against 300 men and killed them and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abishai, Joab’s brother, was the most renowned of the thirty but never reached the first rank, and the record says so plainly.

He did not attain to the three. The official chronicle records that one of Israel’s bravest men was not quite in the first rank, and nobody softens it.

Abishai, the brother of Joab. He spent his life a step behind: behind Joab, who held the command, and behind the three, whom he never joined. He was the man who offered to kill Saul in his sleep (1 Samuel 26:8) and twice to kill Shimei (2 Samuel 16:9; 19:21), and was refused every time. And he stayed. Faithfulness in the second rank is still faithfulness, and God records it.

Uncertain wording. In Hebrew the words for “three”, “thirty” and a kind of officer look much alike and were easily confused in copying. In verses 11, 20 and 21 the wording wavers between them, and the ESV follows what fits the context (its footnotes give the alternatives). Two groups seem to be in view: an inner three, the greatest, and a wider company called the thirty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two heroes of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. And he struck down an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits tall. The Egyptian had in his hand a spear like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and won a name beside the three mighty men. He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benaiah’s feats echo David’s victory over Goliath: the king’s man fights as his king fought.

A valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. Three feats: two of Moab’s heroes, a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and an Egyptian giant, written to recall an older story.

A spear like a weaver’s beam. A giant with a spear like a weaver’s beam sounds like Goliath: that is the phrase 1 Samuel uses of his spear (1 Samuel 17:7), and it will be used once more in this book, of Goliath’s brother (20:5). And a man who goes down to him with only a staff recalls David, who took his staff and five stones out of a brook.

Killed him with his own spear. Benaiah wrenched the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with it, as David killed Goliath with Goliath’s own sword (1 Samuel 17:51). The king’s man repeats the king’s victory in the king’s manner. That is what a good king does to the men around him: they start doing what he does. So it is with the greater King, whose people learn to walk “in the same way in which he walked” (1 John 2:6).

He did not attain to the three. And still he was not in the first rank. Benaiah went on to command David’s bodyguard and Solomon’s army (1 Kings 2:35), and never seems to have complained about his rank.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–47 — The Roll of the Mighty Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The honour roll shows a king surrounded by men from every part of Israel and beyond it. Asahel, long dead, heads the list, and the names come with their home towns, from Bethlehem and Anathoth to Tekoa and Netophah (vv. 26–38). Then come outsiders: Zelek the Ammonite (v. 39), Uriah the Hittite (v. 41), whose story the Chronicler never tells but whose name he keeps, and Ithmah the Moabite (v. 46). The last sixteen names appear only here, several from east of the Jordan (vv. 41–47). The roll remembers the dead, the ordinary and the foreigner alike.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler never tells the story of Bathsheba, yet writes Uriah into the roll of honour. A cover-up would have left the name out.
verseByVerse.examples: An Ammonite, a Moabite and a Hittite among David's men: the King of Israel was never meant to rule Israel alone, and his greater Son gathers his people from every nation (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon, Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll of the mighty men opens with Asahel, long dead, and goes on town by town: the honour roll remembers the fallen and the ordinary places they came from.

Asahel the brother of Joab. Asahel is first, though he had been dead for years, killed by Abner in the retreat from Gibeon after being warned twice to turn aside (2 Samuel 2:18–23). He is on the honour roll all the same, which is what an honour roll is for.

Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth. The roll is mostly geography. Anathoth, the priestly town of chapter 6, sends fighting men; Tekoa will later send a wise woman to bring Absalom home, and later still a shepherd called Amos.

verseByVerse.quote: Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai, Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s men came from all over Israel and beyond it: the people God gathered round his king was never one village or one tribe.

Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth. They come from the hill country and the coastal edge, from Judah and Benjamin, the far north and beyond the Jordan, and one of them is an Ammonite. Joab’s armour-bearer came from Beeroth, one of the Gibeonite towns (Joshua 9:17).

For a small community. The Chronicler wrote for a few thousand people who had come home from one city in one empire. A list like this says what a sermon could not: the people of God was never a single village. His greater Son gathers a multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite, Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uriah the Hittite stands in the roll of honour without comment: the Chronicler leaves out David’s great sin, but he does not erase the man David wronged.

Uriah the Hittite. No note, no explanation; the name sits between Gareb the Ithrite and Zabad the son of Ahlai. In 2 Samuel 23 the list ends with Uriah; the sixteen names after him are found only here, several apparently from east of the Jordan (a Reubenite chief, men probably of Ashtaroth and Aroer), and the Chronicler probably had them from another record.

What Chronicles leaves out. David’s adultery with Uriah’s wife Bathsheba and his killing of Uriah, with Nathan’s rebuke and the child that died, are absent from this book: the largest deliberate omission in Chronicles. Its readers already had 2 Samuel 11–12, and this book was written to show the returned exiles what God had promised David’s house, a promise that stood on God’s faithfulness, not David’s (see the introduction).

Silence, not concealment. It is not concealment, because here is the name: a foreigner faithful to a king who was not faithful to him, set among the men who made David king. The silence around his name is louder than comment. Matthew keeps the same memory in the genealogy of Jesus, “David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6): the Son of David came from that line to save sinners like his ancestor.

Ithmah the Moabite. Zelek the Ammonite and Ithmah the Moabite close the roll, and the man who led them was the great-grandson of a Moabite woman, Ruth, who came home to Bethlehem behind her mother-in-law.

Uncertain wording. Several of the places behind these names, such as the Mithnite, the Tizite, the Mahavite and the Mezobaite (vv. 43–47), are not known from anywhere else.

11.theology:
Twice in six verses the credit is moved off the men and onto God (vv. 9, 14). Neither statement diminishes what the men did; the Chronicler records their feats in detail. He simply refuses to let the achievement be the explanation.

And the kingship rests on a covenant made before the LORD, not on the conquest of a city. David takes Zion in verse 5, but he is already king in verse 3: the covenant made him king, not the conquest.
11.examples:
David would not drink water that had cost three men their safety. Understanding what others spend on us is rarer than courage, and the hardest gifts to receive are the ones we would never have asked anybody to pay for.

Abishai and Benaiah are recorded as not making the first rank, and both went on serving. Some servants can be told exactly where they stand and go on working, and Scripture puts their names in the chronicle.

keyVerse.quote: And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.
keyVerse.note: Set at the start of David’s reign, this verse explains everything that follows: the city, the victories and the loyal men all come because God was with the king he had chosen. It keeps the honour of the mighty men in its place, and it points to the greater Son of David, named Immanuel, God with us.

11.reflection:
Israel made David king because he had already led them and because God had chosen him (vv. 1–3). What do these verses teach about what to look for in leaders, and about Christ as the shepherd King?

Eleazar stood his ground, yet “the LORD saved them by a great victory” (v. 14). How do we hold together hard work and courage with giving God all the credit?

David would not drink water bought with his men’s lives (vv. 17–19), yet Christ gives us his blood to receive. How should the cost of our salvation shape the way we receive it, and the way we treat what others sacrifice for us?

The roll includes an Ammonite, a Moabite and Uriah the Hittite (vv. 39–46). What does that say about the people Christ gathers, and about how welcoming our church is?

12.title: Those Who Came to David: Voluntary Allegiance and the Spirit's Work
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war.<sup>2</sup>They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.<sup>3</sup>The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth,<sup>4</sup>Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah,<sup>5</sup>Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite;<sup>6</sup>Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites;<sup>7</sup>And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.<sup>8</sup>From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains:<sup>9</sup>Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third,<sup>10</sup>Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth,<sup>11</sup>Attai sixth, Eliel seventh,<sup>12</sup>Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth,<sup>13</sup>Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.<sup>14</sup>These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand.<sup>15</sup>These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.<sup>16</sup>And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David.<sup>17</sup>David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."<sup>18</sup>Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.<sup>19</sup>Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.")<sup>20</sup>As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh.<sup>21</sup>They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.<sup>22</sup>For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.<sup>23</sup>These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>24</sup>The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops.<sup>25</sup>Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100.<sup>26</sup>Of the Levites 4,600.<sup>27</sup>The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700.<sup>28</sup>Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.<sup>29</sup>Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul.<sup>30</sup>Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses.<sup>31</sup>Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.<sup>32</sup>Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.<sup>33</sup>Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose.<sup>34</sup>Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear.<sup>35</sup>Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle.<sup>36</sup>Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle.<sup>37</sup>Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.<sup>38</sup>All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king.<sup>39</sup>And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them.<sup>40</sup>And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 told how all Israel made David king at Hebron. Chapter 12, found only in Chronicles, goes back to the years before, when David was an outlaw at Ziklag, and names the men who came over to him then; then it returns to Hebron for the great muster and the feast.

The message. God gathers his people to his chosen king, and he does it one person at a time, often while nothing looks like working. Men came to David when it cost them everything; the Spirit declared that “your God helps you” (v. 18); and the trickle became “a great army, like an army of God” (v. 22). The kingdom came “according to the word of the LORD” (v. 23), and it ended in wholehearted unity and joy.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were few, poor and without a king (see the introduction), and it was easy to think God’s promises had stalled. This chapter showed them how the kingdom had come before: through small, costly decisions of faith made in obscurity, which God gathered into an army and crowned with joy. It called them to the same wholehearted loyalty to David’s house.

How the chapter makes its case. At Ziklag, Benjaminites from Saul’s own tribe come over (vv. 1–7), and Gadites cross the flooded Jordan (vv. 8–15). Men of Benjamin and Judah come, and when David is wary, the Spirit clothes Amasai to pledge them to him (vv. 16–18). Men of Manasseh desert to him as he leaves the Philistine army (vv. 19–21), and day by day the band becomes an army (v. 22). Then the muster at Hebron, tribe by tribe, with Issachar’s wise men and Zebulun’s undivided hearts (vv. 23–37), and three days of feasting and joy (vv. 38–40).

Where it leads. By pattern. David is the rejected and hunted king whose followers came to him before his throne was seen; so Christ gathers disciples while he is still despised, and calls them to go to him “outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured” (Hebrews 13:13). Amasai’s confession is the Spirit’s work, as every confession that Jesus is Lord is (1 Corinthians 12:3). And the chapter ends where the gospel story ends: a multitude from every tribe, gathered to the King at a feast of joy (Revelation 19:9).

For us. Come to Christ now, while following him still costs something, and come with a whole heart, keeping no line open to the other side. Expect his kingdom to grow as it did around David, one person at a time. Nothing done for him is forgotten, and the end is a table and joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Men Who Came While It Cost Something
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men came to David while it cost them everything, trusting God’s promise rather than David’s chances. The clock turns back to Ziklag, where David could not move about freely because of Saul (v. 1). Benjaminites, Saul’s own kinsmen, skilled with bow and sling in either hand, walk out of Israel to join him, and their names and villages are recorded (vv. 2–7). Then Gadites from beyond the Jordan, with faces like lions and the speed of gazelles, are ranked first to eleventh (vv. 8–13). The least was a match for a hundred, and they crossed the Jordan in its spring flood to reach him (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every man in this list backed David when the kingdom God had promised was one hunted man in a foreign town. They went by God’s promise, not by David’s chances.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadites came when the Jordan is hardest to cross and did not wait for the water to drop. Some decisions cannot wait for an easier day.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war. They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while David was a hunted fugitive, men came over to him, beginning with skilled warriors from Saul’s own tribe, because they had seen whom God had chosen.

The men who came to David at Ziklag. Chapter 11 crowned David at Hebron. Chapter 12 goes back to a Philistine border town where he had a price on his head, and names the men who came to him there.

While he could not move about freely because of Saul. The wilderness of Ziph, the cave of Adullam, the sixteen months under a Philistine warlord’s protection (1 Samuel 27:7): all compressed into one clause. Coming to Ziklag was not joining a winning side. It meant leaving the country to attach yourself to a wanted man in enemy territory, with no spoil to share and a good chance of ending on a list of traitors.

Benjaminites, Saul’s kinsmen. The detail ought to stop a reader. Slinging with either hand was what Benjamin was famous for: Ehud was a left-handed Benjaminite (Judges 3:15), and the tribe once fielded seven hundred left-handed men who could sling at a hair and not miss (Judges 20:16). These were Benjamin’s best, and they walked away from the head of their own clan to stand behind a man from Judah. Saul had asked his Benjaminites whether “the son of Jesse” would give them fields and vineyards (1 Samuel 22:7), betting that family loyalty would hold them. It did not hold all of them: some of his own kin had seen what God had said about the throne, and went to the man God had named.

Outside the camp. Following Jesus has often meant the same: leaving loyalties of family and clan to stand with a rejected King before his kingdom is seen. “Let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured” (Hebrews 13:13).
verseByVerse.note: Ziklag was David’s base while he was hiding from Saul among the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth, Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah, Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite; Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites; And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who came are named one by one with their home villages, because God keeps a record of those who come to his king.

Sons of Shemaah of Gibeah. Two come from Gibeah, Saul’s own town; one from Anathoth, the priestly village Jeremiah would come from; and Ishmaiah of Gibeon is marked out as a leader over the thirty. About half of these two dozen men are pinned to a village. They are not legends; they are somebody’s great-grandfather from a place you could walk to in a day.

A word to the returned exiles. The community the Chronicler wrote for was a few thousand people rebuilding a provincial town, and their besetting fear was that they were too small to matter. He hands them a list of men from Gibeah and Gibeon and Gederah who changed the history of Israel by getting up and walking to Ziklag, and lets them draw the conclusion.

Uncertain wording. “The Korahites” (v. 6) is surprising in a list of Benjaminites. They may have been Levites of Korah’s family living in Benjamin, or a Benjaminite clan of the same name; which is meant is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains: Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth, Attai sixth, Eliel seventh, Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth, Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gadite warriors from east of the Jordan, fierce and swift, went over to David in the wilderness, and every one of them, down to the eleventh, is named.

From the Gadites there went over to David. The Gadites lived east of the Jordan, and chapter 5 has already told how their story ended: they “broke faith with the God of their fathers” and were carried into exile (5:25–26). Here, generations earlier, their fighting men cross the river to find a fugitive in the wilderness.

Whose faces were like the faces of lions. A sentence of description no army list needs. A lion’s face is what an enemy sees; a gazelle’s speed is what he cannot catch. Somebody who had fought beside these men remembered them well enough to say both at once.

Ezer the chief, Obadiah second. Eleven names, each with its rank, down to Machbannai eleventh. The ranking was written down, and the man who came eleventh is in Scripture by name: an officer from a tribe that would later be deported for unfaithfulness, recorded because for one season of his life he risked everything for the LORD’s anointed. Nothing done for the true King is forgotten because it came eleventh (Hebrews 6:10).

verseByVerse.quote: These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand. These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gadites were seasoned officers who crossed the Jordan at full flood to reach David, and came out fighting on both banks.

The least was a match for a hundred men. Even allowing for the way soldiers talk about soldiers, the sentence says that David’s band had grown from four hundred debtors and malcontents (1 Samuel 22:2) into a corps of professionals, while nothing outwardly was going his way.

In the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks. The first month is Nisan, in spring, when the snow comes off Hermon and the Jordan runs high and fast: the season nobody crosses if he can help it. It is also the month and the very state of the river when Joshua brought Israel over into the land (Joshua 3:15; 4:19), and the reader will hear the echo. But here there is no ark, no dry ground, no priests standing in the riverbed. These men crossed in flood anyway, and put to flight everyone in the valleys on both sides.

Uncertain wording. “The least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand” (v. 14) may instead mean that the least of them commanded a hundred and the greatest a thousand. The Hebrew is compressed and allows both; either way, they were the pick of the army.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a passage full of men helping David, the Spirit names the real helper: “your God helps you” (v. 18). Men of Benjamin and Judah arrive, and David, often betrayed before, meets them, names his fear of treachery and leaves the judgment to God (vv. 16–17). Then the Spirit clothes Amasai, and his oath of loyalty comes out as poetry and blessing (v. 18). An aside admits that David had marched out with the Philistines against Saul and was sent home by suspicious pagans, while men of Manasseh deserted to him (vv. 19–21). Day by day the trickle becomes “a great army, like an army of God” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: In a passage full of men helping David, the Spirit names the real helper: your God helps you (v. 18). The army is real, and it is not the reason David will reign.
verseByVerse.examples: David could not tell friend from assassin by looking, so he put the question before God and waited: what a man does when discernment runs out and a decision still has to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David. David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When men of Benjamin and Judah came, David could not read their hearts, so he told them his fear plainly and left the judgment to God.

Some of the men of Benjamin and Judah. A strange combination: Benjamin is Saul’s tribe and Judah David’s, and men from both arrive together.

If to betray me to my adversaries. David has grounds for suspicion. Keilah, the town he had just saved, was ready to hand him over (1 Samuel 23:12); the Ziphites twice betrayed his hiding places (1 Samuel 23:19; 26:1); Doeg’s report got eighty-five priests killed (1 Samuel 22:18). A man can smile at you in the morning and sell you before dark.

May the God of our fathers see and rebuke you. He neither pretends the suspicion is absent nor acts on it. He names it aloud, hands the question to the one who can see inside them, and waits to see what God will do, which turns out to be the next verse. That is what to do when discernment runs out and a decision still has to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers David’s question by his Spirit: Amasai, clothed by the Spirit, pledges himself and his men to David and declares that God is David’s true helper.

Then the Spirit clothed Amasai. The verb is the ordinary word for putting on a garment: the Spirit clothed himself with the man, as with Gideon before the trumpet (Judges 6:34) and Zechariah the priest before the words that got him stoned (2 Chronicles 24:20). What comes out is not the man’s own.

O son of Jesse! Son of Jesse was a sneer. Saul used it at his table when he would not say the name (1 Samuel 20:27), Nabal when he refused him food (1 Samuel 25:10), and later the rebel Sheba to call the northern tribes away from David (2 Samuel 20:1). It meant a small farmer’s boy from a village nobody visits. Amasai takes up the sneer and swears by it, pledging himself to the son of Jesse while that man is a fugitive with nothing to offer. The insult becomes the oath. Something like it happened again when the charge fixed to a cross, “The King of the Jews”, proved to be the plain truth, and the church has sworn by it ever since.

Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! We use peace to mean quiet. The Hebrew word, shalom, is far larger: wholeness, things as they should be, a life and a people put right and flourishing. Said three times over, it is a blessing on David and on everyone who stands with him. We tend to look for peace in control, in getting every threat sorted, which is exactly what a hunted man in Ziklag did not have. Amasai gives the real ground: shalom comes from God’s side.

For your God helps you. In a chapter full of men helping David, the last clause turns from David to God: Amasai hands over an army and in the same breath says the army is not why David will win.

He himself is our peace. Isaiah calls David’s greater Son the “Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6); Paul says “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14); and he speaks it to people who once stood on the wrong side: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27). Peace is first a settled state of things between you and God, made by Christ, and the calm feeling follows. This week it may look small: a kind word to someone who was once against you, because Christ spoke peace to you first. See Peace.

Nobody asked for this. David asked about motives; the Spirit answered with a confession of faith, and the suspicion was ended by God speaking through the very men under suspicion. The same Spirit, now given to every believer, still gives the confession of the true King that no one makes on his own: “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). The LORD has never left his anointed standing at a gate without a witness.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.") As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh. They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Manasseh deserted to David after he had marched with the Philistines, and God used the Philistines’ suspicion to keep David out of the battle against Saul.

When he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. A sentence the Chronicler could have left out, and did not. In the days before Gilboa, David and his men were marching with the Philistine army, in line with the enemies of God’s people. The outlaw years had taken him that far.

The rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away. Five warlords decided the Hebrew could not be trusted and sent him home (1 Samuel 29). They were protecting their own necks, and without knowing it they kept the future king from having Israelite blood on his hands on the day the throne fell vacant. David did not get himself out; he was sent out, by men who despised him. It is not a comfortable rescue, but it is a common one: God gets a man out of the mess he walked into through the suspicion of the very people he had leaned on. David’s standing rested on God’s choice, not his record, and God’s mercy reached him in the middle of his worst compromise.

They helped David against the band of raiders. Seven officers of Manasseh came over during that retreat, probably in time for the pursuit of the Amalekites who burned Ziklag and carried off every wife and child (1 Samuel 30). They arrived days before the worst day of David’s life, and he did not know it when he took them in.

verseByVerse.quote: For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men kept coming to David day after day until his band became a great army: the kingdom grew one decision at a time.

For from day to day men came to David to help him. Not a rising, not a moment when the country turned: two men this week and a dozen the next, walking in from Gibeah and Gilead and the far side of the river, over years, until somebody counted and found there was an army. The Chronicler has spent twenty-one verses proving it by naming them. Each made a private decision about a hunted man and a promise, and got up. That is still how God’s kingdom grows: one person at a time, often while nothing looks like working.

Like an army of God. The phrase recalls Jacob, who met the angels of God on the road home and called the place Mahanaim, God’s camp (Genesis 32:1–2). The Chronicler is not saying David’s men were angels. A force assembled out of nothing, around a man with no crown, no capital and no pay, was best compared to a host not of this earth.

Uncertain wording. Hebrew sometimes uses God’s name simply to mean “very great”, so “an army of God” may mean no more than a mighty army. The echo of Jacob’s camp of God suggests more is meant, but both readings are possible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole nation comes to Hebron to make David king, and every free decision is placed under a promise God made years before: they came “to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD” (v. 23). Tribe by tribe they are counted: Judah and Simeon; Levites and priests, the young Zadok among them (vv. 24–28); Benjamin, most of whom had stayed loyal to Saul’s house until then (v. 29); Ephraim and Manasseh in their thousands (vv. 30–31); two hundred chiefs of Issachar who understood the times (v. 32); Zebulun with an undivided heart (v. 33); and, largest of all, the tribes from beyond the Jordan (vv. 34–37).
verseByVerse.theology: A vast number of free decisions are all placed under a promise God made years before anyone counted anything (v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: Issachar's two hundred contributed judgment, not numbers. A community that counts only what it can arm will not notice when it has lost the people who understand what is happening and what to do.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD. The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops. Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100. Of the Levites 4,600. The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700. Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribes came to Hebron in their thousands to make David king, as the LORD had said, and the priests and Levites came armed with them.

According to the word of the LORD. That clause governs everything counted after it. This is not a coup or an election result: God had spoken about a shepherd boy years before, and the numbers are catching up with his word.

The men of Judah … 6,800. Judah’s number is small, fewer than Simeon’s, probably because Judah had crowned David seven years earlier and fought for him since (2 Samuel 2:4). The tribe committed longest had the least to prove at the parade.

The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron. Then the Levites, with Jehoiada of Aaron’s house. The priests came armed, and the Chronicler, who cares more for Levites than any other Old Testament writer, counts them among the troops without apology.

Zadok, a young man mighty in valor. A young man with twenty-two officers behind him. The genealogies have probably listed him (6:8); here the story meets him. He will stand by David against Absalom and anoint Solomon at Gihon, and his line will hold the sanctuary so long that Ezekiel still measures a faithful priesthood by “the sons of Zadok” (Ezekiel 44:15). He enters unannounced, a youngster with a sword who guessed right about the king.

Are 340,000 men credible? The figures may count military units rather than individuals, or have been enlarged in copying; the point is that all Israel came to make David king.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “thousand” can also mean a clan or a military unit of no fixed size, which may explain some of the large totals in verses 24–37. How it is meant in each case is not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul. Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses. Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Most of Saul’s own tribe had held out for his house until then, and the record says so; yet Ephraim and Manasseh came in force, their men named in advance.

Of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul. A clause no propagandist would have written. Most of Saul’s tribe came late, and the record says so. The book that has just honoured the Benjaminites who defected to Ziklag when it was dangerous will not let the exception stand in for the tribe. Writing to encourage a discouraged community, the Chronicler could have left the sentence out. Instead he reports a divided tribe arriving with mixed motives, and the coronation happens anyway: God’s purposes do not wait for everyone to be wholehearted.

Who were expressly named to come and make David king. Ephraim sends 20,800, famous men in their fathers’ houses, and half-Manasseh 18,000. Somebody in Manasseh sat down and wrote out a list of who was going. The commitment was not a mood on the day; it was written down, name by name, by men who intended to be held to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Issachar’s two hundred chiefs are honoured for wisdom: they understood what God was doing in their day and knew what Israel should do about it.

Men who had understanding of the times. Beside Zebulun’s fifty thousand and the east’s hundred and twenty thousand, Issachar is entered with two hundred men, counted because they could tell what time it was. Understanding the times is diagnosis: seeing what is happening rather than what the last ten years trained you to expect. Knowing what Israel ought to do is harder: saying what the next step is, and being trusted enough that the kinsmen under their command would move when they said it.

What did they discern? Not a trend or a mood. Verse 23 has said it: the kingdom was turning to David according to the word of the LORD. They had heard what God said and could see it arriving, and reading the moment meant lining their tribe up with a promise while the outcome was still open.

A test for us. Is our reading of the times governed by what God has said, and does it end in something to do? Jesus rebuked those who could read the sky but not “the signs of the times” (Matthew 16:3). Diagnosis that never reaches a next step is not Issachar’s gift; it is talk with a serious face.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose. Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear. Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle. Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle. Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tribe after tribe came wholeheartedly, Zebulun with an undivided heart and the distant eastern tribes in the greatest numbers of all.

To help David with singleness of purpose. Under the phrase the Hebrew says something plainer: not with a double heart. Zebulun’s fifty thousand came without keeping anything back in case David lost.

Undivided hearts. The word heart runs through the chapter beside the helping: David offering to have his heart joined to theirs (v. 17), Zebulun undivided, and the whole assembly arriving “with a whole heart” (v. 38). A double heart is not treachery. It is a man who marches with you and privately keeps a line open to the other side, and it is the ordinary condition of most allegiance most of the time.

Keeping a line open. A double heart is close to a modern virtue. We are taught to keep our options open, never to commit to a place, a church or a person in a way we cannot undo. The sociologist Zygmunt Bauman argued that our age prefers connections to relationships, because a connection can be dropped with a click and a relationship cannot, and he saw how lonely that leaves people who are never quite held by anything. It feels like freedom, but the man who keeps every door ajar never gets to live in any of the rooms. Yet nobody gets a whole heart by trying harder; Israel’s history after this day is a long record of divided ones. So God promised to give it: “I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them” (Ezekiel 11:19). And the Son of David kept no line open for himself: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and went the whole way to the cross. An undivided heart grows in people who know they were loved by one.

Of the Danites 28,600. Dan and Zebulun are the two tribes the genealogies of chapters 2 to 8 never gave a list to. Missing from the family record, they are both here in strength, making David king. Absence from a register is not absence from the people of God.

From beyond the Jordan, 120,000. The largest contingent comes from the place with the least reason to send one. Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh had asked Moses for land outside the land of promise (Numbers 32), lived furthest from Hebron and the sanctuary, and would be the first taken into exile for breaking faith (5:25–26). On this day they outnumbered everyone. The reach of the king ran out past the river to the people on the edge of the map, and they came.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–40 — Three Days at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter that began with a fugitive ends with a feast. The men come to Hebron “with a whole heart”, and all the rest of Israel is “of a single mind to make David king” (v. 38). They eat and drink with David for three days, supplied by their brothers (v. 39) and by relatives from as far north as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali, with flour, figs, raisins, wine, oil, oxen and sheep (v. 40). The army raised for war fights no battle: the kingdom of God’s choosing arrives as a table. The last words are the point: “there was joy in Israel”.
verseByVerse.theology: An army was raised and no battle fought. The kingdom of God's choosing arrives as a table with enough for everybody and three days to sit at it.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter's last word is joy (v. 40). Unity under the right king is meant to be enjoyed, not merely endured.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king. And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them. And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel, with one heart, made David king and feasted for three days, and there was joy in Israel: the chapter that began with a fugitive ends at a table.

Arrayed in battle order. The armed men march to Hebron in battle order, and there is no battle: they sit down to eat for three days.

Bringing food on donkeys and on camels. The provisioning is described in the detail of somebody who was pleased about it, and it came from as far as Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali, the longest road. Nothing in between was engineered by David. He did not recruit the Benjaminites, could not read the men at the gate, and had marched in a Philistine column. The kingdom assembled around him, day by day, according to a word God had spoken before any of it started.

For there was joy in Israel. Set the two ends of the chapter side by side. It opens with one man who cannot move about freely in his own country and a handful of defectors slipping into a Philistine town. It closes with every tribe in Israel round a table with more than they can eat, and the narrator’s summary is five words long.

A table somebody else provided. This is the shape the gospel keeps: a rejected King with a few followers who came while it cost something; then a countless multitude from every tribe and nation, gathered from the edges of the map (Revelation 7:9), at a table somebody else provided. The last book of the Bible calls it “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), and the King at its head is the Son of David, rejected first and crowned after. The three days at Hebron were a small foretaste of it.

12.theology:
The verb help runs through the first twenty-two verses (vv. 1, 17, 18, 21, 22), and at the centre the Spirit says whose help it finally is: peace to your helpers! For your God helps you (v. 18). The men’s help is real, but it is not what explains David’s rise; the book said the same at 11:9 and 11:14.

And the whole muster stands under one clause: according to the word of the LORD (v. 23). Hundreds of thousands of free decisions, a Benjaminite weighing his family, a Gadite looking at the river, are each treated as real decisions and all together as the keeping of a promise. Scripture never treats the two as rivals.
12.examples:
Coming to David at Ziklag cost something, and coming to Christ still can: a family's disapproval, a career, a reputation. These men are on record because they moved before the kingdom was visible, which is what faith does (Hebrews 11:1), and it is the Spirit, who moved Amasai, who still gives that faith.

Most of Benjamin came late, and the record does not shut them out. Christ's kingdom receives late-comers and those who have hedged: in his parable the last-hour labourers were paid the same as the first (Matthew 20:1–16), because the wage is grace, not a reward for our record.

And the chapter ends at a table where everyone had enough: the church too is gathered one person at a time, around a feast it did not provide.

keyVerse.quote: We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you.
keyVerse.note: Spoken when the Spirit clothed Amasai, this oath is the heart of the chapter. It pledges wholehearted loyalty to God’s chosen king while he is still a fugitive, and it names the real reason he will reign: not the men who help him, but the God who helps him. It is the shape of every true confession of Christ.

12.reflection:
The men who came to David at Ziklag joined a hunted man in enemy territory (vv. 1–2). What does it cost to follow Christ where you live, and what helps you keep going when his kingdom seems small?

When David could not tell friend from foe, he named his fear and left the judgment with God (v. 17). How can we handle suspicion and uncertainty about others in a way that honours God?

Issachar’s men “had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do” (v. 32). What would it look like for our church to read our times by God’s word, and then act?

Zebulun came “with singleness of purpose” (v. 33), and the chapter ends in joy (v. 40). Where are we keeping a line open rather than giving Christ our whole heart, and how does his wholehearted love for us change that?

13.title: The Ark and Uzzah: When Good Intentions Are Not Enough
13.text: <sup>1</sup>David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader.<sup>2</sup>And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us.<sup>3</sup>Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."<sup>4</sup>All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.<sup>5</sup>So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim.<sup>6</sup>And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.<sup>7</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart.<sup>8</sup>And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.<sup>9</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>10</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.<sup>11</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.<sup>12</sup>And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?"<sup>13</sup>So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>14</sup>And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
13.overview:
Where we are. All Israel has made David king and he has taken Jerusalem (chapters 11–12). His first act as king of the whole nation is not a campaign but a question about the ark of God, left in Kiriath-jearim through the whole of Saul’s reign.

The message. God is to be sought, and he is to be sought as he has said. Israel did the right thing, bringing the throne of God back to the centre of its life, in the wrong way, on a cart copied from the Philistines, and the holy God broke out against Uzzah. Sincerity and enthusiasm cannot stand in for obedience. Yet the God who struck at Perez-uzza is the same God who blessed the house where his ark was kept.

Why it was said. The first readers were rebuilding the worship of God at a modest temple after the exile (see the introduction). They needed to know that his presence is a people’s greatest treasure and its greatest danger, and that how he is approached matters to him.

How the chapter makes its case. David consults the leaders and the assembly, and gives the reason for the venture: under Saul nobody sought the ark (vv. 1–4). All Israel goes up to Kiriath-jearim and sets the ark, the throne of the LORD, on a new cart amid music and song (vv. 5–8). At Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah steadies the ark, and God strikes him down (vv. 9–10). David is angry, then afraid, and asks how the ark can ever come home (vv. 11–12). It goes to the house of Obed-edom instead, and the LORD blesses that household for three months (vv. 13–14).
