Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes, and by pattern. No one could touch the ark and live, and the chapter leaves us with David’s question: how can the holy God come home to sinners? The answer lies on the ark itself, in the mercy seat where blood was put once a year, and in the One whom “God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). In Christ the holy God came near in flesh, bore the wrath that broke out at Perez-uzza, and opened the way for sinners to draw near and be blessed.

For us. God is not a household object to be managed, and long familiarity with holy things can wear reverence away. We do not come to him by our own inventions, however heartfelt, but by the way he has given, which is Christ. And through him we come not in terror but with confidence, “by the new and living way that he opened for us” (Hebrews 10:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — All Israel, and a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel rightly resolves to seek God again, and wrongly decides how. David consults every commander and puts the plan to the assembly with two tests, “if it seems good to you and from the LORD our God” (v. 2), and a reason: “we did not seek it in the days of Saul” (v. 3). All Israel, from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, goes up to Kiriath-jearim for the ark of the LORD “who sits enthroned above the cherubim” (vv. 5–6). Then comes the detail on which the chapter turns: a “new cart” (v. 7), the Philistines’ method, with the whole nation singing and playing before it with all its might (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 is the hinge of the book. Saul did not seek the LORD and died for it (10:13-14); David's first act is to seek him. The word will run to the last charge David gives his son.
verseByVerse.examples: The priests and Levites were summoned (v. 2) and then said nothing about the cart. Knowing what God has said is of little use if no one speaks up when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader. And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us. Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s first act as king of all Israel is to bring back the ark, because under Saul nobody sought it, and he means his reign to begin by seeking God.

David consulted with the commanders. The kingdom is new and David calls a council, not about the Philistines, who will attack the moment they hear, nor the treasury or the borders, but about a box that has sat for decades in a private house in the hills.

If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God. He joins two tests in one sentence without ranking them: the people must want it and God must be in it. A king with 340,000 men at his back is asking permission.

We did not seek it in the days of Saul. This is the sentence the Chronicler has waited three chapters to write, and it uses the word of the verdict on Saul, who “did not seek guidance from the LORD” (10:14). Nobody forbade the ark. It had come to Abinadab’s house after a disaster: Israel carried it into battle like a charm, the Philistines captured it, and when plagues broke out wherever it went they sent it back, and the men of Kiriath-jearim took it in (1 Samuel 4:1–7:2). There it sat through a whole reign, and a generation grew up that had never seen the throne of God. No day came when Israel voted to leave the ark in the hills; there were simply years of days when nobody went to get it. That is how neglect of God usually looks from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people. So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole nation, from one end of the promised land to the other, gathers to bring home the ark, the throne of the LORD himself.

From the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath. The assembly agrees, “for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people”, and David summons Israel from the southern edge of the promise to the far northern pass, the whole territory God had described to Abraham and Moses. For a small community around one rebuilt town in a foreign empire, those two place names are not nostalgia but a map of what God said, laid over what they could see out of the window.

Enthroned above the cherubim. The ark is “called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim”. It is not a relic or a national treasure but a throne: a gold-covered lid with two winged figures facing each other across it, and the God of heaven seated between them. Everything that follows depends on that clause being true, and everything that goes wrong goes wrong because the men handling the ark treated it as furniture.

Uncertain wording. Behind “the Nile of Egypt” is the Hebrew Shihor, used elsewhere of a watercourse on Egypt’s eastern frontier (Joshua 13:3); it may be the easternmost branch of the Nile or a border stream. Lebo-hamath may be a town or “the entrance of Hamath”, the pass north into Syria. Either way the phrase means all the land God promised.

verseByVerse.quote: And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart. And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel moved the ark on a new cart, the Philistines’ way rather than the way God had commanded, and all its heartfelt celebration could not make up for that.

On a new cart. The best they had, and exactly what the Philistines had used: their priests and diviners had sent the ark home on a new cart behind two milk cows (1 Samuel 6:7–8). Israel copied the method, and nobody asked whether pagans with no law were the right people to learn from.

What the law said. The law was specific. At Sinai the Gershonites and Merarites received wagons, but to the sons of Kohath Moses gave none, “because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder” (Numbers 7:9). And the Kohathites “must not touch the holy things, lest they die” (Numbers 4:15). The wagon was not a slip over a small detail. It was the one method God had expressly withheld, for the one object now sitting on it, and the Levites summoned in verse 2 were somewhere in the procession, walking beside the cart.

Celebrating before God with all their might. The noise is tremendous and every note of it is sincere. But sincerity is not obedience, and none of it was what God had commanded. Zeal that has not asked what God has said is how well-meaning people do harm in his name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s holiness breaks out against the careless handling of his throne. At the threshing floor of Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark, and the anger of the LORD is kindled: he dies “there before God” (v. 10), at the head of a procession that had been celebrating “before God” (v. 8). The day’s joy collapses. David’s first reaction is anger, recorded without excuse, and the place is named Perez-uzza, meaning roughly the breaking out against Uzzah, a name still on the map when the Chronicler wrote (v. 11). The same verb will describe God breaking through David’s enemies in the next chapter (14:11).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness here is not a mood of God's but what he is. The law had long warned that even Levites must not touch the holy things or they would die (Numbers 4:15), and the warning was itself a mercy, given so Israel could come near and live.
verseByVerse.examples: A reader who has lost someone suddenly may find this passage frightening. It does not teach that every sudden death is a judgment; Jesus denied exactly that (Luke 13:1–5). It records one moment when God made his holiness visible so that a nation would learn to come to him rightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark, God struck him dead: the holy God will not be handled, even with good intentions, and the fault lay with a whole nation that had not asked how he was to be approached.

The oxen stumbled. The cart lurches and Uzzah does what anyone would do. He was not stealing or scoffing; he reached out to stop the ark going down in the dirt in front of the nation.

The danger of familiarity. The ark had stood for decades in the house of Abinadab, probably Uzzah’s father. Uzzah had lived for years beside the throne of God, and that was the problem: familiarity had worn the edge off the holiest object on earth, and his hand went out without a thought in it. His reflex also assumed that God’s honour depends on our protecting it. The God enthroned above the cherubim had not asked to be caught.

Two things held together. The law said no hand touches this, and Uzzah’s did. And there was the larger fault David will name himself: “we did not seek him according to the rule” (15:13). The whole expedition was wrong before the oxen stumbled. Uzzah happened to be walking beside a cart that should never have existed, and the carelessness that killed him was the nation’s before it was his.

Was God unjust? The law was plain and old, the Levites were present, and the ark was the throne of the holy God, not an object Israel could handle as it liked. Scripture’s surprise is not that a sinner died at the throne of God but that sinners are allowed to live near him at all (Lamentations 3:22).

Why do we want a manageable God? To many modern readers this is the most offensive story in Chronicles, and the offence is worth looking at. We are used to having things on our terms, and without noticing we expect God to fit the pattern: available, adjustable, mild, there to help with the life we have already planned. Yet everywhere else we know that greatness is dangerous. Nobody calls the sun unfair for burning, or the sea cruel for drowning the man who treats it lightly, and this is not raw power but a Person who had said plainly, for centuries, what would happen. The surprise of the gospel is not that this God is safer than Perez-uzza suggests. It is that the holy anger which broke out on a cart track fell, in the end, on the one man who had never handled God carelessly. Isaiah saw him “stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4), and Christians see him on the cross, struck so that sinners could come near and not be struck.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s first response is anger at God, and the Chronicler records it honestly; the place keeps the name of what happened there, and the verb “broken out” will return in the next chapter as victory.

David was angry. Scripture says it before it says anything else about him. The music has stopped, a man lies dead on the road, and the king is furious with God. The Chronicler could have left that clause out and did not. Anger at God is not the end of a life with him; what matters is where it goes next, and David’s became fear and a question (v. 12).

Perez-uzza to this day. The name was still on the map when the book was written: Israel kept a marker where God’s holiness had struck, and told the story to its children.

Broken out against Uzzah. Remember the verb, because it comes back almost at once. In the next chapter the Philistines come up against David, God gives him the victory, and David says, “God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood” (14:11). He calls the place Baal-perazim, “lord of breaking through”. It is the same word. One chapter apart, the same God bursts out: the first time it destroys a man on a cart track, the second time it scatters an army in front of the king.

One God, one kind of power. The lesson is not that God is unpredictable but that Israel had been treating his power as manageable. A God who breaks through an army like floodwater is not a God who can be carried about on a farm cart.
verseByVerse.note: “Perez-uzza” means “the breaking out against Uzzah” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Holy fear does not end the story; it makes David ask the right question. Anger gives way to fear, and fear to “How can I bring the ark of God home to me?” (v. 12). Not daring to take it into the city of David, he turns it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite (v. 13). The ark stays there three months, and “the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had” (v. 14). The presence that struck Uzzah blesses the home that shelters it; God has not changed between verse 10 and verse 14. David’s question will be answered in chapter 15, when the ark is carried the way God commanded.
verseByVerse.theology: The ark that killed a man in the road blessed a household for a quarter of a year, and nothing about it changed. The presence of God is neither safe nor hostile; it is holy, and whether it meets a man in blessing or in judgment is not chance.
verseByVerse.examples: Fear that asks how to come to God rightly is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). Fear that simply stays away is not, and David did not stay away.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?" So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger turns to holy fear: David stops and asks how the ark can come home, and while he learns the answer, God blesses the household that shelters it.

David was afraid of God that day. David does not ask why God did it but the right question: “How can I bring the ark of God home to me?” Rather than abandon the project or repeat it louder, he stops and asks. True fear of God does not drive a man away; it makes him careful about the way in.

Finding the rule. The answer took three months, and it had been written down for centuries: only the Levites may carry the ark, and the first attempt failed because “we did not seek him according to the rule” (15:2, 13).

The LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom. The most dangerous object in the world is parked in Obed-edom’s house because the king is afraid to take it home, and for three months that house is blessed. Chronicles later lists Obed-edom among the gatekeepers, with sixty-two descendants and the note “for God blessed him” (26:5, 8). The same holy presence struck Uzzah and blessed Obed-edom. God had not changed; what differed was how he was received.

No hand touched that lid and lived. The ark Uzzah touched was crowned by the mercy seat, where the high priest put blood once a year, on the Day of Atonement. Romans uses the mercy seat’s own word when it says that God put forward his Son “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), a sacrifice that turns away wrath, for all to see. What could not be touched has been displayed and offered. The leper Christ touched did not make him unclean but was made whole (Mark 1:41). Perez-uzza has a real grave in it, and the way home was opened by One who bore the wrath himself, so that sinners could live near God and be blessed, as Obed-edom’s household was.

Uncertain wording. “Obed-edom the Gittite” means he came from a place called Gath. That could be the Philistine city, making him a foreigner loyal to David, like Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 15:19–22), or Gath-rimmon, a town given to the Levites (Joshua 21:24–25), making him a Levite. The gatekeeper Obed-edom of chapters 15 and 26 is a Levite, and many take him to be the same man; the text does not settle it.

13.theology:
Verse 3 carries the word the book is built around, and by chapter 15 David will have learned that seeking God means coming the way he said (15:13). Sincerity was never in doubt; the whole nation was singing with all its might.

And one verb, break out, runs through both halves of God’s dealing with David, against Uzzah (v. 11) and through the Philistines (14:11). Israel's danger was never that God was weak; it was that they had grown used to him.
13.examples:
The man who handled the ark most casually had lived nearest it longest. Long familiarity with holy things is not reverence for them; more often it wears reverence away.

Uzzah's reflex assumed that God's honour is fragile and depends on our steadying it, an assumption that shows up whenever people bend or hide the truth to keep God from looking bad.

David was angry with God, and Scripture records it without excusing or condemning it, then records what the anger became: fear, a question, three months, and a man who came back having learned what he should have known. Anger at God is not the end of a life with him, and the God who met David's failure with a way back still does, because Christ has already come near on our behalf.

keyVerse.quote: And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, “How can I bring the ark of God home to me?”
keyVerse.note: This is the question the whole chapter forces, and the one chapters 13 to 16 answer. David’s anger becomes holy fear, and fear becomes a question about the right way to come near the holy God. The full answer lies beyond the Levites’ poles, in Christ, through whom God makes his home with sinners.

13.reflection:
Israel did the right thing in the wrong way, copying the Philistines’ new cart instead of asking what God had said (v. 7; Numbers 7:9). Where are we tempted to think that sincerity and enthusiasm are all God asks of us?

Uzzah had lived near the ark for years. How can long familiarity with holy things, such as church, Scripture or the Lord’s Supper, wear away reverence, and what renews it?

David was angry, then afraid, and then asked, “How can I bring the ark of God home to me?” (vv. 11–12). What can we learn from the way his anger turned into a question?

The same presence that struck Uzzah blessed Obed-edom’s household (vv. 10, 14). How does Christ, our propitiation, make the holy God a blessing rather than a terror to us?

14.title: David's House, Victories, and the Pattern of Seeking God
14.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him.<sup>2</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>3</sup>And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters.<sup>4</sup>These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>5</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,<sup>6</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>7</sup>Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.<sup>8</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them.<sup>9</sup>Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>10</sup>And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."<sup>11</sup>And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>12</sup>And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.<sup>13</sup>And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>15</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>16</sup>And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer.<sup>17</sup>And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
14.overview:
Where we are. Uzzah lies dead at Perez-uzza and the ark waits in the house of Obed-edom for three months (13:14). Into that interval the Chronicler moves material that 2 Samuel tells before the ark story: Hiram’s cedar, David’s growing family, and two victories over the Philistines.

The message. God had not put David’s reign on hold while David learned how to carry the ark. The LORD establishes his king for the sake of his people, and fights for him. The king who did not seek God according to the rule in chapter 13 now inquires of God twice and wins twice: blessing follows seeking, and the victory belongs to the God who goes out before his people.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had no king, no army to speak of and hostile neighbours (see the introduction). They needed to know that a people’s standing and its deliverance come from the LORD, and that the way forward was not cleverness or past success but seeking him.

How the chapter makes its case. Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen, and David reads the gift rightly: the LORD has made him king, for the sake of Israel (vv. 1–2). His family grows in Jerusalem, and among thirteen sons stand Nathan and Solomon (vv. 3–7). The Philistines attack; David asks God, is told to go up, breaks through them at Baal-perazim and burns their abandoned gods (vv. 8–12). They attack again; David asks again, receives different orders, waits for the sound of marching in the balsam trees, and routs them, and the LORD makes the nations fear him (vv. 13–17).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Nathan and Solomon, side by side in verse 4, are the two sons through whom Luke and Matthew trace the line to Jesus. And David at his best here, asking his God before every move and following where God has already gone, is a faint outline of the Son who said, “the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19), and who won the decisive battle for his people himself.

For us. Whatever standing we are given is a trust, held for the sake of others, as David’s was. Yesterday’s answer from God is no substitute for seeking him today. And the people of Christ fight their battles behind One who has already gone out ahead of them, so that “we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps building David’s kingdom while the ark waits, and David understands why. Hiram king of Tyre, master of the richest port on the coast, sends cedar, masons and carpenters for a palace (v. 1). David reads the gift as evidence about God: the LORD had established him as king, and exalted his kingdom “for the sake of his people Israel” (v. 2). Then his household grows. He takes more wives in Jerusalem, a step the law had warned kings against, and thirteen sons are named (vv. 3–7). Most are no more than names, but two stand together in verse 4: Nathan and Solomon, the brothers through whom the promise will run to Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: An embassy from a great power can persuade a man he has arrived. David read the cedar instead as evidence that God had put him there, for the nation's sake rather than his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Did God approve of polygamy? No. From the beginning marriage was one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), Jesus restated it (Matthew 19:4–6), and the law forbade the king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). The Old Testament records polygamy honestly, and nearly every time it records the jealousy and grief that came with it. God bore with it for a time; he never held it up as his design.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him. And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David reads Hiram’s gift rightly: the LORD had made him king, and had made him king for the sake of his people.

Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers. Tyre ran the richest port on the coast and traded the timber every great court wanted. Its king’s shipment inland is a diplomatic judgment: the new man in the hills is worth an embassy. (Hiram’s reign seems to have begun later in David’s, so both books probably place the gift by theme rather than date.)

For the sake of his people Israel. Both halves of David’s reading are unusual. He takes an international compliment as evidence about God, the timber as proof of what the LORD had done. And he sees that he has been raised up not for himself but for his people. A man surrounded by cedar worked out that the cedar was not the point, and neither was he. Keep the cedar in view: three chapters on, David will sit in the finished house and find he cannot enjoy it while the ark is under a tent (17:1).

The kingdom goes on. All this happens in the three months while the ark stands in another man’s house. David’s great project has stopped dead and a man lies buried at Perez-uzza, yet God does not put the reign on hold while David works out how to carry the ark.

What is success for? Our culture usually tells successful people one of two things: you earned it, so it proves your worth, or you were lucky, so enjoy it while it lasts. The first makes people proud and then frightened, because worth that rests on results has to be defended every quarter; the second makes them restless. Both assume that success is about the person who has it. David draws a third conclusion: God put him there, and put him there for others. That turns success from a trophy into a trust, held for the people under you and one day handed back. It is also the shape of the greatest success story there is. The one to whom all authority was given came, in his own words, “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). People who know they were among the many can hold whatever they are given loosely, and spend it on someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters. These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s household grows in a way the law had warned against, yet among its sons are the two through whom God’s promise will run to Christ.

David took more wives in Jerusalem. The Chronicler neither defends nor condemns it, though he knew the law that a king “shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). This book leaves out the affair with Bathsheba altogether, and then writes this sentence, which shows where the trouble in David’s house grew from. Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah had been born to earlier wives at Hebron (3:1–2), and this verse enlarges the same crowded house that each of them would tear apart.

Nathan, Solomon. Then thirteen names, and two stand next to each other in verse 4. Solomon, the man who will build the temple this whole book is heading towards, is entered fourth, like any other child born in the capital that year. Beside him is a brother nobody remembers, whose line Luke traces when he gives the ancestry of Jesus. Matthew’s genealogy comes down through Solomon (Matthew 1:6) and Luke’s through Nathan (Luke 3:31), and both arrive at the same manger. Two names in one verse of a list, and the whole of the promise runs through the pair of them.

Beeliada. The last name but one is built on the word baal, and in 2 Samuel 5:16 (and 3:8 of this book) the same son is called Eliada, built on El, God. Before Baal-worship poisoned the word, baal simply meant lord or master, and Israelites could use it of the LORD; one of the men who came to David at Ziklag was called Bealiah (12:5), a name joining baal to the divine name. A day came when the word could not be used at all, and God said through Hosea that his people would call him “My Husband” and no longer “My Baal” (Hosea 2:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first battle shows a king who asks before he acts and gives God the credit after. The Philistines, who tolerated a divided Israel, come hunting the moment David is anointed king over all of it, and raid the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem (vv. 8–9). David puts two plain questions to God and receives a plain answer (v. 10). He wins, and names the place Baal-perazim because God broke through his enemies “like a bursting flood” (v. 11), the very verb used of Uzzah a chapter before. The Philistines flee and leave their gods on the field, and David has them burned, as the law commanded (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 10 ended with Saul's armour in Dagon's house. Here the idols are left lying on a battlefield, and Israel's king does with them what the law said.
verseByVerse.examples: David asked, Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand? He would not assume either from the fact that he had just been crowned.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them. Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines come hunting the newly crowned king, and David, who could have trusted his own experience, asks God first and is told to go up.

When the Philistines heard. The Philistines had left David alone for years: he had been their vassal at Ziklag, and a divided Israel suited them. They come the moment he is crowned, “to search for David”, hunting a person. What they tolerated while Israel was in pieces is intolerable now that a shepherd has the whole country behind him: a united people under God’s king is the one arrangement God’s enemies cannot live beside.

David inquired of God. They raid the Valley of Rephaim, almost at Jerusalem’s gates. David, who had beaten them all his life and could have moved on instinct, stops and asks. He will not presume that a crown is a licence to act, or that a righteous cause guarantees a result. The last king went to a medium because heaven had stopped answering (10:13); this one puts a plain question to God and gets a plain answer.

How we seek guidance. David probably inquired, as before, through the priest with the ephod, the priestly garment used in asking God’s will (1 Samuel 23:9–12). Christians do not have the ephod; they seek guidance through God’s completed word, prayer and wise counsel, led by the Spirit given to God’s children (Romans 8:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives the victory through David’s hand, and David names the place for the God who broke through; then he burns the Philistines’ gods, as the law required.

Like a bursting flood. The picture is the bank of a dry stream bed giving way in a spring storm: water building behind an obstruction until the obstruction is simply gone. David does not say he outfought them. God burst through, “by my hand”, which is the doctrine of this book in three words: the flood was God’s and the sword was David’s.

Baal-perazim. Breaking out is the word used a chapter ago of Uzzah (13:11). David had been angry at a God who breaks out; now, in a field of dead Philistines, he makes the same word a name to bless God by. Nothing about God had altered between the two places. It was David who had changed.

They were burned. The idols lie where their people dropped them running, and the king does what the law said: “burn their carved images with fire” (Deuteronomy 7:5). He got the ark wrong; he does not get this wrong. A man just taught what obedience costs is careful with the next commandment he meets. Second Samuel says David and his men carried the idols away (2 Samuel 5:21); they took them, and then burned them.
verseByVerse.note: “Baal-perazim” means “Lord of breaking through” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Wait for the Sound in the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second battle shows that past guidance is no substitute for present seeking. The Philistines raid the same valley again (v. 13). David has a fresh victory and a proven method, but he inquires of God again, and this time the orders are different: do not go straight up, go round behind them, and wait by the balsam trees for “the sound of marching” in their tops, the sign that God has gone out before him (vv. 14–15). David does exactly as God commands, and the Philistines are driven from Gibeon to Gezer (v. 16). The chapter ends where it began, with the LORD exalting his king: David’s fame spreads, and the LORD makes the nations fear him (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's answer is not today's orders. God said go up once and says do not go up now, about the same enemy in the same field, and the only way to know was to ask again.
verseByVerse.examples: Much of the life of faith is like this: not inventing victories but following where God has already gone, and moving when he makes the way plain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley. And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with the same enemy in the same valley, David does not repeat what worked before but asks God again, and God gives different orders and goes out ahead of him.

When David again inquired of God. Same enemy, same valley, and David has a proven method. He had a recent answer from God for this exact situation, and a battlefield named after the result. Repeating it would not have felt like presumption; it would have felt like faith. He asked anyway, and these are the most impressive words in the chapter.

Go around and come against them. The orders had changed: “You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees.” Not up the valley this time but round behind, and then wait.

The sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees. The signal is a rustle overhead that sounds like men on the move, a sound no commander can arrange and no scout can fake, and it means that the God who broke out like a flood is already in the trees ahead of the infantry. By the time David’s men step out of cover the fighting has begun without them. Their whole task is to move when they hear it and finish what Another has started.

The army of God. Two chapters ago the men gathering to David were “a great army, like an army of God” (12:22). Here the army of God is in the treetops going out ahead of them, and all that is required of Israel is to keep step with a march they can hear and cannot see. So it is for Christ’s people, whose decisive battle he has already fought and won, and who follow where he has gone.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “balsam trees” is rare, and no one knows exactly what tree it names. Older English versions said mulberry trees, and others suggest a shrub of the dry valleys that oozes sap. The meaning of the scene is clear either way: a stand of trees whose tops could rustle.

verseByVerse.quote: And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David obeys exactly, the Philistines are driven off, and the chapter closes as it opened, with the LORD exalting his king.

David did as God commanded him. Words that could not have been written of chapter 13. Fifteen miles of pursuit drove the Philistines off Israel’s ridge onto the coastal plain. (2 Samuel 5:25 has Geba, a nearby town easily confused with Gibeon.)

The fear of him upon all nations. His name travelled, and God carried the fear. The chapter opens with the LORD establishing David and closes with the LORD frightening the nations, and the cedar, the sons and the victories sit between the two. Neither David’s asking nor his obeying made the Philistines run. God went out in front, in the treetops, where nobody could see him and everybody could hear him coming.

14.theology:
Twice David asks before he moves, and the second time he was told something different (vv. 10, 14). God's word to us yesterday is not a standing order for tomorrow.

The chapter begins and ends with God’s action (vv. 2, 17). In between David fights and says God broke through by my hand (v. 11), the same refusal to separate God's work from the man's that ran through chapter 11.
14.examples:
Everyone draws a conclusion from his own success; the test is what he concludes (v. 2). David concluded that God had put him where he was for others' benefit.

Scripture often reports a sin without comment and lets the reader watch it grow, as with the wives of verse 3.

And David went out only when God had gone out ahead of him. The Son of David has gone ahead of his people into the battle that matters most, and won it: But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

keyVerse.quote: And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines.
keyVerse.note: The verse holds the chapter together: the king who now seeks God waits for God to move, and the victory is God’s before it is David’s. It answers the failure of chapter 13, where Israel went ahead on its own plan, and it points to Christ, who has gone out before his people and won the battle they could not.

14.reflection:
David took Hiram’s gift as proof that the LORD had made him king “for the sake of his people Israel” (v. 2). How would it change the way we use our position, money or gifts if we saw them as held for others?

The Chronicler records David taking more wives without comment, though the law forbade it (v. 3; Deuteronomy 17:17). How can blessings and blind spots sit side by side in a believer’s life, and what does that teach us about our need of a better King?

David had a winning method from the first battle, yet he asked God again and received different orders (vv. 13–14). Where are we tempted to rely on what worked last time instead of seeking God now?

God went out before David in the treetops (v. 15). What does it mean for us that Christ has already fought and won the decisive battle, and how should that shape the way we face our own struggles?

15.title: The Ark Comes Right: Worship on God's Terms
15.text: <sup>1</sup>David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it.<sup>2</sup>Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever.<sup>3</sup>And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.<sup>4</sup>And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites:<sup>5</sup>of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers;<sup>6</sup>of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers;<sup>7</sup>of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers;<sup>8</sup>of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers;<sup>9</sup>of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers;<sup>10</sup>of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.<sup>11</sup>Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab,<sup>12</sup>and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it.<sup>13</sup>Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."<sup>14</sup>So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy.<sup>17</sup>So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah;<sup>18</sup>and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel.<sup>19</sup>The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;<sup>20</sup>Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth;<sup>21</sup>but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith.<sup>22</sup>Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it.<sup>23</sup>Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>24</sup>Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>25</sup>So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing.<sup>26</sup>And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.<sup>27</sup>David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod.<sup>28</sup>So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.<sup>29</sup>And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
15.overview:
Where we are. Three months after Uzzah died (chapter 13), and after God had blessed David’s house and given him two victories when he sought him (chapter 14), David tries again to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem.

The message. God is to be approached in the way he has given, and when he is, the result is not terror but joy. David confesses that the first attempt failed because “we did not seek him according to the rule” (v. 13), and this time the ark is carried as Moses commanded, with more music, not less. Obedience did not quench the joy; it made the joy safe. Only one person in the chapter does not rejoice, and she is Saul’s daughter.

Why it was said. The returned exiles kept the temple services with their priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers (see the introduction). This chapter showed them that the ordered worship they kept was no dead formality but the way David learned, through grief, to bring God’s presence home with gladness.

How the chapter makes its case. David prepares a tent and declares that only the Levites, whom the LORD chose, may carry the ark (vv. 1–3). Six Levitical houses are mustered by name and number (vv. 4–10). The priests and Levite chiefs are told to consecrate themselves, David confesses what went wrong the first time, and the ark goes up on the Levites’ shoulders with the poles (vv. 11–15). Singers, players, a director, gatekeepers and trumpeting priests are appointed (vv. 16–24). The ark comes up from Obed-edom’s house with sacrifice and shouting, the king dressed in linen like the Levites (vv. 25–28), and Michal watches from a window and despises him (v. 29).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The God no hand could touch at Perez-uzza came among his people in flesh, the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and opened “the new and living way” to God (Hebrews 10:20): a way given, not invented. And David laying aside what set him apart to go up among the servants of the sanctuary is a faint picture of the Son who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and who was despised by those who thought such humility beneath a king.

For us. We come to God by the way he has given in Christ, not by our own inventions, and coming that way frees us to worship with all our heart. Those who have seen what the King laid aside for them will not be too proud to rejoice before him, whatever the watchers at the window think.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — This Time, According to the Rule
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This time David seeks God according to the rule. He pitches a tent for the ark in the city of David (v. 1) and states what he has learned: no one but the Levites may carry it, “for the LORD had chosen them” (v. 2). He assembles all Israel again (v. 3) and musters six Levitical houses, 862 men, most of them from Kohath, the clan the law had charged with the holy things (vv. 4–10). Zadok, Abiathar and the chiefs are told to consecrate themselves, and David says out loud what went wrong: “we did not seek him according to the rule” (vv. 11–13). They obey, and the ark goes up on their shoulders with the poles, “as Moses had commanded” (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 turns the book's key word back on the king. David set out to seek God and found that wanting to was not enough: seeking him includes coming the way he said.
verseByVerse.examples: When God's people have done something wrongly in public, the way back is the one David took: find out from Scripture what should have been done, say so plainly, and do it right in front of the same people, trusting the God who forgives the confessed sin (1 John 1:9) and lets his people begin again.

verseByVerse.quote: David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it. Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever. And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David prepares a place for the ark and, having learned from the law, declares that only the Levites, whom the LORD chose, may carry it.

David built houses for himself. Three months on, with the ark in another man’s house, the first thing verse 1 reports is that David built houses for himself, and then that he prepared a place for the ark of God. The Chronicler leaves the two clauses in that order. He is not scoring a point; he is telling the truth about how things get done.

The LORD had chosen them. The reason for the rule is not that Levites are safer or stronger but that “the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever”. The regulation was never crowd control. God had said who.

David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem. It was the second time. A man who has led a nation into a public disaster must decide whether he will ever ask them to assemble again, and David summons the same crowd to the same road to watch him do it properly.

Two sanctuaries. From this verse until Solomon’s temple Israel has two sanctuaries: the tabernacle with its bronze altar at Gibeon, still standing at the end of the book (21:29), and the ark in David’s tent. It is Chronicles that tells us why Gibeon was “the great high place” where Solomon sacrificed (1 Kings 3:4; 2 Chronicles 1:3).

Opening the book. Somewhere in the three months David found out how the ark was to be carried. The instruction had been in writing for centuries, available to anyone who asked a priest. A man who could raise 340,000 soldiers needed a funeral to make him open the book, and it is often a disaster that sends us back to Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites: of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers; of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers; of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers; of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers; of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers; of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David musters the Levites by family, above all the Kohathites whom the law had charged with carrying the holy things: careful obedience is what his repentance looked like.

The sons of Aaron and the Levites. Verse 4 opens with a distinction the first attempt had ignored. Priests and Levites are two orders with two kinds of work, and the first attempt had used neither. Then six houses, named with their chiefs: Kohath 120 under Uriel, Merari 220 under Asaiah, Gershom 130 under Joel, and three more clans from within Kohath, Elizaphan 200, Hebron 80 and Uzziel 112. Eight hundred and sixty-two men.

Of the sons of Kohath. Kohath, Merari and Gershom are Levi’s three sons, and all three are here, but four of the six contingents come from Kohath, the branch the law had charged with the holy things themselves. When the wagons were handed out at Sinai, Gershon received two, Merari four and Kohath none, because what Kohath carried went on the shoulder (Numbers 7:6–9). This is not a general call for volunteers with strong backs. David has gone to the exact clan the regulation named, and summoned the rest of the tribe to walk with them.

Unlike chapter 13. There nobody had been appointed, and the ark went up the road in the care of whoever happened to be walking beside it. The difference is not zeal; there was no shortage of zeal at Chidon. This time somebody worked out whom God had said should do the job, found them, and wrote down their names, and the Chronicler records the numbers because careful counting was what repentance looked like.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab, and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it. Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tells the priests and Levite chiefs to consecrate themselves, and confesses before them all that the first attempt failed because “we did not seek him according to the rule.”

The priests Zadok and Abiathar. David sends for the two chief priests and the six Levite chiefs. Zadok is here, the young man “mighty in valor” from chapter 12 (12:28), now at the head of the priesthood, and beside him Abiathar, the one man who got out of Nob alive when Saul had eighty-five priests killed in a day (1 Samuel 22:18–20). Two survivors of very different disasters, summoned to handle the ark.

Because you did not carry it the first time. Verse 13 is the sentence this whole part of the book has been moving towards, and every clause does work. “You did not carry it”: the Levites are told to their faces that the failure was theirs too; the men who knew the law had watched the cart go past. “The LORD our God broke out against us”: the verb of Perez-uzza and Baal-perazim, and David now says it was against us, not against Uzzah alone.

We did not seek him according to the rule. That is the word this book keeps returning to (10:14; 13:3). Seeking God is not only a matter of wanting him badly enough; it includes finding out how he has said to come and then coming that way, and the difference had cost a life.

What he does not say. Not that Uzzah was careless, or the oxen stumbled, or God was severe, though three months earlier he had been angry enough to think it. He says we, before the men who did the carrying and a nation that had watched it happen, and then gets on with the arrangements. That is what honest confession sounds like.

verseByVerse.quote: So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time the Levites, made ready, carry the ark on their shoulders with the poles, exactly as God commanded through Moses.

Consecrated themselves. Consecration meant washing, laundering, abstaining, and setting a distance from ordinary life for a set time: slow, unglamorous, invisible in a procession. The men who would touch the poles took time making themselves fit, and the crowd would never know.

On their shoulders with the poles. The rings on each side of the ark had held those poles since it was made, and the poles were never to be taken out (Exodus 25:14–15). Everything needed to carry it correctly had been attached to it all along, including on the day it rode a cart.

As Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD. The authority is stated twice. For readers who might think an old book of regulations a lower thing than a living encounter with God, to obey what Moses wrote is to obey the LORD.

Carried in his mother’s arms. Not wheels or oxen: the throne of God moved through Israel on the shoulders of men made ready for it. Centuries later the God enthroned above those cherubim came among his people in flesh, the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the One no hand could touch at Perez-uzza was carried in his mother’s arms.

Isn’t real worship spontaneous? Many of us assume that what is truly ours comes from inside, and that whatever is received from outside, a set prayer, an old form, a rule in an ancient book, is second-hand and probably hollow. Chapter 13 passes that test easily. It was spontaneous, heartfelt and loud, and a man died. Chapter 15 is worship by the book, with the poles, the clans and the consecrations all done as Moses commanded, and it has far more joy in it. That is less of a paradox than it seems. Love asks what the beloved wants, and is glad to be told; forms that God has given do not crush the heart but give it somewhere safe to go. And underneath, nobody comes to the holy God by self-expression any more than by rule-keeping. We come by a way he opened himself, “the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20). Because the way is given, the worshipper is free to sing with all his might.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Getting the rule right does not make the worship quieter; it organises the joy. David tells the chiefs of the Levites to appoint singers with harps, lyres and cymbals “to raise sounds of joy” (v. 16). Three chief musicians head the list, Heman, Asaph and Ethan, one from each branch of Levi, on bronze cymbals (vv. 17–19), with a second order behind them on harps and lyres in two settings (vv. 20–21). Chenaniah directs the music, “for he understood it” (v. 22). Gatekeepers are posted at the ark itself, Obed-edom among them, and seven priests are to blow the trumpets in front of it (vv. 23–24). Not one of these posts existed in chapter 13.
verseByVerse.theology: Nine verses of appointments stand between the confession and the procession. Worship careful about God's word turns out to have more music in it, not less.
verseByVerse.examples: Not everyone is a Heman or an Asaph. Most of those named here played in the second rank or kept a door, and their names are in Scripture too.

verseByVerse.quote: David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy. So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah; and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel. The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Getting the rule right does not silence the joy: David has the Levites appoint singers and players “to raise sounds of joy”, led by Heman, Asaph and Ethan, whose songs Israel would sing for centuries.

To raise sounds of joy. Before the ark moves, David appoints the choir. One reading of chapter 13 concludes that the lesson was to be more solemn, and this verse forbids it: the aim is joy, and getting the rule right is what made the shouting safe.

Heman, Asaph, and Ethan. Chapter 6 traced Heman to Kohath and Asaph to Gershom, and Ethan is “of the sons of Merari”: one chief musician from each of Levi’s sons, side by side. No branch was left out of the noise. Behind them stand eleven players of the second order, written into Scripture by name. Three men are remembered for the cymbals; these eleven were the sound.

Their psalms. Asaph’s name stands over a dozen psalms still sung, including the one that admits a man nearly lost his footing over how well the wicked were doing: “my feet had almost stumbled” (Psalm 73:2). Two more psalms name a Heman and an Ethan: the darkest prayer in the book, ending on the word darkness (Psalm 88), and the meditation on God’s covenant with David that asks how long the promise will lie in ruins (Psalm 89). Nobody in that street knew the men on the cymbals were being handed a work that would outlast the city, and that Israel would pray their words in a foreign country centuries later.

Is this a model for church worship? David organised the music by God’s command (2 Chronicles 29:25), for the sanctuary. The New Testament calls the church to sing “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16) but sets no pattern of choirs or instruments. Some Reformed churches sing unaccompanied for that reason; others use instruments as aids. Both are faithful if the words come first and “all things should be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth; but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith. Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it. Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark. Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything around the ark is ordered: musical settings, a skilled director, gatekeepers at the ark itself, and priests with the trumpets God himself prescribed.

According to Alamoth … according to the Sheminith. The harps and lyres play in two settings kept distinct, so that the sound had structure, not volume alone. Both words stand in psalm titles (Psalms 46 and 6): somebody kept the performance notes.

For he understood it. Chenaniah got his post because he knew what he was doing, and nothing is added about his piety. That is no slight on piety; leading musicians is a skill, and a consecrated man who cannot hear a wrong note is not the man for it.

Gatekeepers for the ark. Berechiah and Elkanah are stationed at the ark itself. Somebody had to stand between the crowd and the thing that had killed a man, and the post was given names and an order rather than left to whoever was nearest, as at the threshing floor.

The priests, should blow the trumpets. Seven priests go in front with trumpets, the one instrument God specified himself: two of hammered silver, to call the congregation, move the camp, go out to war, and sound “on the day of your gladness” over the burnt offerings (Numbers 10:1–10). Every one of those occasions is happening at once on this road. The column now has silver trumpets at its head, Levites with poles behind, cymbals and strings, doorkeepers beside the ark, a director who understood music, and a king dressed like a porter. Not one of those posts existed in chapter 13.

Obed-edom and Jehiah. Obed-edom, named three times here (vv. 18, 21, 24) and probably the man whose house the ark is leaving, could have watched it go. Instead he took a post at the door and walked beside it to Jerusalem, and his descendants are still on the temple roster later, sixty-two of them, with the note “for God blessed him” (26:5, 8).

Uncertain wording. No one knows for certain what Alamoth and Sheminith mean. Alamoth resembles the word for young women and may mean a high register, like women’s voices; Sheminith means “the eighth” and may mean a lower register or an eight-stringed instrument. In verse 22 the Hebrew word translated “music” can also mean carrying, so some versions make Chenaniah director of the carrying of the ark, here and in verse 27; the ESV and most versions take it as music. On either reading he was chosen because he understood the work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark comes home with joy, and the only discord is in one heart. David, the elders and the commanders go to fetch the ark from the house of Obed-edom “with rejoicing” (v. 25). Because God helped the Levites who carried it, past the place where Uzzah died, they sacrifice seven bulls and seven rams (v. 26). The king wears fine linen like every Levite in the procession, and a linen ephod (v. 27), and all Israel brings the ark up with shouting, horn, trumpets, cymbals, harps and lyres (v. 28). Then the camera moves to a window: Michal the daughter of Saul sees the king dancing and despises him in her heart (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The sacrifice in verse 26 is thanks for being kept alive: nobody had forgotten the threshing floor.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to stand at a window while God comes near and feel only contempt for those rejoicing (v. 29); the danger is not only for Saul's daughter.

verseByVerse.quote: So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing. And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark comes up with rejoicing, and when God brings the carriers safely past the place of judgment, they thank him with sacrifice.

From the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing. Same road as last time, same ark, same king, and many of the same people, walking towards a place with a grave in it and a name that meant the breaking out against Uzzah.

Because God helped the Levites. The clause only makes sense if you remember why they were frightened. God helped the carriers: that is the reason given for the sacrifice, and it means the men under the poles reached the end of the journey alive and knew this was not a foregone conclusion. Fourteen animals were offered in thanksgiving for a walk completed. Doing the right thing in the right way had not made these men casual about being near God; it had made it possible to be near him.

The word help. Helping is the word this part of the book keeps using. Men came to David to help him, and the Spirit told him, “your God helps you” (12:18); now God helps the men carrying his throne up a hill. Every one of them had two hands on a pole, and every one of them was being held.

verseByVerse.quote: David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod. So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day the throne of God enters his city, the king lays aside what marks him out and dresses like a servant of the sanctuary.

A robe of fine linen. The king is in the same fine linen as the porters and the choir. He has come out in the uniform of the men doing the lifting, and over it he has put an ephod, which is not royal dress at all. It is what a priest wore, and what the boy Samuel wore in the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:18).

What David is doing. He is not seizing the priesthood; a later king of Judah tried that with a censer in his hand and came out of the temple a leper (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). He is doing something deliberate and different. On the day the throne of God enters his capital, David takes off the clothes that set him apart and dresses like a servant.

Not a robe but glory laid aside. There is a night in an upper room when the Lord of glory rose from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him (John 13:3–5). David in linen at the head of a procession is a small picture of a very great one: the Son who laid aside not a robe but the privileges of glory, and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Michal, Saul’s daughter, looks down from a window and despises the king who has humbled himself before God: the house that never sought the ark has no joy at its coming.

Michal the daughter of Saul. Michal had been David’s wife since he brought Saul two hundred Philistine foreskins for her, and she had once let him down through a window to save his life (1 Samuel 18:27; 19:12). The Chronicler gives none of that. He gives her father’s name, and the reader who has come through chapter 10 knows what it means: the house that did not seek the ark in the days of Saul is watching the ark arrive.

She despised him in her heart. Second Samuel tells the rest: the quarrel in the doorway, her sarcasm, his answer that he would make himself more contemptible than this, and the note that she had no child to the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:20–23). The Chronicler cuts it all and stops at six words. Nothing was said and nobody in the street knew. The contempt stayed inside, and it was complete already.

Two vantage points. Down in the road is a king in a linen tunic with no crown on, shouting, out of breath, in the middle of a crowd, going up the hill behind the poles. Up in the house is a window, and a woman standing at it, with everything she was raised to value telling her that what she sees is beneath the dignity of a throne. She was not wrong about the dignity; that was the whole point of the linen. What she could not see from a window was that the man in the street had understood something her father never did: when God comes to live among his people, there is no dignity worth keeping that would stop a man going out to meet him. The Son of David would be despised in the same way, and for the same humility (Isaiah 53:3).

What it does not mean. David’s dancing was the joy of a festal procession in the street, not a pattern for the church’s gathered worship, and this commentary does not take it as warrant for liturgical dance in services. But it does forbid us to look down on wholehearted joy in God, or to stand at the window while others rejoice.

15.theology:
Verse 13 completes a lesson begun at 10:14: wanting God is not the same as coming the way he has said. The remedy was not less enthusiasm; it was the book of Moses, read, and 862 men called by name.

Verse 15 joins two authorities as one: as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD. And in verse 26 the God whose rule they kept is the one who helped the Levites who were carrying the ark. Obedience did not put them beyond needing help; it put them where help was given. The same holds for Christ's people, who obey not to earn God's nearness but because in Christ he has already come near, and whose obedience is upheld by his Spirit.
15.examples:
David confessed in the first person plural and named the exact fault. Then he organised the thing properly, which is repentance that goes beyond words.

Chenaniah led the music because he understood music. Competence is a genuine qualification, not something unspiritual, and the chapter most concerned with doing things God's way says so.

Obed-edom saw the ark taken from his house and joined the procession as a doorkeeper. A blessing that moves on can be followed rather than mourned.

keyVerse.quote: Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule.
keyVerse.note: David’s confession explains both chapters: the disaster of chapter 13 and the joy of chapter 15. Seeking God includes coming the way he has said, and David says “we”, owning the failure as his own. The verse points to the way of approach God has given once for all in Christ.

15.reflection:
David confessed, “we did not seek him according to the rule” (v. 13), taking the blame on himself and the leaders rather than on Uzzah or God. What does honest confession look like for a leader, a family or a church after something has gone wrong?

Chapter 15 is more carefully ordered than chapter 13 and far more joyful. How can doing things God’s way free us to worship with all our heart rather than make worship stiff?

“God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark” (v. 26). Where have you known God’s help in a task you feared, and how did you thank him for it?

David laid aside what set him apart, and Michal despised him for it (vv. 27–29). How does Christ’s humility, laying aside his glory for us, challenge the dignity we like to keep in front of others?

16.title: The Psalm of Praise: The Ark at Rest and the Song That Fills the Earth
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.<sup>2</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD<sup>3</sup>and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.<sup>4</sup>Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals,<sup>6</sup>and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.<sup>7</sup>Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.<sup>8</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples!<sup>9</sup>Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!<sup>10</sup>Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice!<sup>11</sup>Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!<sup>12</sup>Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered,<sup>13</sup>O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!<sup>14</sup>He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth.<sup>15</sup>Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,<sup>16</sup>the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac,<sup>17</sup>which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant,<sup>18</sup>saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."<sup>19</sup>When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it,<sup>20</sup>wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people,<sup>21</sup>he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account,<sup>22</sup>saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"<sup>23</sup>Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day.<sup>24</sup>Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!<sup>25</sup>For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods.<sup>26</sup>For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.<sup>27</sup>Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.<sup>28</sup>Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!<sup>29</sup>Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness;<sup>30</sup>tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.<sup>31</sup>Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!"<sup>32</sup>Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it!<sup>33</sup>Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.<sup>34</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!<sup>35</sup>Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.<sup>36</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.<sup>37</sup>So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required,<sup>38</sup>and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers.<sup>39</sup>And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon<sup>40</sup>to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.<sup>41</sup>With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever.<sup>42</sup>Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.<sup>43</sup>Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
16.overview:
Where we are. The ark has come up to Jerusalem with joy (chapter 15). Now it is set in its tent, and the day ends with offerings, gifts of food and the first song sung before it.

The message. When God comes to live among his people, the right answer is thanksgiving: thanksgiving that remembers what he has done, tells the nations who he is, and hopes in his steadfast love. The psalm David appoints moves from memory (the covenant with Abraham) to mission (sing, all the earth) to hope (gather us from among the nations), and rests everything on a God who keeps his word for a thousand generations.

Why it was said. The first readers were few, under foreign rule, with many of their people still scattered (see the introduction). They sang these words in their own temple, and the psalm’s last prayer, “gather and deliver us from among the nations” (v. 35), was theirs. The chapter told them that their praise went back to the day the ark came home, and that God’s covenant and love had outlasted all they had lost.

How the chapter makes its case. The ark is set in the tent with offerings, and David blesses the people and gives food to every man and woman (vv. 1–3). Levites are appointed to invoke, thank and praise the LORD, with Asaph at their head (vv. 4–7). The psalm calls Israel to seek the LORD and remember his covenant with Abraham (vv. 8–22), summons all the earth and all creation to rejoice before the coming Judge (vv. 23–33), and ends in thanks, a prayer to be gathered, and the people’s Amen (vv. 34–36). Then the standing arrangements: Asaph before the ark in Jerusalem, Zadok at the altar in Gibeon, and David home to bless his household (vv. 37–43).

Where it leads. By promise and by the need it exposes. The covenant with Abraham, “the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations” (v. 15), finds its yes in Christ, Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:16), in whom the nations the psalm calls are blessed. The Judge for whom the trees sing is the man God has appointed and raised from the dead (Acts 17:31). And the chapter ends with worship cut in two, the ark in one place and the altar in another, a division healed only in Christ, in whom the presence of God and the one sacrifice meet.

For us. Thanksgiving is a calling, not a mood: remember what God has done in Christ, tell others, and hope in his steadfast love. We may be few and of little account, but we sing under a covenant that cannot fail. And like David, we take that worship home, to bless the people we live with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Ark at Rest, and a Loaf for Everybody
