verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark is at rest, and the first acts before it are sacrifice, blessing and a gift for everyone. The ark is set inside David’s tent with burnt offerings and peace offerings (v. 1). David blesses the people in the name of the LORD and gives bread, meat and raisins “to all Israel, both men and women” (vv. 2–3). Then he makes the day’s praise permanent: Levites are stationed before the ark “to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD” (v. 4), Asaph at their head with harps, lyres and cymbals, and two priests blow trumpets “regularly” (vv. 5–6). Verse 7 dates the founding: on that day thanksgiving was first appointed to be sung.
verseByVerse.theology: Worship at the ark ended not in awe alone but in a meal shared from the peace offerings (v. 3), and nobody was left out.
verseByVerse.examples: Thanksgiving was given a place and people to carry it on (v. 4). A church does well to make room for thanks on purpose rather than leave it to mood.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark is set at rest in its tent, and the day is marked by sacrifice, blessing and a gift of food from the king to every man and woman present.

They brought in the ark of God. After Shiloh, the Philistine capture, decades in a private house on a hill, a death on a threshing floor and three months in Obed-edom’s house, the throne of God is set down in a tent in the capital, and the men who carried it straighten up.

Burnt offerings and peace offerings. A burnt offering went up entirely in smoke; a peace offering was shared, part burned, part to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshipper and his family before God. One says everything here is yours; the other says come and eat with me.

He blessed the people in the name of the LORD. David blesses the people as Aaron’s sons were commissioned to do (Numbers 6:23), and then does something that follows straight from the peace offering: he gives food “to all Israel, both men and women”. The text goes out of its way to name both. Not just the elders or the Levites who had done the work: a woman at the back of the assembly went home with bread, meat and raisins from the king.

A table for everyone. That is the day at ground level: a hand held out with food in it, to everyone, without a list. The God who came to live among his people set a table when he came, and Scripture’s last picture of the finished work is a feast, “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), with guests from every nation.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “a portion of meat” occurs only here and in the parallel (2 Samuel 6:19), and its meaning is not known for certain. Older interpreters took it as a piece of meat; some modern scholars suggest a cake of dates. Either way it was a generous gift, and the point is that every person received it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals, and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David makes the day’s praise permanent, appointing Levites whose ongoing work is to invoke, to thank and to praise the LORD before the ark.

To invoke, to thank, and to praise. Three verbs, and they are the job description. To invoke is to bring God’s acts to remembrance out loud; to thank is to name what he has done as a gift; to praise is to say what he is like. That is the heart of a worship service in three words, and from this day it is somebody’s occupation.

Beyond the law of Moses. The law of Moses said nothing about this. Its regulations concerned blood and bread and incense and the fabric of a tent; there is no order of singers in Leviticus. Yet this is not David improvising: the Chronicler later says the order of Levitical musicians was “the commandment … from the LORD through his prophets” (2 Chronicles 29:25). The God who had regulated how his throne was carried now enlarged his worship with song. Getting the rule right did not make worship smaller.

Asaph was the chief. Behind him nine players on harps and lyres, Obed-edom among them again, and Asaph himself on the cymbals. And two priests, Benaiah and Jahaziel, blow trumpets “regularly before the ark of the covenant of God”.

Regularly. The trumpets that sounded in front of the procession are not put away when the excitement is over. Someone will blow them tomorrow, and the day after, and on the wet ordinary morning when there is no crowd. The most striking word in the paragraph is the dullest one in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thanksgiving that Israel’s singers offered every day began on the day the ark came home, and the psalm David appointed moves from memory to mission to hope.

Then on that day. A date: what the readers heard every day in the temple began the day the ark came home.

Where the psalm comes from. The psalm is recognisable: the opening of Psalm 105 (vv. 8–22), almost all of Psalm 96 (vv. 23–33), and the first and last verses of Psalm 106 (vv. 34–36). Whether it was assembled from three songs or three songs grew from it cannot be settled, and need not be.

Backwards, outwards, forwards. Its shape is deliberate. Remember what God swore to your fathers; tell the nations who is on the throne; ask him to gather you home. Israel’s worship began the day it was given a memory, a mission and a hope, in that order. Its last lines, “gather and deliver us from among the nations”, fit any time Israel was scattered, and the returned exiles would have sung them gladly.
verseByVerse.note: David’s psalm (vv. 8–36) is woven from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–22 — Remember: the Covenant with Abraham
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm’s first movement is memory, and it turns memory into seeking. Israel is to give thanks, call on God’s name and make his deeds known among the peoples (vv. 8–9), and, at the heart of the book’s message, “seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!” (vv. 10–11). They are to remember his wonders and judgments (vv. 12–14), and above all his covenant: made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob, with the land of Canaan as its promise (vv. 15–18). It was made when they were “few in number, of little account”, wanderers whom God guarded by rebuking kings: “Touch not my anointed ones” (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 10 and 11 carry the word the book turns on: the congregation is told to seek God's face, and to keep seeking after they have found it.
verseByVerse.examples: To seek his presence continually (v. 11) is the believer's ordinary daily work, not a stage to be outgrown: turning to God in his word and in prayer, today and again tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually! Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to thank God, tell the nations what he has done, and above all seek him: not an object or a rule now, but his presence, continually.

Make known his deeds among the peoples! The opening commands already have the nations in view. On the day a tent was pitched on a Judean ridge, the congregation is told that what has happened to them is news for everybody else. Verse 9 joins two commands to sing with a harder one: tell. Telling is not performance; it is talking about what God has done, out loud, to someone, the way one person passes on a piece of news.

Seek the LORD and his strength. Three times in verses 10 and 11, seek. The word has carried the book since the verdict on Saul (10:14), and what is sought has changed. In chapter 13 David sought it, the neglected ark (13:3); in chapter 15 he learned to seek him according to the rule (15:13). Here it is neither the ark nor the rule but God himself: “seek his presence continually”, literally his face. A man can get an object into a tent and keep a rule exactly without wanting the face of God, and David was taken through both to arrive at the third.

Seek his presence continually! Continually rules out the obvious mistake. The ark has just been brought home and sits a few steps away, and the command is to go on seeking, every day. Having God does not mean the seeking stops, and the Spirit God sends into his children’s hearts, crying “Abba! Father!”, is the one who keeps them seeking (Galatians 4:6).

Remember the wondrous works that he has done. Verse 12 turns verse 9 inward: the same wondrous works are to be told to outsiders and remembered by insiders, and a congregation that stops remembering will soon have nothing to tell.

The judgments he uttered. A word enters that will not leave the psalm. First they are “the judgments he uttered” (v. 12), then “his judgments are in all the earth” (v. 14), and at the end the trees sing because “he comes to judge the earth” (v. 33): what he has said, what he is doing everywhere, what he is coming to do, all reasons for singing.

His chosen ones! The congregation is addressed not as achievers but as “his chosen ones”, children of Jacob, a man who spent his life being carried by God rather than impressing him. The command to seek rests on that choice.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must keep in mind the covenant God never forgets: the promise made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, with the land as its pledge.

He is the LORD our God. “Our God”, and “in all the earth” (v. 14): the God of one people rules the whole world, and the rest of the psalm holds both together.

Remember his covenant forever. Verse 15 differs from Psalm 105:8, where “he remembers his covenant forever”. Here Israel is told to remember it. Both are true, and the second depends on the first. The covenant is safe whether or not anyone in Jerusalem thinks of it before breakfast. But people who forget it live like people with no covenant, and Israel had just come through a generation of exactly that: nobody cancelled the ark; they simply stopped thinking about it.

The covenant that he made with Abraham. What is remembered is a chain of three: made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob. The promise had outlived all three by close to a thousand years when this psalm was sung, and has outlived them by far longer since.

To you I will give the land of Canaan. The congregation singing of the land of Canaan is standing on it. The first readers of this book sang the same words living on a fraction of it under a Persian governor, a harder and better thing to do.

Where Christians differ. Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists (Christians who read God’s promises to Israel as awaiting a separate, literal fulfilment) hold that it does: the promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. Others note that Joshua already says, “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (Joshua 21:45), and that the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs desired “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).

This commentary’s view. The land is fulfilled in Christ and in the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5). Faithful Christians differ here, and many on both sides expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26); all can share the singers’ confidence that God keeps every word he swears.

verseByVerse.quote: When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made and kept his covenant when his people were few and of no account, guarding them from kings: a word the small community of returned exiles was meant to hear as their own.

When you were few in number. Where the Psalter says “they were few in number” (Psalm 105:12), here it says “you”: the line is addressed to the singers. Consider who sang it when this book was written: a few thousand returned exiles in a half-rebuilt town, of no political weight, moved between empires twice in living memory. Few in number and of little account was not a flourish to them. It was the census.

Why God works in smallness. The point is not that God pities small people. The covenant the psalm rests on was made with three men who had no land, army or standing, at the mercy of whoever hosted them. Smallness was the condition God chose to work in, and always has been; the gospel itself began in a manger and a band of fishermen.

He rebuked kings on their account. God struck Pharaoh’s house and came to Abimelech in a dream over Sarah (Genesis 12:17; 20:3), and both times a king with an army was told to keep his hands off a wandering herdsman. And the titles: “my anointed ones”, using the word that will one day give us Messiah, for a man who owned only a burial cave and a well he had to argue for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second movement turns outward to the whole world. All the earth is to sing and the nations are to hear of his glory (vv. 23–24), because the LORD is great and the gods of the peoples are “worthless idols”, while he made the heavens (vv. 25–26). Strength and joy fill his presence (v. 27). The families of the peoples are summoned to ascribe glory to him and to “bring an offering and come before him”, trembling at his holiness (vv. 28–30). Then heaven, earth, sea, field and forest are called to rejoice, because “the LORD reigns” and “he comes to judge the earth” (vv. 31–33). The song written for one small nation’s tent ends with the whole creation.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD reigns (v. 31) is sung over a tent on a small ridge in a minor kingdom. It is a statement about who holds the throne, by people who could see little evidence of it out of the window.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has suffered a wrong that was never put right may find verse 33 the most hopeful line in the psalm: the Judge is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples! For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song turns to the whole world: the nations are to hear of the LORD’s glory, because their gods are nothings and he made the heavens.

Sing to the LORD, all the earth! The song turns outward here and never really turns back. Every phrase in verses 23 and 24 takes in the whole world. The ark has just been installed in one tent in one city of one small nation, and the song written for the occasion spends its central movement addressing peoples who were not invited.

Worthless idols. The word is a mocking one: nothings, non-entities, a word that sounds in Hebrew like the word for gods and means the opposite. The contrast is not that Israel’s God is stronger. It is that theirs were made and ours makes. Every god in every temple on that coast had a workshop it came out of and a craftsman who could tell you what it cost; “the LORD made the heavens”, and the two cannot be compared at all.

Strength and joy are in his place. One clause describes what it is like where he is: “Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.” Not strength and terror, not joy and sentiment, but power and gladness found together where God is.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are called to give the LORD the glory that is his, and to come before him with offerings, trembling at his holiness: the door is open, and what lies beyond it is holy.

Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples. Now the nations are told to do what Israel is doing. Ascribe means hand over what belongs to him. It is not a request for compliments but the return of property: the glory is his already, the peoples have been assigning it elsewhere, and the psalm calls them to give it back.

Glory and strength! Strength has been running quietly through this psalm. The congregation was told to seek the LORD “and his strength” (v. 11); his sanctuary is where “strength and joy” are (v. 27); and now the nations ascribe strength to him. Israel seeks it, God has it, everyone else is called to admit whose it is, and no one is encouraged to think he has any of his own.

Bring an offering and come before him! This is the surprising part. Foreigners are told to come into the courts of Israel’s God with a gift in their hands: not to admire from a distance, not to send tribute by messenger, but to come. On the day the ark entered Jerusalem, the song appointed for it was already looking at Ammonites, Phoenicians and Egyptians and telling them there was room. That door stands open now in the gospel, which goes to every nation.

Tremble before him, all the earth. The terms come in the same breath: “Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him”. Come, and tremble. The door is wide open and what is on the other side is holy, and both must be said together.

The world is established. A clause that steadies everything: “yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.” It was sung by a nation overrun by Philistines in living memory, and sung again, later, by people who had watched their city burn.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!" Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns now, against all appearances, and the whole creation is called to rejoice because he is coming to judge the earth and put it right.

The LORD reigns! Two words in Hebrew, the summary of the psalm and of the book. He reigns, present tense, over nations who have not yet heard of him. A young kingdom with a tent for a temple and enemies on every side, on a ridge any serious empire could take: the evidence for what they sang was almost nil, and it was true.

Let the sea roar. Then creation joins in: sea, field and forest, the parts of the world with no interest in Israel’s politics, are called to make a noise, and the reason is the one nobody expects: “for he comes to judge the earth”.

Judgment as good news. We hear judgment as a threat, and rightly. But for a forest, a river, or anything that has suffered under human misrule, a judge’s arrival means someone with authority is coming to put things right, and everything groaning applauds.

The judge the trees sing about. The New Testament names him. God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31), and creation waits with eager longing to be set free (Romans 8:19–21). The judge the trees sing about bears the marks of the nails, which is why his coming can be sung about at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–36 — His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends where Israel’s worship would always end: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 34). This line, which would be sung at the temple’s dedication, before battle, and over the foundations of the second temple, is followed by a petition that does not fit the day: “gather and deliver us from among the nations” (v. 35). It fits the Chronicler’s readers, many of whose people were still scattered. The song closes in blessing God “from everlasting to everlasting”, and the people take it as their own with “Amen!” and praise (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 35 is a prayer for exiles in the mouth of a congregation that was not in exile.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 34 is a sentence to take into any day, including the worst: whatever else has stopped, his steadfast love has not.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends in thanks for God’s steadfast love, which never stops, and in a prayer to be gathered from the nations, a prayer the Chronicler’s scattered readers could make their own.

Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good. This line is sung again and again in Israel’s history. It is sung when Solomon’s temple is dedicated and the glory fills the house so that the priests cannot stand to minister (2 Chronicles 5:13–14), and when fire falls on the altar (2 Chronicles 7:3). Jehoshaphat puts a choir in front of his army and sends them out singing it against three nations (2 Chronicles 20:21). Generations later, when the foundation of a much smaller temple is laid and the old men who remembered the first one are weeping, it is what the builders sing (Ezra 3:11–12). A whole psalm was eventually written with it as every second line, twenty-six times over (Psalm 136).

His steadfast love endures forever! Steadfast love is covenant loyalty, the settled determination of God to keep faith with people who do not keep faith with him. The claim made about it is duration: not that it is warm or generous, though it is, but that it does not stop. The people who would need that sentence most were those for whom everything else had stopped.

Gather and deliver us from among the nations. The last petition is sung on the most gathered day in Israel’s history so far, and it does not fit the occasion at all. It fits the readers. They had come back from Babylon, most of their relatives had not, and gather was the word their whole generation lived on. The Chronicler shows that their prayer was already in the first song sung before the ark, so that when they prayed it they were not adding a modern complaint to an ancient liturgy; they were singing what David appointed, and it was already about them.

All the people said, “Amen!” The choir stops and the nation answers with one word, which means: let it be so; this prayer is ours too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the festival come the standing arrangements, and they leave Israel’s worship in two places. Asaph and his brothers minister “regularly before the ark” in Jerusalem, with Obed-edom and the gatekeepers (vv. 37–38). Zadok and the priests stay at the tabernacle in the high place at Gibeon, offering the burnt offerings “regularly morning and evening” as the Law commanded, with Heman and Jeduthun appointed to give thanks, “for his steadfast love endures forever” (vv. 39–42). The ark is in one place and the altar in another, a division the rest of the book works to heal. Then everyone goes home, and David goes “to bless his household” (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worship is in two places, both obedient and neither whole, and everything David does for the rest of the book aims at one house.
verseByVerse.examples: The household that once sheltered the ark became one of the clans that served it (v. 38). Small faithfulness can grow into a family's calling.

verseByVerse.quote: So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required, and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers. And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The standing arrangements leave Israel’s worship divided, the ark in Jerusalem and the altar at Gibeon, a division only a future house, and finally Christ, would heal.

Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers. Obed-edom came into this story as a man who took in an object nobody else would touch, and he is here with sixty-eight brothers on the permanent staff of the ark; by the time the temple rosters are drawn up his family holds the gates with sixty-two more (26:8). The household that sheltered the ark for three months has become one of the clans that serve it.

Before the tabernacle of the LORD. The tent Moses made at Sinai, with the bronze altar in front of it, still stands on another hill at Gibeon, about six miles away. So the priests stay there to offer the burnt offering “regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel”. How it came to Gibeon is not recorded. It had stood at Shiloh, in Saul’s day the priests served at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1–6), and it was probably moved after Saul had the priests of Nob killed (1 Samuel 22:18–19).

Two sanctuaries, one problem. In Jerusalem there is the ark, the throne and the presence, and no altar of burnt offering, so the daily sacrifice cannot be kept there. At Gibeon there is the altar, the daily sacrifice and the full order of the law, and no ark, so the mercy seat is absent and the Most Holy Place is empty. Israel’s worship has been cut in two; each half does exactly what it has been told, and neither half is whole. David cannot resolve it. He keeps both, obediently, and hands the problem to his son. Everything he does in the rest of this book (the site bought on a threshing floor, the plans, the gold, the courses of priests, the charge to Solomon) is aimed at the day the throne and the altar stand under one roof.

No need for a second address. They did, for a while, and then that house came down too. The presence of God and the place where blood is shed were finally brought together on a hill outside Jerusalem, in a man who was himself the offering and the mercy seat, the true temple and the King, and there has been no need for a second address since.

Uncertain wording. Verse 38 is hard to follow. It names “Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers”, then “Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah” as gatekeepers. It may mean one man named twice, first with his kinsmen and then in his office, or two men of the same name, one of them a son of Jeduthun. Chapter 26 counts Obed-edom among the gatekeepers (26:4–8), and the text does not allow certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever. Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Gibeon too, men are appointed by name to give thanks, so that whichever sanctuary an Israelite went to, he heard the same words about God’s steadfast love.

Chosen and expressly named to give thanks. Somebody wrote a list, and it was a list of men whose duty was gratitude: not to guard a gate or kill a bull, but to say thank you, on the record, in a rota, at a sanctuary six miles from where the crowd was.

For his steadfast love endures forever. The refrain returns seven verses after it was sung, as though the Chronicler cannot let it go. It has become the standing text at both sanctuaries: the ark has it in Jerusalem and the altar has it at Gibeon, and whichever hill an Israelite climbed he heard the same sentence about God.

Heman and Jeduthun. Three psalms are headed with Jeduthun’s name (Psalms 39, 62 and 77), and one of them is the prayer of a man who kept silent until “My heart became hot within me”, and who ended by asking God, “Look away from me, that I may smile again” (Psalm 39:3, 13). That prayer carries the name of a man appointed to give thanks. Thanksgiving as an office does not require a man who has never been in the dark.

The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate. Trumpets and cymbals for the music, and the sons of Jeduthun at the gate: the men who play and the men who stand at the entrance are listed in one breath, with the same care.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great day ends as every day of worship should, with the people going home, and the king going to bless his own household as he had blessed the nation.

All the people departed each to his house. The greatest day of worship in the nation’s history so far ends the way every service ends, with people walking home to their own doors, to supper, and to whatever was waiting for them there.

David went home to bless his household. The king goes to do at his own table what he has just done at the ark. He blessed the people in the name of the LORD in verse 2; now he goes home to bless his household. The same man, the same blessing, a smaller room. Whatever was true in front of a nation had to be true in a house with his children in it. The other account follows him through the door to Michal’s scorn (2 Samuel 6:20–23); the Chronicler leaves him on the threshold.

Where the ark was heading. It is a right place to stop: a man going in to pray for the people who live with him. That is where the ark was always heading, not into a building but into the ordinary rooms of a people God had decided to live among. The God who came into a tent on a ridge has since come nearer than that: by his Spirit he lives in his people, and does not go home at the end of the day, because he is already there.

16.theology:
Verses 10 and 11 are the centre of the book's argument, and what is sought has changed: from Saul who did not seek (10:14), to the ark (13:3), to God according to the rule (15:13), to his presence, sought continually. Having God is not the end of seeking God.

And the psalm faces the singers: remember where the Psalter has he remembers (v. 15), you where it has they (v. 19), and a prayer to be gathered on a day nobody was scattered (v. 35). The first song sung before the ark fits people not born for centuries.
16.examples:
Every person in the crowd went home with bread and meat, with no list and no ranking: the chapter's theology with a loaf in it.

The trumpets sounded regularly, the singers as each day required. The hard part was not the procession but the ordinary days after it. Christians who find their own praise fitful can take heart: the Son sings his Father's praise in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:12), and our thanks are offered through him.

The blessing that costs most is usually the one given at your own table, to the people who know exactly what you are like (v. 43).

keyVerse.quote: Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!
keyVerse.note: This is the watchword of the whole book, set at the heart of the first song sung before the ark. In chapters 13 to 15 David learned to seek the ark and then to seek God according to the rule; here what is sought is God’s own presence, his face, and the seeking never stops. In Christ, God’s face is turned towards us, and we seek him with confidence.

16.reflection:
David’s psalm moves from remembering what God has done (vv. 8–22), to telling the nations (vv. 23–33), to hoping in his steadfast love (vv. 34–36). Which of these comes least naturally to you, and how could it grow?

Israel was told to “seek his presence continually” (v. 11) on the very day the ark came home. Why does having God never end the seeking, and what does seeking his face look like in an ordinary week?

The covenant was made when God’s people were “few in number, of little account” (v. 19). How does that encourage a small church, or a Christian who feels insignificant?

After the great day, David “went home to bless his household” (v. 43). What would it mean to carry Sunday’s worship into the home this week?

17.title: The Davidic Covenant: God's Promise That Changes Everything
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent."<sup>2</sup>And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."<sup>3</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>4</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in.<sup>5</sup>For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling.<sup>6</sup>In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>7</sup>Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel,<sup>8</sup>and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>9</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly,<sup>10</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.<sup>11</sup>When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>12</sup>He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever.<sup>13</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you,<sup>14</sup>but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>15</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>16</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>17</sup>And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God!<sup>18</sup>And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant.<sup>19</sup>For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.<sup>20</sup>There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>21</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt?<sup>22</sup>And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>23</sup>And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken,<sup>24</sup>and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>25</sup>For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.<sup>26</sup>And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>27</sup>Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
17.overview:
Where we are. The ark is at last in its tent in Jerusalem, with singers ministering before it (chapter 16), and David lives in the cedar palace Hiram’s craftsmen built (14:1). This chapter is the hinge of the book: everything before it brings the king and the ark to Jerusalem, and everything after it prepares for the house God now promises (see the introduction).

The message. David wants to build God a house, and God answers that he will build David one. The LORD needs nothing from his servants; instead he binds himself by a promise: a son of David whose throne, set inside God’s own kingdom, will stand forever. Grace runs from God to us first, and the right answer to it is David’s: wonder, praise, and prayer that takes God at his word.

Why it was said. The Chronicler’s readers had no king, and no son of David had sat on a throne since the exile (see the introduction). Had the promise died with the monarchy? The chapter answers that the throne was always God’s: “my house” and “my kingdom” (v. 14). And it leaves out the warning about the son’s sins that stands in Samuel, giving them the half they most needed: “I will not take my steadfast love from him” (v. 13).

How the chapter makes its case. David proposes a temple and Nathan approves (vv. 1–2), but that night God says no: he has never asked anyone for a house (vv. 3–6). Then God gives: he took David from the sheep, and he will build him a house, a son whose throne he will establish forever (vv. 7–14). Nathan reports every word (v. 15). David sits before the LORD in astonishment (vv. 16–19), praises the God who has no equal and the people he redeemed (vv. 20–22), and asks God to do exactly what he has promised (vv. 23–27).

Where it leads. By promise, directly. No son of David reigned forever until the angel said of Mary’s child that God would give him “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). Hebrews applies verse 13 to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5), and Peter says God kept this oath by raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). In him the covenant rests, as David saw, on God’s own heart (v. 19).

For us. We keep trying to do something great for God and so put him in our debt; he keeps outgiving us. The gospel calls us to receive before we build, and to pray as David did, with a courage that comes from God’s promise and not from ourselves. What God has blessed in Christ “is blessed forever” (v. 27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A House of Cedar and a Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God needs nothing from David, not even a temple. Settled at last in a cedar palace, David is troubled that the ark of the covenant still lives under a tent, and he plans to build it a house (v. 1). Nathan, warmly and too quickly, tells him to go ahead (v. 2). That same night God overrules his prophet (vv. 3–4). The reason is not that David is unworthy but that God has never asked: for centuries he moved with his people “from tent to tent”, and never once said to any judge, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?” (vv. 5–6). The offer, however sincere, had the relationship the wrong way round.
verseByVerse.theology: God's silence about his own accommodation is the striking thing here. The initiative in this chapter was never going to be a man's, because God had no unmet need for a man to meet.
verseByVerse.examples: Nathan gave sincere, godly-sounding advice on his own authority and was wrong. God corrected him the same night, before the king had laid a stone, and the prophet was humble enough to go back in the morning and say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent." And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settled in comfort at last, David is troubled that God’s ark has less than he has, and Nathan blesses his plan before God has spoken.

When David lived in his house. For the first time in his life David lives somewhere that does not have to be taken down and carried. After caves, a Philistine border town, a wilderness stronghold and Hebron, he has a roof of Lebanon cedar (14:1).

Under a tent. Nothing has gone wrong. The ark is where David put it, in the tent he pitched for it, with singers ministering before it every day (16:1, 37). What troubles him is the comparison: he is the first man in Israel whose house is better than God’s. Comfort gave him time to look around, and it is not a bad instinct: a man in a cave does not compare his roof with anyone’s.

Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you. Nathan’s answer sounds unimpeachable. The heart is devout, and God is indeed with David (11:9). But the prophet has not been told anything: he has admired the impulse and given a verdict in the name of a God who has not yet spoken. Advice is not right merely because it is warm and devout.

verseByVerse.quote: But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in. For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says a plain no to a good man’s best idea, and his reason is that he has never asked anyone for a house. He overturns his own prophet’s advice that same night, before anyone has picked up a tool, a mercy to both men.

It is not you who will build me a house. In 2 Samuel 7:5 God puts it as a question; here it is a flat statement. The reason is not that David is unworthy, nor that the timing is wrong, but that God has gone “from tent to tent”.

From tent to tent. Some four hundred years of it. Each time the tabernacle was taken down, carried and set up again (Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob, Gibeon), the God of heaven went with his people and lived where they lived, a God without a fixed address because they had none either.

Why have you not built me a house of cedar? Through the whole disorderly age of the judges God never complained about his housing. The God who owns the cedars of Lebanon has no need for a king to meet (compare Psalm 50:12; Acts 17:24–25).

The God who pitched his tent among us. The God who went from tent to tent with Israel did the same thing more deeply in his Son. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and John’s word for dwelt means pitched his tent. God’s willingness to live where his people live, homeless when they were homeless, came to its fullest in one who had “nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

Why is it so hard to receive? David’s offer is the most natural thing in the world, which is what makes God’s answer so searching. The anthropologist Marcel Mauss, studying gift-giving across many societies, argued that a gift is never simply free: it obliges the receiver to give something back, and to take without repaying is to be lowered. We still feel it when we insist on paying for dinner, or find it far easier to help than to be helped. Religion left to itself runs on the same instinct: God has been good to me, so I will do something great for him, and then we are square. God will not be squared. He will not let David put him in his debt; he outgives him, “the LORD will build you a house” (v. 10), and in the end gives David’s greater Son, a gift no one could ever repay. The fitting answer to grace is not to settle the account but to be glad, and then to give freely, as people whose account was never open.

Why could David not build the temple? David later gives a further reason: he had shed much blood in war (22:8; 28:3). The temple was to be built in a time of rest, by Solomon, whose name echoes the Hebrew word for peace (22:9). The two reasons stand together: God had never asked for a house, and when one was built, he chose a man of peace to build it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — I Will Build You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having refused David’s gift, God gives instead, and the gift is larger than anything David thought to ask. He retells David’s life in verbs that are all his own: he took him from the sheep, was with him, cut off his enemies, and will make him a name (vv. 7–8). He promises his people a settled place (vv. 9–10). Then the hinge of the chapter: “the LORD will build you a house” (v. 10). One of David’s sons will build the temple, but God will build the dynasty, as a father with a son, and his steadfast love will not be withdrawn as it was from Saul, for this throne stands in God’s own kingdom forever (vv. 11–14). Nathan delivers every word (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The word for house means a building and a family, and the chapter turns on the second meaning. David offered God a roof; God answered with a dynasty.
verseByVerse.examples: The promise had to be delivered by the man whose advice it contradicted, and he delivered all of it (v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel, and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having refused David’s gift, God begins to give: he made David all he is, he will make him a name, and he will settle his people in peace.

I took you from the pasture. God starts with a biography in which every verb is his: took, have been with, cut off. The man in a cedar house is reminded that he was last seen walking behind sheep, and that nothing in between was self-made. The word for his office is not king but prince, a leader appointed under someone else.

I will make for you a name. At Babel people set out to make a name for themselves, and God scattered them (Genesis 11:4–9); then he promised one childless nomad, Abraham, to make his name great (Genesis 12:2). David is given the same gift: he set out to build God a house, and God gives him a name instead.

I will appoint a place for my people Israel. Before the dynasty comes the people: God will plant them and end the wasting by violent men that had gone on since the judges. The king is lifted up for the sake of his people (14:2).

I will subdue all your enemies. The next three chapters are this promise being kept, one campaign at a time (18:6, 13).

Where Christians differ. Does the promise of a place where Israel will be planted (v. 9) mean that the land still belongs to the Jewish people and modern Israel, with its borders, still awaiting fulfilment? Dispensationalists hold that it does.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), the patriarchs looked for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and the place is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5). Faithful Christians differ, and the comfort of verse 9 belongs to all of them: God himself plants his people where no violent man can uproot them.

verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you, but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises David a dynasty: a son who will build the temple, whose throne God will establish forever as a father with his son, inside God’s own kingdom.

A house for David. David offered stone and cedar; God promises a house of another kind, a line of sons on a throne (v. 10), a gift David could not have asked for because it had not entered his head.

When your days are fulfilled. David will be dead before any of it happens. The promise is made to a man who will not see it, about a boy who is at this point a name on a list (14:4).

He shall build a house for me. David’s project is not cancelled, only reassigned, and he spent the rest of his life buying the site, gathering the gold, drawing the plans and organising the priests for a building he would never enter (chapters 21–29).

As I took it from him who was before you. Saul is in the sentence without being named. The last royal house in Israel lasted one generation and ended on Gilboa (chapter 10). This one will not go that way, and the reason given is not how well the son performs but a relationship: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.”

What Samuel adds. The account in Samuel adds that when the son commits iniquity, God will discipline him “with the rod of men” (2 Samuel 7:14). The Chronicler does not deny it; his second volume records that discipline falling on Solomon’s line. But writing for people whose kings were gone and whose city had burned, he gives the half they most needed: the steadfast love will not be withdrawn.

In my house and in my kingdom forever. Samuel says “your house and your kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:16); Chronicles says “my house” and “my kingdom”. David’s son is confirmed inside something that was never David’s to hand on, and later this book calls the throne in Jerusalem “the throne of the LORD” (29:23). Israel’s kings were tenants in God’s own kingdom, which is why that kingdom could survive the loss of every king who held it.

His throne shall be established forever. Is the son Solomon or Christ? Both. Solomon built the temple (v. 12), but his line lost the throne after some four hundred years. No son of David reigned forever except Christ, and Hebrews applies verse 13 to him (Hebrews 1:5). He is also the Son who builds the lasting house of God, not of cedar but of people: “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18). The word forever was always waiting for him.

Where Christians differ. Is Christ reigning on David’s throne now? Dispensationalists look for a future earthly throne in Jerusalem, reading the throne and the place literally.

This commentary’s view. Peter says God fulfilled this oath by raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36), so the throne is Christ’s now and his kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33). This commentary holds that view, and gladly owns those who differ as brothers waiting for the same King.

verseByVerse.quote: In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathan delivers the whole message, including the part that overruled his own advice.

In accordance with all these words. The verse says twice that nothing was left out, and what could most easily have been left out was the beginning, where God said no to the plan Nathan had blessed the day before. The prophet told the king that yesterday’s counsel had been overruled, with no sign of softening it or making excuses, and then drops out of the chapter.

Nathan again. He will come back, in 2 Samuel 12, with a story about a lamb and a rich man and a sin nobody else dared name, and he will not soften that either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace is answered with wonder. David goes in and sits before the LORD, and his first words are a question: “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?” (v. 16). God has spoken of generations to come (v. 17), and David, the great psalmist, runs out of words, content that God knows him (v. 18). The cause of it all is God’s own heart (v. 19). Then David praises two things without equal: there is no God like the LORD (v. 20), and no people like Israel, because God himself went to redeem them and made them his own forever (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer moves from David's house to God himself: before he asks for anything, he confesses who God is and what God has done for Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Faced with a gift he cannot account for, David does not bargain or protest. He sits, asks why, and then praises, and the order is worth copying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God! And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant. For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with God’s promise, David can only wonder that God should do this for him, and he traces it all to God’s own heart.

King David went in and sat before the LORD. Not kneeling or standing; the writer thought the posture worth recording. A man does not stand to attention at his father’s table.

Who am I, O LORD God? He has just been handed an everlasting dynasty, and his opening line is that he cannot see why. There is no false modesty in it and no bargaining; he is genuinely at a loss.

For you know your servant. He runs out of words and says so, a strange admission from the man whose name stands over nearly half the psalms. And he gives the reason he can stop: “you know your servant.” There is no need to explain himself to someone who already knows what he is.

According to your own heart. Verse 19 gives the cause of the whole thing, and it is not David: not his record, not the kingdom’s need, not a reward for bringing up the ark. A covenant founded on what God is like cannot be undone by anything the other party turns out to be, and that is the ground every believer stands on (2 Timothy 1:9).

Uncertain wording. The second half of verse 17 is one of the hardest lines in Chronicles to translate. The ESV’s “have shown me future generations” renders a compressed Hebrew phrase that older versions read quite differently (the KJV has hast regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree), and the parallel in 2 Samuel 7:19 is also obscure. The general sense is not in doubt: God has spoken of David’s house far into the future, and the view stops him.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt? And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David praises two things without equal: the LORD, beside whom there is no God, and the people he went in person to redeem and make his own.

There is none like you, O LORD. The prayer lifts away from David’s house. None like him and none besides him, “according to all that we have heard with our ears”: David believes it because Israel remembered it.

Who is like your people Israel? The second claim rests entirely on the first. Israel is not incomparable because of anything in Israel, but because of who came to fetch it. They were slaves in a brickyard, and the one thing that set them apart was that God himself went down to bring them out.

Whom God went to redeem. Note the verb: God went. He did not send. And the purpose given is not the slaves’ comfort but God’s name: “making for yourself a name for great and awesome things.” God rescued a nation and won a name by it, and then turned round and made a name for David (v. 8). All through the chapter God gives away what he could have kept.

You, O LORD, became their God. Both halves were his doing: he made them his, and he became theirs. It is the covenant’s great promise, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33), and it reached its height when God came in person a second time, in his Son, to redeem a people for himself from every nation (Titus 2:14; Revelation 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–27 — Do As You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks God to do exactly what he has promised. The petition adds nothing of his own: “do as you have spoken” (v. 23), so that God’s name will be magnified and people will say that the LORD of hosts is Israel’s God (v. 24). David explains where his boldness came from: God revealed the promise first, so “your servant has found courage to pray before you” (v. 25). The prayer ends at rest on two facts, that the LORD is God and that he has promised this good thing (v. 26), and on the certainty that what he blesses “is blessed forever” (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The goal David names is not the security of his family but the magnifying of God's name: his house is the means and God's reputation is the end.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 gives the reason a man dares to pray at all, and it is not his mood or his record. God had spoken first. Courage in prayer is a response to a promise, and David says so in as many words.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken, and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to do exactly what he has promised, and the promise is what gives him courage to ask.

Do as you have spoken. He asks for precisely what God has offered and adds nothing of his own. Every petition here was first a promise, which is much of what praying is: handing God’s word back to him as a request.

Your name will be established and magnified forever. His deepest motive is God’s glory, not his family’s security: that people will say, “The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel’s God” (v. 24).

Therefore your servant has found courage to pray. The boldness has a cause outside him. 2 Samuel 7:27 says, literally, that he found his heart to pray, and what gave him heart was not a surge of feeling or a run of good days but a promise, spoken first, by God. Take the promise away and there is nothing to be confident about; leave it there and a shepherd can sit before the ark and ask the Almighty to keep his word.

Still the only door. Hebrews tells frightened people to “draw near to the throne of grace” with confidence (Hebrews 4:16), and the confidence is never in the one approaching. It is in the one who went before, whose perfect obedience stands where ours fails, and in what God has said he will do, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer ends at rest: God is able, God has promised, and what he blesses stays blessed forever.

You are God, and you have promised. You are God, so you are able. You have promised, so you are willing. Everything a man needs to be sure of is in that pair, and David has stopped trying to add to it.

It is blessed forever. Not that it will be blessed if the sons behave. What God has blessed stays blessed, because the blessing never depended on the worth of the one blessed.

Forever, twice. The word forever appears eight times in this chapter, and David uses the last two in his final sentence. Sitting in a tent, in a young kingdom, with a throne no son of his has yet inherited, he says forever twice in one breath.

No end to his kingdom. He was right, though not in a way he could have measured. His line held Jerusalem for four centuries and then lost it, and the last of his sons to wear the crown was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains (2 Kings 25:7). Nearly six hundred years later an angel stood in a village in Galilee and told Mary that her son would reign over the house of Jacob forever, “and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). The house is still standing. “It is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever.”

17.theology:
The covenant rests on God's character and nothing else: according to your own heart (v. 19), not for services rendered and not to meet a need of God's own (vv. 5-6).

Chronicles gives the promise without the discipline clause that stands in 2 Samuel 7:14 and calls the throne God's own (v. 14). Both changes point the same way, at readers who had no king left: the kingdom was never David's property, so its loss was not the loss of the promise. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son is applied in the New Testament not to Solomon but to Christ, and the word forever, used eight times here, finally means what it says.
17.examples:
Being sincerely encouraging is not the same as having heard from God. Nathan's approval was warm and mistaken, and his readiness to reverse it is as much an example as the mistake.

David wanted to build and was told his son would. He spent the rest of his life buying the site, stockpiling the materials, drawing the plans and organising the priesthood for a building he would never walk into. A refused ambition can be worked at for the rest of a life by somebody who has accepted the refusal.

keyVerse.quote: Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.
keyVerse.note: This sentence turns the chapter round. David offered to build God a house of cedar; God answers that he will build David a house of sons and a throne that lasts forever. It is grace in its plainest form, God giving where he could have received, and it finds its fulfilment in Jesus, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end.

17.reflection:
David wanted to do something great for God, and God said no and promised to do something great for David instead (vv. 1–10). Why do we often find it easier to give to God than to receive from him? Where do you try to keep the account square?

Nathan spoke warmly before he had heard from God, and then delivered God’s correction in full (vv. 2–4, 15). What does his example teach us about giving advice, and about admitting we were wrong?

God did all this “according to your own heart” (v. 19), not because of David’s record. How does knowing that your salvation in Christ rests on God’s character change the way you face your own failures?

David found courage to pray because God had promised first (v. 25). Which of God’s promises in Christ could you turn into prayer this week, and what would it mean to pray them with David’s confidence?

18.title: David's Victories: The King Who Subdues the Nations
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>7</sup>And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.<sup>9</sup>When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah,<sup>10</sup>he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.<sup>12</sup>And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>13</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>14</sup>So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>15</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;<sup>16</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary;<sup>17</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
18.overview:
Where we are. God has just promised David, “I will subdue all your enemies” (17:10). Chapters 18 to 20 show him keeping that word, and the Chronicler gathers David’s wars into one place, told at speed, so that the reader sees the promise at work.

The message. The LORD gives his king victory wherever he goes, and the victories have a purpose beyond themselves. The spoil is dedicated to God and stored up for his house, and the peace that is won is used to give justice and equity to all the people. Power given by God is held for God and for others.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were a small province ringed by the old neighbours named here: Philistines, Moabites, Edomites and Arameans (see the introduction). They needed to remember that the LORD had once given his people rest from them all, that wealth was meant for his worship, and what a king of David’s line was for.

How the chapter makes its case. Philistia, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans of Damascus fall in turn, and David cripples the captured chariot horses rather than trust in them (vv. 1–5). The refrain sounds: “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (v. 6). The gold shields go to Jerusalem and the bronze into the furnishings Solomon will make for the temple (vv. 7–8). Tou of Hamath sends gifts, and everything from five nations is dedicated to the LORD (vv. 9–11). Edom falls and the refrain sounds again (vv. 12–13). Then comes the point of it all: justice and equity for all the people, served by a settled government (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. David here is the king Israel longed for: victorious, devoted to God’s house and just to all. He was so only in part, and his sons less. The prophets took the same pair of words, justice and righteousness, and gave them to a coming son of David whose government would have no end (Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 23:5). Jesus is that King. He won his decisive victory not with chariots but on a cross, where he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15), and he brings justice to the nations (Matthew 12:18–21).

For us. Every success God gives, whether ability, money or position, is given for his house and for other people, not to be hoarded. We serve a King whose victories are rescues, and we can bring him our plunder: the strength and resources that once served only ourselves, now set apart for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Victories, and Bronze for a Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD gives David victory on every side, and David refuses to trust in what he wins. Philistia, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans of Damascus fall in turn and become tribute-paying vassals (vv. 1–6). David hamstrings the captured chariot horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots (v. 4), as the law and Joshua’s example taught. Then the refrain that explains every victory: “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (v. 6). The gold shields of Hadadezer’s guard go to Jerusalem, and the captured bronze goes somewhere 2 Samuel never mentions: into the bronze sea, the pillars and the vessels that Solomon will make for the temple (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: David won every war he fought, and the record calls it rescue rather than conquest: the LORD saved him wherever he went (vv. 6, 13).
verseByVerse.examples: Victory did not teach David to trust in horses. He disabled the captured chariot teams rather than build a chariot army of his own (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God begins to keep his word to subdue David’s enemies: the Philistines and the Moabites, who had once hunted or sheltered him, now serve him. “After this” ties the wars to the promise just given: “I will subdue all your enemies” (17:10).

He took Gath and its villages. Gath was Goliath’s town. It was also where David, a young fugitive carrying the giant’s own sword, had run for asylum and escaped only by feigning madness, spittle running down his beard (1 Samuel 21:10–15); later he lived sixteen months there as a vassal of its king (1 Samuel 27:7). Now he owns it. The Chronicler writes the name and moves on.

The Moabites became servants to David. David’s great-grandmother Ruth had walked out of Moab behind Naomi, and when Saul was hunting him David had asked the king of Moab to shelter his parents (1 Samuel 22:3–4). Now the Moabites bring tribute. Servants is the treaty word for a vassal state, which kept its own rulers but paid tribute and owed loyalty to its overlord (so also vv. 6, 13). Samuel adds a grim detail about Moabite prisoners measured with a line (2 Samuel 8:2), which the Chronicler leaves out.

verseByVerse.quote: David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David defeats the greatest power in the region, refuses to build his strength on captured chariots, and the Chronicler gives all the credit to the LORD.

Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath. Hadadezer, an Aramean (Syrian) king whose reach ran towards the Euphrates, is the largest enemy in the chapter, and the fighting has reached the river God named to Abraham as the far border of the promised land (Genesis 15:18).

David hamstrung all the chariot horses. Any other king would have kept the spoil; David cripples nine tenths of the chariot horses, the most valuable weapon of war in his world. Modern readers flinch for the animals; in that world it was the usual way to put captured war horses beyond use.

Why the horses were crippled. God’s law said Israel’s king must not gather many horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), and Joshua had crippled captured horses at the waters of Merom at God’s command (Joshua 11:6). David refuses to build the kind of army that makes a nation trust its weapons instead of God: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). His son Solomon would keep fourteen hundred chariots (1 Kings 10:26).

The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. The verb is the Hebrew word for saving, from the same root as the name Jesus, given “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Each victory was the LORD rescuing his king and people, a foretaste of the greater rescue to come.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Here Chronicles has a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen where the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 has seventeen hundred horsemen, and the Greek translation of Samuel agrees with Chronicles, which points to a copying slip. Neither kind of difference touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds that Scripture as God first gave it is true in all it affirms.

Uncertain wording. “Zobah-Hamath” may mean Zobah towards Hamath, placing the kingdom rather than naming a second one. And it is unclear whose “monument” it was; most readers take it as Hadadezer’s. The word is literally “hand”, a mark of power, and 2 Samuel 8:3 has “to restore his power”.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David brings the gold to Jerusalem, and the bronze becomes, a generation later, the furnishings of God’s house.

The shields of gold. Ceremonial shields, carried by a king’s guard to display his wealth; Hadadezer’s splendour now hangs in Jerusalem.

The bronze sea and the pillars. 2 Samuel does not have this sentence. The bronze sea was the great basin on twelve oxen where the priests washed (2 Chronicles 4:2–6); the pillars were Jachin and Boaz at the entrance (2 Chronicles 3:15–17). The metal came out of a Syrian war fought a generation before the building existed.

Stockpiling for his son. Told he would never build the house, David spent his wars gathering the material for his son. Plunder from a pagan king became the basin where priests washed before they served: what is surrendered to God he puts to holy use.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything David wins is handed over to God. Tou king of Hamath, glad to see his old enemy Hadadezer beaten, sends his son with congratulations and gifts of gold, silver and bronze (vv. 9–10). David dedicates all of it to the LORD, together with the silver and gold taken from five nations: Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines and Amalek (v. 11). Abishai defeats the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, garrisons are set in Edom, and the refrain sounds a second time in identical words: “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A generation later Solomon will build a temple out of a treasury his father never spent, and verse 11 is where it started.
verseByVerse.examples: Even a neighbour's self-interested gifts went into the pile set apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the gifts of a self-interested foreign king, with all the spoil of five nations, are handed over to the LORD.

Tou king of Hamath. Tou had been at war with Hadadezer for years, and now David has beaten Hadadezer for him, so he sends his son Hadoram with congratulations and gifts. It is self-interested diplomacy, and the Chronicler makes no comment on the motive.

These also King David dedicated to the LORD. Five nations are named, and everything taken from every one of them is handed over: not tithed, not shared among the commanders, not put in a royal treasury, but dedicated, set apart from any other use.

Gathering for the temple. Told that his son would do what he most wanted to do, David could have lived out his days in comfort. Instead he gathered wealth for a building he would never see, until by chapter 29 the numbers stop sounding real. He accepted God’s no without sulking, and turned it into years of glad preparation for someone else’s work.
