verseByVerse.quote: And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom falls too, through David’s general Abishai, and the refrain says again that the victory was the LORD’s.

Abishai, the son of Zeruiah. Abishai is the man chapter 11 recorded as the most renowned of the thirty, who “did not attain to the three” (11:21). He is still fighting, still winning and still ranked second.

Three accounts, one battle. Samuel credits this battle to David (2 Samuel 8:13), the title of Psalm 60 to Joab, and this verse to Abishai, who led the action in the field. A king is credited with his generals’ victories. The psalm’s title gives 12,000 dead rather than 18,000, perhaps counting one part of the battle.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wars were for this: a king who gives justice and equity to all his people (v. 14). The victories made room for a settled kingdom, and the Chronicler lists the officials who ran it: Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat the recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech the priests, Shavsha the secretary, Benaiah over the royal guard, and David’s sons as “the chief officials in the service of the king” (vv. 15–17). The care in that last phrase, where Samuel calls the sons priests, shows the book’s concern that God’s worship be served only by those he appointed.
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and equity is the pair the prophets use ever afterwards to test a king, and the phrase to all his people matters as much as the two nouns.
verseByVerse.examples: The king's sons come last in the list, with a civil title (v. 17). In this book even princes do not take a priest's place.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wars were for this: a king who gives right verdicts and a right order of life to all his people, a picture of the King to come.

So David reigned over all Israel. After thirteen verses of armies and tribute, this is not a change of subject but the point of everything before it.

Justice and equity. Justice is the verdict being right; the second word, often translated righteousness, is the whole arrangement being right, so that verdicts do not have to keep rescuing people from a system built to crush them. Jeremiah would ask a later king of David’s line whether being a king meant competing in cedar, and answer that the king’s father had judged the cause of the poor and needy: “Is not this to know me?” (Jeremiah 22:15–16).

To all his people. Not only the tribes that crowned him at Hebron, or the men who joined him at Ziklag. Justice given only to those who have earned it from you is not justice; it is repaying favours. The God who saved David wherever he went asks his people to deal like this.

Justice that reaches all his people. Isaiah used the same two words of a child not yet born, whose government would have no end, and said he would uphold his kingdom “with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore” (Isaiah 9:7). Israel tasted it under David. The rest came with Jesus, the son of David, who brings justice to the nations while “a bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:18–21), and whose kingdom is the one place where justice reaches all his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A settled kingdom has a government, and the list ends with a careful choice of words that guards God’s priesthood.

Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army. Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, Ahimelech, Shavsha: the cabinet of a settled kingdom, with a secretary for a state that now has correspondence.

Over the Cherethites and the Pelethites. Professional soldiers from the Philistine coast, from the people David spent his life fighting, are now his bodyguard.

David’s sons were the chief officials. The account in Samuel says David’s sons were priests (2 Samuel 8:18); this book says “chief officials in the service of the king”. Only the sons of Aaron may offer sacrifice, and Uzzah died for touching the ark (chapter 13): the care over one word at the end of a list is the care that runs through the whole book.

Ahimelech the son of Abiathar. Abiathar was Ahimelech’s son (1 Samuel 22:20), and Abiathar seems to have had a son named Ahimelech in turn; the lists name the son here.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain what Samuel’s word for the sons meant. It is the ordinary word for priest, but it may sometimes have been used of high royal officials (compare 2 Samuel 20:26; 1 Kings 4:5), so the Chronicler may be explaining an older usage rather than correcting it. Either way, no reader can suppose that a son of David served at God’s altar.

18.theology:
The Chronicler is less interested in the battles than in where the metal went (vv. 8, 11). A king told he would never build the house spent his wars supplying it.

And verse 14 is what the fighting was for. Justice and equity to all his people is the standard for every later king of Judah, and Isaiah used the same two words of the true son of David, whose government has no end. Under him, and by his Spirit in his people, justice that reaches everyone is no longer only an ideal.
18.examples: A man who cannot do what he most wants can still spend years making it possible for somebody else. Solomon's priests washed in a basin his father had captured.

keyVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.
keyVerse.note: After thirteen verses of battles, this verse says what the battles were for. God gave David victory so that he could give his people justice, and the same pair of words became the prophets’ description of the coming son of David, fulfilled in Jesus, whose kingdom is the one place where justice reaches all his people.

18.reflection:
Twice the chapter says, “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (vv. 6, 13). How would it change the way you look at your own successes to see them as God’s gifts and rescues rather than your achievements?

David crippled the captured chariot horses rather than build his security on them (v. 4; Psalm 20:7). What are the “chariots and horses” you are most tempted to trust in?

David dedicated everything he won to a house he would never see (vv. 8, 11). What might it look like for you to give generously to God’s work that others will finish?

The wars were for “justice and equity to all his people” (v. 14). How does Jesus fulfil this picture of a king, and how should his rule shape the way we treat people who have no claim on us?

19.title: The Ammonite Humiliation and the Wars That Follow
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away;<sup>5</sup>and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah.<sup>7</sup>They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle.<sup>8</sup>When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.<sup>10</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>11</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites.<sup>12</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you.<sup>13</sup>Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>14</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him.<sup>15</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.<sup>16</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army.<sup>19</sup>And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
19.overview:
Where we are. The victories of chapter 18 continue, but this war begins differently: not with an enemy’s attack but with an act of kindness refused. It is the Ammonite war that ends with the fall of Rabbah in the next chapter (20:1–3).

The message. Kindness offered and despised turns to judgment, and the God who gives his king victory stands behind those who fight with all their strength and leave the outcome to him. David repays kindness with kindness and treats the shamed with patient care; Hanun’s suspicion, and his pride in refusing to admit a mistake, cost him everything.

Why it was said. The returned exiles lived among suspicious neighbours, Ammonites among them (Nehemiah 2:10 names “Tobiah the Ammonite”), with little strength of their own (see the introduction). Joab’s charge was the word they needed: do all you can for God’s people, and leave the result to the LORD (v. 13).

How the chapter makes its case. Nahash of Ammon dies, and David sends envoys to comfort his son (vv. 1–2). Hanun’s advisers call them spies, and he shames them; David shelters them at Jericho until their beards grow (vv. 3–5). Ammon, now a stench to David, hires Aramean armies (vv. 6–7). Joab, caught between two forces, divides his army with Abishai, pledges mutual help and gives his charge: be strong, and may the LORD do what seems good to him (vv. 8–13). Both enemy lines break (vv. 14–15). The Arameans gather again from beyond the Euphrates; David crosses the Jordan himself and wins, and they make peace and will no longer help Ammon (vv. 16–19).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need the chapter exposes. David’s kindness (the word is the one used of God’s own steadfast love) to the son of a man who had been kind to him, and his tenderness to men who had been shamed, are faint pictures of the King who, “despising the shame”, bore it for us (Hebrews 12:2). And Hanun exposes our need: the human heart reads God’s kindness as a trick. The cross is where that suspicion runs out of explanations, and God still sends envoys of peace: “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

For us. Repay kindness, and look for someone to treat better than they deserve, as God in Christ has treated us. Do not let suspicion make you deaf to his kindness. Care patiently for the shamed, and bring your own shame to Christ. And in every battle, do all that is yours to do, and leave the outcome with the Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Kindness Repaid with an Outrage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kindness offered, and despised. When Nahash king of the Ammonites dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, because Nahash had dealt kindly with him (vv. 1–2); the word is the one used of God’s own steadfast love. Hanun’s princes read the visit as spying, and Hanun believes them: he has the envoys shaved and their garments cut off at the hips, and sends them home in disgrace (vv. 3–4). David takes their shame seriously. He sends to meet them on the road and lets them stay at Jericho until their beards have grown (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: David repays a kindness a pagan king showed him when he was nobody. He repays it years later, when no one could have made him.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the measure of the man: he lets the shamed envoys recover out of sight, and sets no date.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David repays an old kindness with kindness, sending envoys to comfort the son of a dead king.

Nahash the king of the Ammonites died. Nahash is probably not a stranger to the story. He is most likely the king who besieged Jabesh-gilead a lifetime earlier and offered its men terms of one gouged-out right eye each, as a disgrace on all Israel; Saul’s first act as king was to rout him (1 Samuel 11:1–11). Ammon lay east of the Jordan on the edge of the desert, and its capital, Rabbah, stood where Amman, the capital of Jordan, stands today.

His father dealt kindly with me. That is very likely why Nahash was good to David: Saul was his enemy, so he had a use for anyone Saul wanted dead. The Chronicler does not say what the kindness was. What he records is that David remembered it. Years have passed, the debt is unenforceable and the creditor is in his grave, and the king of Israel sends an embassy across the Jordan to sit with a bereaved son.

I will deal kindly with Hanun. The Hebrew word for dealing kindly is the word for God’s steadfast love, his loyal covenant love, which the singers at the ark praised in chapter 16 (16:34). That is the logic of a man who knows what he has received: treated better than he deserved, he goes looking for someone to treat better than they deserve. It is a small picture of the kindness God has shown in Christ to people with no claim on him (Titus 3:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away; and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanun’s advisers read kindness as spying, and the envoys are shamed; David answers their shame with patient care.

To spy out the land? The suspicion is plausible. David has been swallowing kingdoms for years, and a hard-headed Ammonite counsellor has reason to wonder what Israelites are doing near his capital. But it takes a visit of sympathy to a young king whose father has just died and reads it as spying. Cynicism like this can never be proved wrong, because it has an explanation for everything: once Hanun accepted it, kindness itself became evidence against David.

Shaved them and cut off their garments. A beard was a man’s dignity, and to shave one off by force was a deep public insult; cutting the robes at the hip left them exposed. Men on an errand of sympathy were sent home that way past every village.

Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown. David does not summon them to the palace. He sends to meet them before they reach the city, so they need not be seen, gives them a town to stay in, and sets no date: “until your beards have grown”, however long it takes. He does not tell them it is only hair, or that the honour of the mission covers it. He assumes that what was done to them will take time to get over, and arranges the time. Men who have been shamed are usually told to be reasonable about it by people who were not there.

A greater King went further than Jericho. Jesus went out himself to people whom shame had driven to the edges, and then, “despising the shame”, was stripped and mocked in public (Hebrews 12:2), so that people disgraced by others or by their own sin could be covered and brought home. The patience David showed his envoys is a small picture of the welcome waiting for every ashamed person who comes to him.

The man who sees through everything. Hanun’s advisers would feel at home today. Suspicion has become the mark of the clever: we assume every kind word has an angle and every generous act a hidden interest, and we think ourselves wise for spotting it. Some of the time we are right. But C. S. Lewis pointed out in The Abolition of Man that seeing through something is only worth doing if there is something on the far side to see: “To ‘see through’ all things is the same as not to see.” The cynic is safe from being fooled and shut out from being loved. The kindness of God has been read Hanun’s way since the garden, as a trick to take something from us, and his envoys are still turned away: “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The cross is where that suspicion runs out of explanations, for nobody dies for people he is only trying to use. God’s kindness “is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4). It cannot, while we are still shaving the messengers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hanun will not admit a mistake, and it costs him dearly. Knowing they have become a stench to David, the Ammonites spend a thousand talents hiring chariots and troops from Aram (vv. 6–7). Joab marches out and finds himself caught between the Ammonites at their city gate and the hired armies in the open country (vv. 8–10). He divides his forces with Abishai, each pledged to help the other, and gives the charge at the heart of the chapter: be strong, fight for God’s people and cities, and “may the LORD do what seems good to him” (vv. 10–13). The Arameans flee, the Ammonites follow them, and Joab returns to Jerusalem (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's charge (v. 13) holds both halves without strain: use your strength, and leave the outcome with the LORD. Neither clause is an excuse for dropping the other, and the man who said it was surrounded at the time.
verseByVerse.examples: Trusting God with the outcome did not stop Joab planning what to do if the battle went badly (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah. They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle. When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rather than admit a mistake, Hanun buys an army, and Joab finds himself caught between two forces.

A stench to David. The word is used of something rotting. The Ammonites now understand what they have done, and instead of apologising they start buying an army.

1,000 talents of silver. A thousand talents of silver, chariots from three states, a whole force camped at Medeba: one of the largest mobilisations in the Old Testament, the direct result of a young king who could not say he had made a mistake.

Joab and all the army of the mighty men. Joab arrives with the mighty men and finds the trap already set: Ammonites drawn up at the city gate in front of him, and the hired kings out in the open country behind.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Verse 18 has seven thousand chariot crews where 2 Samuel 10:18 has seven hundred chariots. The thirty-two thousand chariots of verse 7 probably means chariotry with its crews and supporting troops rather than vehicles: Samuel lists twenty thousand hired men from Beth-rehob and Zobah and twelve thousand from Tob, thirty-two thousand in all, with the king of Maacah and his men named separately, just as here (2 Samuel 10:6). Neither kind of difference touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.
verseByVerse.note: A thousand talents was about 37 tons of silver (a talent was about 75 pounds, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you. Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded, Joab makes the best plan he can, pledges help to his brother, and commits the outcome to God: fight with everything, and leave the result with the LORD.

He chose some of the best men of Israel. First a plan. The best troops face the Arameans, the professionals; his brother Abishai holds the Ammonites at the gate.

If the Syrians are too strong for me. Two commanders, back to back, each promising to break off his own battle to save the other. Neither pretends the plan will certainly work. They agree in advance what to do when one of them starts losing, which is the foresight of men who have lost battles before.

Be strong. Then the charge. “Be strong, and let us use our strength”: there is no sitting back, and no suggestion that trusting God means doing less. “For our people and for the cities of our God”: he names what they fight for, and calls Israel’s towns God’s property. And the last clause hands the result to God: “may the LORD do what seems good to him.” Joab does not tell his men that God is bound to give them victory, nor that the outcome does not matter. Fight with everything for a cause that belongs to God, and leave the result with him. Christians fight their battles the same way, yet with a strength not their own: “be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10).

From Joab, of all men. It comes from Joab, who had knifed Abner in a gateway (2 Samuel 3:27), and who would later kill Absalom against the king’s order and stab Amasa on a road (2 Samuel 18:14; 20:10). That man says the truest sentence about courage and providence in the book, and Scripture records it without comment.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hired Arameans break first, the Ammonites follow, and Joab goes home with Rabbah still standing.

They fled before him. Hired troops with no stake in the quarrel take one charge from Israel’s best and run. The Ammonites, watching their expensive allies disappear, run too, back into the city. The line collapses because the men beside them left.

Then Joab came to Jerusalem. No siege, no sack, no pursuit. He has scattered the field army and goes home, and the Chronicler offers no explanation. Rabbah is still standing, and it will take another spring and another campaign to bring it down, which is where the next chapter opens, and what David was doing while it happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Syrians Sue for Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The war ends with Aram’s submission. The defeated Arameans call up their kinsmen from beyond the Euphrates under Shophach, Hadadezer’s commander (v. 16). This time David gathers all Israel and crosses the Jordan himself (v. 17). The coalition breaks, and Shophach dies on the field (v. 18). Hadadezer’s vassals make peace with David and become subject to him, and the Arameans will not help the Ammonites again (v. 19). Ammon, which bought its allies, is left alone, and the next chapter tells its end.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter began with one young king taking bad advice about an embassy of sympathy. It ends with a coalition broken, a commander dead, and a whole region changing sides.
verseByVerse.examples: Hanun still had the Ammonite army, and no friends left in the world (v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army. And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aram gathers its full strength, David himself leads all Israel against it, and the Arameans submit and abandon Ammon.

The Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. This is no longer about Ammon; it is Aram deciding whether it can live with an Israelite kingdom on its southern border.

He gathered all Israel together. This time David comes out himself. He had sent Joab to the first battle; for the second he calls up the nation, because the scale has changed.

They made peace with David. Seven thousand chariot crews and forty thousand foot soldiers fall, Shophach dies on the field, and Hadadezer’s servants become subject to David, as the promise of 17:10 had said.

Not willing to save the Ammonites anymore. The last line shows what Hanun’s decision cost him. He had bought his allies with a thousand talents, and once they were beaten they would not help him again. Allies who are bought stay only as long as it pays them.

How it began. All of it began with a delegation sent to sit with a grieving young man, and a room full of clever advisers who could not believe that anybody meant it.

19.theology:
Verse 13 holds two things most people hold one at a time: fight with everything you have, and leave the result to God. Joab neither promises victory nor excuses anyone from the battle. For a Christian the strength is not only his own: the Spirit who lives in believers is the power for the fight, and the outcome rests with a Father who has already given his Son.

That the words are Joab's does not make them less true. God's truth is not confined to the mouths of people whose lives commend it.
19.examples:
David repaid a dead foreign king's favour, though the debt was unenforceable, because being kindly treated had made him kind. And with his shamed envoys he did not minimise what had been done or hurry them through it: shame takes time to heal, and the king allowed for that.

One message admitting he had listened to bad advice would have saved Hanun a thousand talents of silver, two armies and every ally he had. An apology always looks costly beforehand. Hanun found out what refusing one costs.

keyVerse.quote: Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him.
keyVerse.note: Surrounded on two sides, Joab joins two things most people hold one at a time: full effort for a cause that belongs to God, and full trust in God for the outcome. It is the right posture for every believer, who fights with a strength the Lord supplies and rests the result with a Father who has already given his Son.

19.reflection:
David showed kindness to Hanun because Hanun’s father had been kind to him (v. 2). Whose kindness to you could you pass on, and who might you treat better than they deserve, as God has treated you in Christ?

Hanun’s advisers read kindness as a trick (v. 3). Where are you tempted to suspect the motives of others, or even of God? How does the cross answer that suspicion?

David let his shamed servants stay at Jericho “until your beards have grown” (v. 5). How can we care patiently for people who carry shame, and what does Jesus offer those who are ashamed?

Joab’s charge joins full effort with trust: “Be strong … and may the LORD do what seems good to him” (v. 13). In what situation do you need to do your utmost and leave the outcome with God?

20.title: The Siege of Rabbah and the Giants: Completing the Conquest
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.<sup>2</sup>And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>3</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued.<sup>5</sup>And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.<sup>6</sup>And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants.<sup>7</sup>And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down.<sup>8</sup>These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
20.overview:
Where we are. The Ammonite war of chapter 19 ends at Rabbah, and the Chronicler closes his account of David’s wars with three Philistine giants. Verse 1 is almost word for word the opening of 2 Samuel 11, the story of David’s sin with Bathsheba, which this book leaves untold.

The message. God keeps his promise to subdue David’s enemies, even the descendants of the giants, and the victories won by David’s servants are counted as David’s. The kingdom’s triumphs rest on God’s faithfulness, not on the king’s private record: the crown comes to David in the very season of his great failure, which the Chronicler’s readers knew well.

Why it was said. Readers with no king needed to know what God had promised David’s house and what that house was for (see the introduction). So the Chronicler tells the story of the throne rather than the private story of the man, and reminds a weak people that the giants who once terrified Israel all fell.

How the chapter makes its case. In spring Joab besieges and takes Rabbah while David stays in Jerusalem (v. 1). The Ammonite crown is placed on David’s head, the spoil is brought out, and the people are set to forced labour (vv. 2–3). Then come three short notices of war with the Philistines, each ending with a giant dead at the hands of David’s men: Sippai at Gezer (v. 4), Lahmi the brother of Goliath (v. 5), and a six-fingered man at Gath (vv. 6–7). All of them “fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants” (v. 8).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by contrast. The giants who taunted Israel fall to the servants of a king who had already beaten their champion. So Christ, David’s greater Son, fought the decisive battle alone and “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15); his people still face, one at a time, what taunts them, and every victory is counted to his name. And the silence about Bathsheba exposes a need. The crown of Rabbah sat on a king who needed mercy (Psalm 51); the King who needed none was crowned with thorns, for sinners like David.

For us. Outward success is no proof of private faithfulness, so guard your heart most when life goes well. And take up the unglamorous work of clearing the field in Christ’s name, one giant at a time, knowing that the decisive battle has already been won.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Rabbah, and What Is Not Here
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ammonite war ends, and the crown comes to David in the very season of his great sin. In spring, “the time when kings go out to battle”, Joab ravages Ammon and besieges Rabbah, but David remains at Jerusalem (v. 1); readers of Samuel know what happened there, and the Chronicler does not retell it. Rabbah falls, the crown of its king, or perhaps of its god Milcom, is placed on David’s head, and the great spoil is brought out (v. 2). The people of the Ammonite cities are set to hard labour with saws, picks and axes, and David and the army return to Jerusalem (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The book keeps the opening sentence of David's worst episode and nothing more. The reader who knows 2 Samuel finds the scene set, the king at home and the army away, and then the fall of a city, with the whole spring in between left blank.
verseByVerse.examples: In 2 Samuel the crowning comes after the prophet Nathan has confronted David with his sin by telling him a story about a lamb. Here nothing comes before it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chronicler writes the sentence that opens the story of David’s great sin, and then passes over the story itself, because his subject is the throne, not the man’s private ruin.

But David remained at Jerusalem. Anyone who has read Samuel will stop at these words, because there the account turns to David walking on his roof in the evening and seeing a woman bathing (2 Samuel 11:1–2). Spring was the season for war, with the rains over, the roads firm and crops ripening to feed an army, so “the time when kings go out to battle” makes David’s staying at home stand out.

The setting, not the scene. Bathsheba appears in this book only as Bath-shua, Solomon’s mother (3:5); Uriah’s death, Nathan and the lamb, Amnon and Absalom are not here.

Not whitewash. Some have called this, the largest omission in Chronicles, whitewash. It cannot be: in the roll of David’s mighty men this same writer prints the name Uriah the Hittite (11:41) and passes on without a word. A man concealing what David did to Uriah does not put Uriah in the honour roll.

What he is doing instead. Writing for people with no king, he tells the story of the throne rather than of the man: how Israel got a king, a city, an ark, a covenant, a site and a temple. David’s private ruin, and the mercy that met his confession (Psalm 51), is not his subject; he assumes his readers know it, writes the sentence that begins it, and moves on. For a reader who knows both books, the silence after the sentence is the loudest thing in the chapter.

A king who needed mercy. The best king Israel had needed a psalm of confession, and the promise of 17:14 never rested on his record. Only one son of David has needed no such psalm, and he took the sins of his people as his own: God “made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
verseByVerse.note: The full story is told in 2 Samuel 11–12.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rabbah falls, the Ammonite crown is placed on David’s head, and the conquered people are put to forced labour.

The crown of their king. It weighed a talent of gold, about seventy-five pounds, far too heavy to wear for long, which fits the reading that it belonged to the statue of the god Milcom (see the end of this note). It may have been held over the king of Israel for as long as the ceremony took.

It was placed on David’s head. A king who stayed at home has a foreign crown placed on his head in a city other men took. For readers who know Samuel, this triumph has those untold months in the middle of it. Centuries later soldiers placed a crown on the head of David’s greater Son, “twisting together a crown of thorns” (Matthew 27:29), and he wore it for the sins of people like David.

The spoil of the city. Then the population is set to work in every town of Ammon: the harsh end of an ancient war, reported without softening and without relish: a nation that hired armies rather than admit a mistake is quarrying stone.

Did David torture the Ammonites? The Hebrew most likely means that he set them to work with saws and picks, as forced labour, not that he killed them with tools. It is recorded, not commended.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are uncertain. In verse 2 the Hebrew can be read their king or, with the Greek translation, Milcom, the Ammonite god (compare 1 Kings 11:5), and the crown’s weight favours Milcom. In verse 3 the Hebrew says literally that he sawed with the saw, while 2 Samuel 12:31 says he set them to the saws, and many think one letter has slipped between the two. The KJV reads that he cut them with saws; forced labour, as in the ESV, is the likelier meaning.
verseByVerse.note: The crown weighed a talent, about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — The Sons of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The descendants of the giants fall one by one to David’s servants. Three short notices of war with the Philistines each end with a giant dead: Sibbecai kills Sippai at Gezer (v. 4); Elhanan kills Lahmi, the brother of Goliath, whose spear was like a weaver’s beam (v. 5); and at Gath David’s nephew Jonathan kills a huge man with six fingers and six toes who taunted Israel as Goliath had done (vv. 6–7). The closing verse gives the verdict: they “fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants” (v. 8). The victories were the king’s, won by his men.
verseByVerse.theology: David killed Goliath himself. Goliath’s relatives were finished off over the years by other men, in David’s name, and the record credits it all to the king.
verseByVerse.examples: Sibbecai of Hushah, Elhanan son of Jair, Jonathan son of Shimea: each has a name, a home town and one sentence in Scripture, and God did not forget them.

verseByVerse.quote: And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued. And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two giants of Philistia fall to David’s men, one of them the brother of Goliath.

Sibbecai the Hushathite. Sibbecai was one line among thirty in the roll of the mighty men (11:29). Here he kills a giant, in one sentence, and disappears.

Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The spear “like a weaver’s beam” is how Goliath’s own spear was described (1 Samuel 17:7). The great spear runs in the family, and so does defeat.

The descendants of the giants. These were the Rephaim, a people of great stature in Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:10–11), and the word here is not the one used of the Nephilim of Genesis 6.

Textual note. This verse says Elhanan struck down “Lahmi the brother of Goliath”; the corresponding verse in 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan struck down Goliath himself. The oldest explanation, and still the most likely, is that a copyist’s eye slipped in the Samuel verse, whose Hebrew has a recognised awkwardness at exactly that point, and that Chronicles preserves the original. Others suppose two men or two names. The KJV, following this verse, adds the brother of in 2 Samuel 21:19, in italics to show the words are supplied. The question is real, and it need not trouble anyone: the killing of Goliath is told at length in 1 Samuel 17, and one damaged line in a list does not touch it.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants. And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down. These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third giant falls at Gath, and the chapter credits all three victories to David and his servants together, the shape of every victory won in Christ’s name.

Twenty-four in number. At Gath the Chronicler counts, as though he wants the reader to have the figure and not just the impression.

When he taunted Israel. The giant taunts Israel as Goliath had done, and somebody comes out to meet him: David’s nephew, the son of one of the brothers who had stood in the valley years before and done nothing while Goliath taunted (1 Samuel 17:13).

By the hand of David and by the hand of his servants. David killed none of these three himself; by the account in Samuel his men had sworn that he would no longer go out with them to battle (2 Samuel 21:17). The text credits him anyway, because the victories were won in his name, by his men, against the family of the champion he had already beaten.

The gospel’s shape. One decisive fight in a valley, settled by one man with a sling while everyone else watched; then years of unglamorous mopping-up by men few remember, against enemies whose champion had already fallen. The victory was the king’s, and the clearing of the field went down on his record. Christians have long heard the gospel’s shape in that. The decisive battle was fought by David’s greater Son alone, who “disarmed the rulers and authorities” at the cross (Colossians 2:15); his people still face what taunts them one at a time, with “the sword of the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:17), and every victory goes down to his name. There is a giant somewhere still taunting, and the church is at Gath and at Gezer with a sword in its hand, and every one of them falls by the hand of David’s Son.

20.theology:
Chronicles omits David's great sin but does not conceal it (see on v. 1). It answers a different question from Samuel: not what David was like, but what God promised to his royal house and what that house was for. Its readers, who had no king at all, needed that answer.

Verse 8 states the principle the honour roll has been working towards since chapter 11: a victory won in the king's name, in the king's manner, by men the king trained, is counted as the king's.
20.examples:
None of these three fought the famous giant; they fought his relatives, years after the story everyone tells was over. Most faithful work is the clearing up after somebody else's decisive victory, and it still has to be done a giant at a time.

Rabbah fell in the spring the king stayed home. The chapter records the crown coming to him anyway. Outward success tells us nothing about how a man has been living in private.

keyVerse.quote: These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
keyVerse.note: The verse closes the account of David’s wars and states its principle: victories won in the king’s name by the king’s men are counted as the king’s. It is the shape of the Christian life, in which Christ has won the decisive battle alone and his people face the remaining enemies one at a time, every victory going down to his name.

20.reflection:
The Chronicler writes, “But David remained at Jerusalem” (v. 1), and does not tell what happened next. Why might he have left the story out, and what does David’s fall in a season of success warn us about?

The crown still came to David in the season of his great failure (v. 2). How does that show that God’s promise rested on his own faithfulness rather than on David’s, and what comfort is that for us in Christ?

None of these men fought the famous giant; they fought his relatives, years later (vv. 4–8). What “giants” still taunt you, and what difference does it make that Christ has already won the decisive battle?

The victories of David’s servants were counted as David’s (v. 8). How does it encourage you that faithful, unnoticed work done in Christ’s name is counted to him?

21.title: The Census, the Plague, and the Altar: Where the Temple Will Stand
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.<sup>2</sup>So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."<sup>3</sup>But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?"<sup>4</sup>But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword.<sup>6</sup>But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.<sup>7</sup>But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel.<sup>8</sup>And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"<sup>11</sup>So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Choose what you will:<sup>12</sup>either three years of famine, or three months of devastation by your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes you, or else three days of the sword of the LORD, pestilence on the land, with the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me."<sup>13</sup>Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man."<sup>14</sup>So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and 70,000 men of Israel fell.<sup>15</sup>And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>16</sup>And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces.<sup>17</sup>And David said to God, "Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father's house. But do not let the plague be on your people."<sup>18</sup>Now the angel of the LORD had commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>19</sup>So David went up at Gad's word, which he had spoken in the name of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>Now Ornan was threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves.<sup>21</sup>As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David and went out from the threshing floor and paid homage to David with his face to the ground.<sup>22</sup>And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor that I may build on it an altar to the LORD—give it to me at its full price—that the plague may be averted from the people."<sup>23</sup>Then Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do what seems good to him. See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings and the threshing sledges for the wood and the wheat for a grain offering; I give it all."<sup>24</sup>But King David said to Ornan, "No, but I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing."<sup>25</sup>So David paid Ornan 600 shekels of gold by weight for the site.<sup>26</sup>And David built there an altar to the LORD and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering.<sup>27</sup>Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.<sup>28</sup>At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.<sup>29</sup>For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time in the high place at Gibeon,<sup>30</sup>but David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
21.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 18 to 20 have shown the LORD giving David victory wherever he went, as promised in chapter 17. Now, at the height of his strength, the king does the one thing in this book that brings death on his people, and the Chronicler, who passes over Bathsheba, keeps it, because of where it ends.

The message. Sin brings real judgment, even on God’s chosen king, but God’s mercy is greater than his anger, and he stops his sword at a sacrifice. The place where judgment halted becomes the place where God will live among his people.

Why it was said. The first readers worshipped at a small rebuilt temple on that same hill and wondered whether it still mattered (see the introduction). The chapter tells them why it stands where it does: not where David triumphed, but where God’s mercy met a sinner’s repentance.

How the chapter makes its case. Stirred up by an adversary, David counts his fighting men over Joab’s protest (vv. 1–6). God strikes Israel; David confesses and chooses to fall into the LORD’s hands, because his mercy is very great (vv. 7–13). Seventy thousand die before the LORD says “It is enough” at Ornan’s threshing floor, and David asks to be struck instead of the flock (vv. 14–17). Sent to build an altar there, he pays full price for the site; God answers with fire from heaven, and the sword is sheathed (vv. 18–27). The closing verses explain why he sacrificed there and not at Gibeon (vv. 28–30), and the next chapter draws the conclusion: “Here shall be the house of the LORD God” (22:1).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. A shepherd king offers himself for the sheep and cannot be accepted, because he is the guilty one; the sword is put away only when blood is shed on God’s altar. On this same ridge, Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1), God had once provided a ram in Isaac’s place. Outside the walls of the same city the innocent Good Shepherd laid down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and the judgment that stopped on Ornan’s floor fell on him, once for all.

For us. When we sin, we can confess as David did, quickly and without excuse, and fall into the hands of the God whose mercy is very great. Our forgiveness costs us nothing because it cost Christ everything, and that sets us free to give God what costs us something, gladly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A King Who Wanted a Number
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride, not need, sets the census in motion, and the one man who sees the danger cannot stop it. An adversary stirs David up, and he orders Joab to count Israel from one end of the land to the other so that he may know their number (vv. 1–2). Joab, no stranger to hard decisions, protests that the people already belong to the king and that the count will bring guilt on Israel; he is overruled (vv. 3–4). The totals come back with Levi and Benjamin missing, because the king’s command was abhorrent to Joab (vv. 5–6). The Chronicler names the tempter, but he never lets David hide behind him.
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever incited him, neither account reduces David's guilt by a syllable: he will say twice, in his own words, that the sin was his.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab said the right thing, was overruled, and could not stop what he saw coming. Being right in the council room does not always mean being able to prevent the harm.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel. So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An adversary stirs David to count his fighting men, and David gives the order because he wants to know how strong he is.

Then Satan stood against Israel. The same episode in 2 Samuel opens: “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them” (2 Samuel 24:1). One book says God moved David; this one says Satan did. It is the plainest case in Scripture of two writers crediting one act to two different actors, and it should not be smoothed over.

Two causes behind one event. Scripture repeatedly puts two causes behind one event and refuses to choose. Satan strips Job, and Job says the LORD has taken away, and does not sin in saying so. A lying spirit deceives Ahab’s prophets, and God sends him. Lawless men crucify Jesus by the definite plan of God, and Peter charges them with murder in the same sentence (Acts 2:23). Samuel looks at the census from above and says God was behind it; Chronicles looks from below and names the adversary who pushed. The Chronicler almost certainly had 2 Samuel in front of him and was not correcting it.

That I may know their number. David is not raising troops or planning a campaign; he wants to see how strong he is, though chapter 18 said twice that it was the LORD who gave him victory wherever he went (18:6, 13).

The devil, and the excuse. What neither writer does is excuse David: twice he says the sin was his (vv. 8, 17), and nobody mentions the tempter again. A man who has been incited is not a man who has been excused. Modern readers tend either to smile at a personal devil, or to find plenty of devils of their own, always outside: the upbringing, the system, the other side. Some of these are real, and Scripture is not naive about forces larger than we are. But Chronicles holds together two things we keep pulling apart: there is an adversary, stronger than we are, and when David is moved, David is guilty. Strangely, that is the hopeful half. Someone who is only a victim can be pitied, helped or managed, but cannot be forgiven, because nothing in the matter is his to be forgiven for. David owns the sin, and so he can pray, please take away the iniquity of your servant (v. 8). The Son of God appeared, John says, “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8), and he does it not by telling us it was never our fault but by bearing what was.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew satan means “adversary”. In Job and Zechariah it has the article, “the satan”, the accuser; here it has none, and elsewhere the same word is used of human enemies: the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, a man called Hadad (1 Kings 11:14). So some read this verse of a hostile power or a human enemy whose threat provoked the count. Most English versions read it as a name, the accuser of Job and the tempter of the Gospels, and that may well be right; the verse alone will not settle it.
verseByVerse.note: God was sovereign over what Satan intended, as in Job 1–2.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?" But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem. And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword. But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab, of all people, sees the danger and protests, but the king overrules him, and Joab carries out the order unwillingly and incompletely.

Why then should my lord require this? Joab’s objection is better than anything the king says in this chapter: three arguments in four lines. Numbers are God’s to give, not the king’s to audit: “May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are!” The people already serve David, so the count adds nothing. And the third argument is the one Joab alone seems to see: this will not stop with David. It will be a cause of guilt for Israel, and seventy thousand deaths will prove him right.

A cause of guilt for Israel. The law had already said why. Every man counted in a census had to pay a ransom for his life, “that there be no plague among them when you number them” (Exodus 30:12). The people were God’s, not the king’s, and the payment said so. Nothing in this chapter mentions the ransom money, and the plague comes exactly as the law warned, which is as close to an explanation as the text offers.

The king’s word prevailed against Joab. Told he was wrong by his most experienced man, David used his authority to end the conversation, and no adviser can answer that.

He did not include Levi and Benjamin. Only this book records it. Levi was exempt from a military census by law (Numbers 1:47–49). Benjamin was not, and Joab simply left it out, for the king’s command was abhorrent to Joab. Neither obedience nor refusal: he carried out an order he believed was a sin, under protest, and handed in an incomplete count, and Scripture reports it without comment.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Samuel has 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah (2 Samuel 24:9). Numbers were easily miscopied in Hebrew manuscripts, and the two accounts may count different things; some think one total includes the standing army of chapter 27 and the other does not. Likewise the three years of famine in verse 12 stand where the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 24:13 has seven, though the Greek of Samuel also has three. Neither touches what the passage teaches; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — Three Days, and a Drawn Sword
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment falls, and mercy sets its limit. God counts the census as evil and strikes Israel, and David confesses at once, before any prophet has come (vv. 7–8). Gad brings three possible punishments, and David chooses the one that leaves him in God’s hands rather than men’s, “for his mercy is very great” (vv. 9–13). Seventy thousand die, yet as the angel reaches Jerusalem the LORD says “It is enough” and the sword stops at Ornan’s threshing floor (vv. 14–15). David sees the drawn sword, takes all the blame and asks to be struck instead of the sheep (vv. 16–17). His offer cannot be accepted, but it shows what is needed.
verseByVerse.theology: The sword in this section is real, and so is the word that stops it. Judgment and mercy meet over the same threshing floor.
verseByVerse.examples: A guilty man appealing to mercy is not asking God to pretend. David names his sin, accepts that judgment is coming, and still trusts the one who judges.

verseByVerse.quote: But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel. And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God counts the census as evil and strikes Israel, and David confesses at once, without excuse, before any prophet has said a word.

God was displeased with this thing. Displeased is a mild word: the Hebrew says the thing was evil in God’s eyes. He struck Israel probably announces at the start the judgment that verses 9–14 describe.

I have sinned greatly. No prophet has spoken yet; no Nathan has come with a story about a lamb, as after Bathsheba. Three sentences, and every one admits something: he sinned greatly, he asks for the guilt to be taken away, and he calls himself a fool.

A ready confession. That readiness to confess was in him from the beginning, and it is the reason God calls him a man after his own heart. It is not that he sinned less than Saul, but that when he was caught he made no excuses. Saul, confronted about the Amalekite cattle, explained that the people had kept the best animals to sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:15).

Please take away the iniquity of your servant. The rest of the chapter shows how God answers that prayer: not by the confession alone, but at an altar where blood is shed (v. 26). Every forgiven sinner since has been answered the same way. God “is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9), just because Jesus Christ “is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying, "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'" So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Choose what you will: either three years of famine, or three months of devastation by your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes you, or else three days of the sword of the LORD, pestilence on the land, with the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me." Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered three judgments, David chooses not the lightest sentence but the kindest judge: he would rather fall into God’s hands than men’s, because God’s mercy is very great.

Gad, David’s seer. A prophet attached to the court, with David since his outlaw days (1 Samuel 22:5), whose task was to bring the king words he had not asked for.

Three things I offer you. The time grows shorter (years, months, days), the severity grows to match, and the one who acts changes: famine works through weather, defeat through enemy armies, and the third comes straight from the LORD, by his angel.

Let me fall into the hand of the LORD. A sentence that never wears out. David is not choosing the shortest option, though it is the shortest; he is picking his judge. He would rather be dealt with directly by the God he has offended than handed over to people, and the reason is God’s character, for his mercy is very great. The third option means an angel with orders to destroy, yet he chooses it, having concluded from a lifetime with this God that even his wrath is safer than human kindness. Men are changeable and can be cruel, and their mercy runs out without warning. God’s does not.

Everyone’s choice. Everyone falls into somebody’s hands in the end. David knew God well enough to choose his, even while they held a sword. We know those hands better than he did: they were nailed to a cross, where the Son of God took the stroke of judgment on himself.

But is it not “a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God”? It is (Hebrews 10:31), for those who go on sinning deliberately and set aside the only sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:26–29). David came as a confessing sinner, and the chapter ends at an altar. The same hands are terror to the defiant and refuge to the penitent.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and 70,000 men of Israel fell. And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plague kills seventy thousand, but as the angel reaches Jerusalem the LORD stops him in mid-stroke, at the threshing floor of Ornan. The judgment is real, and it has a limit God himself sets.

70,000 men of Israel fell. Joab came back from a nine-month tour (2 Samuel 24:8) with one and a half million fighting men. David now has a second figure, and the Chronicler leaves the two nine verses apart without comment. A king asked how many men he had, and God answered with the number he lost.

It is enough; now stay your hand. A handful of words in Hebrew, and one of the great mercies of the Old Testament.

He relented from the calamity. Scripture speaks in human terms, as the moment looked from below; it also says that God is not a man, that he should change his mind (Numbers 23:19). It is enough shows that the punishment had a set measure, and the God who set it was not carried along by his own anger. Wrath that stops at a set point is not a loss of temper. It is the settled response of a holy God who has decided in advance where it ends.

The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Where it stopped is mentioned almost in passing. A threshing floor was a hard, open space on high ground where grain was beaten and tossed for the wind to carry off the chaff, a common biblical picture of judgment. Everything left in this book happens on that piece of ground.

Why did 70,000 die for David’s sin? Second Samuel says God’s anger was already against Israel (2 Samuel 24:1); the nation shared the pride, and the plague judged king and people together. David offered himself in their place (v. 17), a picture of the King who would.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. And David said to God, "Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father's house. But do not let the plague be on your people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the sword over Jerusalem, David takes the whole blame and asks to be struck himself instead of the people: a shepherd offering his life for the flock. The offer cannot be accepted, but it points to one that would be.

Standing between earth and heaven. The king and the elders put on sackcloth and go down on their faces in the open, at the top of the hill. And then David prays, the finest thing he says in this book.

Was it not I who gave command to number the people? Three things, each costing him something. He takes the whole blame: the order was mine. He calls the dying people sheep, the flock God had told him to shepherd, as Israel reminded him at Hebron (11:2). And he asks to be struck in their place, and to have his own house struck with him.

A substitute refused. The shepherd’s offer is refused, and it had to be. David was the one man in Israel who could not stand in for anybody, because he was the one who had committed the sin. A substitute has to be innocent, and there was no such person on that hill.

Where the offer was made. God answers the offer a different way, which is what the rest of the chapter is about. The hill is Mount Moriah, where the temple was built on Ornan’s threshing floor (2 Chronicles 3:1). Abraham had been sent to the land of Moriah to offer his son (Genesis 22:2), long taken to be this same ridge, where a father with a knife was stopped by a voice and shown a ram in a thicket. A substitute had been needed on that hill before, and God had provided one. A thousand years later, outside the wall of the same city, Jesus the good shepherd made the offer David made here, and was not refused: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Where Christians differ. Who is the angel with the drawn sword? Many take him to be a created angel carrying out God’s sentence, since the LORD tells him to stop and to sheathe his sword (vv. 15, 27). Others, noting that he gives Gad the LORD’s command (v. 18) and recalling the commander with a drawn sword whom Joshua met (Joshua 5:13–15), see the Son appearing before his incarnation.

This commentary’s view. Where the angel of the LORD speaks and acts as God, this commentary reads him as the Son before his incarnation. Here the text does not settle it, and the chapter’s point does not depend on it: the sword is in God’s hand and stops at his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The Threshing Floor Bought at Full Price
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sword is put away by an offering God provides the place for and accepts with fire. Through his angel and his prophet, God sends David to raise an altar exactly where the sword stopped (vv. 18–19). Ornan, a Jebusite farmer who has seen the angel too, offers the floor, the oxen, the wood and the wheat for nothing (vv. 20–23). David refuses: he will not offer the LORD what is another man’s, or what costs him nothing, and he pays the full price (vv. 24–25). God answers with fire from heaven on the altar, and at his command the angel sheathes his sword (vv. 26–27). The place of the temple has been found.
verseByVerse.theology: Fire from heaven is how God marks a place as his own, and here it settles where the house of God is to stand: on the spot where the sword stopped.
verseByVerse.examples: The first generosity in this section comes from an outsider: a Jebusite farmer who offered everything he had on the spot.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD had commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. So David went up at Gad's word, which he had spoken in the name of the LORD. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David and went out from the threshing floor and paid homage to David with his face to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself sends David, through his angel and his prophet, to the very spot where the sword stopped, and a Jebusite farmer and his sons see the angel too.

So David went up at Gad’s word. The instruction comes from the angel through Gad, and David goes at once, up the hill towards the angel with the sword.

Ornan was threshing wheat. He is at work with his four sons, doing the most ordinary thing a man can do in that country at harvest.

He turned and saw the angel. No other account gives this detail. It was not a private vision granted to a king: a farmer and his boys looked up from the wheat and saw a figure with a sword over the city, and the sons hid, which is the only sane response.

Ornan the Jebusite. His people had held that ridge against Israel for centuries until David took the stronghold (11:4–6), and he is still there, farming the high ground north of the city, when the king of Israel comes up the path towards him. He goes out and bows with his face to the ground.
verseByVerse.note: Ornan is another form of Araunah.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor that I may build on it an altar to the LORD—give it to me at its full price—that the plague may be averted from the people." Then Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do what seems good to him. See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings and the threshing sledges for the wood and the wheat for a grain offering; I give it all." But King David said to Ornan, "No, but I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David paid Ornan 600 shekels of gold by weight for the site.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David refuses Ornan’s generous gift and pays the full price, because an offering that costs the giver nothing is no offering at all.

I give it all. Ornan offers the floor, the oxen for the burnt offering, the sledges for firewood and the wheat for the grain offering: everything he works with, on the spot, to a king he has just met under an angel’s sword.

Burnt offerings that cost me nothing. David says no. The first half of his answer is about Ornan: it would be Ornan’s sacrifice with the king’s name attached. The second half has been remembered for three thousand years: an offering that cost him nothing would have been a gesture performed with someone else’s oxen.

600 shekels of gold by weight. Six hundred shekels of gold change hands, where the other account has fifty shekels of silver; the likeliest explanation is in the note on these verses, though it cannot be proved. What both accounts agree on is that David insisted on paying, and said why.

The costliest offering ever made was not David’s. Jesus offered himself. It cost him everything, and he had said beforehand that no one took his life from him: he laid it down of his own accord (John 10:18).

Faith that costs nothing. Much modern religion is offered on its low cost: an addition to a full life, with no claim on the diary, the money or the opinions, and churches chosen as a gym is, for convenience. David’s refusal cuts across all of that. A sacrifice which costs nothing says nothing, because worship is giving what we value to the One we value more. Yet the gospel turns even this round. What matters most comes to us free: forgiveness, the sword put away, a place at God’s altar, all paid for by another at full price. That does not make the Christian life cheap. It makes it a response rather than a payment, and a response to love of that size tends to cost everything, gladly. Isaac Watts had the logic exactly: “Love so amazing, so divine, demands my soul, my life, my all.”
verseByVerse.note: Samuel’s fifty shekels probably bought the threshing floor and oxen, and Chronicles’ 600 shekels of gold the whole site.

verseByVerse.quote: And David built there an altar to the LORD and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering. Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God accepts the sacrifice with fire from heaven, and at his command the angel puts away his sword: judgment ends where blood is shed on God’s altar.

Fire from heaven upon the altar. Only this account has it. God lit the altar himself when Aaron first offered at the tabernacle (Leviticus 9:24), and will again when Solomon prays on this very hill (2 Chronicles 7:1) and for Elijah on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). Each time it settles something; here it settles a place. David has offered on a threshing floor because he could not reach the lawful altar, and God comes down on it in front of witnesses and accepts what has been offered there. That is how Israel learns where the temple goes.

Burnt offerings and peace offerings. The burnt offering goes up entirely to God; the peace offering ends in a meal. First judgment is satisfied, then fellowship with God is restored, both on the same fire.

He put his sword back into its sheath. The blade that had been out over Jerusalem goes away, and what put it away was blood on an altar. The sword did not grow blunt, and no one argued it away. Something died in the place where it was pointing, and the sword went home. That is the gospel in a picture: God’s justice is not set aside but satisfied, at the place where a substitute died, so that those who trust Christ are “justified by his blood” and “saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–30 — Why the Altar Had to Be Here
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by explaining an irregular altar, and in doing so shows that God had been leading towards this place all along. David saw that the LORD had answered him on Ornan’s threshing floor, so he went on sacrificing there (v. 28). The tabernacle Moses made, with its lawful altar, stood at Gibeon (v. 29), but David could not go there to seek God, because he feared the angel’s sword (v. 30). The split in Israel’s worship that chapter 16 left behind, ark in Jerusalem and altar at Gibeon, begins to close here, at the place where a plague was stopped, and the next verse names it as the site of God’s house (22:1).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 16 left Israel's worship split between two hills: the ark and the singing in Jerusalem, the altar and the daily offering at Gibeon. This is where the split begins to close, and it closes at the place where a plague was stopped.
