verseByVerse.examples: God did not send David on a journey to the lawful altar. He gave him one on the ground where he stood, and lit it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there. For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time in the high place at Gibeon, but David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Chronicler explains why David sacrificed away from the lawful altar at Gibeon: the angel’s sword barred the way, and God had answered him here instead. The irregular altar turns out to be the one God was aiming at all along.

The tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made. Chapter 16 left the lawful altar at Gibeon (16:39–40), yet David has just sacrificed somewhere else, and this book, which cares more than any other about who may do what and where, accounts for it.

He was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD. Gibeon was a day’s journey off, with a sword over the city and the plague killing people while he travelled. God sent a prophet to say “build here” and lit the fire himself, and the altar on a Jebusite’s floor became the one God had chosen.

Where the rest of the book comes from. Everything after this chapter (the gold, the plans, the divisions of priests, the charge to Solomon, the last prayer of David’s life) is about a building that will stand on this floor and gather the two halves of Israel’s worship into one house at last.

Found at the lowest point. The site was found at the lowest point of David’s life. He wanted a number, seventy thousand people died, and the place where the sword stopped is where God chose to live, bought out of a disaster David had caused himself. God has never needed spotless material to work with, and the mercy seat, the cover of the ark where atoning blood was sprinkled, would stand on the ground where judgment halted.

21.theology:
Verse 1 names Satan and 2 Samuel 24:1 names the LORD (see on vv. 1-2), but neither account lets David off: he says I have sinned greatly (v. 8), and the tempter is never mentioned again.

Verse 13 is the chapter's centre. Offered three judgments, David picks his judge rather than his sentence: let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great. And verse 15 shows he was right: the judgment had a measure, and the one who set it said it is enough while the angel's arm was still raised.
21.examples:
David confessed before any prophet arrived, and ran towards the God whose mercy is very great. That road is still open: the one who confesses is met by a God who is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9), because Jesus, the shepherd David could not be, has already been struck for the flock.

I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing. An offering that costs the giver nothing is not really a gift.

keyVerse.quote: Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man.
keyVerse.note: Guilty and under sentence, David chooses not the lightest punishment but the kindest judge, and he trusts God’s mercy before he has seen it. The rest of the chapter proves him right: the judgment stops at God’s word and the sword is sheathed at an altar. In Christ every penitent sinner may make the same choice with even greater confidence.

21.reflection:
David wanted to know “their number” (v. 2), even though the LORD had given him every victory. Where are you tempted to measure your security by what you can count, and what would it look like to trust God instead?

Chronicles names Satan as the one who incited David, yet David says twice that the sin was his own (vv. 1, 8, 17). Why is it hopeful, and not only humbling, to take full responsibility for our sin?

David chose to “fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great” (v. 13). How does the cross let us run to God when we have sinned, rather than away from him?

David would not offer God anything “that cost me nothing” (v. 24). Since our salvation was paid for by another, what costly offering of love might God be asking of you or of your group?

22.title: David Prepares for the Temple: The Man of War and the Man of Peace
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David said, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel."<sup>2</sup>David commanded to gather together the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, and he set stonecutters to prepare dressed stones for building the house of God.<sup>3</sup>David also provided great quantities of iron for nails for the doors of the gates and for clamps, as well as bronze in quantities beyond weighing,<sup>4</sup>and cedar timbers without number, for the Sidonians and Tyrians brought great quantities of cedar to David.<sup>5</sup>For David said, "Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and glory throughout all lands. I will therefore make preparation for it." So David provided materials in great quantity before his death.<sup>6</sup>Then he called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>7</sup>David said to Solomon, "My son, I had it in my heart to build a house to the name of the LORD my God.<sup>8</sup>But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 'You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth.<sup>9</sup>Behold, a son shall be born to you who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his surrounding enemies. For his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days.<sup>10</sup>He shall build a house for my name. He shall be my son, and I will be his father, and I will establish his royal throne in Israel forever.'<sup>11</sup>"Now, my son, the LORD be with you, so that you may succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as he has spoken concerning you.<sup>12</sup>Only, may the LORD grant you discretion and understanding, that when he gives you charge over Israel you may keep the law of the LORD your God.<sup>13</sup>Then you will prosper if you are careful to observe the statutes and the rules that the LORD commanded Moses for Israel. Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed.<sup>14</sup>With great pains I have provided for the house of the LORD 100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing, for there is so much of it; timber and stone, too, I have provided. To these you must add.<sup>15</sup>You have an abundance of workmen: stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and all kinds of craftsmen without number, skilled in working<sup>16</sup>gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Arise and work! The LORD be with you!"<sup>17</sup>David also commanded all the leaders of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Is not the LORD your God with you? And has he not given you peace on every side? For he has delivered the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land is subdued before the LORD and his people.<sup>19</sup>Now set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God, so that the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God may be brought into a house built for the name of the LORD."
22.overview:
Where we are. The sword has been sheathed over Ornan’s threshing floor, and God has answered David’s sacrifice with fire (chapter 21). Still on that ground, the king names it as the place of God’s house, and from here to the end of the book everything is preparation for a temple he will never see.

The message. God’s work passes from one generation to the next, and each must do its part with what God gives. David may not build, but he can gather, pray and charge; Solomon must build, but he begins inside a promise he did nothing to earn. The work rests on God’s presence and the peace he has given, and the right response is to seek him and get to work.

Why it was said. The first readers had rebuilt the temple on this site, and it looked like nothing beside the one their grandparents remembered (see the introduction). The chapter shows them that the first house was a gift of God’s promise and a father’s labour, not a feat they must equal, and gives them David’s words to live by. Their own prophet Haggai had told them the same: “Be strong … Work, for I am with you” (Haggai 2:4).

How the chapter makes its case. David names the site and starts gathering materials, because Solomon is young and the house must be magnificent (vv. 1–5). In private he tells Solomon why he himself may not build, and that the house belongs to a man of rest whose throne God will establish forever (vv. 6–10). He prays for his son’s wisdom, gives him Joshua’s charge to be strong and courageous (vv. 11–13), and hands over a store past counting: “Arise and work!” (vv. 14–16). In public he tells the leaders to seek the LORD and build (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The words of verse 10, “He shall be my son, and I will be his father”, are applied to Jesus in Hebrews 1:5, and only he holds the throne forever. Solomon, the man of rest who built God a house, foreshadows the greater Son of David, whom Zechariah calls “the man whose name is the Branch … he shall build the temple of the LORD” (Zechariah 6:12). He gives rest to the weary and is building a house of living stones, his people.

For us. We may not see the end of the work we give our lives to. Christ builds his church, and each of us adds what he gives to what others prepared, because he is with us. Seeking God and doing his work are not two callings but one.
22.theology:
The refusal at verses 7-8 is not called a punishment (see on vv. 6-10). A man can do right and still be the wrong man for a task.

Verse 19 turns the book’s key word, seek, into a command with a task attached: set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build. The aim, one house for the ark and the holy vessels, ends the division of 16:37-42.
22.examples:
Most of what is done for God is like David’s nails: plain supplies for someone else’s building, and David was content to supply them.

He said out loud why he was doing it: his son was young and inexperienced and the work was enormous. He saw what his son lacked without contempt, spent the rest of his life making up for it, and then told the boy to these you must add.

Solomon later asked for the wisdom his father had prayed for, and received it. But the prayer was for wisdom to keep the law, and in the end Solomon did not. No son of David kept that law whole but one, and his obedience is counted to all who are his; that is what lets a believer take up the same charge without fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Here Shall Be the House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has fixed the place of his house, and David at once begins to make ready for it. Standing on the threshing floor where the fire fell, he declares that the house of the LORD and the altar of burnt offering will be here (v. 1). Then the gathering begins: resident aliens set to cut stone, iron for nails and clamps, bronze beyond weighing, cedar without number from Tyre and Sidon (vv. 2–4). He gives his reason plainly: Solomon is young and inexperienced, and the house must be exceedingly magnificent, known throughout all lands. So David, who may not build, spends his last years preparing (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The site was fixed where the plague stopped, and fixed by God's fire rather than by David's preference.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness often looks like the least memorable item in the inventory: an old king stockpiling nails (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel." David commanded to gather together the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, and he set stonecutters to prepare dressed stones for building the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing where the fire fell, David declares that this is the place of God’s house and altar, and sets foreigners to cut its stone.

Here shall be the house of the LORD God. He is still on the threshing floor. The sword is sheathed, the wheat still lies where Ornan left it, and the king looks at the ground under his feet and says: here the house, and here the altar. He is not proposing a site but identifying one, because God has just answered by fire on this exact patch of rock. Second Chronicles names it in the same terms: Mount Moriah, the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1).

The resident aliens. The resident aliens (Hebrew gerim) were foreigners settled in Israel. By Solomon’s day the count of them on the works runs to more than a hundred and fifty thousand men (2 Chronicles 2:17–18). It was conscription, and the Chronicler does not dress it up. The stones of the house of Israel’s God were cut and squared by men who could not have gone into it.

A house of prayer for all peoples. Centuries later God promised foreigners who held fast his covenant a place in it, “for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7). Jesus quoted those words when he cleared the temple courts (Mark 11:17), and in him the outsiders who once only cut the stones are built into the house itself (Ephesians 2:19–22).

verseByVerse.quote: David also provided great quantities of iron for nails for the doors of the gates and for clamps, as well as bronze in quantities beyond weighing, and cedar timbers without number, for the Sidonians and Tyrians brought great quantities of cedar to David. For David said, "Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house that is to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and glory throughout all lands. I will therefore make preparation for it." So David provided materials in great quantity before his death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing his son is not yet ready and the house must be glorious, David spends his last years gathering materials for a building he will never enter.

Iron for nails. The first item on the inventory is nails: not gold, not anything anyone would look at, but iron in quantity for the doors and for the clamps that hold dressed blocks together. An old man is buying nails for a building he will never walk into.

Cedar timbers without number. Then bronze beyond weighing, and cedar brought down the coast from Tyre and Sidon by the same trade that had built David his own house (14:1).

Solomon my son is young and inexperienced. Said of his heir without contempt. The house must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and glory throughout all lands, because it is the LORD’s, and its glory will speak of him to the nations. So the father does what the son cannot yet do.

Before his death. The words are plain, and they are the point: he worked at it until he died, for a son he knew was not ready.

The first readers. They had reason to linger over exceedingly magnificent. The house they had rebuilt after the exile was so much plainer that old men who remembered the first one wept when its foundation was laid (Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:3). They were being shown what the first house had cost, and that its glory had always been God’s gift through a father’s labour, not a nation’s achievement it could repeat.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — A Charge to a Young Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David hands his son the work, the promise and the courage to do it. He explains why he himself may not build: he has shed much blood in great wars (vv. 7–8). The house belongs instead to a son who will be a man of rest, and God has promised to be his father and to establish his throne forever (vv. 9–10). Then David prays that God will give Solomon wisdom to keep his law, and charges him in the words once spoken to Joshua, “Be strong and courageous” (vv. 11–13). Finally he lists the vast store he has gathered, tells his son to add to it, and sends him off: “Arise and work! The LORD be with you!” (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 hands the son the covenant of chapter 17 almost word for word. Solomon begins his work already inside a promise he did nothing to earn, and the charge that follows is built on it.
verseByVerse.examples: A father's best prayer for a gifted son (v. 12) is that his gifts will be spent on obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the LORD, the God of Israel. David said to Solomon, "My son, I had it in my heart to build a house to the name of the LORD my God. But the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 'You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth. Behold, a son shall be born to you who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his surrounding enemies. For his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days. He shall build a house for my name. He shall be my son, and I will be his father, and I will establish his royal throne in Israel forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tells Solomon that God barred him from building because he had shed much blood, and that the work belongs to a son of peace whose throne God will establish forever. It is not a punishment but a different calling.

You have shed much blood. It is easy to hear God’s refusal as a punishment, but the text does not say so. The blood was shed in the wars of chapters 18 to 20, and the Chronicler’s verdict on those was that the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (18:6, 13). When David tells the story again he puts it briefly: “you are a man of war” (28:3).

The wrong man for this task. The blood disqualified him for one particular task. A house of rest cannot be raised by the man whose calling was fighting, and that says nothing about whether he did his calling well. He was right, and he was the wrong man, which is harder to accept than a rebuke, because there is nothing to repent of and no decision to appeal against. Some readers think the blood of Uriah is in view as well, and David certainly had that to repent of; but the words given name wars, and they describe a calling rather than a crime.

A man of rest. His name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days. The name and the promise sound alike (Shelomoh, shalom), so that every time anybody called the boy in for supper they were saying what God intended to do with the country.

A house of rest. Rest is the very thing a temple is for. The ark had been carried from tent to tent for four hundred years, and the psalm says of this hill, “This is my resting place forever” (Psalm 132:14). A man of rest builds a house of rest for a God who had never had one. The pattern does not end with Solomon. Someone greater than Solomon has come (Matthew 12:42), who calls the weary to himself and gives them rest (Matthew 11:28), and whose house, Hebrews says, is his people (Hebrews 3:6).

The gift of being the wrong man. Few sentences are harder for a modern person to hear than “not you”. Raised on the promise that we can be anything we set our hearts on, when the door shuts on a good ambition, a career, a ministry, a marriage, we conclude that either we failed or somebody cheated us. David is told no about the best thing he ever wanted, and not that he failed, only that it belongs to someone else. That is a rest the culture of self-realisation cannot give, because it makes every person the hero of his own story and every closed door a small tragedy. Beneath this refusal lies the reversal David had already heard: he wanted to build God a house, and God answered that he would build David one (17:10). Religion says, here is what I will do for God. The gospel begins where David’s plan was set aside, with what God does for us, and ends with a Son of David who did the one work nobody else could do.

How was the throne established forever when Solomon’s line ended? The promise rests on the Son of David who reigns now (Luke 1:32–33). Hebrews applies the words “He shall be my son, and I will be his father” to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s name sounds like shalom, “peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, my son, the LORD be with you, so that you may succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as he has spoken concerning you. Only, may the LORD grant you discretion and understanding, that when he gives you charge over Israel you may keep the law of the LORD your God. Then you will prosper if you are careful to observe the statutes and the rules that the LORD commanded Moses for Israel. Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David prays that God will make his son wise in order to obey, and charges him, as Moses charged Joshua, to be strong and courageous because the LORD is with him.

The LORD be with you. The charge begins and ends with God’s presence (vv. 11, 16), and everything Solomon is asked to do rests on it.

That ... you may keep the law of the LORD your God. The prayer is the surprising part. David asks God to make his son wise, and says what for: not to govern shrewdly or design a building of fame, but to keep the law. In his father’s prayer, intelligence is a tool for obedience. Solomon will one day be offered anything he wants and will ask for wisdom (2 Chronicles 1:10); his father asked for it first.

Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed. These are words from an earlier handover, said to Joshua when Moses died and the river had to be crossed (Deuteronomy 31:7–8; Joshua 1:6–9). David lays them on a young man who has to build a temple. Building is treated as a campaign, with Joshua’s resources: the law, courage commanded, and God’s presence.

The same promise for us. When Jesus sent his followers out to build his church among the nations, he gave them the same assurance: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). That presence is the Spirit given to every believer, who supplies the strength the command calls for.

verseByVerse.quote: With great pains I have provided for the house of the LORD 100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing, for there is so much of it; timber and stone, too, I have provided. To these you must add. You have an abundance of workmen: stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and all kinds of craftsmen without number, skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Arise and work! The LORD be with you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David hands over an immense store gathered through years of hardship, tells his son to add to it, and sends him to work with God’s blessing.

100,000 talents of gold. Figures on this scale (see the note) have long been discussed. Perhaps the Hebrew word for thousand is also the word for a unit or a company, so that ancient totals do not always mean what a modern ledger would mean by them. Nobody can settle it. What the verse plainly says is that the store was past counting, and that a man who could not build had spent everything he had on making it possible.

With great pains. He gathered it out of wars and long campaigns, over decades, while his family fell apart around him.

To these you must add. He does not hand over a finished endowment and take the credit. Each generation receives what the last one gathered and must add its own.

Arise and work! The LORD be with you! The charge ends with a shout, from a man near the end of his life to a young one at the beginning of the only job that mattered.

Uncertain wording. With great pains translates a single Hebrew phrase meaning “in my affliction”. It may mean through all his troubles, by hard toil, or, as some take it, “in my poverty”, out of means that were modest beside the work. The sense of costly, painful labour is clear; the exact shade is not.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note): 100,000 talents of gold is some 3,750 tons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — A Charge to the Leaders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole leadership is called to the work, and the call rests on what God has already done. David tells the leaders of Israel to help Solomon (v. 17), and he begins not with an order but with two questions: is not the LORD your God with you, and has he not given you peace on every side? (v. 18). Only then comes the command: set your mind and heart to seek the LORD, and arise and build, so that the ark and the holy vessels may at last stand together in one house built for his name (v. 19). Seeking God and building his house turn out to be one task.
verseByVerse.theology: David's two questions come before his command. God's presence and the peace he has given are the ground of the work; the work is the answer to them, never the price of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Peace is a gift to be used. David's leaders were told to spend theirs on God's house rather than on their own comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: David also commanded all the leaders of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying, "Is not the LORD your God with you? And has he not given you peace on every side? For he has delivered the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land is subdued before the LORD and his people. Now set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God, so that the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy vessels of God may be brought into a house built for the name of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David calls all the leaders to help Solomon, reminding them first of God’s presence and the peace he has given, and then telling them to seek the LORD by building his house.

Is not the LORD your God with you? Before he asks for anything, David says what God has done: God is with you; God has given you rest. And he treats the rest as something to be used. The wars were not fought so that Israel could sit down. The quiet that has been won makes it possible to build at last, and a nation that thinks rest is the goal will spend it on itself.

Set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Seek is the word the book has stressed since it said Saul died because he did not seek the LORD (10:13–14), and here it comes with a task attached. The way to seek him, this year, in this generation, is to quarry stone, haul cedar and organise labour. Nobody is being told to choose between devotion and work. They are being told which work is the devotion.

So that the ark ... may be brought into a house. The purpose ends a division that has stood since chapter 16. The ark has been in a tent on one hill, and the altar and the vessels on another, for a generation, so that every day the sacrifice has been offered six miles from the ark, God’s throne on earth. One house, at last, with both in it.

The house he never saw. That is what the old man wanted, and he did not get it. He bought the ground, gathered stone and gold, prayed for his son and told the nation to build, and died before the foundations were dug. The house he never entered stood for nearly four hundred years and came down. The house it pointed to, Christ’s people, is still being built out of living stones (1 Peter 2:5), and the Bible’s closing vision has no temple in the city at all, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

keyVerse.quote: Now set your mind and heart to seek the LORD your God. Arise and build the sanctuary of the LORD God
keyVerse.note: Here the book’s key word, seek, is joined to a task: the way Israel seeks God in this generation is to build his house. It comes after David’s reminder that God is with them and has given them peace, so the work answers grace rather than earning it. For Christians it is still the call: seek the Lord, and give yourself to building what Christ is building.

22.reflection:
David was told he could not build the temple, not because he had failed, but because the work belonged to someone else (vv. 7–10). How do you respond when God closes a door on something good you wanted? What helps you rest in his choice?

David prayed that Solomon would be given wisdom so that he could keep God’s law (v. 12). What would change if we prayed for our children, or for younger believers, in the same way?

David worked hard for a building he never saw, and told Solomon, “To these you must add” (v. 14). What have you received from earlier generations of Christians, and what might you be preparing for those who come after you?

David grounded his command in God’s presence and the peace he had given (v. 18). How does knowing that Christ is with us change the way we approach the work he gives us?

23.title: The Levitical Orders: Every Ministry Has Its Place
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel.<sup>2</sup>David assembled all the leaders of Israel and the priests and the Levites.<sup>3</sup>The Levites, thirty years old and upward, were numbered, and the total was 38,000 men.<sup>4</sup>"Twenty-four thousand of these," David said, "shall have charge of the work in the house of the LORD, 6,000 shall be officers and judges,<sup>5</sup>4,000 gatekeepers, and 4,000 shall offer praises to the LORD with the instruments that I have made for praise."<sup>6</sup>And David organized them in divisions corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Gershon were Ladan and Shimei.<sup>8</sup>The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, and Zetham, and Joel, three.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Ladan.<sup>10</sup>And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, and Jeush and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei.<sup>11</sup>Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, therefore they became counted as a single father's house.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to dedicate the most holy things, that he and his sons forever should make offerings before the LORD and minister to him and pronounce blessings in his name forever.<sup>14</sup>But the sons of Moses the man of God were named among the tribe of Levi.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.<sup>18</sup>The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief and Isshiah the second.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.<sup>22</sup>Eleazar died having no sons, but only daughters; their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.<sup>24</sup>These were the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, the heads of fathers' houses as they were listed according to the number of the names of the individuals from twenty years old and upward who were to do the work for the service of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>For David said, "The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever.<sup>26</sup>And so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the things for its service."<sup>27</sup>For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward.<sup>28</sup>For their duty was to assist the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the LORD, having the care of the courts and the chambers, the cleansing of all that is holy, and any work for the service of the house of God.<sup>29</sup>Their duty was also to assist with the showbread, the flour for the grain offering, the wafers of unleavened bread, the baked offering, the offering mixed with oil, and all measures of quantity or size.<sup>30</sup>And they were to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD, and likewise at evening,<sup>31</sup>and whenever burnt offerings were offered to the LORD on Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, according to the number required of them, regularly before the LORD.<sup>32</sup>Thus they were to keep charge of the tent of meeting and the sanctuary, and to attend the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of the LORD.
23.overview:
Where we are. David has named the temple site and charged Solomon and the leaders to build (chapter 22). Now, old and full of days, he makes Solomon king and turns to those who will serve in the house: chapters 23 to 26 set out the orders of Levites, priests, singers and gatekeepers.

The message. Because God has given his people rest and come to dwell among them for good, their service changes shape. The tribe that once carried his tent through the wilderness now serves him day by day in a settled house: cleaning, baking, measuring, and giving thanks every morning and evening. God orders his worship with care, gives every family its place, and counts the humblest daily work in his house as holy.

Why it was said. The first readers served at a humbler rebuilt temple and needed to know that its staff and duties were not improvised but went back through David to Moses, so that their worship stood in an unbroken line with what God had appointed (see the introduction). Lists that look dull to us were their title deeds.

How the chapter makes its case. David makes Solomon king and gathers the leaders, priests and Levites (vv. 1–2). The Levites are counted and divided into four orders: workers in the house, officers and judges, gatekeepers and musicians (vv. 3–6). The three clans are set out house by house, with Aaron set apart for the priesthood forever and the sons of Moses entered as ordinary Levites (vv. 7–23). Finally the reason for the new order is given: God dwells in Jerusalem forever, so the carrying is over, the age of service comes down to twenty, and the daily work of the house begins (vv. 24–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The God who came to rest in Jerusalem came nearer still when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The priesthood promised to Aaron “forever” is fulfilled in Jesus, a priest forever who serves in the true sanctuary (Hebrews 7:23–25), and the Levites’ morning and evening thanks has passed to all his people, who “continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” through him (Hebrews 13:15).

For us. No one inherits a place before God, even from Moses; it is given. And no work done for him is too small to be holy, whether sweeping a court or saying thank you when nobody is listening. Because Christ has opened the house to us, we can serve gladly in the ordinary tasks he gives.
23.theology:
Verses 25-26 give the reason the whole order changed: the LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever. For four centuries the Levites’ work was carrying, because God’s tent moved with his people. Now he has settled in Jerusalem, so the carrying ends and the daily work begins.

And verses 13-14 put two brothers side by side (see on vv. 13-17): a father’s greatness does not pass to his sons. The book that spends nine chapters on family lines also says that descent from Moses, the greatest man in Israel, gave his sons no special rank.
23.examples:
Six thousand Levites were sent out as officers and judges, and four thousand were put on instruments the king had provided. A tribe set apart for God supplied the magistrates as well as the choir, and neither task ranked below the other.

The duties in verses 28-29 run from the cleansing of everything holy to checking weights and measures. Somebody had to make sure a measure was honest, and Scripture lists that duty between the showbread and the morning thanksgiving, as part of the same service.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — An Old King Numbers the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An old king makes his son king and sets the tribe of Levi in order for the house to come. Old and full of days, David makes Solomon king and gathers the leaders, priests and Levites (vv. 1–2). The Levites aged thirty and over are counted, thirty-eight thousand men (v. 3), and divided into four orders: twenty-four thousand to have charge of the work of the house, six thousand officers and judges, four thousand gatekeepers, and four thousand to praise the LORD with the instruments David made (vv. 4–5). He then arranges them by the three sons of Levi, Gershon, Kohath and Merari (v. 6), so that every family has its place.
verseByVerse.theology: Most of the tribe now serves the house itself; the rest keep its doors, lead its music and judge in the towns.
verseByVerse.examples: A king who could not build the house provided the instruments for its praise (v. 5). What we are refused is rarely the end of what we can give.

verseByVerse.quote: When David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel. David assembled all the leaders of Israel and the priests and the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of a full life, David makes Solomon king and gathers the nation to set the temple’s worship in order.

Old and full of days. The phrase is used of Abraham, Isaac and Job at the end. It means a life that ran its full course, and it will be said of David once more, six chapters on, in almost the same words (29:28).

He made Solomon his son king. One sentence for the succession. First Kings 1 gives it a whole troubled chapter: Adonijah proclaiming himself king, Joab and Abiathar going over to him, Nathan and Bathsheba at the bedside of a king too cold to get warm, and a coronation rushed through to stop the plot. None of it is here. His readers knew it; he gives them what they need, that the throne passed as God intended (22:9–10).

David assembled all the leaders. What he has left to do is administrative, and it will take the rest of the book.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites, thirty years old and upward, were numbered, and the total was 38,000 men. "Twenty-four thousand of these," David said, "shall have charge of the work in the house of the LORD, 6,000 shall be officers and judges, 4,000 gatekeepers, and 4,000 shall offer praises to the LORD with the instruments that I have made for praise." And David organized them in divisions corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are counted and divided into four orders, so that the whole tribe has its work.

The total was 38,000 men. The four figures repay the trouble of adding up: 24,000, 6,000, 4,000 and 4,000 make exactly the thirty-eight thousand of verse 3.

6,000 shall be officers and judges. About a sixth of the tribe set apart for God serves in the civil courts. That was not new: the law had already sent hard cases to “the Levitical priests and to the judge” at the place God would choose (Deuteronomy 17:8–9), and Jehoshaphat would later set Levites in the courts of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 19:8–11).

With the instruments that I have made for praise. Four thousand are given to music, with instruments David provided. The king who could not build the house gave it its praise. Long after his death, reforming kings brought out what the record still called the instruments of David (2 Chronicles 29:26–27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–23 — The Three Houses of Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every house of Levi is named and given its place, and no family is left off the roll. Gershon’s line is set out under Ladan and Shimei, with two small families joined into one so that neither disappears (vv. 7–11). In Kohath’s line, Aaron and his sons are set apart forever to offer, minister and bless, while the sons of Moses, the man of God, are simply counted among the tribe of Levi (vv. 12–17). The remaining Kohathite houses follow (vv. 18–20), and then Merari, where Eleazar’s daughters marry their cousins so that his house is kept (vv. 21–23). God’s care reaches the families nobody else would remember.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses is called the man of God in the same breath that his sons are entered as ordinary Levites (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.examples: Even a list of names shows God's care for the household nobody else would remember: his law kept a family with only daughters from vanishing (v. 22).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Gershon were Ladan and Shimei. The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, and Zetham, and Joel, three. The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Ladan. And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, and Jeush and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei. Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, therefore they became counted as a single father's house. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of Gershon is set out family by family, and two small families are joined so that neither drops off the roll.

The sons of Gershon. Gershon divides into Ladan and Shimei, the chief of each house marked out. One small note gets in: Jeush and Beriah had few sons, so they were counted as a single father’s house rather than left to fade off the roster.

The sons of Kohath. Then Kohath, the branch charged with the holy things, on which the next verses turn.

Uncertain wording. Two small puzzles in the names. A Shimei appears in verse 9 among the descendants of Ladan, and again in verse 10 as Gershon’s son; the first may be another man of the same name, or an early slip in copying. And Zina in verse 10 is evidently the Zizah of verse 11, a spelling difference of the kind copyists easily made.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to dedicate the most holy things, that he and his sons forever should make offerings before the LORD and minister to him and pronounce blessings in his name forever. But the sons of Moses the man of God were named among the tribe of Levi. The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer. The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief. The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron’s line is set apart forever for the priesthood, while the sons of Moses, the greatest man in Israel, are counted as ordinary Levites: standing before God is given, not inherited. Two brothers in one line of a genealogy, treated very differently.

Aaron was set apart. Aaron first: three tasks, offering, ministering and blessing in God’s name, and the word forever twice. His descendants get the altar, the sanctuary and the blessing, permanently, by God’s appointment.

The sons of Moses the man of God were named among the tribe of Levi. And that is all. The man who spoke with God face to face and wrote the law this book is trying to keep has sons on a staff list, ordinary Levites in the same columns as everybody else.

Standing is not inherited. Nobody in Israel had a better claim than Moses, and it bought his family nothing; the priesthood went to the line of the brother who made the golden calf. Standing before God is not inherited from a great father. It is given.

How was Aaron’s priesthood “forever”? The word often means for as long as the order God set up endures. Hebrews says the priesthood changed when Jesus came, a priest not by descent from Aaron but “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16), who “holds his priesthood permanently” (Hebrews 7:24). What God promised Aaron’s house is kept, and surpassed, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief. The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief and Isshiah the second. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish. Eleazar died having no sons, but only daughters; their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them. The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of Kohath and Merari are listed, and a family with only daughters is kept alive by God’s law.

The sons of Izhar ... Hebron ... Uzziel. The remaining Kohathite houses go past quickly: Shelomith of Izhar; Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel and Jekameam of Hebron, numbered first to fourth; Micah and Isshiah of Uzziel.

Eleazar died having no sons, but only daughters. Then Merari, and in the middle of the list a family that nearly ended: Eleazar had only daughters, and their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them.

The law of Moses at work. That is a law of Moses still working centuries on. The five daughters of Zelophehad had once asked why their father’s name should be taken away for want of a son (Numbers 27; 36). God told Moses they were right, and that they should marry within their clan so that the inheritance stayed in the tribe. A man died leaving daughters, and the law God gave kept his household’s place on the roll and its name in Scripture.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has come to rest among his people, so the Levites’ work changes from carrying his tent to serving in his house. The age for service comes down to twenty (v. 24), for the LORD has given rest and dwells in Jerusalem forever, and the tabernacle no longer needs to be carried (vv. 25–27). The new duties are set out: helping the priests, caring for the courts and chambers, cleansing the holy things, preparing the bread and the offerings, keeping the measures (vv. 28–29), and standing every morning and evening to thank and praise the LORD, as well as at every Sabbath, new moon and feast (vv. 30–31). So they keep charge of the sanctuary (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The tribe's oldest and most dangerous duty, carrying the holy things on the shoulder, has just been abolished: God has stopped moving, and there is nothing left to lift.
verseByVerse.examples: A settled God does not need fewer servants than a travelling one. He needs different ones, and more of them.

verseByVerse.quote: These were the sons of Levi by their fathers' houses, the heads of fathers' houses as they were listed according to the number of the names of the individuals from twenty years old and upward who were to do the work for the service of the house of the LORD. For David said, "The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever. And so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the things for its service." For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has given rest and dwells in Jerusalem forever, the Levites no longer carry his tent, and the age of service comes down to twenty.

From twenty years old and upward. Numbers counts Levites from thirty (Numbers 4:3) and from twenty-five (Numbers 8:24); after the exile they served from twenty, as here (Ezra 3:8). Verse 3 counted from thirty, the old reckoning for the carrying work; verse 27 says that by the last words of David the age came down to twenty, because the carrying was over (vv. 25–26) and a settled house needed more hands.

No longer need to carry the tabernacle. God has given the rest promised through Moses (Deuteronomy 12:10), and he has come to stay. Carrying had been the Kohathites’ whole task. No wagons were issued to them, because the holy things went on the shoulder (Numbers 7:9), and touching them wrongly meant death (Numbers 4:15), as Uzzah found when the ark was first moved (13:9–10). That is over, not because the rules relaxed but because God has stopped moving, and the tribe whose ancestors had died for touching a holy thing now handle holy things every day.

verseByVerse.quote: For their duty was to assist the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the LORD, having the care of the courts and the chambers, the cleansing of all that is holy, and any work for the service of the house of God. Their duty was also to assist with the showbread, the flour for the grain offering, the wafers of unleavened bread, the baked offering, the offering mixed with oil, and all measures of quantity or size. And they were to stand every morning, thanking and praising the LORD, and likewise at evening, and whenever burnt offerings were offered to the LORD on Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, according to the number required of them, regularly before the LORD. Thus they were to keep charge of the tent of meeting and the sanctuary, and to attend the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites’ new duties are ordinary and daily, and at their heart is thanks to God every morning and evening.

All measures of quantity or size. The duties are strikingly ordinary: cleaning, baking and, in the same sentence as the sacred bread, all measures of quantity or size. God had said that a just balance and honest weights were his concern (Proverbs 16:11), and here they are, kept by Levites between the wafers and the morning praise.

Every morning, thanking and praising the LORD. The standing order of the whole tribe: thanks every morning and evening, and on every Sabbath, new moon and feast. Even in winter, when the court was empty and nobody was listening, somebody stood there saying thank you, and it went on for four hundred years.

The daily duty. A settled God takes away the heroic duty and gives the daily one, which turns out to be the harder and the better of the two.

A share in the morning thanks. The God who came to dwell in Jerusalem has come nearer still in Christ: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). And the morning and evening thanks has passed to his people, who through him “continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15), by the Spirit who now lives in them, not to earn a place in the house but because he has given them one.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever.
keyVerse.note: This is the reason for everything new in the chapter. Because God has given rest and come to stay, the Levites stop carrying his tent and begin the daily service of his house. The promise of God dwelling with his people is fulfilled in Christ, in whom God has come to live among us, and it will be complete when he dwells with them forever.

23.reflection:
The sons of Moses were counted as ordinary Levites, while the priesthood went to Aaron’s line (vv. 13–14). What does this teach about whether our standing with God can be inherited or earned? How does the gospel answer that question?

God’s law and David’s arrangements made sure that small families and a household with only daughters were not lost from the roll (vv. 11, 22). Who in your church might feel overlooked, and how could you make sure they know they belong?

The Levites’ new work was ordinary: cleaning, baking, measuring, and giving thanks every morning and evening (vv. 28–31). Why might faithfulness in daily, unseen tasks be harder than one heroic act? Where is God calling you to that kind of faithfulness?

Through Christ, all believers now “continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15). What would it look like for you to make thanksgiving a morning and evening habit this week?

24.title: The Priestly Divisions: Order in the House of God
24.text: <sup>1</sup>The divisions of the sons of Aaron were these. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>2</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests.<sup>3</sup>With the help of Zadok of the sons of Eleazar, and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, David organized them according to the appointed duties in their service.<sup>4</sup>Since more chief men were found among the sons of Eleazar than among the sons of Ithamar, they organized them under sixteen heads of fathers' houses of the sons of Eleazar, and eight of the sons of Ithamar.<sup>5</sup>They divided them by lot, all alike, for there were sacred officers and officers of God among both the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar.<sup>6</sup>And the scribe Shemaiah, the son of Nethanel, a Levite, recorded them in the presence of the king and the princes and Zadok the priest and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar and the heads of the fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites, one father's house being chosen for Eleazar and one chosen for Ithamar.<sup>7</sup>The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah,<sup>8</sup>the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim,<sup>9</sup>the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin,<sup>10</sup>the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah,<sup>11</sup>the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah,<sup>12</sup>the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,<sup>13</sup>the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab,<sup>14</sup>the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer,<sup>15</sup>the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez,<sup>16</sup>the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel,<sup>17</sup>the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul,<sup>18</sup>the twenty-third to Delaiah, the twenty-fourth to Maaziah.<sup>19</sup>These had as their appointed duty in their service to come into the house of the LORD according to the procedure established for them by Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him.<sup>20</sup>And of the rest of the sons of Levi: of the sons of Amram, Shubael; of the sons of Shubael, Jehdeiah.<sup>21</sup>Of Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, Isshiah the chief.<sup>22</sup>Of the Izharites, Shelomoth; of the sons of Shelomoth, Jahath.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, Jekameam the fourth.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Uzziel, Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir.<sup>25</sup>The brother of Micah, Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi.
