These were the sons of the Levites according to their fathers' houses.<sup>31</sup>These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.
24.overview:
Where we are. David has counted the Levites and set out their new duties for a settled house (chapter 23). Now he turns to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and arranges them in twenty-four courses to take turns at the altar, before giving the rest of the Levites their places on the same terms.

The message. God is to be served his way, and he himself assigns his servants their places. The chapter opens with two priests who died for offering what God had not commanded, keeps the service exactly as God gave it to Aaron, and settles who serves when by lot, in public and on record, so that no one is favoured and every assignment comes from God. Faithful order of this kind, kept week after week, carried God’s purposes further than anyone in the room could see.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had only a few priestly families left (Ezra 2:36–39), and they needed to know that their priesthood and its rota went back through David to Aaron and to God’s command (see the introduction). This chapter gave them the pattern, and they kept it.

How the chapter makes its case. Nadab and Abihu died childless, so the priesthood came through Eleazar and Ithamar (vv. 1–2). With Zadok and Ahimelech representing the two lines, David forms twenty-four houses in proportion to their size, and the order is drawn by lot, all alike, before witnesses and written down (vv. 3–6). The courses are listed as the lots fell, the eighth to Abijah (vv. 7–18), each to serve by the procedure God gave Aaron (v. 19). The other Levite houses are listed and cast lots in the same way, eldest and youngest alike (vv. 20–31).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. The courses were still running a thousand years later, when Zechariah of the division of Abijah was chosen by lot to burn incense and was told of the son who would prepare the way for the Lord (Luke 1:5–17). And the very rota shows the weakness of that priesthood: many priests, taking turns and dying in their turn. Jesus “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24), and he is never off duty.

For us. We may approach God only in the way he has given, and that way is now Christ. In his church no one has a better claim than another, for every place is a gift. And ordinary faithfulness, kept up week after week, is one of the ways God carries his purposes forward.
24.theology:
Verse 19 marks a line David keeps everywhere: he arranged when the priests served and did not change what they did (see on vv. 13-19).

And the appointments were made by lot, in public, with a written record, even inside each family: the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike.
24.examples:
A rota is how anything outlasts the enthusiasm of the people who begin it. Twenty-four courses serving a week at a time were still running after the exile, the return, and centuries of foreign rule.

Eleazar of Mahli (not Aaron's son of the same name) had no sons, and childlessness did not take him off the record of God's people. Nothing else is known about him, but somebody thought it worth writing down that he had been there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Two Families Left, and a Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priesthood is ordered with care, because God must be approached his way, and the order is fixed by God’s choice rather than human influence. The chapter begins with Nadab and Abihu, who died childless after offering what God had not commanded, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar (vv. 1–2). Working with Zadok of Eleazar’s line and Ahimelech of Ithamar’s, David forms twenty-four heads of houses, sixteen and eight, in proportion to their numbers (vv. 3–4). The order of service is settled by lot, all alike, and a Levite scribe records it before the king, the princes and the heads of both priestly lines (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's instructions for worship are not formalities, and the first sentence of an administrative list says so.
verseByVerse.examples: Fairness that can be seen is a kindness to everyone who has to live with the result.

verseByVerse.quote: The divisions of the sons of Aaron were these. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priesthood runs through Eleazar and Ithamar alone, because their brothers died for offering what God had not commanded.

Nadab and Abihu died before their father. Anyone who knew Leviticus knew what that meant. On the day the tabernacle was dedicated, just after fire from the LORD had consumed the offering and the nation fell on their faces, Aaron’s two eldest took their censers and “offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them” (Leviticus 10:1). Fire came out again, they died in front of the tent, and their father was told not to mourn.

So Eleazar and Ithamar became the priests. Every course in this chapter, every priest at Solomon’s altar and in the second temple, comes down through these two.

Approaching God his way. It is the lesson of Uzzah and the cart in chapter 13, set without comment at the head of a list: how God is to be approached is not a formality. For us the way he has given is his Son: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). In Christ we may draw near with confidence, but only in Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22).

verseByVerse.quote: With the help of Zadok of the sons of Eleazar, and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, David organized them according to the appointed duties in their service. Since more chief men were found among the sons of Eleazar than among the sons of Ithamar, they organized them under sixteen heads of fathers' houses of the sons of Eleazar, and eight of the sons of Ithamar. They divided them by lot, all alike, for there were sacred officers and officers of God among both the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar. And the scribe Shemaiah, the son of Nethanel, a Levite, recorded them in the presence of the king and the princes and Zadok the priest and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar and the heads of the fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites, one father's house being chosen for Eleazar and one chosen for Ithamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David divides the priests fairly and settles their order by lot, in public and on record, so that the choice is God’s and no one is favoured.

Zadok ... and Ahimelech. Both high priests stand with David, one from each line, and neither family is placed under the other. The division is proportional: the larger house gets sixteen places because it has more men, not more influence.

They divided them by lot, all alike. The order of service is settled in the one way no one can influence. No priest could arrange to be on duty in the best weeks, and no family could be quietly kept out of them. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33), and that is why it was used here: to take the rota out of human hands and put it in God’s.

The scribe Shemaiah ... recorded them. A named Levite clerk wrote it down with the king and both high priests watching: fair, seen to be fair, and on record.

Should Christians decide things by lot? Scripture last records it in the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:26), before the Spirit was poured out; after that the church decided by Scripture, prayer and counsel (Acts 15:28), and this commentary holds that God now guides chiefly in those ways.

Uncertain wording. Sacred officers and officers of God are probably two titles for leading priests, but whether they name different offices is not known. The end of verse 6 is compressed in Hebrew; it may mean the two lines were drawn by turns, or describe how sixteen and eight were fitted together. Either way, both lines were in one draw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The twenty-four courses are recorded in the order the lots fell, and each serves by the procedure God gave Aaron. The list runs from Jehoiarib, first, to Maaziah, twenty-fourth, with the eighth lot falling to Abijah (vv. 7–18). The names look like a page to skip, yet the rota they record was still in use when Luke began his Gospel. Verse 19 draws the line that matters: the courses came into the house of the LORD according to the procedure established for them by Aaron, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him. David arranged when the priests served; he did not change what they did (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The rota was David's idea; the procedure inside the house was Aaron's, and Aaron's had come from God. New arrangements, old obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithful routine can carry God's purposes further than anyone who set it up could see (see on vv. 7-12).

verseByVerse.quote: The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah, the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim, the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin, the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah, the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah, the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lots fall one by one, and the eighth, to Abijah, fixes the week in which, a thousand years later, God would announce the forerunner of Christ.

The eighth to Abijah. Nearly a thousand years later the arrangement is still in force. Luke opens his Gospel with a priest named Zechariah, and the first thing he tells us is his course: “of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1:5). Only four priestly families came back from Babylon (Ezra 2:36–39), and by later Jewish tradition they were divided again into twenty-four courses under the old names, so the arrangement outlived even the loss of most of its families. The draw made before David and Zadok was still deciding, after the Persians, the Greeks and the Romans, which week an old priest from the hill country came up to Jerusalem.

Chosen by lot. And in that week Zechariah “was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke 1:9), his one turn at the incense, and found an angel standing at the right side of the altar with news of a son: John, who would go before the Lord to make ready a people prepared (Luke 1:17).

A page readers skip. It is the kind of page a reader skips, and the arrangement on it outlasted the building it was made for and carried God’s purposes to the threshold of the gospel. Faithful routine can reach further than anyone who sets it up will see.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah's division is named in Luke 1:5.

verseByVerse.quote: the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab, the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer, the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez, the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel, the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul, the twenty-third to Delaiah, the twenty-fourth to Maaziah. These had as their appointed duty in their service to come into the house of the LORD according to the procedure established for them by Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list is completed, and every course is to serve exactly as God commanded Aaron: David arranged when the priests served, not what they did.

The twenty-fourth to Maaziah. Each course served, as later practice shows, a week at a time, about twice a year, with all present at the three great feasts. One family serving continuously would have been exhausted inside a generation.

According to the procedure established for them by Aaron their father. Two authorities, carefully distinguished. The rota is David’s: nothing in the law of Moses mentions twenty-four courses drawn by lot. But what a priest did once he was through the door was Aaron’s procedure, and Aaron’s had come from God, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him. That is the same line David drew over the ark and over the music: the manner of carrying was commanded, and he obeyed it to the letter (15:13–15); the choir was not, and he arranged it. Knowing which is which is most of the art of ordering the worship of God.

He is never off duty. The priests served a week and went home, and their sons took their places when they died. Hebrews draws the contrast: “The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24), and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He is never off duty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — The Levites Draw on the Same Terms
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the Levites take their places on the same terms as the priests. The register of chapter 23 is repeated with the next generation added: the houses of Kohath (vv. 20–25) and of Merari, where Eleazar is again remembered as having no sons (vv. 26–30). Then all of them cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, before the king, Zadok, Ahimelech and the heads of houses, the head of each family and his younger brother alike (v. 31). The tasks in God’s house differed, but no man’s claim to his place was higher than another’s, because every assignment came from God.
verseByVerse.theology: The last verse is the point of the chapter: the tasks differed, but no man’s standing was higher than another’s.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody in the court was too senior, or too junior, to be sent wherever the lot fell.

verseByVerse.quote: And of the rest of the sons of Levi: of the sons of Amram, Shubael; of the sons of Shubael, Jehdeiah. Of Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, Isshiah the chief. Of the Izharites, Shelomoth; of the sons of Shelomoth, Jahath. The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, Jekameam the fourth. The sons of Uzziel, Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir. The brother of Micah, Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Jaaziah: Beno.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites who are not priests are listed again, with the next generation added: the working register of God’s house.

The rest of the sons of Levi. It is a working document rather than a history, kept because it is how the house of God was actually staffed.

Uncertain wording. Beno (vv. 26–27) is also the ordinary Hebrew for “his son”, and some read the line as “of Jaaziah, his son”. Jaaziah himself is not named among Merari’s sons anywhere else, so whether this is a name, a phrase, or a line imperfectly preserved cannot now be known.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Merari: of Jaaziah, Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri. Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons. Of Kish, the sons of Kish: Jerahmeel. The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites according to their fathers' houses. These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites cast lots just as the priests did, eldest and youngest alike, because every place came from God.

Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons. Verse 28 repeats what the last chapter said (23:22). A man whose family stopped with him is written into the record in two consecutive chapters, and nothing else is said about him; childlessness did not take him off the roll of God’s people.

Cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron. This is where the chapter has been going. The Levites drew on exactly the same terms as the priests: the man who would never touch the altar put his hand in the bag beside the man who would. And within each family the head of the house and his younger brother drew alike, so being the eldest gave no advantage.

The same claim for every man. Every man in that court had a different job and precisely the same claim on it, which was none, because the assignments came from God and not from anyone in the room. So it is in the church: there are “varieties of service, but the same Lord” (1 Corinthians 12:5), and no one’s place is earned.

keyVerse.quote: These had as their appointed duty in their service to come into the house of the LORD according to the procedure established for them by Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him.
keyVerse.note: David could arrange when the priests served, but not what they did: the service itself came from God’s command to Aaron. The chapter begins with two priests who ignored that command and died. It points to Christ, the priest God appointed, through whom alone we now come into God’s presence.

24.reflection:
The chapter begins by remembering Nadab and Abihu, who offered what God had not commanded (vv. 1–2). Why does it matter that we worship God in the way he has given? How does Christ being “the way” shape our approach to God?

David arranged the rota, but he kept Aaron’s procedure exactly as God commanded (v. 19). In church life, how can we tell what God has commanded from what is simply wise arrangement, and why does it matter to know the difference?

The lots made sure that no family or eldest son was favoured (vv. 5, 31). Where do favouritism or rank creep into church life, and how does the gospel answer them?

A rota drawn up under David was still running when the angel came to Zechariah (Luke 1:5–9). What ordinary, faithful routines in your life or church might God be using further than you can see?

25.title: The Temple Musicians: Prophecy Through Song
25.text: <sup>1</sup>David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king.<sup>3</sup>Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth.<sup>5</sup>All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.<sup>6</sup>They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.<sup>7</sup>The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288.<sup>8</sup>And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.<sup>9</sup>The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve;<sup>10</sup>the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>11</sup>the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>12</sup>the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>13</sup>the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>14</sup>the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>15</sup>the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>16</sup>the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>17</sup>the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>18</sup>the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>19</sup>the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>20</sup>to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>21</sup>to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>22</sup>to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>23</sup>to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>24</sup>to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>25</sup>to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>26</sup>to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>27</sup>to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>28</sup>to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>29</sup>to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>30</sup>to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>31</sup>to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
25.overview:
Where we are. David is near the end of his reign and setting the worship of the coming temple in order: the Levites have been counted and given their work (chapter 23) and the priests divided into twenty-four courses (chapter 24). Now he turns to the musicians, before the gatekeepers and treasurers in chapter 26.

The message. Singing God’s praise is a ministry of his word. The men who led Israel’s song are said to have prophesied, because through their songs God spoke to his people, and the word could lodge in a nation’s memory. God himself gave the gifted families, the training was taken seriously, and the places were assigned by lot, so that no one’s rank decided who sang when.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had singers again, sons of Asaph who praised the LORD with cymbals when the foundation of the second temple was laid “according to the directions of David king of Israel” (Ezra 3:10). This chapter told them where their singers came from, and that their modest song stood in the line David had set up by God’s command (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David and the leaders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, whose music is three times called prophesying (vv. 1–3). Heman’s fourteen sons are named, the gift of God’s promise to exalt him (vv. 4–6). The 288 trained and skilful singers draw lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike (vv. 7–8), and the draw is written out in full, twenty-four courses of twelve (vv. 9–31).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. Israel’s singers stood among the people and gave them God’s word in song; the Son of God himself sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Mark 14:26), and Hebrews hears him say to the Father, “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). The one in whom God has spoken finally now leads his people’s praise, and gives the ministry of the song to the whole church (Colossians 3:16).

For us. What we sing teaches us, so it matters that it is true, and it is worth the work of doing well. In Christ no one has a better claim to serve than another, and the long faithfulness of ordinary people, week after week, is one of the ways God keeps his praise alive.
25.theology:
Singing is called prophecy, and the word is not used loosely (see on vv. 1-3). The Bible’s longest book by chapters is a hymn book, and the men in this chapter took what God had said and set it to music, so that a nation could remember it.

And the same chapter insists the singers were trained and skillful (v. 7). Nothing here treats craft as a rival to inspiration. It gives the work of prophesying to men who had been taught and could play.

The New Testament gives this ministry to the whole church. Believers are to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16), and Hebrews hears Christ himself say, in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Hebrews 2:12). Some of these men's songs became Scripture (Psalms 50 and 73–83 bear Asaph's name). This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such inspired prophecy ended with the closed canon, while respecting brothers who see it otherwise; what has not ended is the task of setting God's word where a people can carry it, and singing it with the Son who leads the song.
25.examples:
The lots were cast small and great, teacher and pupil alike, and master and pupil both had to live with the result.

God's promise to exalt Heman arrived as seventeen children, and fourteen of the twenty-four musical courses carried his sons' names.

Most of these men are named once in Scripture and never again. A rota is duller than enthusiasm, and it lasts longer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s singing is a ministry of God’s word, given to gifted and trained men whose places God himself assigns. David and the leaders set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, and three times their music is called prophesying (vv. 1–3). Heman’s large family is presented as God’s fulfilled promise to exalt him (vv. 4–6). The whole company, 288 men trained and skilful in singing to the LORD, casts lots for its duties, and the lot treats the famous and the obscure, the teacher and his pupil, exactly alike (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: To sing what God has said is to speak for him to his people, which is why these musicians can be said to prophesy.
verseByVerse.examples: Gift and practice are not rivals: the men who prophesied with lyres had also learned to play them (v. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was: Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king. Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of Israel’s music are set apart for a ministry the Chronicler calls prophesying: through their songs God’s word was given to his people.

Who prophesied. The word nobody would predict for temple musicians comes three times in three verses, of the sons (v. 1), of Asaph (v. 2) and of Jeduthun (v. 3), and every time the men have instruments in their hands.

Music and prophecy elsewhere. Samuel told Saul he would meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute and lyre before them, prophesying (1 Samuel 10:5). Elisha, asked for a word from God, called for a musician, and while the man played the hand of the LORD came upon him (2 Kings 3:15). Heman is called the king’s seer (v. 5). The three leaders are the men David first appointed when the ark came up (15:17–19), one from each of Levi’s three clans: Asaph from Gershon, Heman from Kohath, and Jeduthun, probably the same man as Ethan, from Merari (6:33–47). The whole tribe had a voice in the song.

What the singers did. They gave God’s word back to the people set to music, and some of their songs became Scripture. Israel learned much of its theology by singing it.

Why sing what you believe? We tend to file beliefs as private opinions and music as the soundtrack to a mood. Israel did not divide a person that way: its music carried the truth further in than an argument could. Augustine remembered weeping in Milan as the church sang, soon after his baptism: the voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth was distilled into his heart. A truth you have only thought about can be argued away in an afternoon. A truth you have sung for twenty years is still there when your mind is too tired to argue, at a hospital bedside or beside a grave. So Paul joins the two in one breath: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly,” and then, “singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16). And on the night he was betrayed the Lord himself sang a hymn with his disciples before he went out to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26).

Under the direction of the king. This sounds alarming until it is clear what it can and cannot mean. David set the rota, appointed the men and made the instruments (23:5). He directed the arrangements; he did not tell a prophet what God says.

Uncertain wording. The chiefs of the service is literally officers of the host, usually a phrase for army commanders. It may mean David’s military leaders joined in the appointment, or the word may refer, as it sometimes does (Numbers 4:3), to the Levites’ service. Either way the appointment was made publicly, by the king and the leaders together.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth. All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman’s large family is God’s promise to exalt him, kept in the form of children: fourteen sons, three daughters, and fourteen of the twenty-four courses.

The promise of God to exalt him. The exalting arrived as children: not office or land, but a full house, and more than half the courses of temple song bearing his sons’ names (compare Psalm 127:3).

And three daughters. The daughters are counted as part of God’s gift. Whether they sang in the temple is not clear: they were all in verse 6 most naturally means the sons, and should not be pressed further. What can be said plainly is that women did sing in Israel’s worship: the returning exiles counted two hundred singers, men and women (Ezra 2:65), and a psalm puts young women playing tambourines in the middle of a procession into the sanctuary (Psalm 68:24–25).

Uncertain wording. The last nine names in verse 4, from Hananiah to Mahazioth, are odd as names and ordinary as Hebrew words, and read in order they seem to make a petition, something like: be gracious to me, LORD, be gracious to me; you are my God; I have magnified and exalted help; sitting in trouble, I said, give visions abundantly. It cannot be proved. If it is right, a prayer has been standing inside a staff list for three thousand years, and a father named his sons one line at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288. And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The 288 singers were trained and skilful, and they took their duties by lot, so that neither seniority nor reputation decided who served when.

Trained in singing to the LORD. Two hundred and eighty-eight is twenty-four courses of twelve. Two words matter here: trained, taught by a master, and skillful. Somebody spent years on these men. Chenaniah had been given charge of the music when the ark came up, for he understood it (15:22). Gift and training are not rivals in God’s service.

Small and great, teacher and pupil alike. The master and the student put their hands in the same bag. The veteran might draw a quiet week while the boy he taught drew a feast. Nothing in the system rewarded seniority, and nothing protected reputation, because the appointments were not being made by anyone in the room: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). Moses told Israel’s judges, “You shall hear the small and the great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17); here the same refusal to favour rank has been built into a duty roster.

In Christ. In his church every gift is given, not earned, which leaves no room for pride in the gifted or envy in the overlooked (1 Corinthians 12:22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The draw is written out lot by lot, because the Chronicler wants his readers to have the real record of who served. Twenty-four lots fall in turn, and almost every line closes with the same words, his sons and his brothers, twelve (vv. 9–31). Asaph’s four sons, Jeduthun’s six and Heman’s fourteen make exactly the twenty-four leaders, and twenty-four courses of twelve make exactly the 288 of verse 7. The repetition is the point: a rota that every family could check, in which each course had its turn and none was left out.
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-four courses of twelve is exactly the figure verse 7 gave. The Chronicler has set out a rota whose numbers add up, and written it out in full.
verseByVerse.examples: The repetition is the design and not a fault in the writing: a rota reads like this because a rota works like this, and somebody was willing to be dull on paper.

verseByVerse.quote: The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve; the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lots fall one after another, the three families shuffled together, so that no family chose its place.

His sons and his brothers, twelve. On it goes (Bukkiah, Jesharelah, Jeshaiah, Mattaniah, Shimei, Azarel, Hashabiah), the same clause every time, the same number every time.

The families mixed by lot. The sons of Asaph and Jeduthun come up by turns in the first lots, with Heman’s sons among them; nobody chose the order. Some names are spelled a little differently from verses 2–4 (Izri for Zeri, Jesharelah for Asharelah, Azarel for Uzziel), as often happens with Hebrew names, but they are the same men.

verseByVerse.quote: to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the lots fall mostly to Heman’s sons, and the list ends having given every course of twelve its turn, a pattern of ordinary faithfulness that outlived the temple itself.

The twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer. The second half of the list belongs largely to Heman’s family, down to Romamti-ezer at the twenty-fourth.

Week after week. Each course took its turn, twelve trained men replaced by twelve more, most of them unknown to anyone outside.

The rota outlived the house. The house they sang in was burned about four hundred years later, yet the sons of Asaph were singing again when the new foundation was laid (Ezra 3:10). God has never needed his praise to be interesting to be worth having.

keyVerse.quote: David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the whole chapter in its true light. These are not entertainers but ministers of God’s word: their singing is called prophesying, because through it God spoke to his people. It is why what the church sings still matters so much, and why it must be true.

25.reflection:
The Chronicler says these musicians “prophesied” with their instruments (vv. 1–3). What does it mean that singing is a ministry of God’s word? How should that shape what we choose to sing, and how we listen to the words?

The singers were both gifted and “trained” (v. 7). Why do you think Scripture values both? Where do you see a false choice between gift and hard work in your own service?

The lots were cast “small and great, teacher and pupil alike” (v. 8). Where do rank, reputation or seniority creep into church life, and what in the gospel answers them?

Most of these names appear nowhere else in Scripture. What ordinary, unnoticed faithfulness has God used in your life, and where is he asking you to keep at it?

26.title: Gatekeepers and Administrators: Guarding the Holy and Serving the Community

(In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.)<sup>32</sup>King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
26.overview:
Where we are. This is the last of the four chapters in which David gives the Levites their work for the coming temple (chapters 23–26). The priests have their courses and the singers their rota; now come the gatekeepers, the keepers of the treasuries, and the Levites who served as officials across the land.

The message. Guarding God’s house and keeping what is given to him are holy service, as truly as singing or sacrifice. God put at his doors families whose very presence told of his mercy, chose capable men and men of judgment, settled their posts by lot, and had every gift brought to him stored and recorded honestly. His service did not stop at the temple wall: the same Levites carried the work of the LORD into the courts and districts of the whole land.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had their gatekeepers again (Ezra 2:42), and their storerooms were a live question: Nehemiah had to appoint treasurers “for they were considered reliable” after a storeroom had been handed over to an enemy of the work (Nehemiah 13:4–13). This chapter showed them that the doors and the accounts belonged to the order David received from God (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The gatekeeping families are listed: Korah’s descendants, Obed-edom’s large household for God blessed him, and the sons of Hosah, all able men (vv. 1–12). The gates are assigned by lot, small and great alike, and the daily watch covers every side, most heavily the east (vv. 13–19). Named men keep the treasuries, including the dedicated spoil of war given by Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab (vv. 20–28). Other Levites serve as officers and judges on both sides of the Jordan (vv. 29–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need it exposes. The gates were guarded because sinful people could not walk freely into the presence of the holy God. Jesus says, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9), and through him we draw near “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain” (Hebrews 10:20). The city to come has gates that “will never be shut by day” (Revelation 21:25), because the one who guards them is the one who opened them. And the sons of Korah at the doors show the grace he brings: rebels’ children kept alive and given a place in God’s house.

For us. No work in God’s house is beneath notice, from the door to the accounts. What is given to God should be handled faithfully and openly, and our ordinary work outside the church, in court, office or home, is still service of the Lord.
26.theology:
The doorkeepers are Korah's descendants, a rebel's line kept alive by mercy (see on vv. 1-5), and they are the family who sang of being glad to keep a door in the house of God.

And verse 28 keeps Saul's dedicated gifts in the treasury beside Samuel's. The verdict of chapter 10 stands: he broke faith and did not seek the LORD. What he gave was not thrown out with him.

The gates were guarded because the house was holy and the wrong person could not simply walk in. The New Testament announces that the way has been opened: through the blood of Jesus believers may enter the holy places with confidence, by the new and living way he opened through the curtain (Hebrews 10:19–20). The sons of Korah stood at the threshold, glad to be there at all; the children of God, rebels by nature as Korah was, are now welcomed all the way in.
26.examples:
The house was guarded for nearly four hundred years by people nobody can name, chosen by lot and described only as able men.

A descendant of Moses kept the accounts of the storerooms (v. 24): real, necessary, unglamorous work, and Scripture records his name.

In the fortieth and last year of his reign, David sent men over the Jordan to find capable administrators for a temple that had not been begun. He knew he would not see it. He was still hiring.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The doors of God’s house were entrusted to capable men from families marked by God’s mercy, and their posts were assigned by God’s lot, not by rank. The Korahites come first, descendants of a rebel whose sons were spared (vv. 1–3). Obed-edom’s household is large for God blessed him, and his sons are men of great ability (vv. 4–8). Meshelemiah’s and Hosah’s families follow, with a younger son made chief (vv. 9–11). All of them are said to minister in the house of the LORD just as their brothers did (v. 12). Then the lots assign the gates, small and great alike, and the daily watch is set, twenty-four men on duty, most of them at the east (vv. 13–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Mercy runs through this list: a rebel's line kept alive, and a family blessed for sheltering the ark, both now trusted with the doors.
verseByVerse.examples: If he is the same man, as seems likely, Obed-edom is here for the fourth time. He took the ark into his yard when the king was frightened of it, walked to Jerusalem beside it as a doorkeeper, stood on the permanent staff with sixty-eight brothers, and now heads a family of sixty-two on the gates.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph. And Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh. And Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first gatekeeping families carry stories of mercy: Korah’s line, spared when their rebel ancestor died, and Obed-edom, blessed for sheltering the ark.

Of the Korahites. Korah stood up in the wilderness with two hundred and fifty men and told Moses and Aaron they had taken too much on themselves. The ground swallowed him and his household, and fire took the two hundred and fifty with their censers (Numbers 16). Then, buried in a census ten chapters later, one sentence: “the sons of Korah did not die” (Numbers 26:11). Centuries on, here they are at the doors of the house of God.

Of the sons of Asaph. Not Asaph the singer, who was a Gershonite, but almost certainly Ebiasaph, the Korahite ancestor named in the gatekeepers’ list at 9:19, in a shortened form.

A doorkeeper in the house of my God. Eleven psalms carry the name of the sons of Korah, and one of them says: “a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psalm 84:10). The family whose ancestor grasped at the priesthood wrote the song about contentment at the threshold, and was kept alive by mercy to sing it.

For God blessed him. Beside the name of Obed-edom’s eighth son comes the reason there are so many: for God blessed him. That is the sentence from chapter 13, when the ark stood in his house for three months (13:14). The register still remembers why. This Obed-edom, a Levite, is probably the man who kept the ark (13:13), called a Gittite because he had lived in Gath-rimmon, a Levitical town (Joshua 21:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: Also to his son Shemaiah were sons born who were rulers in their fathers' houses, for they were men of great ability. The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad, whose brothers were able men, Elihu and Semachiah. All these were of the sons of Obed-edom with their sons and brothers, able men qualified for the service; sixty-two of Obed-edom. And Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen. And Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief), Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen. These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gatekeepers were capable men chosen for a demanding post, and their work at the doors is counted as ministry in the house of the LORD, just as their brothers’ was.

Men of great ability. The word is used of soldiers and fighting strength, and it runs through the chapter (vv. 6–9, 30–32). Someone had to hold the doors against festival crowds and stop the wrong people going in. Later Jehoiada the priest stationed the gatekeepers “so that no one should enter who was in any way unclean” (2 Chronicles 23:19), and they also kept the keys and the storerooms (9:26–27).

His father made him chief. Of Hosah’s sons a note is dropped in without explanation: though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief. The Chronicler does not say why, but again, as in 23:14 and 24:31, the expected order does not hold.

Just as their brothers did. Verse 12 counts the doorkeepers’ duties, like the singers’ and the priests’, as ministering in the house of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates. The lot for the east fell to Shelemiah. They cast lots also for his son Zechariah, a shrewd counselor, and his lot came out for the north. Obed-edom's came out for the south, and to his sons was allotted the gatehouse. For Shuppim and Hosah it came out for the west, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. Watch corresponded to watch. On the east there were six each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, as well as two and two at the gatehouse. And for the colonnade on the west there were four at the road and two at the colonnade. These were the divisions of the gatekeepers among the Korahites and the sons of Merari.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gates were assigned by lot without regard to rank, and the watch was arranged so that every side of the house was guarded every day.

Small and great alike. That is the third time in three chapters: priests, head of house and younger brother alike (24:31); singers, teacher and pupil alike (25:8); doorkeepers, small and great alike. Nobody in the service of that house got a posting because of who he was.

Zechariah, a shrewd counselor. Gatekeeping needed judgment as well as strength, for a doorkeeper decided who came in.

Watch corresponded to watch. The numbers in verses 17–18 add up to twenty-four men on duty each day, six of them on the east, the front, the way the sanctuary faced. Nobody has heard of any of them.

The door that was opened. All this guarding said that the holy God could not simply be walked in upon; Christ is now the door through whom sinners enter (John 10:9).

Uncertain wording. The gate of Shallecheth (v. 16) is named only here. Colonnade (v. 18) translates a rare word, parbar, probably some court or annex on the west side; exactly what is not known. The sense is clear: the west was guarded like the rest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What was given to God was kept honestly, and God’s service reached far beyond the temple walls. Named Levites have charge of two kinds of treasury, the stores of the house and the dedicated gifts, with a descendant of Moses as chief officer (vv. 20–24). The dedicated gifts include spoil from David’s wars and offerings from Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab, all kept on record (vv. 25–28). Other Levites serve outside as officers and judges, thousands of capable men overseeing the tribes west and east of the Jordan, for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king (vv. 29–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The treasury belongs to holiness as much as the altar does: what is given to God has to be kept honestly and recorded.
verseByVerse.examples: A Levite settling a boundary dispute in Gilead was as much in God's service as one standing at the temple door (v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: And of the Levites, Ahijah had charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated gifts. The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers' houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli. The sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and Joel his brother, were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD. Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites— and Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries. His brothers: from Eliezer were his son Rehabiah, and his son Jeshaiah, and his son Joram, and his son Zichri, and his son Shelomoth. This Shelomoth and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated gifts that David the king and the heads of the fathers' houses and the officers of the thousands and the hundreds and the commanders of the army had dedicated. From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD. Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated—all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What was given to God was stored, guarded and recorded by named men, and the gifts of flawed people, Saul among them, were kept.

The treasuries of the house of God. The stores of the house and the stores of dedicated gifts both needed accounts.

Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses. (Son of in such lists can skip generations.) The sons of Moses were entered among ordinary Levites (23:14), and here is what that meant: the descendant of the man who spoke with God face to face kept the accounts of the storerooms.

From spoil won in battles. The stores hold what David, the heads of houses and the commanders brought back from Edom, Moab, Ammon and Philistia (18:11), dedicated for the maintenance of the house of the LORD.

Saul the son of Kish. Saul is on that list. The king whose obituary in chapter 10 says he died for breaking faith with the LORD and for not seeking him had, at some point in his forty years, set things apart for God. Nobody had melted them down or removed his name from the ledger. Beside them sit gifts from Abner and from Joab, two generals who spent years killing each other’s men and both died by violence, kept on the same shelf as Samuel’s.

What this says to us. God kept what Saul gave him. That does not undo chapter 10, but it speaks to anyone who has wondered whether the good they did before they went wrong was wasted.

We erase names; God blots out sins. Our culture is quick to remove names from buildings, prizes and history once a person’s worst deed comes to light. Sometimes justice does require an honour to be withdrawn. But a society that has lost any way of dealing with guilt except purging the guilty leaves every life one revelation away from being struck out. The opposite instinct is no better: the whitewash that keeps the name and quietly loses the file. This inventory does neither. Chapter 10 tells the truth about Saul’s unfaithfulness, and this ledger still keeps his gift. For those who come to him, God goes further than any ledger. It is the sins he blots out: “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake” (Isaiah 43:25). The names he keeps, and Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that theirs were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). We erase people and keep the record of their sins. God, at the cost of his Son, erases the record and keeps the people.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges. Of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 men of ability, had the oversight of Israel westward of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites of whatever genealogy or fathers' houses. (In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.) King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levites also served outside the temple, as officials and judges across the whole land, where the LORD’s work and the king’s service were one commission.

For all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. Chenaniah, Hashabiah and Jerijah, with thousands of capable men, served as officers and judges on both sides of the Jordan, and their task is not divided into sacred and secular. Israel was a nation under God’s covenant, where temple and throne belonged together. The church today is not a state, but the principle stands: the believer’s daily work, in court, office or home, is service of the Lord (Colossians 3:23).

In the fortieth year of David’s reign. In David’s last year search was made for able men at Jazer in Gilead: an old man who has handed the throne to his son is still combing the far side of the Jordan for capable men to staff a building that has not been started.

keyVerse.quote: These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The men at the doors are counted with the singers and the priests: their work too is ministry in God’s house. The chapter is about the service no one notices, the guarding of the gates and the keeping of the stores, and this verse says it matters to God as much as any other.

26.reflection:
The sons of Korah, whose ancestor rebelled against God, became doorkeepers in his house (vv. 1–3; Psalm 84:10). What does that show about God’s mercy? How does it encourage those who come from difficult family histories?

The gatekeepers guarded the way into God’s house, but Jesus says, “I am the door” (John 10:9). What does it mean for you that the way to God is now open through him? How should it shape the way we welcome others?

The treasuries were kept by named, accountable men (vv. 20–28). What does faithful handling of money given to God look like in a church today, and why does it matter for the gospel?

Levites served for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king (v. 30). How does knowing that your ordinary work can be service of the Lord change the way you do it this week?

27.title: The Civic Order of David's Kingdom: Twelve Months, Twelve Tribes, One King
27.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000:<sup>2</sup>Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>3</sup>He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month.<sup>4</sup>Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>5</sup>The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000.<sup>6</sup>This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.<sup>7</sup>Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000.<sup>8</sup>The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>9</sup>Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>10</sup>Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>11</sup>Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>12</sup>Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>13</sup>Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>14</sup>Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>15</sup>Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.<sup>16</sup>Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah;<sup>17</sup>for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok;<sup>18</sup>for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael;<sup>19</sup>for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel;<sup>20</sup>for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah;<sup>21</sup>for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner;<sup>22</sup>for Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.<sup>23</sup>David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven.<sup>24</sup>Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.<sup>25</sup>Over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the treasuries in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers, was Jonathan the son of Uzziah;<sup>26</sup>and over those who did the work of the field for tilling the soil was Ezri the son of Chelub;<sup>27</sup>and over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite; and over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite.<sup>28</sup>Over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah was Baal-hanan the Gederite; and over the stores of oil was Joash.<sup>29</sup>Over the herds that pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai.<sup>30</sup>Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite; and over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite.<sup>31</sup>Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite. All these were stewards of King David's property.<sup>32</sup>Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king's sons.<sup>33</sup>Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend.<sup>34</sup>Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.
27.overview:
Where we are. With the worship of the coming temple set in order (chapters 23–26), the Chronicler turns to the rest of David’s kingdom: the army, the leaders of the tribes, the royal estates and the king’s inner circle. It is the last list before David’s farewell to the nation and to Solomon (chapters 28–29).

The message. The kingdom God gave David was ordered for the long term, its burdens shared across the whole people and the whole year, every tribe in view, and faithful men in their places. But it remained a kingdom of men: at its centre stands a remembered sin, the census, and among its officers a counsellor who would betray the king and a commander no one could control. Israel belonged to the LORD, who had promised to make it beyond counting, and even its best-ordered days were waiting for a better king.

Why it was said. The first readers had no king and no army, and lived in a small province made up mostly of Judah, Benjamin and Levi (see the introduction). This register reminded them that Israel had once been all twelve tribes under David’s house, and that God’s promise of a people like the stars of heaven had not been cancelled.

How the chapter makes its case. Twelve divisions of 24,000 serve a month each, commanded by men from David’s roll of mighty men (vv. 1–15). Each tribe has its chief officer (vv. 16–22). Two verses return to the census: those under twenty were not counted because of God’s promise, and Joab’s unfinished total brought wrath and never entered the official record (vv. 23–24). Stewards run the royal farms, vineyards, orchards and herds (vv. 25–31), and the list closes with the king’s counsellors, his friend, and Joab still in command (vv. 32–34).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need it exposes. The people no king was allowed to number has become, in Christ, the “great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9), for those who belong to him are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). And Ahithophel, the trusted counsellor who turned traitor and hanged himself, foreshadows the betrayal the Son of David would suffer at the hand of a friend (John 13:18). The best administration in Israel’s history could order a kingdom; it could not change a heart. Christ rules his people by his Spirit and loses none of them.

For us. God cares about faithful, ordinary administration, and serving steadily in the background after years on the front line is no comedown. Our security is not in numbers but in the God who keeps his promises, and our King is better than David.
27.theology:
Verse 23 supplies what chapter 21 left out: the young were not counted for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven (see on vv. 23-24).

And verse 24 says the total was never entered in the annals, while the sin and its confession were.
27.examples:
David put the men who understood the animals in charge of them, wherever they came from (vv. 30-31).

Asahel had been dead for years and his name still heads the fourth division, with his son entered after him. An organisation can honour the man who began a thing while getting on with the work he left.

Abner's son holds royal office over Saul's own tribe (v. 21). Old enmities between two houses did not have to pass to the next generation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Twelve Divisions, One a Month
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The defence of the kingdom was shared by the whole people across the whole year, and led by men already proved faithful. The army is organised as a rota: twelve divisions, each of 24,000, serving one month in turn (v. 1). The commanders are named month by month, and almost all of them come from the roll of David’s mighty men in chapter 11: Jashobeam, a descendant of Perez and chief of the commanders; Benaiah the priest’s son, with his own son in charge of his division; Asahel, killed long before, with his son after him; and on through the twelve (vv. 2–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The defence of the kingdom was spread across the whole year and the whole people, so that no one carried all of it and no one was excused.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who were there at the beginning ended up running the timetable (see on vv. 7-15).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000: Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000. He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month. Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000. The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000. This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s army was a rota of citizen soldiers, twelve divisions each serving a month, so that the defence of the kingdom was shared by all and owned by none.

Month after month throughout the year. Every soldier served one month in twelve (see the Jewish calendar) and spent the other eleven on his own land. A nation with no force is at everybody’s mercy; a permanent army under a king has its own costs (1 Samuel 8:11–12). David built neither. He built a timetable.

Each division numbering 24,000. The singers came to 288 and the priests to twenty-four courses; the army comes to 288,000. It may be no more than the tidiness of twelves.

A descendant of Perez. The first commander, chief of all the commanders, comes from the line of Perez, Judah’s son by Tamar, the line that runs through Boaz and Jesse to David and on, as the first page of Matthew records, to Jesus (Matthew 1:3–16).

Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest. The third month belongs to a priest’s son, the man who killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day (11:22). He would command Solomon’s army in the end (1 Kings 2:35).

Uncertain wording. Dodai the Ahohite (v. 4) is probably connected with “Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite”, one of David’s three greatest warriors (11:12). Either the father’s name stands for the son’s, or the son’s name has dropped out; which is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000. The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000. Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000. Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000. Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The twelve commanders are almost all David’s mighty men from chapter 11: the heroes of the hard years became the steady administrators of the settled kingdom.

Asahel the brother of Joab. Asahel, brother of Joab, was dead, killed years before with the butt of Abner’s spear in the retreat from Gibeon, after being told twice to turn aside (2 Samuel 2:18–23). Yet his name still heads the division, with his son Zebadiah after him. Either the list keeps an arrangement from the Hebron years, before his death, or the division kept his name after he fell; the text does not say.

The rest of the twelve. The rest read like a page from chapter 11: Shamhuth, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Helez the Pelonite, Sibbecai the Hushathite who killed a giant’s descendant at Gezer (20:4), Abiezer of Anathoth, Maharai of Netophah, Benaiah of Pirathon, Heldai the Netophathite. Almost every one is on the roll of the mighty men (11:26–31).

From heroes to administrators. Men who came over to David when he was a hunted man, or stood their ground in a barley field when everyone else ran (11:13–14), are now running a duty roster. It is not a comedown. Faithfulness in the dull years is God’s service too.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — The Tribal Officers, and the Number That Was Not Entered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel was one people of many tribes, and it belonged to God, not to the king. Each tribe has a chief officer, including one of David’s brothers over Judah and the son of Saul’s general Abner over Benjamin, though Gad and Asher are missing (vv. 16–22). Then two verses return to the census of chapter 21 and add what that chapter did not say: David did not count the young, because the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars, and Joab’s count was never finished, brought wrath, and was left out of the royal annals (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: A people God has promised to make beyond counting is not a resource for a king to total.
verseByVerse.examples: A confessed sin stays in the record so that it can be learned from, not so that it can go on accusing.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah; for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok; for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael; for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel; for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner; for Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every tribe had a named leader under David, a reminder that Israel was one people of twelve tribes, though the list has gaps and surprises of its own.

Over the tribes of Israel. Each tribe gets a chief officer, with Levi and Aaron’s priestly house listed separately and Manasseh in its two halves. Gad and Asher have no officer in this list, and nobody knows why. It may be damage to the text, or an arrangement lost to us. The gap is there, and it should not be papered over.

For the first readers. To a small province of Judah, Benjamin and Levi, a register with an officer for every tribe said that Israel was still the whole people, the same hope that fills the book’s opening genealogies with the northern tribes.

Elihu, one of David’s brothers. Judah’s officer may be Eliab, the eldest, under another form of his name, the brother who stood in the valley of Elah while David, the shepherd boy, went out to Goliath (1 Samuel 17:28); or he may be a brother not otherwise named, since 1 Samuel 16 implies Jesse had eight sons and 2:13–15 names seven.

Jaasiel the son of Abner. Abner was Saul’s general, who put Ish-bosheth on a throne against David, killed Asahel, and was murdered by Joab in the gateway at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:27). His son is a royal officer over Saul’s own tribe. Whatever peace was made between the two houses is recorded in one line.

verseByVerse.quote: David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven. Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The census was wrong because Israel was God’s people, promised to be beyond counting, not a resource for the king to total; the wrath was recorded, but the number was left out.

The LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven. Verse 23 gives the reason chapter 21 never gave. God had told Abraham to “number the stars, if you are able to number them” (Genesis 15:5). A man who totals a people God has promised to make uncountable has already contradicted the promise.

The number was not entered. Joab never finished, and though chapter 21 prints a figure, the total never went into the royal annals. The wrath is recorded, and the sin, with the king’s own confession; what was struck out was the total he had sinned to obtain. Scripture keeps what a man needs to remember and drops what he wanted, and the confessed sin is met with mercy, not held on account against him.

The promise still stands. Nor did the census cancel the promise it contradicted. Those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29), and John saw before the throne and before the Lamb “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9). The people no king was allowed to total have become countless because the Son of David has been gathering them from the whole earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — Stewards, Counsellors, and a Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s wealth was the land and its life, and it was managed by capable people chosen for their skill. Twelve stewards oversee the treasuries, the fields, the vineyards and wine cellars, the olive and sycamore trees and their oil, the herds, the camels, the donkeys and the flocks, with an Ishmaelite over the camels and a Hagrite over the flocks (vv. 25–31). Then the king’s inner circle: his uncle Jonathan as counsellor and tutor to the princes, Ahithophel the counsellor, Hushai the king’s friend, Ahithophel’s successors, and Joab still commanding the army (vv. 32–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Farming and herding take their place in Scripture beside the army and the priesthood as part of the kingdom's order.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler gives Ahithophel and Hushai their job titles and moves on (v. 33); 2 Samuel tells how that pair ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the treasuries in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers, was Jonathan the son of Uzziah; and over those who did the work of the field for tilling the soil was Ezri the son of Chelub; and over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite; and over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite. Over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah was Baal-hanan the Gederite; and over the stores of oil was Joash. Over the herds that pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai. Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite; and over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite. Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite. All these were stewards of King David's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s wealth was land, trees and animals, and it was managed by stewards chosen for their skill, some of them from outside Israel.

Stewards of King David’s property. Only one of the twelve looks after money; the rest have separate charges for vineyards and wine cellars, for olive and sycamore-fig trees in the lowland hills and their oil, for herds on the coastal plain and in the valleys.

Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite. Ishmaelites and Hagrites were desert peoples who knew camels and flocks, and David put them in charge, though they came from outside Israel. He already had foreign soldiers, the Cherethites and Pelethites, as his bodyguard (18:17). Competence and faithfulness were what counted, as they still do in good stewardship (1 Corinthians 4:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king's sons. Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend. Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list closes with David’s inner circle, and its names recall that even the best-ordered court held a counsellor who would betray the king and a commander no one could control.

Jonathan, David’s uncle. David’s uncle, counsellor and tutor to the princes, is described first as a man of understanding, then as a scribe.

Ahithophel ... and Hushai. Two names, no comment, but 2 Samuel tells more. Ahithophel went over to Absalom; David, climbing the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, prayed, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness” (2 Samuel 15:31), and sent Hushai back into the city to do it. It worked, and Ahithophel went home, “set his house in order and hanged himself” (2 Samuel 17:23). Verse 34 names his successors without saying why.

The betrayed king. Many hear Ahithophel behind David’s lament: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Jesus applied those words to Judas (John 13:18), and the Son of David crossed the Kidron to the Mount of Olives as David had, betrayed by a friend who then went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). David could not save his betrayer; the greater King was betrayed in order to save.

Joab was commander of the king’s army. Joab is still there. He had won the command by being first up into Jebus (11:6), murdered Abner and Amasa, killed Absalom against orders, opposed the census, and said the finest sentence about courage and providence in the book: “Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him” (19:13). Nobody could remove him, and the register of David’s kingdom closes with his name and his rank: David’s kingdom was not yet the kingdom of God.

keyVerse.quote: David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of a register of officers, this verse says whose people Israel really was. They were not a resource for a king to total but the fulfilment of God’s promise to Abraham, a people beyond counting. That promise is kept in Christ, who gathers a multitude no one can number from every nation.

27.reflection:
The army served one month in twelve, so the burden was shared by all (v. 1). What does that say about how responsibility should be shared in a church or family? Where are a few people carrying what many should share?

David’s mighty men ended up running a duty roster (vv. 2–15). Why is steady, unnoticed faithfulness so important in God’s service, and how do you feel when your work moves out of the spotlight?
