Verse 23 says the census contradicted God’s promise to make Israel as many as the stars. In what ways are we tempted to count, measure or compare, as churches or as individuals, when we should be trusting God’s promise?

Ahithophel betrayed David, and Jesus was betrayed by a friend (John 13:18). How does it help to know that Christ understands betrayal from the inside? How does his response shape ours?

28.title: David's Final Charge: The Blueprint from the Spirit and the Call to Seek
28.text: <sup>1</sup>David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors.<sup>2</sup>Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building.<sup>3</sup>But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'<sup>4</sup>Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel.<sup>5</sup>And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.<sup>6</sup>He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.<sup>7</sup>I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'<sup>8</sup>Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.<sup>9</sup>"And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.<sup>10</sup>Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."<sup>11</sup>Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat;<sup>12</sup>and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts;<sup>13</sup>for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service,<sup>15</sup>the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,<sup>16</sup>the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables,<sup>17</sup>and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each;<sup>18</sup>for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.<sup>21</sup>And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
28.overview:
Where we are. The preparations are complete: materials gathered, Solomon charged in private, and priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, soldiers and stewards all in their places (chapters 22–27). Now the old king calls the whole leadership of Israel together for his public farewell, and in the next chapter the people give, and Solomon is made king.

The message. The kingdom and the temple belong to God. He chose the king, he gave the plan, and he will stay until the work is finished. So the one thing asked of God’s people is to know him and seek him with a whole and willing heart: “If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever” (v. 9).

Why it was said. The first readers had no king and a modest temple, and wondered whether God’s promise to David still meant anything (see the introduction). This chapter told them that the throne had always been the LORD’s, that the temple was his design and not a king’s vanity, and that the way forward was the one the book has urged from the start: seek the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. David stands before the assembled leaders, speaks of the house he was not allowed to build, and repeats God’s reason (vv. 1–3). He traces God’s choosing from Judah to his father’s house, to himself, to Solomon, who will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD, with a condition attached (vv. 4–7). He charges the assembly to seek out God’s commandments (v. 8), and his son to know and seek God with a whole heart (vv. 9–10). Then he hands over the plan, down to the weight of gold for the forks, received in writing from the hand of the LORD (vv. 11–19), and ends with the words once given to Joshua: be strong, for God will not leave you until the work is finished (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. God said of David’s son, “I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father” (v. 6), and Hebrews hears that promise fulfilled in Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). Solomon did not continue strong (v. 7); the Son of David did, perfectly, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him. The temple built to a heavenly pattern was “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and the reality has come: Jesus called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21), and he is building his church as a house for God that will be finished.

For us. No one can know God on a parent’s faith; each must seek him for himself, and in Christ the promise holds that he will be found. Our part in his work may be smaller than we hoped, as David’s was, but the work is his, the plan is his, and he will not leave it half-built.
28.theology:
Verses 4-6 set out election, God’s free choosing, as a funnel, in David’s own words, about his own throne (see on vv. 4-7). And the throne is called the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel, which is why its loss centuries later did not cancel the promise attached to it.

Verse 7's if stands beside chapter 17's unconditional word, and history shows how the two worked: whether a generation enjoyed the covenant’s blessings depended on that generation’s obedience, but the covenant itself did not. Solomon did not continue strong, and the promise ran on underneath the wreckage until the Son of David came who did, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him. That is why a reader who has not continued strong is not cast off for it: the way back is confession, and the God who searches hearts is found by those who seek him.

And verse 19 names the temple's origin with the word used of the pattern Moses was shown on the mountain (see on vv. 16-19).
28.examples:
A dying man who could not be kept warm under blankets rose to his feet to make the speech. Nothing in the chapter required him to stand, and the record says he did.

Parents can point their children to the God they have known, but they cannot know him on their children's behalf (v. 9).

The king who once put the ark on a cart handed his son a plan with the forks itemised. Nothing in the house of God is too small to be done with care.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom is God’s, so his king, his son and his people are called above all to seek him. David assembles every leader in Israel and stands to speak (vv. 1–2). He wanted to build a resting place for the ark, but God refused him as a man of war (v. 3). He traces God’s choosing step by step, the tribe, the family, the man, the son, so that Solomon will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel, with a condition attached (vv. 4–7). He charges the assembly to keep and seek out God’s commandments (v. 8), and then his son: know God, serve him wholeheartedly, seek him, and be strong and do it (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Four times in three verses the verb is chose, and it narrows each time: the tribe, then the family, then the man, then the son. David is standing in front of the nation explaining his own throne, and not one clause of the explanation is about him.
verseByVerse.examples: David's first words to the whole kingdom are about his own refusal (v. 3), and he says them without complaint.

verseByVerse.quote: David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors. Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building. But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the whole leadership of Israel, David speaks first of the temple he was not allowed to build, and accepts God’s refusal without complaint.

All the officials of Israel. Everyone listed in chapters 23 to 27 is standing in one place: officials, commanders, stewards, palace staff, the mighty men.

King David rose to his feet. He is near the end of his life. First Kings describes a man so cold no bedclothes could warm him, with his sons already reaching for the throne (1 Kings 1:1–5). Whatever it cost him, he speaks standing.

The footstool of our God. That is what he calls the ark, and the psalms call it that too: “worship at his footstool! Holy is he!” (Psalm 99:5). It shows the true scale. The gold-covered box between the cherubim is the stool under the feet of a God who says, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” (Isaiah 66:1). The building David wanted, with its cedar and bronze and a hundred thousand talents of gold (22:14), was a room for a footrest.

You are a man of war and have shed blood. Then the refusal, in God’s own words, said aloud in front of the kingdom. God does not here accuse David of a particular sin. He describes what David was, a warrior whose victories God himself had given (18:6, 13), and the house of rest was to be built by a man of rest (22:9). David says it standing on his feet, without a word of complaint. It is possible to be refused by God, to know it, and still to serve the work gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel. And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s throne, and Solomon’s after him, came from God’s free choice, and the throne itself is the LORD’s; yet each king’s enjoyment of the promise depends on his keeping God’s commands.

The LORD God of Israel chose me. David describes God’s choosing as a funnel. Out of twelve tribes, Judah. Out of Judah, a farmer’s household in Bethlehem. Out of that household, the youngest (1 Samuel 16 implies eight sons; the list at 2:13–15 names seven, perhaps because one died without heirs), who was not even called in from the sheep. Each stage is God’s doing.

He took pleasure in me. No reason is supplied: not Judah’s faithfulness or Jesse’s piety or David’s courage. He took pleasure in me gives no reason outside God himself, and is not meant to. Moses had told Israel, “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you” (Deuteronomy 7:7). That is grace, and it leaves no room for boasting.

The throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. Not “the throne of Israel”. In chapter 17 God called it “my house” and “my kingdom” (17:14), and in the next chapter “Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king” (29:23). Israel’s kings were tenants; the throne belonged to God.

I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. The promise of 17:13 is repeated, and Hebrews hears its full meaning in Jesus, the Son greater than the angels: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (Hebrews 1:5).

If he continues strong. Verse 7 does not sit easily beside chapter 17. The promise made through Nathan had no condition on it; this one does. Both are true (see the chapter’s theology): whether a king enjoyed the covenant’s blessings depended on his obedience, but the covenant itself did not. Solomon did not continue strong, and the kingdom was torn in half under his son. Yet the promise ran on underneath the wreckage until a son of David was born who did continue strong, and in whom forever finally meant what it said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David charges the whole assembly, with God as witness, to keep and search out all God’s commands, so that they may hold the land and hand it on.

In the sight of all Israel ... and in the hearing of our God. David names two witnesses, the assembly and God: this is said on the record, as a dying man speaks.

Observe and seek out all the commandments. The verb is the book’s own word, seek. That is more than obeying the commands you already know: it means going looking for what God has said. David himself had failed to do it the first time he moved the ark, and confessed, “we did not seek him according to the rule” (15:13).

That you may possess this good land. The promise attached is the land, held and handed on to the children. The Chronicler’s first readers lived on a fraction of that land under a foreign governor, and knew which commandments had been ignored while it was lost. To them the sentence was not nostalgia but explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s charge to his son is the heart of the book: know God for yourself, serve him with a whole and willing heart, because he sees every heart; seek him and he will be found, forsake him and he will cast you off.

And you, Solomon my son. The old man turns to his son in front of everybody.

Know the God of your father. Not know about him. The God of your father points to a life the boy has watched from the inside, and says that none of it passes to him automatically. A father’s faith can show his son the way, but it cannot be handed down. For a believer today the charge is just as personal: to come to God for himself through Christ, in the means he has given, his word read and heard, prayer, and the worship of his people, rather than leaning on a parent’s faith or a church’s reputation.

With a whole heart and with a willing mind. The whole heart is what this book keeps asking for: the men who came to Hebron came “with a whole heart” (12:38). And the second phrase is stronger than it looks in English: literally it is a delighting soul, service a man actually wants to give. God does not want grudging duty. The prophets would promise that God himself would give that new heart and put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26–27), and he does so in everyone who belongs to Christ.

The LORD searches all hearts. That is why wholeness is demanded rather than suggested. A divided heart can deceive people, but not God, who told Samuel that “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

If you seek him, he will be found by you. Saul did not seek the LORD and died (10:14); David learned to seek him and told the nation to keep seeking (16:11). Here it comes as a plain promise. Moses had said it to a people facing exile: “you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 4:29). Jeremiah said it to people already in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:13). And the Son of God said it in five words on a hillside: “seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).

But if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. David does not soften it for his own child in public. And the hardest thing about the sentence is what happened next: the son who received this charge built the house, saw the glory fill it, heard God speak to him twice, and ended his life building places of worship for Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7–9). He had been warned in words nobody could misunderstand.

Be strong and do it. The charge ends practically. The truth has been set out; now act on it.

Can a believer be cast off forever? The warning is real, and it describes those who forsake God for good, who show they never truly knew him (1 John 2:19). Those who truly seek God find him (Jeremiah 29:13), and he keeps them (John 10:28). A troubled believer who fears this verse is about him is usually showing, by the fear itself, that he still wants God; the one who forsakes God for good does not lie awake over it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The temple was not David’s design but God’s, received in writing and handed on, and nothing in it was too small for God to care about. David gives Solomon the plan of the porch, the rooms and the room for the mercy seat, and of the courts and treasuries (vv. 11–12). The rotas of priests and Levites are part of the plan (v. 13), and so is the weight of gold and silver for every vessel, down to the forks and the cups, and the golden chariot of the cherubim over the ark (vv. 14–18). The source is named: in writing from the hand of the LORD (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The temple was given, not designed: a king received it in writing and handed it on.
verseByVerse.examples: A God who specifies the forks has not overlooked the smallest part of anyone's service.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat; and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts; for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD, the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service, the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plan David hands over covers not only the buildings but the people who would serve in them and the weight of every vessel: God’s house was designed whole, by God.

The room for the mercy seat. The plan reaches the innermost room, where the ark stood and where once a year blood was sprinkled for the sins of the people (Leviticus 16:14–15). The whole building was arranged around the place of atonement.

For the divisions of the priests and of the Levites. Verse 13 is not architecture at all. The rotas of the last five chapters are filed inside the plan, between the chambers and the vessels: who would work there was part of the design, not something added once the roof was up.

The weight of gold for each lampstand. Somebody had specified how much gold went into a lamp, a figure for each item according to its use. It is the same care that would not let the ark travel on a cart.

Uncertain wording. All that he had in mind (v. 12) is literally all that was in the spirit with him. It may mean David’s own spirit, his mind, as the ESV takes it, or the Spirit of God, who gave him the plan. Verse 19, which says the plan came from the hand of the LORD, shows that either way its source was God.

verseByVerse.quote: the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables, and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each; for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. "All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Down to the forks, and up to the golden cherubim over the ark, the temple was built to a pattern God gave in writing, a copy of the heavenly reality.

Pure gold for the forks. The list of weights gets smaller as it goes: tables, forks, basins, cups, bowls, each by weight. God is not indifferent to the small fittings of the place where he is worshipped, and nothing in that house was too small to matter. Nor is any part of anyone’s service to him too small to matter now.

The golden chariot of the cherubim. The last item is the greatest. The two great figures that would stand in the Most Holy Place, wings stretched over the ark (1 Kings 6:23–28), are called a chariot, the thing a king rides. It is the picture Ezekiel would see by a canal in Babylon (Ezekiel 1; 10), and David sang of the LORD who “rode on a cherub and flew” (Psalm 18:10). The ark was not a box God sat in, but the footstool of the King of heaven, who goes where he wills.

According to the plan. The word translated plan is the word used of the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, when he told him to make the tabernacle and everything in it accordingly (Exodus 25:9, 40). So the temple was not a rich king’s monument but a copy, and the copying was the point.

A copy and shadow. Hebrews says the priests “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), quoting the instruction to Moses. Every measurement in this chapter pointed beyond itself to the true presence of God, which Christ has entered for us (Hebrews 9:24). The building was a shadow; he is the substance.

Uncertain wording. Verse 19 is compressed in Hebrew, and it is not certain how the writing from the hand of the LORD came about: whether David wrote under God’s guidance, as prophets did when the LORD’s hand was on them, or received a written plan some other way. Either way the plan came from God, and David was its keeper, not its author.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–21 — Be Strong and Do It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon can take up the work without fear, because God will stay with him until it is finished, and he will not be alone. David repeats the charge once given to Joshua, be strong and courageous, and adds his own testimony, the LORD God, even my God, is with you, with the promise that God will not leave him until all the work is done (v. 20). And the help is in place: priests and Levites in their divisions, every willing and skilled worker, and leaders and people ready to follow (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise has an end point, and it is not Solomon’s death or his best effort. God will not leave him until all the work ... is finished, which means the finishing itself is promised.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who will help are described twice over: willing, and skilled. Neither on its own was thought sufficient to build a house for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished. And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David sends Solomon to the work with the promise that God will stay with him until it is finished, and with every helper he needs already in place.

Be strong and courageous. These are, very nearly, the words Moses and then God spoke to Joshua before the Jordan crossing (Deuteronomy 31:6–8; Joshua 1:6–9), and David has been using them on Solomon since chapter 22 (22:13).

The LORD God, even my God, is with you. David puts something of his own in the middle. He cannot help saying my. Forty years of being carried by this God are compressed into even my God, and it is the only proof the old man offers.

He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work ... is finished. The promise has an end point, and it is not Solomon’s best effort but the finished work. Hebrews gives the promise to every frightened believer: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5); and Paul is sure that “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The God who finished his house through Solomon will finish his greater house, the church Christ is building (Matthew 16:18).

Every willing man who has skill. The last verse answers a young man’s obvious fear: you are not doing this alone. The rotas are drawn up, the staff in post, every willing and skilled worker beside him, and the people at his command.

keyVerse.quote: And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.
keyVerse.note: This is the sentence the whole book has been travelling towards. Saul died because he did not seek the LORD (10:14); David learned to seek him and called the nation to do the same (16:11); now the charge passes to the next generation, with a promise and a warning. In Christ the promise stands for all who seek God: he will be found.

28.reflection:
David says God chose him and took pleasure in him without giving any reason outside himself (vv. 4–5). How does God’s free choice humble us and comfort us at the same time?

David tells Solomon to know “the God of your father” (v. 9), not to rely on his father’s faith. Why can faith not simply be inherited? What would it look like for you, or for the young people you care about, to seek God personally?

The temple was built to a plan God gave, down to the forks (vv. 11–19), and Hebrews calls it “a copy and shadow” of heavenly things. What does it teach us that Christ is the reality the temple pointed to?

David was not allowed to build the temple, yet he prepared everything for it gladly (v. 3). Where might God be asking you to serve a work you will not finish or see completed? How does verse 20 encourage you?

29.title: The Offering of All Things: Generosity, Prayer, and the Passing of the Kingdom
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God.<sup>2</sup>So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble.<sup>3</sup>Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:<sup>4</sup>3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house,<sup>5</sup>and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"<sup>6</sup>Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work.<sup>7</sup>They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron.<sup>8</sup>And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.<sup>9</sup>Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.<sup>10</sup>Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.<sup>12</sup>Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all.<sup>13</sup>And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.<sup>14</sup>"But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.<sup>15</sup>For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.<sup>16</sup>O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own.<sup>17</sup>I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.<sup>18</sup>O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you.<sup>19</sup>Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.<sup>21</sup>And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel.<sup>22</sup>And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.<sup>23</sup>Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.<sup>24</sup>All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.<sup>25</sup>And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.<sup>26</sup>Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.<sup>27</sup>The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>28</sup>Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer,<sup>30</sup>with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
29.overview:
Where we are. David has gathered the leaders of Israel, handed Solomon the plan of the temple and charged him to seek the LORD with a whole heart (chapter 28). Chapter 29 is the last day of David’s reign and the last chapter of the book: the gifts, the prayer, the coronation and the obituary.

The message. Everything belongs to God: the gold, the kingdom, even the willingness to give. So his people can give gladly and hold everything lightly, as his guests, looking to him to keep their hearts. And the throne of Israel was never David’s own: it was “the throne of the LORD” (v. 23), kept by God for the son of David he has chosen.

Why it was said. The first readers were few, poor and without a king, rebuilding a modest temple out of their own freewill offerings (Ezra 2:68–69; see the introduction). The chapter showed them what such giving had meant at the beginning, set their poverty and short lives in the hands of the God to whom all things belong, and reminded them that an empty throne in their day did not mean a broken promise, because the throne was the LORD’s.

How the chapter makes its case. David gives his own fortune for the house and asks who will consecrate himself to the LORD (vv. 1–5). The leaders give an enormous offering, and the people rejoice because they have given willingly (vv. 6–9). David blesses God: yours is the kingdom; everything comes from you; we are guests whose days are a shadow; keep your people’s hearts and give Solomon a whole one (vv. 10–19). The assembly worships, feasts and makes Solomon king; he sits on the throne of the LORD (vv. 20–25). David’s obituary closes the book, written to be read against Saul’s in chapter 10 (vv. 26–30).

Where it leads. Above all by promise: Peter preached that God had sworn to set one of David’s descendants on his throne, and had done it by raising Jesus to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36), so the throne of the LORD now belongs to Christ. The chapter also exposes a need. David prays for a whole heart for Solomon, whose heart was not wholly true (1 Kings 11:4); only the Son who came to do the Father’s will (Hebrews 10:7) answers that prayer, and he gives his people the new heart David asked for. And it shows God’s character: the one to whom all things belong became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Nothing we give to God was ours first, so we can give gladly and without pride. Our days are a shadow, but we are guests of a generous Host, and the King on the LORD’s throne has risen and reigns. Ask God, as David did, to keep your heart, and your children’s, set on him.
29.theology:
Verse 14 is the theology of giving in one line: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. Nobody has handed God anything he did not supply first, including the willingness, which is why David's next petition is that God would keep it in place (v. 18). Hearts do not hold themselves steady; holding them is the work God has now given his Spirit to do in his people.

And verse 23 finishes what 17:14 began: Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD (see on vv. 23-25).

That is also why the New Testament can preach this throne as Christ’s. Peter told Jerusalem that God had sworn to seat one of David's descendants on his throne, and that he had done it by raising Jesus and exalting him to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). And the giving that opens the chapter has its own answer in him: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). Every willing gift since is a small echo of that one.
29.examples:
After forty years of having his victories written down, David gave his own gold for the plating of the walls, where no one would know it was his (vv. 3-4).

Parents who have prayed for a child's whole heart and watched the child go astray have not prayed wrongly. David's request for Solomon was still the right one, and God answered it in the end in a greater Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Who Then Will Offer Willingly?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Giving to God begins with the heart, and a whole-hearted gift brings joy. David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work great, because the palace is not for man but for the LORD God (v. 1). He lists all he has gathered as king (v. 2), then gives his own private treasure out of delight in God’s house, gold and silver for the walls, where no one would see whose it was (vv. 3–5), and asks who will consecrate himself to the LORD today (v. 5). The leaders answer with an immense offering (vv. 6–8), and the whole people rejoice, not because the fund is full but because they have given willingly and with a whole heart (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Bringing a gift to this house is described in the words used for setting a priest apart (see on vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.examples: They were glad because they had given, not the other way round (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God. So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble. Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tells the nation that its young king cannot do this alone, then gives first: all he had gathered as king, and his own private fortune on top, out of love for God’s house.

Young and inexperienced. David tells the whole kingdom that the new king is not ready (as in 22:5). It is the ground of his appeal: if the young man is not equal to it and the work is enormous, everyone in the room has something to do about it. And the standard is set: the “palace” (a late word, used of the citadel at Susa, Nehemiah 1:1) is not for man but for the LORD God, so the cost cannot be trimmed.

So far as I was able. Gold for the things of gold, silver for the silver, bronze, iron, timber and stone, each matched to its purpose, gathered out of forty years of tribute and war (18:7–11; 22:14).

Because of my devotion. Verse 3 turns the chapter: the private fortune of an old man, given on top of all he had arranged as king. The reason is not duty or example but my devotion, a word meaning delight. He wanted to. The king who would not offer the LORD what cost him nothing (21:24) now gives what is his alone.

The King who gave himself. David gave treasure for a house he would never see. The Son of David gave himself for a house of living stones (1 Peter 2:5): he “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

Uncertain wording. Several materials in verse 2 are rare words. Which stone “onyx” was (Genesis 2:12; Exodus 28:9) is not certain. “Stones for setting” is literally “stones of filling”, probably gems for mounting. “Antimony” is the dark eye-paint of 2 Kings 9:30; here probably dark stones or a dark setting (compare Isaiah 54:11, “I will set your stones in antimony”). “Colored stones” may be stones for inlay. The sense is plain: the finest stone of every kind.

verseByVerse.quote: 3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house, and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s gift went into the walls, where no one would know whose it was, and then he asked who would give themselves to the LORD that day. In Scripture’s language, to give willingly is to be consecrated.

Of the gold of Ophir. Three thousand talents of the finest gold known (Job 28:16), and seven thousand of refined silver, for overlaying the walls: not a vessel with his name on it, but the walls.

Who then will offer willingly? “Offer willingly” is the verb of the freewill offering, and it runs through the chapter (vv. 5, 6, 9, 14, 17). “Consecrating himself” is literally “filling his hand today for the LORD”, the language of a priest’s ordination: when Moses is told to “ordain” Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:41), the Hebrew is to fill their hands, the sign that a man was set apart for God’s service.

Giving oneself to God. So David is not simply asking for donations. He asks who will be set apart for God today, and a man answers by putting something in his own hand and holding it out. Giving a gift and giving oneself are one act; the Macedonians “gave themselves first to the Lord” (2 Corinthians 8:5).

The hand filled for us. Christians have a Priest whose hands were filled not with gold but with the offering of himself (Hebrews 9:14), and through him their small gifts become “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18).

Where Christians differ: does the tithe bind Christians today? This freewill offering does not settle it; it teaches willing, generous giving from what God first gave (v. 14). Some teach that believers must give exactly a tenth, since Abraham tithed before the law (Genesis 14:20) and Jesus did not set the tithe aside (Luke 11:42). Others hold that Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and belonged to that order. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and for churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). A tenth is a good benchmark and starting place; it is not a ceiling, many should give more, and it is not a debt.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work. They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron. And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite. Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders followed the king with an enormous offering, and the joy came after the giving: the people rejoiced because they had given willingly.

Made their freewill offerings. Heads of families, tribal leaders, commanders and royal officials give first, and precious stones go to the treasury under Jehiel, of the Gershonite family already in charge of the treasuries (23:8; 26:21–22).

10,000 darics of gold. The daric was a Persian coin, not struck until nearly five hundred years later. The Chronicler has turned an ancient sum into money his readers used, as a writer today might give a medieval price in modern currency. They may have recognised the scene: when the exiles came home, heads of families made freewill offerings for the house of God and gave 61,000 darics of gold (Ezra 2:68–69). Their giving stood in a line that began here.

Because they had given willingly. Three words for willingness are piled into one sentence (willingly, whole heart, freely), and the joy comes after the giving: they rejoiced because they had given, an order most people never test and every generous person knows. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7), and he is one: Christ “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2).

David the king also rejoiced greatly. The clause stands on its own. The old king, refused the one thing he had wanted to do (17:4), watched others fund it and was gladder than any of them.

What it does not mean. Not that giving should be stirred by public pressure. The text praises a whole heart, not a large sum, and Jesus praised a widow’s two small coins above the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44).

Can the totals be real? Three thousand talents is over a hundred tons of gold, and with chapter 22’s figures the sums exceed any known treasury of the age. Some think they were rounded or enlarged in copying; others note that ancient kings did boast of enormous hoards. What the text plainly teaches does not hang on the arithmetic: the gifts were vast, willing and glad.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “darics” is rare. Most take it as the Persian daric, first minted under Darius I (who came to the throne in 522 BC); some connect it with the Greek drachma. Either way it is a coin of the Chronicler’s own day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything belongs to God, so praise, humility and prayer are the right answer to a great offering. David blesses the LORD before the whole assembly: greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty, the kingdom, riches and honour are all his (vv. 10–13). Then he turns: who are we, that we could give at all? All things come from God, and we only hand back what is his, as guests whose days are a shadow (vv. 14–15). He lays the gift before the God who tests hearts (vv. 16–17), and ends with two petitions: that God would keep his people’s hearts set on him, and give Solomon a whole heart to obey and to build (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: After forty years of answered prayer David still asks the question of chapter 17: who am I? (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer hands everything back to God before it asks for anything. Asking comes best from open hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever. Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all. And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David hands back to God everything a king is praised for, greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty, riches and honour, because all of it is God’s and comes from his hand.

Yours, O LORD, is the greatness. David blesses the God of “Israel our father”, that is, Jacob, and the last great prayer of his life opens with five nouns a king is congratulated on. He has all five by any human measure: he took Jerusalem, beat the Philistines (14:8–17), broke the Syrian coalition (chapter 19) and rules from Egypt’s border to the Euphrates (13:5; 18:3). He hands the whole list over in one breath.

Yours is the kingdom. In this book that is no figure of speech: his son is to sit on “the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel” (28:5).

Both riches and honor come from you. Hold those two words. Sixteen verses later David dies “full of days, riches, and honor” (v. 28). The obituary is written in the vocabulary of the prayer, so that nobody mistakes where his wealth and standing came from.

In your hand it is to make great. Greatness is something God does to people. Through Nathan he had promised, “I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth” (17:8), and David says it back to him as settled truth. Then, after all the majesty, a plain thank you (v. 13).

In the Lord’s Prayer. Christians have long closed the Lord’s Prayer with words that echo verse 11 (see the note). An old king at the end of his reign gave the church the words it uses to hand everything back.

Handed to the Lamb. In heaven the same list is given to Christ: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12). What David gave back to the LORD is given to the slain Lamb, who shares the glory that belongs to God alone, and whose way to the throne went through the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The closing words added to the Lord’s Prayer in later manuscripts (“yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory”) closely echo v. 11.

verseByVerse.quote: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the ability to give came from God, and the givers are only guests on his earth whose days pass like a shadow; so the offering is God’s own gift handed back.

But who am I. He asked this when Nathan brought him the covenant: “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house” (17:16). Decades later, after a capital taken, a son lost and the dead of a plague he caused buried, the question returns, only wider: not my house now, but my people.

Able thus to offer willingly. What astonishes him is not the throne but that the assembly has just been able to give something away. The capacity for generosity is itself the gift.

Of your own have we given you. Every talent in that pile had passed through God’s hands before it reached theirs. The offering was not a transfer of wealth from Israel to God but Israel handing back a fraction of what it held, and being thanked for it. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Strangers before you and sojourners. Resident foreigners, with no title to the ground they stand on. God had said of Israel, “the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23), and David had prayed, “For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12). Said beside storehouses of gold, it is neither morbid nor a slight on what he has. It says on what terms they hold it: as God’s guests.

Our days on the earth are like a shadow. The clause holds no comfort; there is nothing here to keep (compare Psalm 144:4). The comfort is in the one he speaks to. Abraham and his family “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth”, and God “has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:13–16). David says it in prayer, in public, on the best day of his old age: for anyone who feels how fast life runs, the right thing to do with that is to tell God.

Who owns your life? One of the deepest assumptions of modern life is that I belong to myself. John Locke wrote that every man has a property in his own person, and much good grew from that: no king owns you, and no master may sell you. But stretched into a philosophy of life it becomes a weight. If my life is my property, its success is my achievement and its failure my bankruptcy, and I alone must make it worth something before the shadow passes. David speaks as a guest, and that sounds like a demotion until you see what kind of owner this is. The Lord of the house gave away what was his: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). So when Paul says, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), he is not describing a cell. He is describing a home.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own. I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David says again that the whole offering is God’s, tells the God who tests hearts that he gave with an upright heart, and rejoices to have seen his people give with joy.

Comes from your hand and is all your own. He repeats it, lest the first time be taken for modesty. And the house is “for your holy name”: it exists to make God known, not David.

You test the heart. He had just told Solomon, “the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought” (28:9). God weighs a gift by the heart that gives it.

In the uprightness of my heart. A clean motive claimed aloud to the God who examines motives. Not a claim to a clean life: this is the king who ordered the census and took Bathsheba. It is a claim about one act. He knows why he gave, he knows God is testing exactly that, and he says what he found when he looked.

Offering freely and joyously. An old leader’s last public satisfaction was not that the fund was full, but that he had seen his people’s faces while they gave.

The one wholly upright heart. David could vouch for one act; Jesus could say of his whole life, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Our gifts are accepted not because our motives are pure, for they rarely are entirely, but because we come in him.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you. Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s last petitions ask God to do what no gift and no leader can: keep his people’s hearts turned to him, and give Solomon a whole heart.

The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. He appeals to the God who made covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and kept his word through every generation, to keep it in this one.

Keep forever such purposes and thoughts. Looking at gold given gladly, he asks God to make the willingness last, because it will not last by itself. He had seen the ark neglected through a whole reign (13:3) and felt his own heart go where it should not. No one can hold his own heart steady, so he asks God to.

Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart. Not a long reign, wealth or sons, but a whole heart, as he had urged (22:12–13; 28:9): the last prayer this book records him praying. The temple comes second; a builder whose heart is God’s matters more than the building.

What became of the son. When Solomon was old, “his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father” (1 Kings 11:4), and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7). That does not make the prayer wrong.

The Son with the whole heart. Its full answer came about a thousand years later out of the same family, in a Son whose heart was never divided for an instant: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). His obedience stands for every divided heart that trusts him, and through him God answers David’s first petition too: “I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26), for “it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

In everyday life. Pray for your children’s hearts above their success, and leave the answer with the God who answered David in a greater Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Solomon on the Throne of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom passes to Solomon in worship, because it is the LORD’s kingdom and his to give. At David’s call the assembly blesses God and bows before the LORD and the king (v. 20). Next day come a thousand bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs, and a feast before the LORD with great gladness, and Solomon is made king a second time, anointed as prince for the LORD, with Zadok as priest (vv. 21–22). He sits on the throne of the LORD, and the leaders, the warriors and every one of David’s sons pledge their allegiance (vv. 23–24). God himself makes him great, with a majesty no king before him had known (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The kingdom is handed on with worship, sacrifice and a shared meal: the throne is received before the LORD, not seized.
verseByVerse.examples: Feasting before God is part of worship, not a break from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king. And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel. And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly blesses God, worships with lavish sacrifices and a glad feast before the LORD, and makes Solomon king in full view of the nation, with Zadok beside him as priest.

Bless the LORD your God. David has spent ten verses doing it; now he tells them to, and they bow their heads and pay homage to the LORD and to the king.

What it means to bless the LORD. Blessing usually comes down: the greater blesses the lesser (Hebrews 7:7). We cannot add anything to God; to bless him is to speak well of him, to tell him and anyone listening what is true and good about him. Our hearts are always praising something, very often ourselves; blessing God turns the praise to the one it belongs to. And we never bless him first: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3). Our praise answers his gift, which is why it can be glad rather than dutiful. This week, before you ask God for anything, name one thing he has done and say it to him. See also Bless in the Theological Dictionary.

To the LORD and to the king. One bow, two honours: worship to the LORD, homage to his anointed servant. In the Son of David the two meet, for every knee will bow to Jesus and confess him Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

They ate and drank before the LORD. A sentence this book keeps arriving at. So it was when the tribes made David king at Hebron (12:39–40), and when the ark came home and everyone went away with bread, meat and a cake of raisins (16:3). Whenever this kingdom gets something right, the record closes with people eating; and the kingdom of the Son of David ends at a table too: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

King the second time. The first is probably the brief notice in 23:1; readers of Kings will remember the hurried anointing at the Gihon spring while Adonijah claimed the throne (1 Kings 1). This one is done in daylight, before the nation. Solomon is anointed as prince for the LORD, the title God gave David (17:7): a ruler under God, not over him.

Why does Chronicles leave out the bedridden David and Adonijah’s bid for the crown? Not because it denies them: its readers had Kings, and verse 24 alludes to the rival brothers. It tells the handing on of God’s kingdom from one chosen king to the next, the side of a day Kings tells from the palace. Both are true accounts of one succession, written for different ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him. All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon sits on the throne of the LORD: the kingdom belongs to God, its king rules for him, and God himself makes his chosen king great.

The throne of the LORD. Not the throne of Israel, nor of David, and the book has said so before. God called it “my house” and “my kingdom” in the covenant (17:14), and David “the throne of the kingdom of the LORD” (28:5). Now a man sits down on it, and the chronicle records whose throne it was.

The hope of the book. Its first readers had no king, and if the throne had been David’s own, it was gone. But it never was. The kingdom was the LORD’s, held in trust by a family he had chosen, and when that family lost the throne the kingdom was still his.

The throne now filled. Peter told Jerusalem that God “had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne”, and had done it by raising Jesus to his right hand (Acts 2:30–33). Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD for forty years; Christ sits on it now and forever (Hebrews 1:8). This commentary holds that he reigns there already, not only in a kingdom still to come.

All the sons of King David. The leaders, the mighty men and all David’s sons, including the older brother who had tried to take the throne, pledged their allegiance (literally, “gave the hand under” Solomon).

Such royal majesty. Majesty is the word David had just handed over: “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty” (v. 11). He gave it away in the prayer, and God put it on his son. In God’s hand it is to make great, and what is handed back to him is never lost.

Does generous giving make a person rich? No. This is God honouring a king he had chosen, not a rule that gifts come back as money. God promises to supply what the generous need, so that they can go on giving (2 Corinthians 9:8–11), and some of the most generous people in Scripture stayed poor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David’s life ends in honour, held by God from first to last, and its record is kept by the prophets. In a few sentences the Chronicler sums up the reign: king over all Israel for forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (vv. 26–27). He died at a good age, full of days, riches and honour, the very gifts his prayer said come from God, and Solomon reigned in his place (v. 28). The acts of his reign, his power and all that befell him and the nations around were written by Samuel, Nathan and Gad, the prophets who had told him the truth (vv. 29–30). Read against Saul’s death in chapter 10, the paragraph closes the argument of the whole book.
verseByVerse.theology: What separates the two obituaries in this book (10:13-14 and here) is not talent or success but whether the king sought the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: A name once used as an insult becomes a title of honour when God writes the record.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place. Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer, with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s reign is summed up in a few sentences, a good old age, riches and honour from God, and a record kept by prophets who told him the truth, and the whole book stands between this death and Saul’s.

He died at a good age. Turn back nineteen chapters: Saul died for his breach of faith, because “He did not seek guidance from the LORD” (10:13–14). One king died on a hill, his armour hung in a Philistine temple. The other died full of days, having spent his last years buying a threshing floor, weighing out gold and praying for his son’s heart. Everything in between is the difference between those two sentences.

David the son of Jesse. Saul used that phrase when he could not bear to say the name (1 Samuel 20:27); Nabal used it to refuse a man food (1 Samuel 25:10); a rebel raised the northern tribes with it (2 Samuel 20:1). But in the wilderness the Spirit came on Amasai, and he made the insult his oath: “We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse!” (12:18). The official chronicle uses the sneer as his name.

The Chronicles of Samuel the seer. Samuel, Nathan and Gad are each remembered for bringing a king a word he did not want to hear. Samuel told Saul the kingdom was torn from him. Nathan told David someone else would build the house, and later told him a story about a lamb. Gad brought him three punishments to choose from. The record of the reign was kept by the men who had told the king he was wrong.

The circumstances that came upon him. The word is simply “the times”: what happened to him. The chronicle of a reign is not only what a king did but all that was done to him, and the prophets wrote down both.

A life in summary. A shepherd from Bethlehem, a fugitive at Ziklag, a king who got the ark wrong and then right, who counted his soldiers and buried seventy thousand of his people, who bought a threshing floor at full price, and who died without laying a stone of the house he gave his life to. The house was built, filled with glory, and burned nearly four hundred years later. But the throne was the LORD’s, promised to this family forever. Nearly six hundred years after the last of David’s reigning sons was led away in chains, an angel in a village in Galilee said that “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David”, and that “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

Are these lost books Scripture? They were the prophets’ records and annals the inspired writer drew on, as Luke drew on earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–3). Not every writing of a prophet was given to be Scripture; God has preserved all of his word that he meant the church to have (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

keyVerse.quote: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.
keyVerse.note: David’s prayer names the truth the whole chapter rests on: the gold, the kingdom and even the willingness to give all come from God. It turns giving from an achievement into gratitude, and it points to the God who in Christ gave first, and gave himself.

29.reflection:
David gave his own treasure for walls where no one would see it, and the people rejoiced because they had given willingly (vv. 3–9). What makes giving joyful rather than grudging, and what does 2 Corinthians 9:7 add?

“All things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (v. 14). How would your attitude to money, time and abilities change if you truly believed they were God’s, and that you were his guest (v. 15)?

David prayed that God would keep his people’s hearts and give Solomon a whole heart (vv. 18–19), yet Solomon’s heart turned away. How does Jesus, the Son with the undivided heart, give hope to those praying for their own hearts or their children’s?

Solomon “sat on the throne of the LORD” (v. 23). What difference does it make to your week that Christ now sits on that throne (Acts 2:30–36)?
